19:25:56 KST

The White House has published the terms of its Venezuela oil deal, naming the private company at its centre and confirming Washington's majority control of more than 65 billion barrels, as President Trump vowed the US would be taking "all" of it.
Days after announcing what it calls the largest oil deal in history, the Trump administration has filled in the details.
A fact sheet released on Monday night by the White House named North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) as the operator at the centre of the arrangement, disclosed the ownership structure for the first time and set out what Washington gets in return.
Venezuela's interim authorities have granted NABEP 100-year concessions over 17 fields with the agreement signed by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
The Venezuelan reserves dwarf America's own, as the 65 billion barrels covered by the concessions compare with roughly 46 billion across US territory.
Speaking in the Oval Office on Monday, US President Donald Trump called the reserves "unbelievable value that was sitting dormant" and added that the US is "going to be taking all of that. We're going to be taking that oil out."
The US president also reasserted that American majors were queuing up to be a part of the takeover of Venezuelan oil fields.
"We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in, we have our big oil companies going in, and everybody's bidding," Trump stated.
What Washington gets
In exchange for the inclusion in the deal, NABEP has given the US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent, which the White House says is worth up to hundreds of billions at zero cost to taxpayers.
The US State Department also secures the right to buy 20% of output from all current and future NABEP fields at production cost, intended to partly refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, plus right of first refusal on the remaining 80%.
Washington holds a veto over board appointments, a majority of directors must be US citizens and the agreement falls under US law and courts.
NABEP has committed to investing up to $100 billion (€86bn) in Venezuelan oil infrastructure and is expected to pay around $200 billion (€172bn) in royalties and taxes over 25 years.
Most of the fields were previously run by Russian or Chinese firms, which the White House casts as a reassertion of the Monroe Doctrine.
Signatures expected, questions unresolved
Further energy contracts are due to be signed this week, but reports suggest the arrangement is causing unease among the very majors that Trump says are queuing.
NABEP is controlled by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, investigated by US and European authorities over past dealings with the Venezuelan government, though never charged, and who denies wrongdoing.
Reportedly, oil majors negotiating their own contracts want assurances they will not find themselves seated alongside him.
Exxon and ConocoPhillips both left Venezuela in 2007 after their assets were nationalised, and each says its requirements on legal certainty and contract sanctity remain unmet.
Former US energy advisers have warned of political risk, since a future government in Caracas or Washington could challenge the terms. NABEP reportedly produces between 170,000 and 200,000 barrels a day, second among private operators behind Chevron.
Betancourt said Venezuela is "blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential," and that the deal would "unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans."
Venezuela's Acting President Delcy Rodríguez has also backed it as a chance to modernise the industry, insisting in the face of criticism that the country cedes nothing of its sovereignty.
Lawmakers on Capitol Hill said on Monday they were seeking further information about the agreement, which was negotiated without congressional involvement.
Whether the majors share the Trump administration's confidence should become clearer within days, when the contracts are due to be signed.

Sporting Diplomacy in Odesa: Ukrainian Servicemen Take on Italian Pacifists

19:25:38 KST

Odesa was the setting for a friendly sporting encounter between Italians and Ukrainians: a football match pitting Ukrainian servicemen against Italian activists from a civic movement committed to non-violent action. It was an unusual example of informal Italian diplomacy – and, at the same time, of civic courage.
From August 25 to 28, Odesa was cheerfully invaded by more than 130 activists from MEAN, the European Nonviolent Action Movement. The initiative probably caused a few headaches at the Italian Embassy in Kyiv, which goes to considerable lengths to discourage Italians from travelling to Ukraine on safety grounds. Yet it is worth emphasizing just how much it means to Ukrainians to meet foreigners willing to come and support their country at their own risk.
And the risk was very real. On two of the three nights of their stay, Russian forces launched kamikaze drones at central Odesa, striking precisely the areas where some members of the Italian group were staying. For people unused to air-raid warnings, those two frightening nights certainly lent the mission an added touch of realism.
The purpose of the MEAN mission – the Italian acronym carries a rather unfortunate meaning in English – was to demonstrate civil resistance to war and peaceful support for Ukraine. The activists visited cities battered by Russian attacks and took part in a series of activities and meetings with residents and local institutions. MEAN had previously travelled to Kyiv and Kharkiv as well.
‘Russia Always Calculates Its Strikes to Destroy Lives’: Zelensky Says After Deadly Overnight Attack
Among the many events organized in Odesa was a five-a-side football tournament held on Aug. 27, the final day of the visit. It was arranged in partnership with the International Association of Defenders of Ukraine and took place at Odesa’s Academy Sports stadium.
The Italians were hardly going to pass up an opportunity to play football. Someone observed, with a certain irony, that Italians have not had many chances to compete abroad lately – a reference to the national team’s absence from the World Cup. During their stay in Odesa, the activists therefore hastily assembled two Italian sides with suitably evocative names: “Civilian Corps” and “Nonviolent Action.” Waiting for them on the pitch were teams representing the Ukrainian Navy and Air Defense Forces.
The Ukrainian organizers staged the occasion with considerable ceremony. The Ukrainian Navy band welcomed the Italian visitors and played both national anthems.
In the square facing the assembled teams, the customary minute’s silence was observed for the fallen. Senior military representatives of the host association then addressed those present, followed by six military chaplains representing different faiths, each of whom offered a prayer before play began.
The teams played four matches, including the semi-finals and final. In the end, the superior fitness of the young servicemen – who play regularly – prevailed over that of the Italian teams, which had been assembled for the occasion. The Italians nevertheless compensated for their lack of training with their country’s natural calling for football, scoring several goals that gave their opponents something to think about.
At the awards ceremony, the Italian visitors were overwhelmed with gifts, while the Ukrainian winners received artistically crafted trophies made in Italy. Flags were exchanged as mementoes of the occasion: Italian flags for those of Ukraine and the Ukrainian Navy.
In a moment of unintended irony, the captains of the Italian pacifist teams were presented with two large bronze cylinders decorated with the Ukrainian trident and commemorative inscriptions. The objects were, in fact, two empty artillery shell casings – a reminder that even an instrument of war can be transformed into a work of art and a symbol of friendship.
Col. Andriy Maydachenko, the highest-ranking Ukrainian officer present, gave an oversized bottle of Ukrainian craft wine to the mayor of Casalbuono Attilio Romano, in the province of Salerno. For the occasion, the mayor wore his official tricolor sash, both as a representative of the Italian mayors who support Ukraine and as a footballer who had taken part in the tournament.
MEAN president Angelo Moretti also received a bottle of Ukrainian wine from the colonel, together with instructions to drink it on the day Russia’s war on Ukraine ends. Naturally, the footballing mayor and the movement’s president reciprocated with two bottles of Italian wine.
The event concluded with a convivial dinner of traditional Uzbek plov rice and a screening of videos provided by the Ukrainian Navy and Air Force.
Battered by Russian drone and missile attacks, Odesa continues to welcome courageous supporters of Ukraine with generosity – and still finds room for a sporting event and a shared meal. It is proof that the war has not dehumanized Ukrainians, who have not relinquished their ability to bring a touch of irony into everyday life.

Mecca defense pact not directed against any state, Pakistan premier tells SCO summit in Bishkek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:24:14 UTC
19:24:14 KST

Faisal Mahmud, Riyaz ul Khaliq
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Tuesday that the trilateral Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense, involving his country, is “fundamentally defensive” and is not aimed at any other state.
“It is neither directed against any state nor intended to create any confrontation or division,” Sharif told the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of State summit in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan.
Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the pact on Aug. 7 and held the first meeting of its Strategic Political and Defence Committee in Istanbul on Monday.
Turning to regional tensions, Sharif said Pakistan had acted as an “honest and sincere mediator and facilitator,” with diplomatic efforts culminating in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran aimed at regional de-escalation.
He described the memorandum as a “critical step towards restoration of peace” and the “most viable and enduring pathway” toward lasting regional peace.
Sharif also said water “must never be weaponized” and cannot be used as an “instrument of coercion” or for political leverage, while stressing Pakistan’s commitment to combating terrorism.
The statement comes as India has stopped sharing water details with Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty since last year after an attack in Indian-administered Kashmir left 26 people dead.
“Water is the life, blood of our region. It sustains millions of lives, nourishes our land and secures the very future of our coming generations,” said Sharif, without directly naming New Delhi.
“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit.”
He said more than 90,000 Pakistanis had been killed and the country had suffered economic losses exceeding $150 billion in its fight against terrorism over the past 25 years.
Pakistani prime minister called on the international community to “honour its commitment to help the Palestinian people alongside all other oppressed nations to secure their fundamental right to self-determination.”
 
As Pakistan assumes the SCO chairmanship, Sharif said Islamabad would prioritize connectivity, artificial intelligence, energy, poverty reduction, disaster management and health.
He also proposed establishing an SCO sovereign AI infrastructure and governance framework to promote “responsible and inclusive” development of the technology.

Two tankers carrying Saudi oil attacked in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:23:11 UTC
19:23:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Two tankers carrying Saudi Arabian oil attacked in Strait of Hormuz
Two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday, according to shipping intelligence and tracking firms Marisks and Kpler.
"The near-simultaneous incidents represent a further escalation in the threat environment within the Omani corridor," Marisks said.
The tankers each loaded 2 million barrels of Saudi crude at the Juaymah terminal last week, Kpler data showed. Saudi Aramco resumed oil loadings and sales from inside the strait in August.
Iranian and US blockades of the Strait of Hormuz have sharply curbed energy exports from the Gulf as both sides tried to assert their authority over the waterway.
Efforts by mediators including Qatar and Oman to broker a deal to reopen the strait, which carried about a fifth of global oil supplies before the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran more than six months ago, have so far proven inconclusive.
Oil prices gained on Tuesday after US President Donald Trump threatened further strikes against Iran, following the first exchanges of fire since late July.
In the latest attacks on shipping, the Saudi Arabian-flagged very large crude carrier Sidr was struck by unknown projectiles about 16.6 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman at about 1952 UTC (GMT), Marisks said.
Minutes later, the Liberian-flagged VLCC Senegal Prosperity was reportedly struck by three unknown projectiles approximately 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, Marisks said. All crew aboard were reported safe, it added.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported three projectiles striking a tanker in the same location as it sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz, in what appeared to be the same incident.
Bahri, operator of Sidr, and Sinokor, operator of Senegal Prosperity, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Earlier on Tuesday, Iranian media reported that a Saudi oil tanker was stopped while transiting through the southern corridor of the Strait of Hormuz.

US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
September 1, 2026
G20 finance ministers and central bank heads gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for two days of talks.
The session is being overshadowed by dissatisfaction over the White House welcoming Russia to the meeting but not some critical reporters, the war with Iran and its economic fallout, and Donald Trump's latest trade dispute with Canada.
Who is representing Russia at the meeting?
Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made an unexpected appearance as talks opened late on Monday. He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
"We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters when asked about the first in-person Russian invite since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The US currently holds the rotating G20 presidency and so is hosting the session.
The US government told several news agencies on condition of anonymity that Bessent used the meeting to tell Siluanov that the US would not give Russia economic relief until it brings its four-and-a-half-year invasion to a close.
How did European delegates respond?
"Receiving the Russian finance minsiter here sends a troubling signal," German Finance Minsiter Lars Klingbeil said.
He said he and his European colleagues made clear that they would not appear in the traditional "family photo" alongside the Russian media, saying this was a common EU position.
The photo was ultimately taken without Siluanov and away from the media.
Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told the Reuters news agency that he recognized the right of the G20 hosts to invite guests, but that he was unhappy to see Moscow represented.
"We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them," he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia."
Which reporters and outlets were excluded?
As leaders gathered in Asheville, three giants of the US media landscape complained of either no or limited access toe the meeting.
The business-focused Bloomberg News said that its team was not allowed access, while the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both complained that certain journalists who would typically cover such events were refused media credentials.
Following a challenge from the DJV German journalists' union on Monday, Klingbeil was critical on the matter.
"I believe the press has a completely legitimate interest in reporting openly and freely on this G20 summit," he said. "I consider it unacceptable for journalists or entire editorial teams to be excluded."
Intractable Iran war weighing down global economy
Klingbeil had also said in a German political podcast last week that he would bring a simple message to the US regarding what he called Donald Trump's "irresponsible" war in Iran — that it needed to come to an end.
Host Bessent, however, was trying to drum up support among allies for the US plans for what it calls "Operation Economic Outcast," an intensified sanction regime against Iran reliant in no small part on third parties outside the US who still do business with Tehran.
Iran has withstood decades of extensive US and western sanctions, but Bessent tried to argue when asked by reporters that it could swiftly be made to collapse if its remaining trading partners joined in.
"I think it could be within weeks or months — and the economy doesn't have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses," he said.
Trump's latest Canada meltdown unsettles allies
The other major source of strain at the meeting was last week's sudden deterioration in trade talks between the US and Canada.
This quickly descended into the tit-for-tat imposition of tariffs, and President Trump launching various social media jabs before unilaterally redesignating Lake Ontario as Lake America, at least on the books in the US.
Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne sought to stress that even the recent friction did not impact his participation.
"Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," he told reporters, stressing the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade."

Russia to respond to Japan’s deployment of US missile systems — Foreign Ministry
Unknown

2026-09-01
10:22:32 UTC
19:22:32 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 1. /TASS/. Russia has warned Japan of countermeasures after it deployed US made Typhon missile systems near the Russian borders during exercises with the United States and Australia, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"Attention was drawn to the information that, as part of these exercises, it is planned to use American ground-based Typhon systems designed to launch medium-and shorter-range missiles. The [Japanese] embassy was clearly informed that the deployment of this type of weaponry on Japanese territory, including under the pretext of military exercises, is absolutely unacceptable, as it poses a threat to Russia’s security. We warned about Moscow’s retaliatory measures aimed at ensuring an adequate level of national security," she said at a briefing on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum.
Zakharova pointed out that the statement was made to the Japanese embassy in Moscow in connection with the military exercises conducted by Tokyo, Washington, and Canberra.
"In connection with the joint Japanese-American-Australian Orient Shield exercises scheduled to take place from September 8 to 24, including on the island of Hokkaido and in the regions near the borders of the Russian Federation, the representation was made to the Japanese Embassy in Russia on August 11, expressing concern regarding these maneuvers. The Japanese side was firmly told that provocative military activity near the Far Eastern borders is categorically unacceptable," the diplomat added.
According to the Japanese Ground Forces command, the exercises will include firing drills, training in the deployment of personnel, and the transportation of equipment. About 1,700 military personnel will take part in the maneuvers, which will be a record for joint exercises involving Japan, the United States, and Australia. Kyodo news agency said that the Typhon systems will also be involved.
They will be used for joint exercises in Japan for the third time. In September 2025, they were temporarily deployed at the US Marine Corps’ Iwakuni base in Yamaguchi Prefecture, Japan, and in June of this year - at the Kanoya air base for joint Japan-US exercises. Earlier, Japanese media reported that after a series of exercises in Japan, starting in mid-October, Typhon would be moved to one of the US bases in the country for storage.
The Eastern Economic Forum is taking place from September 1-4 in Vladivostok, at the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University. Its main theme this year is "The Far East - development for the benefit of people." The organizer is the Roscongress Foundation, with the support of the government.

Partner of missing Australian in Nepal says waiting for news has been 'hell'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:22:32 UTC
19:22:32 KST

Australian families holding on to hope their loved ones missing in Nepal are still alive
A week after the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet flood, 23-year-old Sarada Viswanathan is refusing to give up on her partner Rishab Iyer, also 23, who is still missing.
"It's been genuinely just hell for us," she told 7.30.
Mr Iyer was travelling with his parents and brother in Nepal on a Hindu Indian pilgrimage.
They too have not been heard from since last Wednesday.
"It's been really difficult just not having any answers and not knowing where they are, how they're doing, whether they need help, whether they're drinking water, whether they're eating. Are they injured?" she said.
"It's just 24/7, we're just thinking about them, thinking about ways that we can bring them home. What can we do for them? How can we help them?"
Ms Viswanathan has set up a DIY search operation at her family home in north-west Sydney, scanning location tracking websites, clinging to any detail that might pinpoint the Australians.
"We all have them on Find My iPhone and Life360," she explained.
"The last location I have of Rishab is outside that hotel. The last location we have of his brother is slightly up onto the highway."
The Iyers were staying at the Royal Himalaya Hotel & Lodge, close to the river that flooded.
"We're just hoping that they managed to climb somewhere and they managed to escape and that they just are in a remote region that's blocked off and they're not able to get in contact with anyone," Ms Viswanathan said.
Other relatives of the Iyer family are already on the ground in Nepal and have been feeding back any scintilla of information to Ms Viswanathan.
But the disaster zone has been difficult to access on foot, and Ms Viswanathan has set up a petition to push the Australian government to send defence force personnel to help with the search and rescue.
Australia has committed $8 million towards sending aid supplies and has dispatched a crisis response team of 18 people, including consular staff and the AFP.
Ms Viswanathan believes the government should assist with on-the-ground patrols, helicopter searches and thermal drones.
"You never stop at anything to get your family back when they're missing. We appreciate all of the money and all the humanitarian aid that has been given. We're just hoping that we can get actual people there," she said.
Nepal has already knocked back offers of rescue assistance from foreign governments.
"The Australian government continues to offer search and rescue assistance to the Nepali authorities, but that offer hasn't been taken up," a spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs told 7.30 in a statement.
"We are working with telecommunications companies to support Nepali search, rescue and recovery efforts, and assist us in ascertaining the location of those Australians who remain unaccounted for."
Missing Sydney man due to become an intern doctor
Ms Viswanathan and Mr Iyer have been friends since childhood and both became medical students in Sydney.
Mr Iyer was due to start a new job next year as an intern doctor at Gosford Hospital.
"My search will never end," Ms Viswanathan said.
"I will keep looking for him until anything is confirmed. I will never give up on him, and I know none of us will ever give up on them."
Mr Iyer and his brother, Rudhra, 20, were keen cricketers and played for West Pennant Hills.
Their mother Lakshmi and father Sreedharan ran a childcare business and were well-loved in Sydney's Indian community.
John Kurian, 23, has been friends with Rishab since high school.
"We played cricket together since 2018 and we've lost four grand finals together," he told 7.30.
"So we've always joked around saying that we need to win another premiership. He has tried every season that he can. He's always our best player. He leads from the front verbally and with his bat and the ball."
Mr Kurian has joined Ms Visawanathan in her cause.
"I'm here because he's my brother. Rishab and Rudhra are my brothers, and Sreedharan and Lakshmi are also my mum and dad," he said.
"They are out there somewhere right now. Maybe they can't be reached … because they are stuck or the communication towers are knocked down. The least we can do is try and get more people out there to help."
Son flies to India to search for missing parents
The Iyer family was staying at the same hotel as another missing Sydney family, the Sharmas, who were all on the same pilgrimage tour.
The two families were close.
Chitrak Sharma, 23, was in Sydney when he heard about the disaster in Nepal.
His mother Krishna and father Umesh are still missing.
"They're true Australians who lived by generosity, inclusivity, and just giving back to the community," Mr Sharma told 7.30.
"The first thing I did was I tried calling. Of course, [I got] nothing.
"I tried calling someone else that I know was with them. No contact was able to be made. Still, I didn't take it too seriously because I mean, just what are the odds?"
Mr Sharma decided to fly to India and is now south of Delhi, where he is deciding whether to continue to Nepal.
"What made me take a flight here? It had been four days and no concrete news, and I figured I may have to head to Nepal very soon for any reason," he said.
"So that's why I'm basically on stand-by mode here in India with the rest of my extended family."
Mr Sharma remained hopeful but said he was prepared for the worst.
"I've thought about it, and just for assumption's sake I have brought some DNA samples with me. I brought hair in case, but I don't want to think too much about that right now," he said.
"My hope is that we find them safe and sound."
Families of the missing face racist comments
Amid their desperation, some of those related to the missing said they had seen racist comments on social media that denied their Australian identity.
"It's been quite disheartening to see a lot of racial comments towards the families that have gone, about 'they're not Australians'," Mr Kurian told 7.30.
"Rishab and Rudthra are as Australian as they come. They've grown up here their whole life, their education, their work, their sport, their academia, everything is here.
"So for anyone that's been saying those things, they need to really have a deep look and reconsider what they're saying."
Mr Sharma said he had also seen racist comments and wished they would stop.

Rising energy prices due to the Iran
war are continuing to push up Italian inflation, which was 3.3%
in August, a near three-year high, Istat said Tuesday.
                                    
                                       
				According to preliminary estimates, in August 2026, the national
consumer price index (NIC), excluding tobacco, will increase by
+0.5% month-on-month and +3.3% year-on-year (from +2.9% the
previous month).
                                    
                                       
				"In August 2026, inflation will rise to +3.3% (from +2.9% in
July), supported by the trend in energy prices (from +11.6% to
+17.0%), which are still affected by international tensions,"
explains the national statistics institute.
                                    
                                       
				The 'acquired' inflation for 2026 (i.e., the inflation that
would occur in the year assuming that the index itself remains
at the same level as the latest available monthly data for the
remainder of the year) is equal to +2.9% for the general index
and +1.9% for the core component, Istat said.
                                    
                                       
				The inflation rate recorded in August (3.3%) is the highest in
almost three years.
                                    
                                       
				In fact, we need to go back to September 2023, Istat reports, to
find a higher rate of change than the preliminary estimate
recorded in August 2026.
                                    
                                       
				In September 2023, inflation had reached 5.3%.
                                    
                                       
				Finally, the stats agency said that In August, the annual rate
of change in prices for the so-called "shopping basket" (food,
household goods, and personal care products) remained stable (at
+1.0%), while the rate of change for frequently purchased
products increased (from +3.4% to +4.3%).

China holds memorial services for flood victims in Tibet, 10 penalized over ‘misinformation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:18:29 UTC
19:18:29 KST

Faisal Mahmud, Riyaz ul Khaliq
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
China held memorial services Tuesday for victims of last week’s deadly flash floods and mudslides in Tibet, while authorities announced legal action in 10 cases involving alleged online misinformation about the casualty figures from the disaster.
The memorial services were held Tuesday morning in Gyirong County in southwest China’s Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet, to mourn those killed in the Aug. 26 disaster, according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.
China has deployed some 700 personnel to restore access to the mudslide-hit Gyirong border crossing with Nepal.
"Road repairs continue, rescuers have spent four consecutive days searching a 0.7-square-kilometer area around the border gate using life detectors and other equipment," said Norbu Tsering, deputy head of the emergency rescue headquarters and acting mayor of Xigaze City.
Separately, China’s cybersecurity police disclosed 10 cases involving what authorities described as online rumors related to the mudslide that devastated Gyirong Port along the border with Nepal, the state-run Global Times reported.
Authorities said legal action had been taken against people accused of fabricating information about the disaster, exaggerating casualty figures and misleading the public about the situation.
Police said the measures were aimed at preventing false information from disrupting ongoing search, rescue and relief operations.
The disaster struck on Aug. 26 after a glacier on Nepal’s Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet), triggering an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the Nepal-China border.
Official data from both countries showed Tuesday that the combined death toll had risen to 1,019, including 1.003 fatalities in Nepal and 16 in China.
Some 4,462 people remained missing across the border, including 844 foreigners, as rescue teams continued searching areas devastated by the floods and mudslides.

Finland answers America's Nato "loyalty test"
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:18:00 EEST
19:18:00 KST

Finland has responded to a US questionnaire asking Nato allies whether they support Washington's foreign policy priorities.
The Pentagon sent the questionnaire to allies in July. Finland's response was prepared by the defence ministry in consultation with the foreign ministry, the president's office and the government.
Washington is seeking allies' views on Nato participation and on shifting more of the alliance's defence costs and responsibilities to European countries. Most of the questions focused directly on defence.
Europeans avoid antagonising US
Nato allies have sought to avoid antagonising President Donald Trump, hoping to preserve his pledge that America will continue to help defend Europe.
Some questions in the survey addressed each country's relationship with America. Finland's answers described the relationship in broad terms. One Yle source characterised the response as "fact-based, not flattering".
News network Bloomberg, which first reported on the letter in July, dubbed it a "loyalty test". The questionnaire is part of America's plans to reduce its military presence in Europe in countries Washington believes are not spending enough on their own defence or supporting American foreign policy.
Some questions also touched indirectly on America's military action against Iran and Venezuela, including the capture and transfer to the United States of Venezuela's president, Nicolás Maduro.
Finland did not answer these more politically sensitive questions directly, instead highlighting issues it wanted to emphasise.
Nato allies have previously said they would help secure the Strait of Hormuz after hostilities end and uphold the rule of law.
Finland is among the European Nato members spending the most on defence and plans to raise spending further, towards Nato's target of 3.5 percent of GDP. The country is also buying new fighter jets from America and continuing close cooperation with the US armed forces.
Yle was unable to reach Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) for comment on Finland's response.
In July, however, Häkkänen told Yle that Finland had taken the right steps by investing in national defence, strengthening its defence industry and deepening cooperation with the US.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Michelin-starred Wok by O’bond and 50 Best Discovery-listed Tei by O’bond partnered with Bangkok’s Chai Jia Chai to host a two-night collaboration dinner titled “Taiwan Tsai” (T.W.C.) on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1 in Taipei.
Priced at NT$6,980 (US$230), the event featured a 13-course tasting menu accompanied by four Taiwanese tea-inspired beverage pairings.
The collaboration stemmed from a friendship between Tom Liu (劉明杰), founder of Wok and Tei by O’bond, and Chai Jia Chai founder Tsai Shih-wei (蔡世偉). Chai Jia Chai is one of two Bangkok restaurants awarded two diamonds by the Black Pearl Restaurant Guide.
Tsai, an Iron Chef Thailand champion with nearly 30 years of culinary experience across Hong Kong and Shanghai, co-hosted the event alongside Wok Executive Chef Tseng Chih-huai (曾治淮).
The title “Taiwan Tsai” plays on multiple references: “Tsai” honors Tsai’s surname while evoking the Mandarin word cai (菜), meaning food or cuisine. “T.W.C.” represents Tei, Wok, and Chai Jia Chai.
The menu combined Taiwanese flavor profiles with Western structural deconstruction and traditional Chinese dried-goods preparation.
Opening bites included “Tomato and egg,” combining Spanish tomato gazpacho infused with 50-year-old Jinhua ham inside a crisp, egg-like shell, and “Black gold cup,” featuring Taiwanese black plum sauce, asparagus, and celery.
Street-food-inspired dishes followed. “Kha khoo png” paired Thai braised pork knuckle with French terrine techniques over a pan-fried mustard green rice cake topped with pickled chili and kumquat jam, while “Century egg tart” combined pickled peeled chili, century egg, and shacha mayonnaise.
Warm courses focused on traditional ingredient preparation. “Yan du xian” used Jinhua ham from Taipei’s historic Feng Chi cured meats shop to cure Japanese green citrus without added salt. It was served over chicken egg custard, pickled mustard green stems, and crispy yuba in charred bamboo shoot broth.
“Sautéed tiger prawn” adapted Cantonese glass-prawn techniques with botan shrimp, Thai lime, and prawn oil.
“Taiwanese spicy fish maw” featured herbal hotpot spices balanced by garlic sprout sabayon and pig’s blood cake.
“Shacha aged duck” was dry-aged for 21 days after a 15-spice marinade, while Tsai presented his signature “Braised aged abalone two ways” over sticky rice.
The dessert sequence combined modern pastry and tea elements. “Bird’s nest almond tea” fused bird’s nest, almond parfait, and Baozhong tea aromas, while a reinterpreted “Mango sticky rice” paired clarified mango juice and rice cream with caviar.
The meal concluded with an “Abalone sauce pound cake” infused with salted egg yolk and Biluochun green tea.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Tuesday it will push for Taiwan’s participation in the United Nations when the General Assembly opens in New York on Sept. 8, CNA reported.
Vice Foreign Minister Baushuan Ger (葛葆萱) said Taiwan remains excluded from the UN system as China increases political and military pressure on the country. He said Beijing has misrepresented UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 to argue that it has the right to represent Taiwan at the UN.
The ministry outlined three priorities for this year’s campaign. First, it said Resolution 2758 does not exclude Taiwan from meaningful participation in the UN system and should not be used to bar the country from UN activities.
Second, the ministry said peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait are important to global security and prosperity. Taiwan will continue to defend the status quo and oppose unilateral attempts to change it, it said.
The third priority is to resolve disputes peacefully and uphold international law and the UN Charter. Ger said any attempt to change the cross-strait status quo by force would violate the charter’s principles prohibiting the use of force.
The ministry said China has increased pressure on Taiwan through military threats, cyberattacks, and economic coercion. Ger also warned that a new Chinese ethnic unity law could be used to extend Beijing’s control overseas and support transnational repression.
Ger said stability in the Taiwan Strait is important to global trade and supply chains. He said Taiwan will work with allies and like-minded countries to expand its participation in international organizations.

Princess Cruises ends local sales operations in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:17:28 UTC
19:17:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Princess Cruises has ended its local sales operations in Taiwan, stopping new bookings through its Taiwan branch while existing reservations and scheduled sailings this year remain unaffected.
The cruise line announced Monday that the website, social media platforms, and local sales operations of its Taiwan branch, Carnival Taiwan, ceased operations Aug. 31. It will no longer accept new bookings through the local operating entity, per UDN.
The move effectively ends Princess Cruises’ direct sales presence in Taiwan after 13 years of local operations. Travelers needing assistance will be provided with contact information. Future itineraries and new bookings will have to be handled through Princess Cruises’ international website or other overseas sales channels.
Princess Cruises, founded in 1965 and owned by Carnival Corp., is one of the world’s major cruise brands and became widely known through the television series “The Love Boat.” The cruise line has historically used Keelung as a home port and port of call, offering itineraries linking Taiwan with destinations including Okinawa, Ishigaki, and South Korea.
Taiwan International Ports Corp. Chair Chou Yung-hui (周永暉) said Tuesday that the withdrawal from local sales will not affect Princess Cruises’ scheduled calls at Taiwan ports this year. The strategy change could affect sailings in 2027 and 2028, but the ports corporation will continue discussions with Princess Cruises, per CNA.
Chou said the decision was ultimately a strategic adjustment by the operator. He added that Taiwan has seen a significant increase this year in cruise lines making maiden calls at Keelung and Kaohsiung and that the ports corporation will continue seeking opportunities to expand the market.
The withdrawal comes as Carnival Corp. adjusts its sales operations in Asia. Sources familiar with the matter said Carnival has ended local sales operations in several Asian markets, including Taiwan, China, Hong Kong, and South Korea, while retaining direct operations in Japan and Singapore.
Princess Cruises’ departure from the local sales market also highlights the challenges facing Taiwan’s cruise industry, particularly its reliance on regional itineraries centered on destinations such as Okinawa and Japan, per CNA.
Chou said Taiwan should seek to attract more international cruise lines and develop a wider range of itineraries to strengthen the country’s position as a cruise destination.

Taiwan’s drone capabilities will remain insufficient as long as the KMT weaponizes them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:17:10 UTC
19:17:10 KST

On Aug. 27, the Legislative Yuan passed a six-year, NT$240 billion (US$7.3 billion) act for the development and procurement of unmanned vehicles, as well as the development of Taiwan’s indigenous drone industry.
The KMT-backed version replaces the Cabinet’s original NT$210 billion (US$6.5 billion) special procurement proposal, which would have run through 2031.
The act provides a framework to fund the three types of unmanned systems that the Ministry of National Defense (MND) deemed crucial: coastal attack drones, coastal reconnaissance drones, and small one-way attack unmanned surface vehicles.
While finally overcoming the deadlock over a vital component of Taiwan’s national security should be welcomed, it is impossible to ignore that, as with the special defense budget passed in May, the KMT has once again weaponized national security through delays, cuts, and reshaped plans.
The last-minute addition of the three unmanned systems identified as critical by the MND, the persistent funding uncertainty that risks discouraging drone manufacturers, and the likelihood of further delays are all signs of the same problem: the KMT does not seem to consider how its actions undermine Taiwan’s readiness.
A flawed act
The problem lies in the difference between money announced and money made available. Although NT$240 billion appears more generous than the Cabinet’s NT$210 billion proposal, the two figures are not directly comparable.
First, the new act places the funding within the regular annual budget process, with approximately NT$40 billion to be allocated each year for six years. Additional expenditure remains possible, but it will require further legislative approval.
The Cabinet’s proposal instead concentrated special-budget funding on the acquisition, production, maintenance, engineering, and training of the three unmanned systems previously mentioned, leaving the funding of other large and medium-to-large drones to be included separately in annual budgets or other procurement programs.
Procurement also becomes less precise. Unlike the Cabinet’s plan, which requested funding for 208,200 attack drones, 1,446 reconnaissance drones, and 1,320 unmanned surface vehicles, the new act contains no procurement numbers.
Second, the new framework has a much broader mandate, also covering industrial development and testing facilities. Consequently, the larger headline figure does not necessarily translate into more money for the systems identified by the military as its most urgent requirements.
The KMT has therefore transformed what could have been one multi-year funding decision into a series of annual negotiations. Every budget cycle will offer another opportunity to delay procurement, reduce individual programs, or demand that the government reshape its plans.
To justify this approach, the KMT argues that annual reviews will strengthen oversight and allow the military to adjust its purchases as drone technology evolves.
Recent experience provides little reason to trust that this mechanism will progress smoothly. The Cabinet submitted the 2026 central government budget on Aug. 31, 2025.
The Legislative Yuan did not pass it until Aug. 14, 266 days after the statutory deadline.
During that dispute, the KMT threatened to cut drone-related funding by 70% before eventually approving the full amount. Its reversal is welcome, but this final approval does not erase the uncertainty created for ministries and manufacturers during almost a year of political deadlock.
The same pattern shaped the special defense budget passed in May. The opposition reduced the government’s proposed ceiling from NT$1.25 trillion to NT$780 billion and, by excluding domestic drone programs, seriously weakened Taiwan’s drone industry and capabilities.
The passage of the drone act therefore seeks to resolve a problem that the earlier opposition-backed legislation helped create. It also leaves future funding exposed to the same political process.
Taiwan’s drone industry and asymmetric readiness cannot afford annual funding delays that undermine the industrial guarantees and political clarity manufacturers need to scale up drone production.
Moreover, it increases pressure on the MND, which may be forced to adapt to procurement cycles different from those it originally envisioned, while diluted funding could reshape its capability-development plans.
The issue therefore reaches beyond the design of the act. By potentially exposing capabilities considered urgent by the MND to repeated political delays, the KMT’s approach raises a broader question about the responsibility that comes with legitimate legislative opposition.
National security should be a key consideration
Far be it from me to suggest that the Legislative Yuan should blindly follow any policy from the government, or that the act does not support Taiwan’s asymmetric preparedness.
The KMT has every right to oppose the government and defend its position, and the DPP’s defense vision should remain open to scrutiny.
Nobody should want one-party rule in Taiwan. However, legitimate opposition still carries a responsibility to consider the consequences of repeated delays for national security.
The new act is a positive outcome, and it can strengthen Taiwan’s drone industry and asymmetric preparedness if its funding is delivered on time. However, each future delay will be a political choice with direct consequences for Taiwan’s national defense.
What is apparent with the act is that the KMT has embraced the popular appeal of funding drones while preserving repeated opportunities to use delays as political leverage, even if this means endangering Taiwan’s national security.
This raises serious questions about the party’s credibility on national defense issues and makes accusations of alignment with Beijing increasingly difficult to disregard.
It remains to be hoped that the KMT will finally understand that political competition does not need to come at the expense of Taiwan’s national security.

Italy's new far-right party becomes fourth most popular in polls
Unknown

Italy's new far-right party becomes fourth most popular in polls
ROME, Sept 1 - Italy's far-right movement led by former army general Roberto Vannacci has overtaken co-ruling Forza Italia in opinion polls, a survey showed on Tuesday, becoming the country's fourth most popular political force only seven months after its launch.
Futuro Nazionale was founded in February after Vannacci broke away from the coalition's League party, building a movement centred on fierce opposition to mass migration and the defence of what he describes as traditional values.
Vannacci's popularity has long outstripped that of the League, which was seen at 5.7% in the latest survey by pollster SWG, and his movement has now moved ahead of Forza Italia as well.
Forza Italia, the party founded by former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi and now the second-largest force in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's coalition, was seen at 7.1%, compared with 7.5% for Futuro Nazionale. The findings broadly confirmed a survey published by pollster BiDiMedia at the end of August.
Vannacci's steady rise poses a challenge for Meloni, as the new party is siphoning support from her ruling alliance ahead of elections due next year.
Meloni's coalition currently trails the centre-left bloc led by the Democratic Party (PD) by a narrow margin. Her Brothers of Italy party remains the country's most popular political force, with 26.8% support, but its backing has weakened in recent months.
It remains unclear whether Futuro Nazionale will eventually join Meloni's coalition, an option that has so far received a lukewarm response from the alliance's leaders.
With her hopes of securing another term under pressure, Meloni is pushing through parliament an electoral reform that opposition parties and some analysts have denounced as an attempt to improve her prospects and disadvantage the centre-left.
The government rejects that criticism, saying the reform, which is due to be approved by the Senate this month after receiving a first green light at the lower house, is intended solely to help ensure elections produce stable governments. REUTERS

Russia has become "more desperate" in recent weeks, and is stepping up its hostile activity towards NATO, Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, told Euronews.
Speaking on Euronews' flagship morning Europe Today show, she said European unity was key to deterring Russia from further aggression on NATO territory.
The minister was responding to reports of a significant uptick in hybrid-war activities across Europe in recent weeks. The most significant was the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport, Germany in early August.
"We see a more desperate Russia," she said.
"Russia is losing territory, losing influence, losing men, and now they are obviously more desperate testing us and testing our unity," she told Euronews correspondent, Shona Murray.
"We have seen a lot of incidents lately and we have seen united response from NATO," she said.
Meanwhile, German Chancellor Frederic Merz is due to announce he is to formally accuse the Kremlin for the drone incident in Leipzig and vowed to respond accordingly.
It'll be the first time a European country has formally accused Russia of such aggression, and it's likely his response will raise tensions further.
Malmer Stenergard spoke to Europe Today ahead of a gathering of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers to be held in Ireland this week.
EU foreign affairs ministers are also meeting in Wicklow for the so-called Gymnich informal session Wednesday. They’ll be joined by their Ukrainian, British and Canadian counterparts where European and transatlantic security is top of the agenda.
Meanwhile, Stockholm is calling for the European Commission to revisit the issue of using frozen Russian state assets – most of which are held in Belgian financial repository, Euroclear - to fund Ukraine.
Leaders of Sweden, Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands want to reopen the issue and pledge to accommodate Belgium’s concerns.
The Belgium government put up the strongest resistance to the measure late last year saying it would create too much risk to the financial sector.
Prime Minister Bart de Wever insisted on limitless guarantees in exchange for his government’s imprimatur. "We cannot stay in the same position as we were before Christmas," said Malmer Stenergard.
"We have to move on because this is what is fair to Ukraine, it's what is fair to the taxpayers," she said.
"And we have to find a way to make sure that Belgium feels comfortable with this," said Malmer Stenergard.

Iranian woman cyclist Dehghan targets gold in Nagoya
TEHRAN - Iranian women’s cyclist Mandana Dehghan is aiming to return home from the Nagoya Asian Games with the most coveted medal.
Dehghan, who is currently in China training and competing with her club team, told Tehran Times in an exclusive interview that she hopes to make history at the Asian Games.
“Despite all the difficulties this year, particularly the wartime conditions and the events that affected our training, I tried not to miss even a single training session,” Dehghan said.
The Iranian cyclist has spent around a month in China competing in races as she looks to sharpen her competitive edge and reach peak form ahead of Nagoya.
“I hope to reach 100 percent fitness by the Asian Games and compete in one of the best conditions of my career,” she said.
Asked about her medal expectations in Nagoya, Dehghan was clear about her ambition.
“My goal is definitely to win the most coveted medal at the Asian Games,” she said. “But regardless of the result, I will continue my journey with even greater strength and motivation, because I feel this is what I was born to do.”
Dehghan also highlighted one of the major challenges facing road cyclists in Tehran and Karaj: the lack of suitable and safe training routes.
“Unfortunately, the absence of proper roads for road cycling is one of the biggest problems for cyclists in Tehran and Karaj,” she said.
“Our discipline is road cycling, and professional athletes need to spend hours riding on roads to train. Many roads in Tehran and Karaj are either extremely congested or prohibit cycling, so athletes face serious difficulties finding suitable routes.”
She called for greater attention from city officials and proposed developing a dedicated professional cycling facility.
“Ordinary cycling paths built across cities are excellent for recreational and public use, but they cannot meet the needs of professional athletes or replace a standard training route,” Dehghan said.
“If I were the mayor of Tehran, one of the options I would definitely consider would be the second phase of Chitgar Park. The area has great potential, and with proper planning, we could create a technical and attractive cycling circuit of around 10 kilometers. By restricting vehicle access, it could become a completely safe and standard training venue.”
Dehghan believes such a project could provide a major boost to cycling in Iran.
“We could have a professional cycling track, or something like a specialized cycling park, where amateur cyclists could enjoy the sport while professional athletes could carry out their training under standard conditions,” she said.
“In my opinion, establishing such a facility would be one of the greatest services we could provide to cycling in Iran, particularly in Tehran and Alborz provinces.”

New evidence links Teltonika devices to Russia as Lithuania’s export control system stalls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:11:00 UTC
19:11:00 KST

Lithuania’s system for controlling exports of high-priority goods to third countries remains stalled a year after it was proposed, as a Belarusian investigative centre has published new evidence that Teltonika devices continue to be traded in Russia.
The issue dates back to late 2024, when Lithuania introduced restrictions on the export by air to most third countries of telemetry equipment, internet routers and other goods with potential dual-use applications.
The measure was introduced by the conservative government of Prime Minister Ingrida Šimonytė. Teltonika founder Arvydas Paukštys publicly criticised the rules. The subsequent social democratic government of Prime Minister Gintautas Paluckas amended them in January 2025 and only land exports of dual-use goods to third countries remained restricted.
Exporters were also required to include clauses prohibiting the re-export of goods to Russia in contracts with buyers and provide customs authorities with written confirmation that recipients had been informed about possible physical inspections.
Those rules remain in effect.
The latest allegations concern a supply chain traced by the Belarus Investigative Center (BIC), an independent research organization operating in exile, in cooperation with the Lithuanian investigative journalism centre Siena.
The BIC said Western-made products continue to reach Russia and Belarus despite European Union restrictions. It traced one supply route involving GPS tracking devices made by the Lithuanian technology group Teltonika.
According to the investigation, Russian company Laboratoriya Interneta Veshchei (Laboratory of Internet of Things) supplied Teltonika equipment to Belarusian company BelTransSputnik, partly sourcing the products through Hong Kong-based Sinalex. BelTransSputnik then sold Teltonika tracking devices to Russian company Evrosvyaz.
The investigation examined trade data from February 2023 through March 2025 and said BelTransSputnik sold 345 Teltonika GPS controllers and vehicle trackers worth more than USD 100,000.
In a comment to LRT.lt, Teltonika said it does not tolerate violations of sanctions or export controls and has ended commercial relationships with customers in Russia and Belarus.
The company also said it had responded to the BIC’s questions before publication and offered to review the documents underlying the report’s conclusions, which it said contained factual inaccuracies and assumptions. Teltonika said no follow-up request or opportunity to review the documents was provided.
The controversy comes as Lithuania’s planned system for tighter control of high-priority exports remains unresolved.
The Economy and Innovation Ministry was tasked last year with assessing exported goods and determining which should be subject to licensing. It initially proposed an exporter self-declaration system instead of licensing all high-priority goods.
A new proposal registered in February would establish a system under which commissions assess exporters’ applications and recommend whether licenses should be required for specific goods.
The proposal has drawn objections from several institutions. The Defence Ministry and State Security Department called for a simpler system with a single commission, while the Lithuanian Business Confederation opposed the new national controls as excessive and disproportionate.
The Economy and Innovation Ministry said in late June that the legislation should be finalised within two weeks after consultation with government institutions and the public. However, the cabinet had not considered the proposal as of Tuesday.
The ministry estimates licensing all conventional high-priority goods would cost the state about 5 million euros annually. Its proposed system would cost about 60,000 euros per year, mainly for two additional positions.

In Serbia's scorched dunes, foresters plan for an even hotter future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:10:56 KST

In Serbia's scorched dunes, foresters plan for an even hotter future
BELGRADE, Sept 1 - More than a month after flames tore through Serbia's Deliblatska Pescara reserve, foresters are facing tough choices as they work on plans to restore its unique dunes and woodlands and give them a better chance against future wildfires.
One core dilemma — what to keep and what to replace in a still-smoldering area where forest fires used to be rare, but are now expected to become more common with the ravages of global warming.
The changes, when they come, will take years to settle in, said Jovana Devetakovic, a lecturer at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Forestry.
“For the first 15, 20 or even 25 years, it likely won’t look like a forest — it will look like low shrubland,” she told Reuters.
Damage assessment on its own is a year's work, she said.
Then will come the removal of ravaged material, including half-burned or weakened trees — a very gradual process to make sure it does not fuel new blazes or create breeding grounds for bark beetles that threaten healthy forests.
Then there are the choices on what to replant — birch, poplar, ash and oak could all replace highly flammable conifers in the reserve about 80 km (50 miles) from the capital Belgrade.
Black pines and black locust trees have studded its horizon for more than two centuries. But replanted plots of those trees have fallen victim to past blazes, particularly major fires in 1996 and 2007.
"The real question is: do you want Robinia (black locust) and Pinus nigra (black pine) in this ecosystem?” asked Alexander Held, a senior expert with the European Forest Institute, an organisation backed by 30 European states.
He advised against rushing into large-scale replanting, and recommended a three-to-five-year observation period in areas without immediate risks of erosion.
Data from the European Forest Fire Information System show that 2023 to 2025 was the worst three-year period for fires in Serbia this century.
In a sign of how far things have changed, experts are now drawing parallels with traditionally much drier regions.
Greece faced a similar problem when it reforested sandy parts of the West Peloponnese after the wildfire of 2007, said Theocharis Zagas, Emeritus Professor of Forestry and Natural Environment at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki.
"Special methods must be applied, using organic material in planting holes and materials that catch water and improve soil humidity,” he said. REUTERS

US May Have Burned Through 17% of Its PAC-3 Stockpile in a Single Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:08:49 UTC
19:08:49 KST

- Category
- World
US May Have Burned Through 17% of Its PAC-3 Stockpile in a Single Night
US forces may have used as many as 96 to 128 PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a single night while defending military bases in Jordan from an Iranian ballistic missile attack—potentially consuming up to 17% of estimated US stocks, Defense Express reported on August 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The calculation is based on reports that Patriot crews may have fired three to four interceptors at each incoming ballistic missile. Defense Express stressed that the reported launch rate has not been officially confirmed, meaning the estimate remains provisional.
Iran reportedly launched around 32 medium-range ballistic missiles of several types at US military facilities in Jordan in response to recent American strikes. Patriot air defense systems deployed around the bases were used to engage the incoming missiles.
According to Defense Express, such multiple-missile engagements can be used to increase the probability of interception, although the number of interceptors assigned depends on the threat and engagement conditions.
Defense Express also pointed to a documented case during the US operation “Epic Fury,” when three PAC-3 interceptors were launched against a single ballistic missile but failed to destroy it.
Ukraine, by comparison, has at times used only one Patriot interceptor against an incoming ballistic missile because of limited missile availability, according to previous Defense Express reporting.
If all 32 Iranian missiles were engaged with three to four PAC-3 interceptors each, US forces could have launched between 96 and 128 interceptors during the attack.
That potential expenditure would represent a substantial share of estimated US PAC-3 reserves.
Defense Express cited estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies suggesting that the United States may have had around 759 to 827 PAC-3 interceptors available, including newer PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) missiles and older PAC-3 Cost Reduction Initiative (CRI) variants.
Against that estimate, the upper-end expenditure of 128 missiles would amount to roughly 15% to 17% of the estimated inventory. A launch total of 96 interceptors would still represent approximately 12% to 13%.
The figures should not be treated as confirmed US ammunition expenditure. Neither the total number of interceptors fired nor the reported use of three to four missiles against each target has been independently verified.
The scale of the US PAC-3 inventory has become increasingly important as Patriot systems remain deployed across multiple regions while Washington continues supplying interceptors to allies and partners.
According to the figures cited by Defense Express, a stockpile of 759 to 827 PAC-3 missiles would equal roughly 13 interceptors for each of approximately 60 US Patriot batteries. That comparison is illustrative, however, as actual missile distribution varies depending on deployment and operational requirements.
Patriot launchers can also carry different numbers of missiles depending on the interceptor variant. Launchers configured with the older PAC-3 CRI can carry more interceptors than those loaded with the larger PAC-3 MSE.
Defense Express emphasized that there is currently no reliable confirmation that US Patriot crews fired three or four interceptors at every Iranian ballistic missile during the attack.
As a result, both the estimated expenditure of 96 to 128 missiles and the calculation that as much as 17% of the US PAC-3 stockpile may have been used depend on an unverified launch-rate assumption.
The potential scale of US PAC-3 expenditure comes as Ukraine is seeking additional Patriot interceptors ahead of winter.
On August 22, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was looking to secure 300 missiles for its winter air defense needs, while the Ukrainian Air Force had requested 360. Zelenskyy said Ukraine hoped the US could provide 5% to 10% of its existing stocks, with Kyiv prepared to pay for the missiles.

Indian Citizen Among 12 Killed as Russia Pounds Kyiv and Ukraine With Ballistic Missiles, Drones
An Indian citizen was among 12 people killed as Russia unleashed ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones across Ukraine overnight, striking homes, a Kyiv railway depot, businesses and critical infrastructure.
An Indian citizen was among 12 people killed in a massive Russian missile and drone barrage across Ukraine, with strikes hitting apartment buildings, a Kyiv railway depot, businesses and critical infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 1.
Dozens more were injured as Russia deployed large numbers of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles against Kyiv and several other regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In many cities and communities, work to address the aftermath of the Russian attack has been ongoing since last night—nearly 350 first responders are involved in Kyiv and the region alone. A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were among the sites hit.
“Unfortunately, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure have been damaged,” the Ukrainian leader stated.
Boryspil, east of Kyiv, was among the hardest-hit cities. A five-story apartment building was damaged there, forcing emergency crews to evacuate 50 people. Businesses were also struck.
“In Boryspil, an ordinary five-story residential building was damaged. Fifty people were evacuated. All necessary services are on the ground. Businesses were also struck. Overall, 4 people were killed and 13 injured in the city. My condolences,” Zelenskyy said.
Kyiv itself suffered a deadly ballistic missile strike on railway infrastructure.
Russian forces deliberately targeted a railway depot and other railway facilities in the capital, according to Ukrzaliznytsia CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
Seven people were killed at the depot, six of them Ukrzaliznytsia employees. Another railway worker was hospitalized with injuries.
Dozens of employees survived because they had moved into shelters during the air raid alert.
The strike caused extensive destruction around the depot, including the complete destruction of a workshop, while emergency crews continued fighting several fires.
Rail traffic was temporarily suspended along two sections following the strike before service was restored.
“All of this is nothing compared with the terrible loss of our colleagues,” Pertsovskyi wrote, adding that the company was contacting the families of those killed and providing support.
Zelenskyy later confirmed the death toll at the railway facility.
“In Kyiv, a strike on a railway depot killed 7 people,” he said.
Russian strikes also continued against Odesa and the surrounding region, leaving thousands of households without electricity.
“Since last evening, guided aerial bomb and drone strikes have continued against Odesa and the region. Thousands of families were left without electricity, and work is ongoing to restore power to people as quickly as possible,” Zelenskyy stated.
Russia also damaged a border crossing with Romania and infrastructure used for Ukrainian exports.
“A border crossing with Romania was deliberately damaged, as was export infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said.
The Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy and Dnipro regions also came under Russian strikes.
“Overall, 12 people were killed, among them an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured in the attack. My condolences to everyone who has lost family and loved ones,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader said the casualty toll once again showed how strongly civilian survival depends on the availability of air defense systems.
“Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defense capabilities are insufficient,” Zelenskyy stated.
He called for increased deliveries of systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, particularly through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL, and bilateral assistance from Ukraine’s partners.
“I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine receive anti-ballistic capabilities through PURL and bilateral supplies, and it is very important that these deliveries increase this fall,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that additional air defense support has an immediate impact on civilian casualties.
“The number of victims of Russian terror directly hinges on every new package of assistance. I thank everyone who is helping make Ukraine more resilient,” Zelenskyy added.
Previously, a large-scale aerial attack struck the city and region of Odesa, with local authorities reporting multiple explosions across the area.
The assault involved high-speed airborne targets, standard and jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, missiles, and guided aerial bombs launched from both northern directions and the Black Sea.

Enzo Bianchi, a monk who was one of

problems.

spiritual guide for entire generations.

Ukraine Hits Ust-Luga Port With Drones as Fire Breaks Out in Russia’s Leningrad Region
Unknown

- Category

Ukraine Hits Ust-Luga Port With Drones as Fire Breaks Out in Russia’s Leningrad Region
Ukrainian defense forces struck the Russian port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region with drones overnight on September 1, causing a fire and damage within the port area.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko first reported drone activity in the region at around 2 a.m., later saying that Russian air defenses had been activated and had intercepted aerial targets.
Following the attack, however, damage and a fire were reported at the port of Ust-Luga.
“As a result of the UAV attack, damage was recorded in the Ust-Luga port area, and a fire broke out. Emergency services are working at the scene. Information on the consequences is being clarified,” Drozdenko wrote on Telegram.
The Ukrainian OSINT monitoring project Exilenova+ also published footage showing the overnight attack on the port of Ust-Luga in Russia’s Leningrad region.
Ust-Luga is one of Russia’s key seaports on the Baltic Sea. Although it handles a range of cargo, its primary role is the export of energy resources. The port serves as the terminus of the Baltic Pipeline System-II (BPS-II).
Russia uses the port to export crude oil and petroleum products, including shipments carried by tankers belonging to the so-called “shadow fleet.”
The port is located in Luga Bay in the Gulf of Finland, approximately 110 kilometers from St. Petersburg and near the Estonian border. It lies roughly 900 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
The Ust-Luga port area also hosts major industrial and transshipment facilities, including sites operated by Novatek and EuroChem.
The September 1 strike follows another reported drone attack on Ust-Luga less than three weeks earlier. Overnight on August 14, a fire broke out at the port after the facility was targeted by drones.
At the time, Drozdenko reported that the attack had caused damage and sparked a fire, prompting emergency crews to begin extinguishing the blaze. By 6:21 a.m. local time, he claimed that Russian air defenses had downed 51 drones over the Leningrad region.

Three more London-listed companies are set to be taken over as the value of deals removing firms from the capital’s under-pressure stock market passes $100bn (£74bn) so far this year.
On Tuesday, Bodycote, the FTSE 250 industrials group that has been listed on the London Stock Exchange since 1972, agreed a £1.84bn takeover by the US private equity group Veritas.
The Macclesfield-based company, which offers services including heat treatment for manufacturing, metal joining and protective metallic coatings, had been the subject of a bidding war against the rival European buyout group CVC.
Veritas said Bodycote’s prospects would be better served by being taken out of public markets.
“As a private company under Veritas’ ownership, Bodycote will benefit from enhanced flexibility and long-term perspective to support continued investment in the business and pursue targeted organic and inorganic growth opportunities,” the US group said.
Meanwhile, the telecoms company Gamma Communications recommended a £1.1bn offer from the UK private equity company Epiris, days after confirming it was in possible takeover talks with the European buyout company Waterland.
Epiris first indicated its interest in a potential takeover in June. On Tuesday it said: “The additional flexibility that comes from a private company environment will enable Gamma to invest further and focus on sustainably improving the growth of its business over the long term.”
Separately, the Scottish energy company Capricorn is set to end 38 years on the FTSE all-share after striking a deal with the Norwegian rival DNO for $396m. Capricorn had recommended an offer from Genel Energy, but the company switched its recommendation after receiving a higher offer from DNO.
The takeovers put further pressure on the LSE, which has been hit by an exodus of companies so far this year in deals totalling almost $110bn, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
The flurry of dealmaking includes easyJet’s £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity company Apollo, the warehouse landlord Segro’s £14bn takeover by the US rival Prologis, and the sale of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming business to the Sky owner, Comcast, for £1.6bn.
Earlier this year the historic British asset management group Schroders agreed a £9.9bn takeover by a US investor.
Other deals include the £10bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by a consortium led by the Swedish private equity company EQT in June and Beazley, the specialist insurer with clients including Lloyds of London, which agreed an £8bn deal to be acquired by the larger rival Zurich in February.

Germany news: FM says Algeria can provide gas supplies
