Russia slams Japanese drills with US and Australia, says US Typhon missile systems pose threat
VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 1 - Russia on Tuesday condemned upcoming joint military exercises between Japan, Australia and the United States and said it had formally complained to Tokyo about the deployment of U.S. Typhon missile launchers for the drills, something it said posed a threat to its own national security.
The "Orient Shield" drills are due to run from September 8-24 in Japan and, according to Japan's Kyodo News, will involve 3,700 personnel from the three countries, making the exercise the biggest of its kind yet. The drills will for the first time also involve U.S. Typhon mid-range missile systems which can launch SM-6 and Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Maria Zakharova, a spokeswoman for Russia's Foreign Ministry, told reporters at a news briefing in Vladivostok that Russia wanted Japan to return to a policy of pacifism and was concerned that the exercises would take place in Japanese regions close to Russia's own borders in the far east. Russia had lodged a complaint with the Japanese embassy in Moscow on Monday, she said.
"The Japanese side was firmly informed that provocative military activity near our country’s far eastern borders is categorically unacceptable,” said Zakharova.
"Attention was also drawn to reports that, as part of these exercises, it is intended to deploy American Typhon ground-based systems. It was made clear to the embassy that the deployment of such weapons on Japanese territory, including under the pretext of military exercises, is absolutely unacceptable as it poses a threat to Russia’s security. A warning was issued regarding compensatory countermeasures by Moscow aimed at ensuring an appropriate level of national security.”
The U.S. military sent its powerful Typhon midrange missile system to Kagoshima Prefecture for joint exercises with the Japanese Self-Defence Forces in June, the Japan Times reported at the time. It said the missiles were then scheduled to take part in this month's joint exercises before being moved to a U.S. military base in Japan from around mid-October.
Russia and Japan have exchanged a series of protests in recent weeks following a rare visit by President Vladimir Putin to a disputed Russian-controlled island off northeast Japan.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the trip "absolutely unacceptable", and Moscow then summoned the Japanese ambassador to complain about what it called anti-Russian remarks by Takaichi and her foreign minister. REUTERS

Helsinki and Lithuania, 1 September 2026 – Capalo AI, a sustainable technology company specializing in optimization and trading of renewable and hybrid energy assets, has entered into a partnership with Future Energy, a Lithuanian renewable energy developer, to manage and optimize a 56 MW / 168 MWh standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) in Raseiniai, Lithuania.
The project brings together infrastructure investment, EPC delivery and AI-driven optimization in one of Lithuania’s most significant new battery storage developments.
The BESS is planned to be completed by the end of 2026 and is expected to reach commercial operation in Q1 2027. Under the partnership, Capalo AI will provide route-to-market services for the asset, including Day-Ahead, Intraday and balancing market trading, as well as Balance Responsible Party (BRP) services, delivered through the Capalo Zeus VPP™.
With a storage capacity of 168 MWh, the Raseiniai BESS will be one of the largest facilities of its kind in Lithuania and among the country’s first commercial battery storage projects capable of storing and supplying energy for up to three hours. The longer storage duration enables more efficient participation across balancing and wholesale electricity markets while providing a broader range of services supporting the electricity system.
The facility is being delivered by MT Group, a European EPC contractor specializing in energy infrastructure. MT Group is responsible for the engineering, procurement and construction of the BESS infrastructure and its integration into Lithuania’s high-voltage electricity system. The battery park will be connected to the Litgrid 110 kV transmission network through the expanded Raseiniai transformer substation.
Together, Future Energy, MT Group and Capalo AI combine energy infrastructure investment, EPC delivery and advanced market optimization, connecting the physical infrastructure required for the energy transition with the digital capabilities needed to operate it efficiently.
The project has also been welcomed by the Raseiniai District Municipality as a significant investment in the region and a contribution to Lithuania’s ongoing energy transformation.
“Lithuania’s storage market is scaling quickly, with grid operators fast-tracking new battery connections to keep pace with the country’s growing renewable capacity. We already manage a substantial number of assets in the market, and this partnership with Future Energy extends that footprint and reflects the confidence Baltic developers continue to place in our trading and optimization approach” said Dainius Velykis, Regional Manager Baltics, Capalo AI.
Rimvydas Štilinis, CEO, Future Energy, said: “Energy storage is becoming an essential part of Lithuania’s energy system. As renewable generation continues to grow, the ability to store electricity, provide flexibility and respond efficiently to market and grid needs becomes increasingly important. The Raseiniai project is a significant long-term investment in this infrastructure. By combining MT Group’s EPC capabilities with Capalo AI’s route-to-market access and AI-driven optimization, we are building an asset designed not only to store energy, but to operate efficiently across Lithuania’s evolving electricity markets.”
“Battery storage is becoming a fundamental part of Europe’s energy infrastructure. Projects such as Raseiniai demonstrate that the next generation of energy systems requires not only new renewable generation, but also large-scale flexibility, intelligent operation and strong grid infrastructure. At MT Group, our role is to turn this transition into physical infrastructure – engineering and delivering the assets that make a more flexible and resilient energy system possible. We are pleased to deliver this project together with Future Energy and to see Capalo AI bring advanced optimization capabilities to its operation,” said Phd Kristina Norvaišienė, Executive Director of MT Group.
Capalo AI’s Capalo Zeus VPP™ provides route-to-market access, AI-optimized trading and operational management of BESS assets, combining automated dispatch with a data-driven approach to maximizing revenue across multiple electricity markets.

Labor MP Ed Husic says he is 'very lucky' to walk away from serious Sydney car crash
In short:
Labor MP Ed Husic has returned to work after a serious car crash in Sydney last month.
The backbencher, who sustained a concussion and fractures, says he has no recollection of the incident.
What's next?
Mr Husic is hoping to attend parliament when it returns next week.
Labor MP Ed Husic says he feels "very lucky" to have walked away from a serious car crash, revealing the extent of his injuries as he returns from several weeks out of the public eye.
The Member for Chifley was travelling on Sydney's M7 motorway on August 4 when his vehicle was involved in a crash with a truck and another car.
Mr Husic was taken to hospital for assessment and treatment, and was discharged the next day with minor abrasions, fractures, and a concussion.
In his first public remarks since the incident, Mr Husic said he had no recollection of the incident, and said he was trying to piece together what happened on the day of the crash.
"I am completely blanked of my memory from midday of the day in which the accident occurred through to when I regained consciousness in the emergency department," he told ABC's Afternoon Briefing on Monday.
"I sustained a hairline fracture in one of the vertebrae, and a concussion is a new experience for me.
"I can tell you sneezing is a new experience. I always have to brace myself when I'm going to sneeze because the back introduces me to a new kind of pain and ache."
The Labor backbencher said he was fortunate to have had a speedy recovery.
"In terms of the sum of what I went through, I am very, very lucky because I am conscious, very conscious, other people don't necessarily have that type of experience," he said.
"I am very much counting my blessings."
'Keen' to get back to work
Mr Husic returned to work last week and said he was "overwhelmed" by well wishes he received from parliamentary colleagues and across the community.
On Tuesday, he released dash cam footage of the collision, which he has also provided to police.
He hoped to attend parliament when it sits next week after he missed the previous sitting fortnight.
"I am very keen to get back doing the work that I need to for my community and also obviously as a parliamentarian getting involved in different issues that I care deeply about," Mr Husic said.
"The key has been to not rush back and to take it easy as a result of concussion.
"I have been told I cannot return to parliamentary basketball. I cannot be involved in contact sports for some time, so I'm out from that."
Mr Husic previously served in cabinet as Industry and Science Minister, but has been sitting on the backbench since the 2025 election.
He was first elected to his seat in Sydney's outer west in 2010.
The outspoken MP tried to gather support for a motion at Labor's national conference in July that aimed to recognise claims of genocide in Gaza.

Kurds in Syria, Iraq fight against 'Arabization' with language, but might need to push harder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:36:49 UTC
17:36:49 KST

Kurds in Syria are concerned that changes in the country may erode Kurdish language education that has been common in eastern Syria for more than a decade.
Meanwhile, in Iraq, a Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) official on Monday warned of demographic changes in the disputed Kurdish-majority city of Khanaqin in eastern Diyala province. According to Rudaw, a Kurdish media outlet, he called the changes a “clear constitutional violation.”
In both countries, Kurdish political parties will need to tackle these issues.
Syrian Kurds adapting to last six months of changes
The issue in Syria relates to changes over the past six months. During the long Syrian civil war, the Kurdish regions of what Kurds call Rojava were largely cut off from Damascus. The local authorities instituted Kurdish language instruction in schools, something that the Assad regime had suppressed. As such, what developed since 2012 was more freedom for Kurds, and a generation of young people was raised with their language being taught in school.
Now, the area of eastern Syria, which had been governed by the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (DAANES) with the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) defending it, will be governed by Damascus.
A deal between the SDF and the new Syrian government has led to the Kurdish forces being dissolved. Rudaw media noted that “Kurdish students, parents and teachers rallied in northeast Syria's Rojava region on Monday against a Syrian government decision to end full Kurdish-medium schooling, arguing it falls short of their demands for language rights.”
The issue at stake is clear: Kurds who have been learning in Kurdish may find advancing in the education system difficult without Arabic language skills, while reducing Kurdish education will be seen as reducing the rights of Kurds.
It’s not a zero-sum game; there are many ways to have language instruction in both Arabic and Kurdish. Kurds are a minority in Syria, perhaps around ten percent of the country’s population. Education appears to be an issue that affects not only the Kurdish region. A dispute over where people from the Druze area of Suwayda are allowed to travel to take national tests has also created a crisis in this area.
The issue is not a simple one. Local people may want locally tailored instruction. However, if they can’t progress to national levels via testing and language, then how will they enter university in Syria or abroad? What the Kurdistan Region of Iraq shows is that one can establish an autonomous system with education tailored for locals, but also create success via universities and avenues for growth for young people. In eastern Syria, this remains to be seen.
North Press Agency in Syria notes that “Presidential Decree No. (13) of 2026, concerning the cultural and linguistic rights of the Kurds in Syria, has reopened the debate about the future of education in the Kurdish language, amid a dispute between the Syrian government and the educational institutions affiliated with the Autonomous Administration regarding the mechanism for implementing these rights in schools.”
It adds that “while the government is moving towards teaching the Kurdish language as a subject within the official curriculum with two lessons per week, the Kurdish side is demanding that its teaching be expanded to become a language of education alongside Arabic, especially in predominantly Kurdish areas.”
In many ways, the new decree is important. It changes the old Assad-era discriminatory laws that were rooted in a census dating to 1962. The report quotes Dr. Samar Habib, a faculty member at the Higher Institute for Population Research, as saying “she believes that the decree, from the perspective of educational and social sciences, represents a shift from policies of exclusion and forced Arabization to a context of legal recognition and national symbolism, but at the same time she points to a gap between symbolic recognition and educational empowerment.”
It notes that “Habib proposes a three-track educational model, which can be implemented gradually over a period of three to five years, to overcome the limitations of the two-weekly lesson model. She explains that the first path is parallel bilingual education, through teaching science and social studies in Kurdish and Arabic in areas of high concentration, including Hasakah, Qamishli, Afrin and Kobani.”
In contrast, the report also quotes Ibrahim Khalil, a Kurdish writer and linguist residing in Germany. “He adds that teaching two optional classes per week cannot be considered a national gain or a correct step towards solving the Kurdish issue in Syria, but rather, in his opinion, it represents ‘a step in the wrong direction on the path of national assimilation and Arabization of what remains of the Kurds.’” It notes that “Khalil believes that the national solution lies in recognizing the Kurdish language as a second official language, and opening official primary schools in Kurdish areas where instruction is only in Kurdish, with a daily lesson allocated to the Arabic language.”
Another concern in Syria is the issue of official names for towns and areas. This dispute is most clear in Kobani, which has also been called Ayn al Arab. Kobani is the Kurdish name for the city. In “predominantly Kurdish areas, particularly in the east and north of the country, the issue of place names has been linked over the past decades to a broader conflict over language and identity,” North Press notes.
“Most of those areas acquired dual names, one official Arabic name which is the one used in government records, and another Kurdish name used by the residents among themselves.” The concern is that Kurdish names of areas will continue to be “Arabized” in official documents. This was common during the Assad era, as the Assad regime was an Arab nationalist regime, similar to the Saddam regime in Iraq.
Kurds can't speak their language in government offices
In Iraq, Kurds continue to struggle for their rights. “A blacksmith in the Kurdish-majority city of Khanaqin in the eastern Diyala province was arrested Monday over what his family says was his addition of Kurdish to his shop's billboard - an incident that has further stoked tensions in a region already fraught with demographic manipulation concerns,” Rudaw noted this week.
According to the KRG official, speaking to Rudaw, “Kurdish-speaking residents of Khanaqin are being prevented from using Kurdish in government offices, calling it "’a dangerous indicator.’ He further noted that ‘the issue is not entirely on Baghdad's shoulders - we share in it, too,’ criticizing Kurdish parties representing Khanaqin in federal institutions for falling short.”
As Kurds demonstrate in Rojava for their language rights, in Khanaqin in Iraq the issue relates to demographics. There are disputed areas between the KRG and Baghdad, including Khanaqin and parts of Diyala, Kirkuk, Nineveh, and Salahaddin provinces. The Kurds have long been concerned about attempts to change the demographics in these regions, often by government authorities trying to increase the number of Arabs in the regions.
This demographic change goes back to the Saddam era and attempts at mass movement of people and even collectivizing areas into various villages while moving Bedouin and other tribes into areas to link them more closely with Baghdad.
Rudaw says that Kurds have put off a planned mass demonstration in Khanaqin. However, there have been “arrest warrants against activists, political figures, and youths who had intended to take part.”

Why can't Lebanese women pass citizenship to their children?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:33:36 UTC
17:33:36 KST

Breadcrumb
'Foreigners in their own home': The Lebanese mothers fighting for their children's right to belong
When a Lebanese woman marries a man from a foreign land, she is reminded that, on a political, financial and societal level, in the eyes of the state, her children are not truly Lebanese. She may have been born in Beirut, voted in elections, paid her taxes, and never lived elsewhere. Yet, because she married a non-Lebanese man, her child inherited only his nationality.
This is the result of Lebanon's 1925 Nationality Law, born of the French Mandate era, which creates a system of unequal citizenship by preventing Lebanese women who marry foreign nationals from passing their citizenship to their children or spouses.
For families affected by the law, however, the consequences extend far beyond legal status. The restrictions shape access to residency, employment, education, healthcare and other essential services throughout a family's life.
In some cases, children can even be left vulnerable to statelessness, highlighting how a legal distinction rooted in patriarchal hierarchies between men and women continues to produce lasting social and economic inequalities.
For Ramzi Kaiss of Human Rights Watch, the central issue is straightforward: "Lebanon's nationality law should be amended so that men and women have access to the same rights," he tells The New Arab.
Ramzi notes that under Nationality Law No. 15, Lebanese women cannot pass citizenship to their children or spouses, whereas their male counterparts generally have the right to pass citizenship to their families.
"The sex of a person should not determine what legal benefits they may enjoy in the country," Ramzi adds.
He describes the impact of the law on a personal, financial and political level, saying the legal framework "affects their ability to work in certain sectors, to participate in elections, to access services that other people with the nationality have access to."
Locked out of equal opportunities
For families living under these restrictions, those legal differences can have immediate and practical consequences.
When Lebanese mothers are prevented from passing on their citizenship, the consequences can extend far beyond questions of identity. Their uncertain legal status places them at greater risk of exploitation, trafficking and homelessness.
Given that they are not recognised as natural-born Lebanese citizens, foreign spouses and children must repeatedly obtain residency and, where applicable, work permits to remain and work lawfully in the country. Their status as legal residents rather than citizens also means that children are generally ineligible for free public education, greatly limiting their overall prospects in the country.
Education is one area where this uncertainty becomes particularly visible. For example, although some children of Lebanese mothers might be eligible to attend public schools free of charge, their status as foreign nationals often creates additional obstacles.
Each year, the Ministry of Education prioritises the enrolment of Lebanese citizens, meaning children considered 'non-Lebanese' under the Nationality Law face greater uncertainty and longer waits to secure a place in the classroom.
For Amanda, who spent her childhood in Lebanon before leaving for college, the prospect of returning is complicated by the restrictions she could face.
"The possibility that I'd come back to the country is slim. I'm anticipating a lot of difficulty applying for work permits and going through residency again. It feels like a lot of doors are shut before I even get there," she says.
The sectarian argument
The difficulties do not end with education or residency. For the most part, children and spouses of Lebanese women are also excluded from Lebanon's National Social Security Fund and subsidised care provided by the Ministry of Public Health.
For Danya, a Lebanese woman married to a Palestinian, this has meant having to be hyper-aware of minor medical expenses at all times.
Her family once had private insurance, but they decided to abandon their policy after weighing the costs against the uncertainty of whether an insurer would continue covering them if a chronic illness developed. Even a minor injury could leave the family facing expenses that extend far beyond their means.
For these families, the absence of citizenship is therefore not just about their legal status in the country. It determines how and if they can access basic healthcare in a secure and affordable way.
These consequences have also raised wider questions about the law itself. Not only does the implementation of a legal framework that discriminates based on sex violate international law, but it also directly contradicts Lebanon's own constitution, with Article 7 stating that all Lebanese are guaranteed equality before the law, regardless of identity.
Yet despite these concerns, the debate over reform has repeatedly returned to Lebanon's sectarian balance.
For years, Lebanese politicians have framed nationality reform as a threat to the country's sectarian balance. Many campaigners have long argued that this explanation quickly unravels under scrutiny.
If Lebanon's nationality law were truly about preserving the country's delicate demographic balance, many campaigners ask: why do those concerns only seem to arise when women seek the same rights as men?
While multiple successive governments have repeatedly cited demographic concerns to justify preventing women from passing on their citizenship, the same logic has never been applied to Lebanese men, who retain the unrestricted right to confer nationality on their foreign spouses and children.
For Human Rights Watch activists such as Ramzi, this inconsistency reveals that the debate is driven less by constitutional necessity than by political calculations rooted in gender discrimination.
"Politicians in Lebanon regularly refer to sectarian and demographic concerns to spark fear. These same leaders have regularly resorted to sectarian or demographic-related arguments to bar women from passing nationality to their children or spouses. But somehow those arguments cease to exist when it comes to men's ability to pass their nationality," he says.
The battle to change Lebanon's nationality law
The political argument has persisted despite years of campaigning for reform. While it is true that some ministries have offered minor amendments to increase access to basic rights for those impacted by the law, these have been widely criticised as fragmented attempts to appease the wider public without offering tangible and reliable resolution.
Lebanese women's rights groups, such as Collective for Research and Training on Development-Action (CRTDA) and Masir, have spent over 20 years pushing multiple governments to amend the nationality law and grant women the same right as men to pass on their citizenship.
Despite this hardline campaigning effort, reform has repeatedly been blocked by a familiar political argument: extending nationality rights to women married to Palestinian refugees would greatly disturb Lebanon's fragile sectarian balance and, therefore, the law must remain intact.
But campaigners point to figures they say challenge the scale of that concern.
A 2016 census of Palestinians in Lebanon recorded just 3,707 households in which a Palestinian man married a woman of another nationality. According to activists, this figure alone immediately undermines claims that reform would trigger a major demographic shift.
Instead, advocates highlight an overwhelmingly glaring inconsistency: while politicians lean into their own self-interested sectarian concerns to justify restricting women's nationality rights, Lebanese men continue to pass citizenship to foreign spouses and children without the same objections being raised.
For the women caught in the middle of Lebanon's nationality law, the debate over sectarian balance is not an abstract political argument. It is felt in the residency office, at the school gates and when their family needs medical care.
Despite living, paying taxes and co-existing in Lebanon, they are treated as foreigners in their own home.
Those who do decide to stay, or rather are unable to leave, face immeasurable scrutiny and a never-ending bureaucratic nightmare that limits their basic rights and freedoms as nationals.
For more than two decades, campaigners have challenged a system that gives Lebanese men a right that Lebanese women are denied.
Yet reform remains enmeshed in competing political calculations and aspirations, with the prospect of sectarian imbalance repeatedly invoked to justify maintaining the status quo.
That leaves a question at the heart of the debate: if demographic concerns are the sole reason for withholding nationality from the children of Lebanese women, why is this not a concern for Lebanese men?
Until that contradiction is adequately addressed at a political and state level, Lebanese women will continue to face a deeply unequal form of citizenship, which allows them to be recognised as Lebanese in almost every facet of public life except where it means the most: at home with their children.
Lucy Rafaela Farha is a London-based freelance journalist and digital creative

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Tuesday that Tehran would immediately reciprocate if the US returned to its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, the presidency said.
“I state clearly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the memorandum, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in an address at the 26th summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Kyrgyzstan’s capital Bishkek.

Islamabad MoU

The agreement included provisions concerning an end to hostilities, the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
Turning to the SCO, Pezeshkian proposed establishing a bank, creating an export insurance and investment union, and forming an energy consortium as three measures to strengthen the organisation’s role, according to the presidency.
The SCO summit brings together leaders of its 10 member states to discuss regional security as well as political and economic cooperation.
Founded in 2001, the SCO comprises Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
Iran became a full member in 2023.

UK house prices rise for first time since April, says Nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:32:48 UTC
17:32:48 KST

UK house prices increased for the first time in four months in August, according to a leading index, as buyers and sellers remained in a “holding pattern” before an expected increase in interest rates later this year.
The average price of a British home rose 0.2% month on month in August to £275,465, the first increase since April, according to Nationwide. Analysts had forecast a 0.1% rise.
The increase follows a three-month decline in prices after Nationwide revised a month-on-month 0.1% rise in July to a fall of 0.1%.
Ian Futcher, a financial planner at Quilter, said the UK housing market was awaiting the outcome of the next vote by the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee on 17 September on whether to raise the base rate of interest from its current 3.75%.
“Over recent months, expectations for interest rates have been driven by the stop-start nature of the conflict in the Middle East,” Futcher said. “That leaves the housing market in something of a holding pattern ahead of the next interest rate decision.
“While a hold remains the most likely outcome, it is becoming increasingly difficult to call with confidence. For borrowers, the key message is that rates may not have peaked. Until that uncertainty lifts, buyer confidence is likely to remain subdued.”
After three months of falling prices, the average UK property remains valued more than £3,000 less than the £278,880 Nationwide estimated in April.
On an annual basis, house prices were up 1.6% on the same month last year, ahead of the 1.4% year-on-year increase in July. However, that was below economists’ forecast of a 2% annual increase.
Markets currently do not expect the MPC to raise rates this month but are pricing in a 0.25% increase by December.
Robert Gardner, the chief economist at Nationwide, said the latest increase in the energy price cap, which will result in bills hitting a three-year high this winter, had not yet affected buying and selling activity.
“While the latest energy price shock poses inflation risks, there have been encouraging signs that it is not feeding through to underlying price pressures,” he said. “Underlying affordability is improving as house price growth remains well below earnings growth, although some of these gains have been offset by higher mortgage rates. Nevertheless, this suggests that activity should regain momentum in the quarters ahead, providing the energy shock wanes and confidence returns.”

Captain arrested after northern Cyprus ferry disaster leaves 8 dead, 20 missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:32:08 UTC
17:32:08 KST

A deep-sea search team from Turkey was expected to arrive in northern Cyprus on Tuesday to help locate 20 people still missing after the Filo Jet ferry sank two days earlier, killing at least eight people.
Authorities in northern Cyprus have arrested nine people in connection with the disaster, including the ferry’s 66-year-old captain, Mustafa Oz. Some reports cited witnesses as alleging that he abandoned the vessel after it capsized, though that claim has not been independently confirmed.
Other detainees reportedly include shareholders in the company that operated the ferry.
The Filo Jet was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members on Sunday afternoon when it ran into trouble while sailing from Kyrenia in northern Cyprus to the Turkish port of Tasucu.
About seven kilometers off the northern Cyprus coast, water began entering the vessel and the captain sent a distress signal.
Witnesses said the wide-bodied catamaran began listing and rocking violently before slamming back onto the water. Part of its bow reportedly broke apart on impact, creating a breach as passengers heard what they described as an explosion.
Passengers then began jumping into the sea in an attempt to survive.
Footage from the scene showed suitcases and other belongings scattered across the water as the ferry went down.
Authorities believe there is a significant possibility that passengers who failed to escape were trapped inside cabins when the ferry overturned.
Of the 20 people still missing, 18 are Turkish citizens and two are from northern Cyprus. Children are among the missing.
The wreck now lies more than 500 meters below the surface, beyond the reach of equipment currently available to authorities in northern Cyprus, prompting the deployment of a specialist team from Turkey.
The cause of the disaster remains under investigation.
Authorities said the vessel, built around 2000, apparently held the required permits, including safety certification.
A court on Monday extended the detention of nine people connected with the ferry’s operation for three days.
Several survivors have also alleged that there were not enough life jackets on board.
“Some people had to jump without a lifebuoy or a life jacket. It was a fight for survival,” survivor Efe Multici told CNN Türk.
Turkish newspaper Sabah reported that one victim, Fahri Ates, went back inside the ferry in an attempt to find life jackets for his wife and child but became trapped. His wife and child survived.
One of the most harrowing accounts came from Ayten Bicer, who was returning to Turkey with her family after a vacation in northern Cyprus.
Her six-year-old son Mehmet and 12-year-old daughter Saliha remain missing.
“I lost two of my children,” Bicer told Turkey’s DHA news agency as she cried. “My daughter slipped out of my hands right in front of my eyes. She said, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go.”
Bicer said a suitcase fell on her during the chaos, causing her daughter to slip from her grasp.
She managed to grab the girl by the leg, but said her daughter’s shoe had become covered in engine oil from the overturned vessel and slipped from her hands.
“Mehmet was holding onto his father here,” Bicer said, pointing to the collar of her shirt. “He shouted, ‘Baba,’” the Turkish word for father.
Her husband, Hayri Bicer, said the disaster unfolded too quickly for the family to react.
“We couldn’t do anything,” he said. “We lost two of our three children. We’re leaving and leaving them behind on this island.”
Northern Cyprus has declared three days of mourning following the disaster.
The territory has been controlled since 1983 by the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is recognized only by Turkey. The internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus controls the rest of the island.

Taipei Fubon Bank advances FSC’s Financial Giveback Initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:31:53 UTC
17:31:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — In alignment with Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) Financial Giveback Initiative, Taipei Fubon Bank continues to leverage its financial expertise and resources to create long-term social value.
Guided by the initiative’s four key pillars — financial literacy, support for local communities and underserved populations, green finance and sustainable development, and corporate social responsibility — the bank has expanded its efforts in financial education, inclusive finance, net-zero transition, and fraud prevention.
Taipei Fubon Bank has been recognized by the FSC three times as ranking among the top 25% in the Performance in Treating Customers Fairly Evaluation. In addition, the National Development Council selected the bank this year as a Model Bank for One-Stop Banking Services for Foreigners, recognizing its commitment to financial inclusion and customer-centric services.
“Financial institutions play an important role beyond providing capital,” said Taipei Fubon Bank President Tim Kuo (郭倍廷). “By strengthening financial literacy, improving access to financial services, supporting the low-carbon transition, and upholding fair treatment principles, we aim to maximize the positive impact of finance on society.”
Financial literacy and inclusion
The bank has developed a comprehensive financial empowerment ecosystem through partnerships with schools, nonprofit organizations, and community groups, reaching children, youth, and underserved populations.
In 2025, the bank continued its popular Budding Tycoon Money Management Camp and partnered with the CommonWealth Education Innovation Hub to launch a youth financial education initiative. Together, these programs reached more than 2,600 students aged 8 to 18, providing courses on financial literacy, fraud prevention, risk management, and financial planning.
To promote equitable access to financial knowledge, the programs have also been extended to rural communities, students with hearing and speech impairments, immigrant families, and Indigenous students.
The bank further collaborated with Taipei Municipal Songshan High School of Commerce and Home Economics and National Taiwan Normal University’s Special Education Center on the “Wings Branch Financial Empowerment Program for Students with Disabilities.”
The initiative equips special education students with workplace and financial skills, with 32 students completing professional training and internship placement by the end of 2025.
Inclusive financial services
Taipei Fubon Bank continues to enhance financial accessibility for seniors, people with disabilities, foreign residents, new immigrants, and migrant workers. Its initiatives include senior-friendly financial products, dedicated service counters, multilingual ATM services, and accessibility enhancements across banking channels.
The bank’s designation as a National Development Council model bank also reflects its ongoing efforts to create a more welcoming and inclusive banking environment for residents from diverse backgrounds.
Local economies and communities
As part of its commitment to Taiwan’s real economy, Taipei Fubon Bank further strengthens its presence in central and southern Taiwan and deepens its engagement with local communities and industries.
By providing financial support to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), youth entrepreneurs, and regional industries, the bank supports inclusive economic growth and regional development.
Beyond financial services, the bank promotes sustainable local development through its “Fubon Green Action” Sustainable Marketplace initiative. By increasing procurement from social enterprises and local farmers, Taipei Fubon Bank contributes to both environmental sustainability and local economic vitality while advancing responsible procurement practices.
Green finance
Taipei Fubon Bank is integrating climate-related risks and ESG considerations into its lending and investment decisions to accelerate the transition to a sustainable economy.
As of year-end 2025, the bank’s green financing balance reached NT$648.5 billion (US$20.08 billion). The bank also expanded sustainability-linked loans and green bond financing while providing carbon reduction workshops to help businesses, especially SMEs, in their net-zero transition efforts.
By the end of 2025, the bank had completed three industry-focused workshops covering the bicycle, manufacturing, and metal fastener sectors, helping participating companies develop decarbonization roadmaps and transition strategies.
To further strengthen sustainable finance, Taipei Fubon Bank issued NT$2.5 billion in green bonds and NT$2.5 billion in social bonds in 2025. For retail customers, the bank also introduced green mortgage and energy-efficiency loan programs to encourage the adoption of green buildings and energy-saving technologies.
Fraud prevention
To combat increasingly sophisticated fraud schemes, Taipei Fubon Bank has deployed AI-powered fraud detection solutions, including its Eagle Eye Anti-Fraud Model and “Eagle Eye Care+” services.
In 2025, the bank prevented 717 fraud cases, safeguarding more than NT$838 million in customer assets through frontline intervention. It continues to promote fraud awareness through multilingual education materials and targeted outreach programs.
Kuo emphasized that the FSC’s Financial Giveback Initiatives are not only about returning value to customers but also about creating broader social impact.
“Finance can be a force for positive change,” he said. “Taipei Fubon Bank will continue to advance financial literacy, inclusive finance, green finance, and social responsibility, helping build a more sustainable, resilient, and inclusive future.”

“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP.
The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran.
It left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, have made headlines in the US and provoked criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the carrier would dock just after midnight on Wednesday (about 5pm GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. About 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups before the carrier departs on Sunday.
After meeting US officials on Monday, Poramase said service members would be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and cannabis use. Medical cannabis was legalised in Thailand in 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities.
Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam war in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation.
The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied this was linked to the US arrivals.
Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge US sailors, and Poramase said there would be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya beach and Walking Street.
The city’s police chief, Anek Srathongyoo, said law enforcements agencies had been ordered to step up security measures to prevent undesirable situations. He said that if any US service members broke Thai law, they would be prosecuted accordingly.
Local business owners feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war are eager for the new arrivals. A banner hung over a local bar near a beach read: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”
Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee, said she had seen US service members during past visits but she did not expect many from this crew. “They said 5,000 people will come here but how many will reach us?” she said.
Earlier in August, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East. The Lincoln, one of the US navy’s largest warships, was part of American efforts in the Iran war, which flared back up over the weekend for the first time in a month.
The deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 270 days. Trump downplayed concerns over conditions onboard and said the deployment was “not nearly long enough”.
Thai officials have said the Lincoln will return to the US after its port call in Thailand.

U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s resignation Monday triggered a wave of public criticism directed at Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, with veterans, lawmakers and commentators accusing Hegseth of driving out serious military leadership through a pattern of firings tied to personal loyalty rather than competence.
Retired Army Maj. Richard Ojeda, a combat veteran, wrote on X that the military has “a Pete Hegseth problem.”
“Our troops are not props. The Pentagon is not a playground for incompetent fox news hacks with something to prove about their manliness,” Ojeda wrote. “I carry the names of 13 brothers I lost in war tattooed on my body. I know exactly who pays the price when the people at the top screw up. It sure isn’t Pete Hegseth. It’s the kid strapping up his gear and walking outside the wire.”
Former Democratic congressional candidate and retired Marine Lt. Col. Amy McGrath wrote that the Army now lacks both a permanent secretary and a permanent chief of staff.
“No Secretary of the Army. No permanent Army Chief of Staff, Hegseth fired Gen. Randy George in April with no explanation. And we’re in the middle of a war and perhaps the biggest transformation in land warfare in generations,” McGrath wrote. “So who exactly is running the Army? The serious people keep leaving or getting fired. Meanwhile, Pete Hegseth is giving political stump speeches in Iowa and bringing internet trolls into the Pentagon. This isn’t serious leadership. It’s chaos, and America is much weaker for it.”
Attorney and commentator Ron Filipkowski offered a shorter assessment.
“Hegseth has taken out more American generals than Iranian ones,” Filipkowski wrote.
The criticism centers on an account, reported by multiple outlets, of why Driscoll resigned. Fox News national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin cited a senior source familiar with the matter.
“According to a senior source familiar: Driscoll brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible,” Griffin wrote.
That account matches reporting from NBC News, which cited a source saying Driscoll’s resignation raised concerns about “Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible,” and from CNN, which reported an Army official’s description that Driscoll “spoke to the president about the current state of the Army and submitted his resignation.”
The criticism draws directly on Hegseth’s firing of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George in April, along with two other generals, without public explanation. Driscoll and George had worked closely together, and Driscoll defended George publicly before Congress that same month.
“No person has more respect for Gen. George and his 42 years of service, his Purple Heart, his wife Patty, their grandkids, their kids,” Driscoll said at the time, according to CNN. “I adore them. And he was an amazing, transformational leader.”
McGrath’s and Ojeda’s posts each drew tens of thousands of likes and reshares within hours, according to engagement figures visible on their posts, reflecting the scale of the online reaction to Driscoll’s departure.

German vice-chancellor confronts Russia's finance chief at G20, calls his presence 'irritating'

German vice-chancellor confronts Russia's finance chief at G20, calls his presence 'irritating'
German Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil confronted Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov over Moscow's war against Ukraine at the Aug. 31 G20 meeting of finance ministers and helped lead a push to exclude him from a group photo, Klingbeil told journalists after the meeting.
The summit in Asheville marked Siluanov's first in-person attendance at a G20 finance ministers' meeting since Russia launched its all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"The signal to welcome the Russian finance minister here I perceive as irritating, because I would have wished for clarity from the U.S. side, and that you do not receive him here like a normal guest," Klingbeil said. "This is a regime that has been leading a brutal, illegal war against Ukraine."
Klingbeil said he spoke directly with Siluanov during the meeting, telling him that Russia must end its war and that Germany remains firmly on Ukraine's side.
"I told him directly in his face that the Russian government must end this war, and that the consequence of this war is that we are clearly on the side of Ukraine," he said.
Klingbeil said he opposed taking a joint "family photo" with the Russian finance minister. Other European representatives supported the move, and organizers ultimately took the photo without Siluanov and away from reporters.
When asked why the U.S. invited Siluanov to the meeting, President Donald Trump told reporters on Aug. 31 that the current White House is "getting along with everybody."
Siluanov met with his U.S. counterpart, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on Aug. 31, to discuss a peace plan for Ukraine. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv does not "know anything about this meeting."
Klingbeil warned that Siluanov's return after four G20 meetings without Russian participation risked contributing to the normalization of relations with Moscow despite its ongoing war.
"Just the fact that the Russian finance minister is back after four G20 meetings without them shows an attempt to normalize," Klingbeil said. "All the more we have to resist. There is no normal situation, especially with Russia."

Why US sanctions threats against China aren’t credible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

Why US sanctions threats against China aren’t credible
Weaponising global payments against Beijing risks triggering a major shock at home – one America’s fragile debt and stock markets cannot afford
The US talking up economic war on Iran reflects the reality that it is running out of ammunition for a hot war. The US has imposed economic and financial sanctions on Iran for decades. Now it aims to impose secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners. As China is Iran’s main trading partner, the US is essentially targeting China.
China and the US have traded places since US President Donald Trump initiated the trade and tech war during his first term. At the time, China was grappling with a massive property bubble and a bloated shadow banking system. The government managed to deflate both without triggering a major economic downturn. Today, while China’s growth rate is muted, the economy is resilient and can withstand shocks.
The US’ financial fragility and China’s resilience make it unlikely that the former will initiate an action that can shock its financial system. In a game of chicken, the US will blink first.
The US has been sanctioning China in trade and technology through any means it can find. So far, China has been able to absorb the blows without suffering a recession. China is in the crosshairs of US politicians, with or without Iran. Hence, China has no incentive to respond to US pressure on additional sanctions.

“The UK is yet to have a national reckoning around its role in colonialism”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Lavinya Stennett on the importance of teaching Black history in schools
Lavinya Stennett, 29, is founder and CEO of The Black Curriculum, an educational tool that enables young people across the UK – and beyond – to learn about the history of colonialism.
Here, she shares what inspired the idea, why reparatory justice matters and the impact her organization is having on young people…
In 2016, I received my A Level results. I didn’t get my first-choice university, so went through clearing [how universities and colleges fill any places they still have on their courses]. I received a place at SOAS to do African Studies. I didn’t know much about the university, but my mum insisted I go.
The course changed my life. Prior to my degree, I hadn’t been able to access any information around African history that was empowering or wasn’t just focused on enslavement.
I started learning from African lecturers and it was such a grounding experience. I received a scholarship to go to New Zealand, where I learned a lot about Māori land law, as well as issues around the colonization and theft of land, and it just put everything into context.
The main aim of The Black Curriculum is to empower all students with a sense of identity and belonging.
Lavinya Stennett
I realized that the UK hadn’t had a national reckoning around its role in colonialism and the impact it’s had on young people today. We often see Saturday schools and other forms of alternative Black education pop up, but there’s nothing in the official curriculum – so that’s how the Black curriculum was born.
Inspiring a new generation
The main aim of The Black Curriculum is to empower all students with a sense of identity and belonging, allowing young people from all backgrounds to access knowledge on their cultural or national history.
Our work primarily focuses on training teachers, working directly with young people, and campaigning because it is our aim to embed Black history into the national curriculum.
We work with people across the education sector, as well as with people in prisons and museums to make sure they have access to our curriculum – so it’s really about societal education for all young people.
There are so many things that inspired this idea. Initially, we started speaking to teachers directly and there were three schools in South London that were excited to work with us. Once we had worked in those schools, The Black Curriculum took on a life of its own. We were approached by teachers across London, as well as Manchester. Then, after George Floyd was killed, we were contacted by schools in Canada and the USA, eager to know how they could incorporate it into their curriculum.
Our course is having an incredible impact across the world, and our reports from 2020 to 2024 show that students gain an improved sense of confidence from learning about their history once they’ve completed our course – and this goes for both Black and white students.
We don’t just have one scheme of work for the term that we give to teachers, we work with what they have. So, for example we have a zine our young people have created, as well as animations, podcasts and digital and physical learning resources.
Why reparatory justice matters
Through our course, I’ve realized how important it is to continue to seek reparatory justice because the work we’re doing around truth-telling in our histories and across the curriculum must lead to something. It’s not just about retelling a long history for history’s sake, it’s about building a consciousness within the peoples of the world to shift structures and systems that are affecting us.
Reparations are about repairing the harms still taking place, as well as the harms that people of African descent have experienced, in particular. Enslavement has impacted our countries, our cultures, our languages, our everything.
Enslavement has impacted our countries, our cultures, our languages, our everything.
Lavinya Stennett
I think it is about re-educating people truthfully about what’s happened so that we can then think really clearly about what needs to be rectified for a better future.
Aside from the obvious moral wrong, Britain and other colonial powers have a duty to readdress a lot of the ills that we see today from discrimination in access to healthcare to education disparities – and a lot of this stems from colonialism, so it needs to be brought under a framework of reparations.
I’m from Jamaica in the Caribbean, and for many people of African descent we don’t know where we’re from. Even if you do a DNA test, it doesn’t even give you the specific community you’re from, so it’s about reconciling our cultural identities that were lost historically. Families were forced into migration when Britain brought back its “citizens” from the colonies to help rebuild itself postwar and we were essentially forced into poverty – we didn’t have a choice.
Finding where I fit in
I have always been attracted to history and the more social side of education, but I couldn’t figure out where I fitted in. So going through primary school, secondary school and onto university, I had to go and find that for myself. I was lucky I had the opportunities I’ve had, but there’s people that haven’t and will continue to stay lost and not have that sense of identity that their white counterparts may be privileged to have because they’ve seen themselves in history and in the curriculum taught at school. We want everybody to be able to see themselves in what they’re learning and use that to guide them forward and to build on themselves. To date we’ve reached well over 25,000 educators and that’s young people and teachers combined. We’ve also amassed a huge following on social media.
But outside of that, it’s incredible to share our message across the world. I recently travelled to Ghana and Kenya, and connected with young people who understand the legacies of colonialism very well and are passionate and want to bring it back into a larger space.
It’s not a privilege, but it feels like a rite of passage that I’m very honoured to walk on.
In our series, Voices of Reparatory Justice, we speak with artists, activists and leaders who share their stories of repair and resilience in fighting against the negative impacts of historical injustices, slavery, and colonialism. Despite existential challenges, their journey to secure dignity and rights of racialised groups, restores hopes for our collective future, humanity must always prevail. This is one of those stories. Find out more about our work.

Thailand jails activist over royal motorcade live streaming

Thailand jails activist over royal motorcade live streaming
She had questioned the conduct of police who dispersed farmers protesting along the route of King Maha Vajiralongkorn’s motorcade in Bangkok
A Thai court has sentenced a 25-year-old activist to two years in prison for violating the country’s strict royal insult law, a rights group said, with her lawyer on Tuesday vowing to appeal.
A criminal court convicted Tantawan Tuatulanon on Monday over a live streaming she aired near a royal motorcade in March 2022, legal advocacy group Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said in a statement.
The court found Tantawan intended to defame Thailand’s highly revered monarchy when she questioned the conduct of police who dispersed farmers protesting along the route of King Maha Vajiralongkorn’s motorcade in the capital, Bangkok.
The court said she had insulted the monarchy on multiple occasions, showing her conduct was “not a good-faith exercise of rights”, the group said.
Tantawan denied charges of breaching Thailand’s strict lese-majeste law.
Her lawyer Khumklao Songsomboon said that she would file an appeal, insisting on her client’s innocence.
“This is simply an exercise of freedom of speech questioning the police’s work and right to assembly,” said Khumklao.

Andrey Gyurov launches presidential bid with Georgi Kandev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:28:17 UTC
17:28:17 KST

Tuesday 1 September 2026 11:11
Tuesday, 1 September 2026, 11:11
Andrey Gyurov, left, and Georgi Kandev announced their candidacies for president and vice-president.
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, who served as Interior Ministry Chief Secretary during his government, have formally entered Bulgaria’s presidential race. They announced their candidacies for president and vice-president outside the History Museum in their home town of Gotse Delchev.
“You all want to hear whether I will enter the race to become Bulgaria’s head of state, and the answer is yes, I will – and Georgi Kandev and I will do it together,” Gyurov said.
He went on to pose a series of questions: “Do we have a state that explains its decisions and knows how much those decisions cost? Do we have a state that does not make its citizens pay for poor planning, incompetence and dependence? Do we have a state that relies on those who are capable, rather than those who are loyal to those in power?”
Gyurov said the initiative committee nominating the pair was made up of citizens rather than representatives of a political party.
“No one sent us here and we owe nothing to anyone. We are working Bulgarian citizens and we have proved ourselves in the highest positions,” he said.
According to Gyurov, the two know Bulgaria from different perspectives: his own experience is in finance, the economy and academia, while Kandev’s is in law, security and the practical implementation of government decisions.
Kandev said he had chosen to stand alongside Gyurov because, from working with him, he knew him to be a man of integrity who loved Bulgaria.
“I know, and I can tell you, when a policy is actually being implemented. I have no hidden agenda. I was brought up to respect and uphold the law,” Kandev said.
The pair have set out four main priorities for their campaign: Bulgaria’s European path, economic competence, independence, and security and public order.
Among the first to address the event was internationally renowned scientist and philanthropist Prof. Minko Balkanski, who voiced his support for Gyurov and Kandev in a video message.
The presidential elections in Bulgaria will be held on October 25.

Russian drone struck a Ukrainian fire truck on its way to a house fire—four rescuers injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:28:00 UTC
17:28:00 KST

A Russian drone hit a fire truck driving to a call in the village of Kushuhum outside Zaporizhzhia on 1 September, injuring four rescuers, the head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ivan Fedorov, reported. The crew was on its way to a house fire that Russian shelling had started. The strike came hours after a countrywide Russian air assault overnight.
A drone hit the crew before they reached the fire
Fedorov said a Russian drone struck the State Emergency Service vehicle in Kushuhum as it drove to put out a fire. The truck took damage, and the crew was hurt. He said the men were under the supervision of medics.
The Main Directorate of the State Emergency Service in Zaporizhzhia Oblast confirmed the attack, and added that all four injured firefighters had been taken to hospital with injuries of differing severity. The directorate specified what the crew had been sent to: a fire in a detached house in the suburb, started by Russian shelling.
Over the past 24 hours, Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia city and district killed two people and injured eight, Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out strikes on 57 settlements across the region.
The night before: a countrywide strike
Overnight into 1 September, Russia attacked with ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-radar missiles, Banderol munitions, and 218 Shahed-type strike drones, about a third of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force reported. By preliminary data, air defenses downed or suppressed 199 targets. Odesa and Kyiv oblasts were the main directions of the strike.
Russia killed 12 people across Ukraine, among them a citizen of India, and injured dozens, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russia killed four people and injured 13 and damaged a five-story residential building, and 50 people were evacuated. Nearly 350 rescuers worked in Kyiv and the surrounding oblast alone.
Russia’s 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head’s visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year
In Kyiv, a ballistic strike on Ukrzaliznytsia railway facilities killed seven people, six of them railway workers, and one more employee remains hospitalized. The capital's overall toll for the night stood at eight killed.
In Odesa Oblast, Russian drones, guided bombs, and missiles injured seven civilian men, four of whom went to hospital, and struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the border with Romania again, the regional prosecutor's office found.
Ukraine has documented Russia striking the people who respond
As of May, Ukraine has documented 11,000 Russian first-person-view drone attacks on civilians, among them repeat strikes on the same spot once medics and firefighters arrive. Ukraine's UN envoy has built part of the case for expelling Russia from the Security Council on that practice.
Rescue workers in Zaporizhzhia have been caught that way before. After a strike on a Poltava Oblast gas site, Russia hit the crews who came to the fire. Firefighters in Chernihiv Oblast went to hospital mid-rescue. In Kryvyi Rih in August, a second Russian attack reached rescue workers thirty minutes after a drone strike on a shopping center, and a repeat strike killed a 20-year-old volunteer paramedic in Kyiv the same month.

Russia Wanted Its Own Starlink. Now Its Satellites Are Falling Before the Network Even Takes Off

Russia Wanted Its Own Starlink. Now Its Satellites Are Falling Before the Network Even Takes Off
Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink is encountering severe operational setbacks, with satellites deployed in orbit losing altitude while newly launched units fail to reach their designated positions, French technology portal Numerama reported.
Moscow allocated 102.8 billion rubles ($1.3 billion) from its state budget for the "Rassvet " program. Commercial operations were set to launch in 2027, with plans to expand the constellation from 250 to 900 satellites in orbit by 2035.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Deploying the intended satellite group requires at least 18 Soyuz-2.1b rocket launches. However, Russia conducts only six to eight such launches per year.
On the night of August 15, the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Progress Space Center in Samara—the sole facility manufacturing the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to place the Rassvet satellites into orbit.
Following claims that several hundred satellites would be in orbit by next year, the first spacecraft are already beginning to lose altitude earlier than anticipated. According to orbital tracking data, at least two satellites are losing altitude, while several others are unable to enter their assigned orbits.
As noted by the specialized website Russian Space Web, while the initial 16 launched satellites performed somewhat better—though one fell back in June—a July launch delivering another 16 spacecraft proved unsuccessful.
The goal was to place the satellites at an altitude of 800 kilometers, but several ended up below 500 kilometers, with some dropping below 400 kilometers.
Nine satellites began maneuvering to rise a few additional kilometers, while others appear to have stopped ascending and started falling. Currently, not a single satellite has managed to rise above 360 kilometers, while two have dropped below 300 kilometers on trajectories resembling a descent.
Even the spacecraft that continue to ascend remain significantly below the altitudes reached by the first group of satellites at the same phase of deployment.
Remaining at lower altitudes carries direct physical consequences. The lower a satellite travels, the higher the atmospheric drag it encounters, requiring it to burn more fuel to avoid falling and thereby shortening its operational lifespan. Consequently, even the spacecraft that stabilize at around 500 kilometers risk degrading much faster than originally anticipated.
With only 32 satellites in orbit and a portion of them barely reaching the required altitude, Rassvet remains far from becoming a fully functional network.
At present, Russia lacks the capacity to expand the satellite constellation to the 250 units planned for 2027, the report noted.
In early February, Starlink CEO Elon Musk deactivated devices not included on Ukrainian “whitelists,” following a request from Ukraine’s Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, which significantly weakened Russian command-and-control capabilities in several parts of the front.
Previously, reports emerged that Russian low-Earth-orbit satellites developed under the Rassvet program may already provide intermittent battlefield connectivity over Ukraine, creating an early-stage alternative to Starlink for Russian forces.

Russia’s Finance Minister Makes First US Visit Since Russia’s Invasion of Ukraine
Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 31, marking his first trip to the United States since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
During the visit, the sanctioned official held discussions with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent regarding Donald Trump's 28-point peace plan, which was prepared last year and stalled following several unsuccessful rounds of negotiations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg, Siluanov did not speak with Bessent alone, as he was accompanied by a Russian delegation, though the agency did not specify who was part of the negotiating team.
The presence of Siluanov at the summit drew pushback from European representatives in Asheville. According to The New York Times, Germany's Vice Chancellor threatened to skip the traditional group photograph of attendees if Siluanov was included. The objection led to Siluanov being excluded from the official photo session.
The Russian minister’s trip came just six days after US CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s unannounced visit to Moscow.
Reports from The New York Times state that Ratcliffe met with Foreign Intelligence Service Director Sergey Naryshkin and Federal Security Service Director Alexander Bortnikov to assess whether Russian officials could influence Vladimir Putin to re-engage in peace discussions.
Sources cited by The New York Times indicated that Ratcliffe delivered a "gloomy assessment" of the outlook for the Russian military and economy, urging the officials to reach an agreement before conditions worsen. He additionally proposed a potential three-way summit featuring Putin, Trump, and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Previously, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for an immediate end to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine during a meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek.
Emphasizing that every day of war pushed humanity backward, Modi stated that it was necessary to work toward ending military actions and transition to peace, reiterating India's support for peace negotiations between Ukraine and Russia.

Putin Expands His Security Service’s Staff Once Again—Fourth Time Since Invasion

- Category

Putin Expands His Security Service’s Staff Once Again—Fourth Time Since Invasion
Russian leader Vladimir Putin signed an order to expand the core personnel of the Federal Protective Service, marking the fourth increase since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Under the updated decree, the maximum staff allowance for the central office of the agency increases from 785 to 812 people, as reported by The Moscow Times on August 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The prior increase went into effect on January 1, 2025, raising the limit to 785 personnel, following earlier expansions to 775 on January 1, 2024, and to 760 from 725 in late 2022.
Prior to the full-scale invasion, the agency had not expanded its central leadership structure for nearly 13 years.
The structure includes a dedicated personal security division for Vladimir Putin that accompanies him during travel and guards his residences and facilities. The agency also oversees specialized communication systems and tracks public opinion.
Following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the organization shifted into an independent center of influence due to its direct access to the leader and confidential data regarding top officials. Security precautions around the Russian leader have intensified in recent months, according to Financial Times.
Kremlin officials have voiced growing concerns over potential assassination attempts involving drones or possible coup scenarios. These anxieties grew after American military forces captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. As a result, Vladimir Putin reduced public travel while security screening procedures for meetings grew stricter.
During an official trip to Kazakhstan in late May, Putin’s convoy featured an armored vehicle fitted with a roof-mounted machine gun, an electronic warfare vehicle, and a helicopter.
The Russian leader's fear for his own life has reshaped his movements for months. Since early March, Putin has suspended visits to his usual residences near Moscow and at Valdai, and has been operating instead from hardened, modernized bunkers in the Krasnodar region.
The Federal Protective Service has meanwhile expanded its priority-protection roster to include at least 10 senior military figures.
The mood among the Russian elite is even more pessimistic. Insiders cited by The Economist reveal a growing consensus that the nearly five-year war is a failure because of the sheer amount of time wasted, regardless of the outcome. However, the criminal logic guiding Putin’s regime dictates that he can never show weakness.
A failure to achieve even his minimum goal of capturing the entire Donbas region could put his life in physical danger. “They will hang me,” he reportedly confessed to cronies earlier in the war, The Economist wrote.

Russian seventh-grader attacks teacher with knife and pepper spray at a Siberian school. Seven people injured.
A seventh-grader attacked a teacher with a knife during a school assembly in Kansk, Krasnoyarsk Krai, local outlets Ngs24.ru and “Prospekt Mira” reported.
The incident took place at School No. 2, according to media reports. One account holds that the student sprayed pepper spray at her physics teacher and then tried to stab her with the knife, and that a woman believed to be another student’s mother rushed to the teacher’s aid and forced the girl out of the classroom.
A second account says the seventh-grader attacked both teachers and students with the knife and also set fire to a door. The motive for the incident remains unclear.
The school has declined to comment on the incident. Russian National Guard officers and ambulance crews responded to the scene, and the Internal Affairs Ministry of Krasnoyarsk Krai stated that it is establishing the circumstances of the incident.
The regional Health Ministry told Ngs24.ru that seven people — five children and two adults — were injured in the attack on the school in Kansk. “All those injured were examined, received the necessary medical care, and were referred for outpatient observation,” the ministry stated.

Helmet required on scooters that can do more than 20km/h
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:23:59 UTC
17:23:59 KST

From 1 September, helmets are compulsory for riders of electric scooters capable of travelling at speeds exceeding 20 kilometres per hour. The regulation has been introduced by the Federal Mobility Ministry.
The helmet requirement does not depend on the speed at which a rider is travelling, but on the maximum speed the scooter is capable of reaching according to the manufacturer. The Royal Decree that enters force today states that the requirement applies to riders of “a motorised personal mobility device whose maximum speed, as determined by its design, exceeds 20 kilometres per hour”.
The rider may choose either a moped helmet or a cycling helmet that also protects the temples and the back of the head.
According to the Mobility Ministry, the measure is intended to improve road safety. “International studies and medical and accident statistics all point in the same direction: in serious and fatal accidents involving motorised vehicles, and in particular electric scooters, head and brain injuries are particularly common,” it states. Furthermore, the risk of serious injury increases as speed rises.
In Belgium, only electric scooters capable of travelling at a maximum speed of 25 kilometres per hour are permitted. The new compulsory helmet rule therefore applies to scooters with a design speed of between 20 and 25 kilometres per hour.
According to the government, one of the reasons why the requirement does not apply to all e-scooters is the desire not to discourage people from swapping their car for a (share) scooter for short journeys.
For share e-scooters, a helmet is not compulsory if the operator has limited the maximum speed to 20 kilometres per hour. According to the Mobility Ministry, this is often already the case in practice, and this speed limit is usually included in the operating licence.

Russia faces space setback in rapid deployment of Starlink analogue – ISW
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:22:00 UTC
17:22:00 KST

Russia faces space setback in rapid deployment of Starlink analogue – ISW
Ukrinform reports, citing the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), that none of the 16 Rassvet satellites from the second batch launched on July 19 had reached the expected altitude of 550 kilometers above Earth as of August 31, according to satellite tracking data from N2YO.
Many of these satellites were at altitudes of between 300 and 400 kilometers, and at least two satellites were heading toward Earth’s atmosphere.
These altitudes are significantly below the planned operational altitude of 870 kilometers for the Rassvet satellites.
The report notes that satellites operating at lower altitudes have shorter service lives because of increased atmospheric drag from the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere and greater fuel consumption compared with satellites operating at higher altitudes.
Overall, only 12 of the 16 Rassvet satellites launched on March 24 had reached the expected altitude of 550 kilometers as of July 31. They remained at that altitude as of August 31.
These 12 satellites provided Russian forces with two daily communication windows with ground terminals over Ukraine, each lasting up to 1.5 hours.

Lake Annecy gun linked to unsolved 2012 murder of British family in French Alps
French officials say a Luger pistol fished out from the bottom of Lake Annecy shows similarities to the weapon used in the notorious 2012 killings of a British-Iraqi family and a French cyclist in the nearby village of Chevaline, opening up a new lead in a case that has befuddled investigators for over a decade.
French officials are examining a Luger pistol found at the bottom of Lake Annecy which could have been used in the murders of a British-Iraqi family and a French cyclist 14 years ago.
The 2012 Alps killings saw three members of a British-Iraqi family and a French citizen shot dead on a mountain road near the southern end of Lake Annecy.
Saad al-Hilli, 50; his wife Iqbal, 47; her mother Suhaila al-Allaf, 74 and French cyclist Sylvain Mollier, 45, were found dead on a mountain road.
The al-Hillis' two daughters survived the attack. One, aged four, was found hidden under the legs of her dead mother in the rear footwell while the elder one, aged seven, was shot in the shoulder and also suffered a head wound.
French prosecutors in the western Paris suburb of Nanterre told AFP on Monday the Luger was fished out from the bottom of the lake by British tourists swimming there on August 20.
It shows similarities to the weapon used in the 2012 attack.
French and British police had investigated al-Hilli's past in Iraq as an engineer on sensitive topics, as well as his work at the time of his death, as a potential motive for the attack.
