War on words: Russia destroyed a third of Ukraine’s annual book production this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

Russia continues to devastate Ukraine’s cultural heritage. Attacks on the book market, already under threat from the war, have intensified recently – over the summer, a third of Ukrainian publishers’ annual output, including a large proportion of textbooks, was destroyed in warehouses or printing works. Industry representatives are warning of a collapse of the sector, which would deprive Ukraine of the right to speak with its own voice.
“The whole world should know what has happened here,” said Viktor Kruhlov, director of the Ranok publishing house, which specialises in children’s and educational literature, to RFI. The Russians attacked the company’s largest warehouse in Kharkiv on August 1.
“It was a deliberately planned attack on the bookshop,” noted Kruhlov, according to Reuters. “Two explosions followed one after the other, a few minutes apart. There were about fifty employees on the premises at the time, and it is a miracle that no one died. Everything melted as a result of the heat following both explosions,” RFI quoted him as saying.
It was the biggest blow to the Ukrainian publishing industry since the start of the war. In a 10,000-square-metre warehouse, where not only Ranok but also the KnyhoLand chain stored books, eight million books were destroyed in the fire caused by the attack.
Around a million of these were textbooks; Ranok prints roughly a third of the total number of these in Ukraine. Although the company has other warehouses, the one in Kharkiv was the largest and housed the majority of its output.
“We learnt that during the Second World War, the Nazis burnt thousands of books. Now the Russians are routinely destroying millions of Ukrainian books. It is a deliberate strategy to undermine Ukrainian culture and identity, because Russia refuses to accept a prosperous Ukraine,” added Kruhlov.
Systematic attacks
Russia is systematically targeting the Ukrainian publishing industry. It carried out its first such attacks as early as spring 2022, specifically in Kharkiv.
Further attacks followed, which intensified significantly in 2024. In May of that year, Moscow destroyed the Faktor-Druk printing works in Kharkiv, killing seven workers who were printing children’s books. The facility produced around a third of all books in Ukraine, according to the Ukrainian Publishers’ Association.
Last year, Russia extended its strikes to include warehouses in Kyiv and Dnipro, and its attacks on Ukrainian books reached their peak this summer. In July, it struck, amongst other targets, a warehouse belonging to the BookChef publishing house, destroying 800,000 copies – the majority of its stock. In the same month, it also destroyed two other warehouses, the office of a publishing house and a printing works in the capital.
The attack on Ranok in Kharkiv in early August was followed by further strikes; for example, in the middle of the month in Kyiv, several warehouses belonging to various companies were targeted once again, including BookChef’s backup warehouse, where 100,000 copies were reduced to ashes. The Počajna open-air book market in Kyiv was also targeted.
A third of the annual output was destroyed by fire
The attacks mentioned above are among the largest, but by no means an exhaustive list. The attacks over the last two months have caused losses to dozens of publishing houses and bookshops – whether through direct destruction or indirect consequences.
In July, the Russians destroyed 1.5 million copies and in August ten million, which represents roughly a third of Ukraine’s annual book production, reported Ukrayinska Pravda (UP).
The Ukrainian Publishers’ Association reports as many as thirteen million books destroyed over the summer and direct losses amounting to 1.2 billion hryvnias (roughly six hundred million korunas) – though, according to the association, the actual losses are significantly higher. The Ukrainian Book Institute estimates them to be in the billions of hryvnias.
The Ukrainian book market as a whole is, however, relatively small; according to the publishers’ association, its annual turnover is around seven to eight billion hryvnias, which is comparable to the turnover of a small shopping centre.
Hundreds of schools have also been affected, as nine per cent of new textbooks were destroyed shortly before the start of the school term. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Education, this amounts to more than 1.2 million copies. In the case of some subjects, Russia has even destroyed the entire print run for the 2026–2027 academic year, according to Serhiy Babak, chair of the parliamentary committee on education, as reported by UP.
“Russia’s genocidal policy”
As well as book warehouses, printing works, bookshops and publishers’ offices, Moscow is also destroying Ukrainian libraries. The Ukrainian Ministry of Culture reports that, since the start of full-scale war, 228 libraries have been destroyed and 678 damaged as a result of Russian attacks. The actual damage, however, is likely to be greater, as the figures do not include damage in the occupied territories.
Attacks on libraries and book publishing in general form part of a wider Russian campaign aimed at destroying Ukrainian monuments and cultural heritage. The Ukrainian Ministry of Culture has recorded – in the unoccupied territories alone – thousands of such cases.
Ukrainian Minister of Education Andriy Butenko described the Russian attacks on bookshops and printing houses as an attempt to destroy the Ukrainian language, history and memory, “everything from which our children’s identity grows”. Similarly, Oleksandra Matviychuk, director of the human rights organisation Centre for Civil Liberties, which was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022, described the destruction of Ukrainian books as “part of Russia’s broader genocidal policy”.
“We know from history that the burning of libraries has accompanied genocides for centuries – as a means of erasing someone else’s identity. (Russian dictator Vladimir) Putin openly states that there is no Ukrainian nation, no Ukrainian language and no Ukrainian culture,” says Matvijčuková, alluding to Russia’s questioning of the existence of an independent Ukraine.
The Struggle for Survival
“One in three planned new releases either never sees the light of day or reaches shop shelves with a significant delay and in reduced print runs. All of this is accompanied by colossal additional costs for an industry that is already struggling to survive,” summarises the consequences of the Russian strikes, reports the UA News website.
Like other sectors of the Ukrainian economy – with the exception of the defence industry – the book sector is struggling as a result of the Russian war, even in the absence of direct attacks.
The cost of printing books has risen by around forty per cent over the last two years, and fewer and fewer Ukrainians can afford to buy them regularly, according to Reuters. Demand for books is so low that a number of bookshops have had to close this year, reports UP.
Russian raids on warehouses and printing works are further complicating the situation – the publishing houses affected will find it very difficult to replenish their stocks, as they have had to temporarily suspend operations, RFI adds. According to Reuters, it can take between six and eighteen months to produce books.
‘The right to speak with a Ukrainian voice’
The Publishers’ Association is therefore warning that the entire sector is on the brink of collapse, and is calling on the country’s leadership to convene the National Security Council and introduce support measures. These include state-subsidised loans, insurance to cover the cost of books, tax relief and subsidies for shop rent, as well as the resumption of state purchases for libraries, which were suspended in 2022.
The association also warns that if domestic publishers are unable to recover, they will be replaced by foreign companies, which would mean that the Ukrainian book market would lose not only books written in Ukrainian, but also support for Ukrainian authors, national values and identity.
A similar appeal was published by the Ukrainian Book Institute. “We are facing the risk of the collapse of the entire book ecosystem,” it states, calling on the international publishing community to support their Ukrainian colleagues and to cease cooperation with their Russian counterparts.
“Supporting Ukrainian publishers today is not just about preserving the industry. It is about defending Ukraine’s right to speak with its own voice and shape its own narrative on the world stage,” the institute added.
Article initially published on August 27, 2026, 06:00 (CEST).

Commission warns of worsening health of Palestinian women detainees in Israeli jails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:14:21 UTC
15:14:21 KST

The health of several Palestinian women detainees in Israeli custody has deteriorated amid intensified raids, searches and punitive measures, the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said on Monday.
The Palestinian prisoners’ body said testimonies from women prisoners documented overcrowding, shortages of basic necessities, poor food and inadequate medical care in prisons and interrogation centres.
It said the conditions were taking an increasing physical and psychological toll on detainees.
Among them is Abeer Odeh from Tulkarem in the occupied West Bank, who suffers from asthma as well as problems affecting her oesophagus and back, according to the commission.
Odeh, who underwent surgery before her detention, said she was receiving only stomach medication despite needing further treatment.
She said prison authorities raided rooms holding women detainees at Damon Prison on August 17 and carried out another crackdown the following day, forcing prisoners out and confiscating clothes and personal belongings.
Detainees report medical concerns
The commission said Yasmine Shaaban from Jenin also requires treatment for a uterine condition.
Shaaban previously spent around nine years in Israeli prisons before being detained again in May 2025. She has since been issued five administrative detention orders, according to the commission.
It also reported that Nadine al-Daghamin from as-Samu, south of Hebron, suffers from a severe skin rash and allergies, while Shahd Adi from Beit Ummar has contracted scabies.
The commission said Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir entered Damon Prison on August 19, where he threatened Palestinian prisoners and spoke about measures imposed on them.
It also raised concerns over the health of 54-year-old Palestinian physician Dima Mohammed Amin, who was detained on August 18.
Amin experienced symptoms of a heart attack and underwent cardiac catheterisation, while also suffering from low blood sugar, unstable blood pressure, high cholesterol and dizziness, the commission said.
After a lawyer visited her at the Russian Compound interrogation centre, Amin described shortages of food and clothing, repeated searches, shouting and psychological pressure.
She also said women detainees were forcibly dragged from their cells and made to stand in a corner without being allowed to move.
The commission warned that Amin’s detention conditions posed further risks to her health and said she required continuous medical care.
Around 92 Palestinian women are currently held in Israeli prisons and detention centres, according to the commission.
Palestinian figures put the total number of Palestinians in Israeli prisons at around 9,400 as of early July, including more than 350 children, 3,244 administrative detainees and 1,320 people Israel classifies as “unlawful combatants”.

A fire has been reported in Russia following a drone attack on the port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region, according to monitoring resources and Russian authorities, UNN reports.
Details
A fire broke out in the Ust-Luga port area as a result of a UAV attack, the governor of the Leningrad region said on Telegram.

At the same time, there were loud reports in the Samara region: explosions were heard in Chapayevsk, Novokuibyshevsk and Tolyatti," the statement said.

Rain, internet outages hit first day of Hong Kong’s robot convenience stores
But visitors praise humanoid robots at new Galbot Stores in Hung Hom, Wan Chai and Kai Tak
Heavy rain and internet outages marred the launch of Hong Kong’s first humanoid robot-operated convenience stores on Tuesday, but visitors said they still appreciated the work of the new robots.
Embodied-intelligence robotics company Galbot opened two outdoor stores in Hung Hom and Wan Chai and an indoor shop in Kai Tak.
The Galbot Stores offer a mix of snacks and drinks, along with local offerings such as pineapple-bun and egg-tart-themed merchandise, with prices ranging from HK$14 to HK$139 (US$1.79 to US$17.73).
Customers order using a screen and pay by card, WeChat, Alipay or China UnionPay, before the robot retrieves their purchases.
Patrons are also welcome to have a casual chat with the robots in Cantonese or English without making a purchase.
“Do not miss it – the big star who’s appeared on the Spring Festival Gala is working right here!” one of the robot managers said as it greeted passers-by in Cantonese.

Ex-gang leader ‘Keffe D’ found guilty of killing rap legend Tupac Shakur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:10:29 UTC
15:10:29 KST

Ex-gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
Jury finds Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, guilty of murdering the chart-topping artist in the 1996 shooting.
Former gang leader found guilty of Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
A former gang leader accused of orchestrating the killing of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in the United States in 1996 has been convicted of murder for his role in the long-unsolved crime.
A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours on Monday before finding Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a courtroom in the city of Las Vegas.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Suspect in rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing makes first court appearance in US
- list 2 of 4Who killed Tupac? What to know about the trial of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis
- list 3 of 4‘Truth or fiction’: US trial of Tupac Shakur’s accused killer begins
- list 4 of 4Tupac Shakur murder trial begins thirty years after his death
Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13. He told the judge “he plans to appeal this matter”.
Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang in Los Angeles, was accused of ordering the drive-by shooting that killed Shakur on September 7, 1996. Prosecutors said he was enraged because members of Shakur’s entourage had beaten his nephew at a Las Vegas casino hours earlier.
“Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” prosecutor Binu Palal said during closing arguments. “So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together and went hunting for Mr Shakur.”
Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight, was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.
According to prosecutors, Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records cofounder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.
The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has been one of the US’s most notorious cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it and why.
The investigation into Shakur’s murder sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the case was revived when Davis’s memoirs were published in 2019. Davis has repeatedly boasted over the years of involvement in Shakur’s murder, in interviews with law enforcement and media and ultimately in his autobiography, Compton Street Legend.
He has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
Palal, the prosecutor, played clips from Davis’s various alleged confessions as part of his closing arguments.
Michael Sanft, Davis’s defence attorney, characterised his client’s confessions as fiction and lies partly designed to promote his book.
“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact,” Sanft told the jury. “But the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession, that he was there and present at the time of the shooting.”
Sanft said there was no evidence implicating Davis in Shakur’s murder other than his own statements.
In the run-up to the trial, Davis’s lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008.
Shakur, who was 25 when he was killed, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting US East Coast rappers against West Coast artists.
Known for hits including “California Love” and “All Eyez on Me”, Shakur – the son of a Black Panther – was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but became the epitome of California hip-hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.

Oil prices jump as US, Iranian attacks stoke fears of escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Oil prices jump as US, Iranian attacks stoke fears of escalation
Brent crude tops $92 a barrel following first strikes between Washington and Tehran in over a month.
Oil prices have jumped amid fears of escalation in the Middle East following the first exchanges of fire between the United States and Iran in more than a month over the weekend.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 2 percent on Tuesday to top $92 a barrel, extending a more than 2.5 percent gain from the previous day.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4African NGOs demand probe into six bodies found in Guinea mass grave
- list 2 of 4New York police kill knife-wielding woman in Times Square
- list 3 of 4Toxic haze from Indonesian forest fires chokes Malaysian Borneo
- list 4 of 4US brings back Russia’s finance minister to G20 talks, angering Europe
Brent scheduled for November delivery stood at $92.31 a barrel as of 08:45 GMT, up from just over $88 a barrel when markets closed on Monday.
The latest rise came amid renewed tensions in the Middle East following US strikes on Iran’s Larak Island and Iranian attacks on two bases used by US forces in Jordan.
In a television interview on Monday, US President Donald Trump pledged to respond to Tehran’s strikes on the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan.
“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a monitoring centre operated by the British Royal Navy, reported late on Monday that a tanker was struck by three unknown projectiles while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian forces have carried out numerous attacks on commercial shipping.
No casualties were reported in the attack, and no government or group has claimed responsibility.
Oil prices have been volatile since a 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran expired in mid-August, denting hopes of a return to pre-war levels of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for about one-fifth of global oil supplies in peacetime.
After peaking at nearly $94.40 a barrel on August 21, Brent has been trading in the range of $86-$91 since the truce between the sides lapsed without an extension or permanent peace deal.
“Hopes of a near-term deal to open the strait have faded as the conflict appears back on an escalatory trajectory in the wake of recent attacks,” Saul Kavonic, head of energy research at MST Financial, told Al Jazeera.
“The oil market is increasingly realising we may be in for a protracted ‘no war, no peace’ situation, with only partial volumes flowing through the strait, that could last well into 2027,” Kavonic said.
Traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which saw roughly 130 daily transits before the war, remains heavily constrained, with many vessels sailing “dark” with their Automatic Identification System turned off to lessen the threat of Iranian drones and missiles or interception by the US Navy.
The strait saw 107 transits from August 24 to August 30, down from 121 crossings the prior week, according to ship monitoring platform MarineTraffic.
Tony Sycamore, a senior market analyst at IG Markets, said oil prices could ease in spite of the latest flare-up in violence if “dark” shipments tick up again in the strait.
“I think after the latest skirmish, and the risk of further exchanges of fire, the path of least resistance for oil is higher in the short term,” Sycamore told Al Jazeera.
“However, if this flare-up were to fade by the weekend and those dark-ship and ship-to-ship transfers resume, you would expect this week’s geopolitical premium to get stripped out pretty quickly,” Sycamore said.
“Overall, what we are dealing with is a day-to-day proposition.”

Four members of Syria’s internal security forces were wounded on Monday while confronting attacks by “outlaw groups” in rural Sweida, southern Syria, state media reported.
Alikhbaria TV reported that the security forces were targeted near the villages of Al-Mansoura, Walgha, and Tall Hadid, with four personnel sustaining injuries.
The security forces also inflicted direct casualties on the attackers, the broadcaster said without providing a figure.
It added that the groups targeted Al-Mansoura with a drone.
No further details were immediately available on the condition of the wounded security personnel.
A ceasefire has been in place in Sweida since July 2025 following clashes between Bedouin tribes and Druze militias that left hundreds dead and wounded.
Groups affiliated with Hikmat al Hijri, a controversial Druze leader, have repeatedly violated the deal by targeting military positions, while the Syrian government has maintained the arrangement and facilitated evacuations and humanitarian aid deliveries.
Al-Hijri’s positions and calls for Israeli intervention have drawn widespread controversy amid government efforts to consolidate control and preserve Syria’s territorial unity.
Since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, Syrian authorities have sought to restore security across the country, while some armed groups have continued to operate independently. Damascus has said it will not allow a return to lawlessness and is determined to extend state authority nationwide.

Russia attacks Ukraine with different missiles and 218 drones: 199 aerial assets destroyed
Russia attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles, Zircon anti-ship missiles, Kalibr cruise missiles, Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles, S8000 Banderol loitering munitions and 218 drones of various types on the night of 31 August-1 September. Strikes have been recorded at 28 locations.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Quote: "Early reports indicated that as of 08:30, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 199 aerial assets:
- 5 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles
- 2 S8000 Banderol missiles
- 5 Kalibr cruise missiles
- 187 Shahed, Gerbera and other types of drones
Details: Hits by missiles and attack drones have been recorded at 28 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at 10 locations.
Some Russian missiles also failed to reach their targets, and information about them is being confirmed.
Ukraine's defence forces have managed to destroy or jam 199 Russian aerial assets, but the attack is still ongoing. More than 10 Russian drones remain in Ukrainian airspace.
Odesa and Kyiv oblasts have been the main targets of the attack.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces.
Overall, starting at 18:00 on 31 August, Russia attacked Ukraine:
- with Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles and Zircon anti-ship missiles launched from Russia's Bryansk, Kursk, Voronezh and Rostov oblasts
- with sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from Novorossiysk
- with Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles launched from airspace over the Black Sea
- with S8000 Banderol loitering munitions launched from Bryansk Oblast and over the Sea of Azov
- with 218 Shahed attack drones (around one-third of them jet-powered) and Parodiya decoy UAVs launched from the Russian cities of Kursk, Millerovo, Oryol and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea

It's the sixth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Ukraine's capital. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
Brussels floats fresh plans to increase sanctions against Russia
Beyond ramping up intelligence sharing and police cooperation, the EU is trying to raise the cost of the war for the Kremlin by bolstering support for Ukraine and hitting Moscow with sanctions.
Brussels has floated fresh plans to add 1,600 more firms and individuals to its already long list of Russians sanctioned over the war.
Meanwhile discussion has resurfaced on whether the bloc should tap some 200 billion euros ($235 billion) of frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
A proposal to use the funds failed last year after opposition from Belgium, where the bulk of the assets are held, and the EU came up with a 90 billion euro loan for Kyiv off its own back. But there is already a sense that the money might not last the two years it was intended for and the EU may need to find a way sooner or later to use the immobilised Russian funds.
"As each day passes, the cost of the war is rising," the top diplomats of the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden wrote in a letter last week.

Over the course of the month of August, Russia launched more than 2,800 jet-propelled drones at Ukraine, a type of drone that is harder to shoot down.

Autumn will begin with contrasting weather - meteorologist gives forecast

Autumn will begin with contrasting weather - meteorologist gives forecast
Kyiv • UNN
Rain, thunderstorms and wind are expected in western Ukraine, while the south and east will remain dry and sunny. Up to +28° in Kyiv.
In Ukraine, on September 1, the weather in the west will be determined by an atmospheric front, bringing rain, while part of the country will still be under the influence of high atmospheric pressure, sunny and dry weather, forecaster Natalka Didenko said on social media, reports UNN.
Details
"In the western regions of Ukraine tomorrow, September 1, a cold atmospheric front will bring rain and, in some places, even thunderstorms, as well as gusty winds. This rain will reach the central region of Vinnytsia, as well as the northern regions of Zhytomyr and Kyiv. In the rest of Ukraine — namely Chernihiv and Sumy regions, most of the central regions, the entire southern part and the eastern regions — there will be high atmospheric pressure, sunshine and dry weather," Didenko said.
According to her forecast, air temperatures will be divided between the Left Bank and the Right Bank.
In the western regions, as well as Zhytomyr region, Vinnytsia region, and parts of Kyiv and Chernihiv regions, temperatures of +23°...+26° are expected, while in the rest of the country it will still be a summery +25°...+29°; with more intense sunshine, temperatures could even reach +30°. However, this is more likely to apply to the eastern regions and the southern part of the country, as well as Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava regions and Kropyvnytskyi and its surrounding areas.
Weather in Kyiv
According to the forecast, on September 1, air temperatures will be +26°...+28°. "In the morning, it will be practically perfect for wearing a vyshyvanka with long sleeves, that is, around +21°...+24°," Didenko noted.
"Rain in Kyiv is possible both in the morning and during the day, but, to be honest, it will most likely be just a few drops to moisten the excessively dry air, smoky after these unbearable fires. I think the rain will come in handy, but I repeat — nothing significant is expected," the forecaster wrote.
"From the perspective of the coming days, September 1 in Kyiv is expected to be the warmest day, that is, the day with the highest air temperature.
Because already on September 2, 3 and 4, and even more so on September 5, 6 and 7, it will be cooler," she added.

A walking tour of Andalucía’s historic white villages: ‘Nightingales serenade us as we wind along lush river valleys’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

‘The wind is in from Africa / Last night I couldn’t sleep.” Joni Mitchell has ear-wormed her way into my head as my wife and I step out from Zahara de la Sierra into the mountains of Sierra de Grazalema natural park. The Africa bit probably comes from yesterday’s visit to Zahara’s castle museum. Here, high above the tiled terracotta mosaic of village rooftops, we learned how the recapture of this picturesque hill town was a turning point in the Reconquista – the military campaign of the 1400s that saw the Catholics retake southern Spain after seven centuries of Moorish control. As for sleep deprivation, I may just have overdone it on last night’s tapas.
Either way, Africa feels present as we tramp through the countryside of Andalucía, if only in the wildlife. The painted lady butterflies drifting over the flower-spangled verges, the turtle doves purring from the olive groves and the booted eagle drifting overhead: all are summer visitors recently blown in from the great continent to our south.
It’s day two of our White Villages of the Ronda Mountains walking tour, a self-guided seven-day route from On Foot Holidays that explores this alluring corner of southern Spain. We arrived yesterday by bus from Málaga, winding up through the mountains until the whitewashed dwellings of Zahara appeared like teeth in the hillside ahead. This was the first of the week’s four pueblos blancos, all tucked picturesquely into the natural park’s rugged 51,695 hectares (127,740 acres) of limestone peaks and serpentine river valleys.
I’ve walked with On Foot before, so the routine is familiar: water bottles and packed lunches stashed in daypacks, laminated map around neck on lanyard and route app open on phone (belt-and-braces navigation). Best of all, our luggage is already wending its way by taxi to the next destination.
The conditions couldn’t be more perfect. The hillsides burst with blossom and birdsong, the May temperature is a pleasant mid-20s (midsummer out here would be punishing), and the peaks stand proud against the clear blue sky. It’s hard to believe February brought such heavy rains that much of our route was then impassable – and some areas of the park were affected by wildfires later in the summer.
But each month here has its own character. September/October – also prime walking season – sees the chestnuts and cork oak forests turn russet and gold, and the spring irises and orchids replaced by the post-summer bloom of wild asparagus and autumn crocus. Overhead, those booted eagles will be massing for their return journey – along with bee-eaters, honey buzzards and other winged voyagers – back to Africa.
Today’s hike takes us south towards Grazalema: pueblo blanco number two. We skirt a reservoir then wind along a lush river valley, nightingales serenading us from the oleander thickets, and by late morning are rising into the mountains, the vista gaining grandeur as we gain height.
Lunch is in a high meadow, where we unwrap our bocadillos while bees buzz and butterflies busy themselves among the blooms. Afternoon brings a long uphill slog, then finally a cool descent through shady pines to sleepy Grazalema. Another 11 miles (18km) under our belts.
We stay two nights in Grazalema at the Hotel la Mejorana, meeting wild ibex on a mountain circuit high above town, and eating at the cosy Cádiz el Chico restaurant, where a menu featuring partridge and wild boar (though, thankfully, not ibex) reflects the region’s hunting traditions. At night, the cobbled streets are quiet beneath a canopy of stars.
Benaoján, the third of our pueblos blancos, lies about 16 miles to the south-east. We exit Grazalema early in the morning, beneath the Los Peñascos mirador. Roosting griffon vultures line the cliffs like pterodactyls, warming up in the morning sun before, one at a time, flapping off on table-top wings for another day combing the plains.
Our route leads down through the oak woods before rising again into the hills. Here we enter a limestone wonderland, the karst formations sculpted by wind and rain into Henry Moore-like statues. Bee-eaters dart overhead, their liquid chirrups audible long before we lay eyes on them. A passing walker greets us with a cheery “Buen camino!” He’s returning with his father to see the farmhouse where they grew up. We find Dad sitting on a nearby rock, devouring an empanada. They’re the only other walkers we meet all day.
Our hideaway at Benaoján is the Molino del Santo hotel, where we dine beside a chuckling stream on a terrace crowded with potted geraniums. From here, it takes us two hours to hike to the Cueva de la Pileta, an immense cave system discovered in 1905 when a local farmer spotted bats streaming from a fissure in the hillside.
Local guide Ainhoa Bullón leads us down cool, narrow passages into measureless caverns, her thin torch beam illuminating flowstone formations as enormous and elaborate as a Gaudí cathedral – formed, she explains, by the drip-drip of lime at the rate of 1cm every 400 years. The farthest recesses hold exquisite shamanic rock art, some more than 25,000 years old. Ainhoa overflows with information, talking us through the cave’s successive ages of antiquity, from Neanderthal to Neolithic. Most important, she delivers us safely back to the blazing sunshine outside.
Our week ends at Ronda, perched atop the precipitous El Tajo gorge. The celebrated clifftop town seems to beckon us onward like some mythical sky citadel as we tramp our final kilometres towards it. Below the cliffs, we find ourselves back in tourist land, sharing the steep climb to the top with a gaggle of selfie-snapping day trippers.
We make it, slumping at the first available cafe table to lever off boots, fold away the map and order a celebratory cold cerveza. Tomorrow, we catch our bus back to Málaga. For now, a final night lies ahead, with a stirring panorama from our room at the Parador de Ronda and the promise of a slap-up meal down in the old town. Our beers arrive, and any lingering strains of Joni are soon lost to a busker’s volley of flamenco guitar.
The trip was provided by On Foot Holidays. It costs from £985pp for a seven-night self-guided route in Grazalema natural park, ending in Ronda; five-, six- and eight-night routes also available. The walking season is February-May and September-December (April, May, September and October being optimum)

How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily | Jeremiah A Carew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

A year has passed since I and thousands of colleagues lost our jobs at USAID. Asking myself “Why us?” I have come to the conclusion that the American public had very little idea of what we were doing and why.
Doge, the “department of government efficiency”, began its work in January 2025, with USAID as its first target, in a reckless campaign that even Elon Musk has said he would not repeat. At that moment of chaos, Americans lacked the knowledge that could contradict the false narrative presented by Musk, who called the agency a “criminal organisation” and “a viper’s nest of radical left-marxists who hate America”.
But what if Doge had eliminated Nasa, not USAID? Such a scenario seems highly implausible. Despite the rise of private space companies, Nasa remains an icon of national prestige, with broad bipartisan congressional support. How many kids want to be astronauts when they grow up? I sure did. And that’s because Nasa has spent decades carefully communicating its results and cultivating its image with the public.
In contrast, USAID is not well known or understood. One expert on USAID’s brand noted that the agency’s handclasp emblem and the tagline “from the American people” were “well known in the developing world, even if not well known in Washington”. How much worse is that brand recognition in middle America?
Misunderstandings around foreign aid abound. In March 2025, a Kaiser Family Foundation survey reported: “Nearly nine in 10 (86%) adults overestimate the share of the federal budget spent on foreign aid, saying on average that the US spends about a quarter (26%) of its budget on foreign aid.” In fact, about 1% of the federal budget goes on foreign aid.
Unfortunately, that lack of recognition and those gross misunderstandings were key factors in USAID’s elimination. It may never be resurrected, but the question remains important: what could future foreign assistance learn from Nasa’s approach to public communications, to ensure broad public understanding and support?
Without a doubt, stories were there to be told. In Colombia, where I was deputy director of the largest USAID mission in the hemisphere from 2021 to 2025, we contributed to solving major regional challenges. We helped tens of thousands of Venezuelans take advantage of generous Colombian migration policies by processing legal residency cards, training them for jobs and establishing healthcare access. That meant they could stay in Colombia legally, rather than add to the thousands of migrants trying to enter the US.
We guaranteed hundreds of millions of dollars in loans Colombian banks made to new businesses. These businesses promoted tropical forest products such as açaí to keep the Amazon’s trees standing. Other loans helped poor farmers build businesses with legal crops instead of coca, which is turned into cocaine, causing addiction and death in the US and Europe. These loan-guarantee programmes cost the US government pennies on the dollar to reduce risk so that Colombian banks would extend their loans to new, unfamiliar businesses.
And after Colombia’s government successfully negotiated a historic peace accord in 2016, ending 50 years of civil conflict, USAID was the largest donor to help them implement it. Among many things, that meant helping prosecutors gather testimony from thousands of victims of violence so the truth could be told and justice done.
When fighters turned in their guns to lead peaceful lives, efforts such as ours helped Colombians achieve some form of reconciliation and turn the page.
These are not simple stories to tell. As these examples illustrate, real development work is not handing out goodies for a photo op. It is making strategic nudges to a country’s own efforts to do the things that solve global challenges – illegal migration, climate breakdown, illegal drugs and yes, world peace – while reflecting its national interest.
Telling USAID’s story to the American public accurately – describing projects far from home, in complex and unfamiliar foreign contexts – is challenging.
Yet faced with its own challenges in communicating technically complex scientific work performed thousands of miles from home, Nasa succeeded where USAID failed. The 2014 book Marketing the Moon, by David Meerman Scott and Richard Jurek, focuses on the Apollo programme, when 94% of American televisions were tuned to the first lunar landing. They argue that “without strong public support abetted by high-profile, enthusiastic public relations, the entire achievement and its funding would have been unthinkable”.
Echoes of these strategies are still seen, and Nasa still excels in communicating with the public. There are three ways it does this:
Helping voters understand 
  Rather than use woolly phrases such as “capacity building” and “democracy strengthening”, as we did at USAID, Nasa goes to great efforts to help viewers grasp what it is doing. Computer visualisations and animations show orbits and flight paths. Saying a Mars rover is “about the size of a small SUV” explains in everyday terms what its scientists have built. The media are willing allies to show these graphics and allow Nasa spokespeople to explain the mission and its impact.
Telling stories that link to the US’s highest national aspirations 
 In the Apollo programme, astronauts became superheroes, signing exclusive agreements with Life magazine to profile them. On unmanned missions, Nasa has linked its efforts to timeless questions of science: was there water on Mars, for instance, and did it support life? As its website says: “For more than 65 years, Nasa has made the seemingly impossible, possible.” Nasa has connected its work to national pride, reminding Americans of its cutting-edge science, world-class innovative tech and heroic astronauts.
Talking about positive side-effects 
 Nasa is highly vocal about how technology developed for space missions has been repurposed for everyday use and benefited our lives, from memory foam to infrared ear thermometers to cordless tools. Given the prestige associated with Nasa, there is even a small cottage industry of inventions that are falsely attributed to the space programme, such as lasers, Velcro and Teflon.
Decades of effective PR and brand recognition may not have been enough to overcome the onslaught of misinformation that USAID faced in 2025. Its international focus – on cultures and contexts completely unfamiliar to Americans – made it vulnerable. The sheer quantity of projects made it easy to find some that would appear indefensible, so when the attacks did come, the gas tank of “brand equity” was nearly empty and the public outcry was muted, with many only just learning of the agency’s existence. USAID was shuttered with startling speed.
When an information vacuum allows Americans to overestimate how much of the federal budget goes to foreign assistance, they fail to see it for the bargain it truly is for our nation. Americans spend several times more on pet food and treats than the government did on USAID. What USAID spent on some aid programmes in a year was the equivalent of a few dozen Patriot missiles.
In short, as the US aspires to be a great nation – generous, admired and strategic in solving global challenges – the work USAID did seems an absolute bargain. As we reimagine what foreign assistance looks like, let’s be more like Nasa, communicating that value and making Americans proud.
Jeremiah A Carew was a senior Foreign Service Officer for USAID; his final tour was as deputy mission director of USAID/Colombia from 2021 until the mission’s closing in 2025.

My partner packed up and disappeared with his children while I was out with friends. I was left having to foot all our bills, including rent, which has made me financially stressed.
We had a family plan with O2 which meant family phones were all registered to my account. When my partner left, he stopped paying his share of the monthly phone bill, so I set about trying to remove his, and his children’s, phones from the account. O2 explained he would need to join a conference call with me and O2 to agree the transfer of the numbers in question.
Getting my ex to engage with this involved support from a mutual friend; then he claimed he could not join the conference calls. O2 had only one suggestion: that he and I meet in person for the call.
My ex is an emotionally aggressive and manipulative man. He does not know where I now live, and I want to keep it that way, so I met him in a busy park, and we spent an hour on the phone together with O2. His children’s numbers successfully transferred. His number did not. O2 said it would keep working on it and ended the call.
Two weeks on, nothing has happened. O2 insists I either make another joint call with my ex, or pay his outstanding bills and cancel his phone plan.
I’ve explained about my financial situation and concerns about meeting up with him.
I discovered an O2 form allowing customers to flag up difficult family situations and filled it out but was told I did not qualify. I have now been sent a £164 early termination fee for the children’s numbers that were removed from the plan.
My ex is deliberately manipulating this situation. I am baffled that O2 does not have a better process for women during relationship breakdown as forced meet ups could be really risky in some cases.
Name and address withheld
I felt rage when I read of your plight. You had, by then, spent four weeks trying to get O2 to understand the potential risks of meeting your ex and the financial hardship his departure caused. Its response that you meet up, or pay up, was almost certainly in breach of the regulatory duty of care to vulnerable customers telecoms companies are obliged to fulfil.
When I pointed this out, O2 managed, within hours, what it had failed to do in weeks, and called you. It admitted you had been led on a debilitating wild goose chase.
Instead of subjecting you to a painful encounter in a public park, it should have served a disconnection notice giving him seven days to transfer the numbers to a new account. It duly did after a push from its press office, and cancelled the £164 charge. It has offered you £200 in compensation but you, understandably, feel this does not reflect the anguish and expense the blunders caused you.
O2 says: “We have a range of policies to protect and support customers who have been victims of domestic abuse, ensuring they can safely disconnect unwanted numbers without having to meet an ex-partner in person. This existing support was not accurately offered, and we apologise for the experience she had, and the time taken to resolve her issue.”

Solar cuts ‘at least £400 from bills in even the cloudiest British areas’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:00:46 UTC
15:00:46 KST

Households in Great Britain’s cloudiest regions could still save more than £400 a year on their energy bills by installing rooftop solar panels, research has found.
Rising wholesale energy prices mean the potential savings from a home solar panel system have climbed in recent years, as the cost of installation has continued to fall, leading to increased demand.
An analysis carried out for the Guardian has found that in areas with the fewest sunny days, solar panels could bring annual savings of about £450 a year on the average household electricity bill. In areas with the brightest skies, this figure could climb to more than £600.
The findings, provided by the UK solar firm Recharge Renewable, show that households in southern Scotland could save on average £440 a year, based on the estimated solar generation in Glasgow over a year, while homes in the north-west of England could save £463, based on the generation likely in Manchester.
In southern England, where brighter weather means more solar generation, savings on bills could climb to between £571 and £618 a year for households in Brighton and Southampton, respectively, according to the figures.
The potential savings have increased in recent years as conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East have compounded Britain’s rising electricity prices, leading to a boom in rooftop solar installations. Large-scale installations have also climbed under the Labour government, which has set a target to triple the UK’s solar farms by 2030.
A Guardian analysis of the government’s official figures revealed there were more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, the year the UK built its first large-scale solar farm, in Cornwall.
Most of the new solar panels recorded are on household rooftops, with these smaller solar installations making up slightly less than a third of the country’s total solar power capacity.
The increase in capacity allowed solar power to supply 14.4% of Great Britain’s electricity in July, more than in any previous month, after some parts of the UK recorded almost twice the average sunshine hours for the time of year. The rise was due to the summer heatwaves, made more severe by the climate crisis, which has triggered drought and record temperatures across Europe.
Recharge Renewable, a Somerset-based solar provider, warned that households hoping to save on their energy bills from solar panels need to pay attention to the set-up of each rooftop system as well as the regional potential.
“Even in cloudier parts of Britain, a typical 4kW system can still be worth around £450 a year in electricity used at home under the current price cap,” a spokesperson said.
“The catch is that this is the value of the units displaced, not a finished bill, and a north-facing or shaded roof will not match a modelled south-facing array. Households should compare any regional headline with their own annual use, then look at whether a battery or more daytime demand would keep more of that generation on site.”
The company’s analysis used the typical electricity output from a standard, south-facing 4kW rooftop solar system, and data for the average energy use of the typical household. These figures were then adjusted for each of Great Britain’s 14 regions, using satellite imagery to measure the different levels of annual sunshine across big cities and accounting for varying electricity rates.
The calculations do not include the use of a battery and assume that each household uses only 50% of the electricity generated over a year. This means that bill payers who use more solar power while working from home, for example, or by timing appliances to run during daylight hours, could make even greater savings.
However, a typical 4kW solar system costs about £7,000 after the government removed VAT for solar upgrades. This puts the upfront cost out of reach of many families and has prompted calls for the government to step in to help make rooftop solar more affordable for people on lower incomes.
Plug-in solar panels went on sale in the UK for the first time last week, allowing households unable to use rooftop set-ups to generate power from their balconies.

‘Alarm bells were going off’: parents tell of ordeal at Send school closed down after abuse allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:00:46 UTC
15:00:46 KST

Annette and Kevin Maxwell were nervous about sending their son Jonah to a residential home for children with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Jonah has severe autism – he is non-verbal, has epilepsy and behavioural problems and needs round-the-clock care.
“It was a huge decision, but we almost had no choice because with Jonah at home, you can’t work and we had two other children to think about. He’s beautiful, but he is very, very complicated,” said Annette. “Outsourcing parenting is just foreign to us and it’s horrible, but we didn’t have another option.”
When he first arrived at St Christopher’s in Bristol, Jonah was thriving, receiving different therapies and doing activities such as horse riding. Then, in 2016, the charity that ran the home collapsed and the centre was acquired by the Aurora Group, which runs more than 30 Send schools and is owned by Octopus, an investment management and real estate company.
The Maxwells, who live in Bath, noticed a change almost immediately. They said the food quality went downhill, there were plans – later suspended – for an overnight nursing position to be cut and they began to have concerns about Jonah’s wellbeing. Whenever he came home to visit he seemed very tired.
“Alarm bells were going off. But every time we spoke to management and staff, they would always reassure us that everything was OK,” said Annette.
At this point, the Aurora Group was being paid £292,000 a year by their local authority to care for Jonah. The company was expanding rapidly by acquiring several established providers to become one of the UK’s largest specialist education and care operators.
Then, in 2019, it was announced that St Christopher’s was being closed down by Ofsted after serious allegations of child cruelty came to light. Vulnerable children had to move out at short notice, their belongings hastily packed into black bin bags. They were sent across the country to new placements.
The police began an investigation into alleged child cruelty and safeguarding concerns and this concluded after two years without any criminal charges being brought.
The Maxwells were told by police there had been allegations involving Jonah. In one incident, he was said to have been roughly grabbed and shoved into his room by a staff member. They also found out a carer had allegedly been waking him up every two hours through the night to go to the toilet to avoid having to clean soiled sheets, which police said could be classified as child cruelty.
“I just wish I’d been more pushy at the time and tried harder to get to the bottom of things. I really, really regret that I didn’t do more,” said Annette.
Police later confirmed they were unable to interview the directors of the Aurora Group, who parents believed had questions to answer over cost-cutting that may have contributed to alleged abuse. Child cruelty legislation applies only to those who directly commit an alleged offence.
St Christopher’s was classified as a school, not a care provider, meaning it could not be investigated under legislation that might implicate both a corporation and individuals.
Kevin said: “Our kids have become a moneymaking tool for these companies, and they squeeze it, because they know that, ultimately, they can walk away. There has to be better accountability.”
The couple pursued civil action against Aurora, alleging a breach of Jonah’s human rights. The company agreed to pay £18,600 without admission of any guilt.
The Maxwells are pushing for stricter laws to ensure private Send providers face the same levels of accountability and transparency as other schools.
As part of sweeping Send reforms announced earlier this year, the government promised to “crack down” on private companies running schools, imposing fee caps and minimum standards.
Those in the sector said they had been raising the alarm for years and urged the government to create more state schools in the Send sector to wrest back control from private companies, which charge significantly more.
Darren Northcott, the national officer for education at the NASUWT teaching union, said: “There is a big problem where public money which should be being spent on children, young people and the staff working with them is leaking out of the system in the form of profits and surpluses. That’s not acceptable.”
He said many Send schools, in the state and private sector, had become incredibly challenging places to work because of a lack of staffing or resources to deal with children with complex needs. He said staff were increasingly expected to accept violence from children as “part of the job” and in some cases “the level of care and investment in staff falls short of would reasonably be expected”.
Hayley Harding of the Let Us Learn Too campaign said many parents were frustrated by the lack of Send places in state schools, leaving private providers as the only option for many. “There’s a huge issue with local authority capacity and lack of planning – for so many years they have been firefighting, rather than actually planning for how many children need this,” she said.
“Nobody wants people making profit out of our children. But we want them to be educated, and that’s often the only option available.”
A spokesperson for the Aurora Group said it was the only B Corp accredited provider in the sector. B Corp certification is a private credential for for-profit companies that prove high social and environmental standards through independent evaluation. Aurora also said 96% of its services were rated by Ofsted as good or outstanding.
The spokesperson added: “St Christopher’s was in serious difficulties under different ownership and under close Ofsted scrutiny when we responded to a campaign to keep the school open. We invested substantially in improving staffing, facilities and overall provision.
“We regret that we were ultimately unable to overcome the school’s challenges, and we remain saddened by the circumstances surrounding its eventual closure in 2019. We did all that we could at the time to support the Maxwell family and wish them well.
“The police thoroughly investigated the allegations and agree that we did all we could to support their inquiries. Police took no further action.”
The spokesperson said all the Aurora Group’s profits were reinvested in establishing new schools in partnership with local authorities, bringing “relief to families and making it far easier for children to go to school nearer to home”.

German-French rover set for October launch on journey to Mars moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:59:16 UTC
14:59:16 KST

By Annett Stein, dpa.
Berlin (dpa) – A Japanese space probe carrying a German-French rover is set to begin its journey to Mars in October, with the rover eventually due to become the first to explore the surface of one of the planet’s moons.
Japan’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is currently scheduled to launch on October 19, the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) said on Monday, citing plans by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency.
The launch window runs until November 7.
As part of the mission, the German-French rover Idefix is due to land on the Martian moon Phobos in 2029. A return capsule is then to bring samples from Phobos back to Earth in 2031 – the first samples ever returned from the Martian system.
Idefix is expected to explore the moon’s surface for around 100 days.
“Our rover Idefix and the MMX spacecraft of our Japanese partners will begin their journey to the Martian system as one unit,” DLR project manager Markus Grebenstein and Julien Baroukh, project manager at French space agency CNES, said in a joint statement.
Their paths will separate only once they reach Phobos. “There, Idefix will make history – as the first rover ever to leave tracks on a Martian moon.”
The rover takes its name from Idefix, the small white dog in the French “Asterix” comics, who is known as Dogmatix in English.
Rover the size of a drinks crate
One of Idefix’s distinctive features is its compact design. The rover is about the size of a drinks crate and weighs around 25 kilograms, but still contains essentially all the components of a fully fledged scientific rover, according to the DLR.
Because of its low weight and Phobos’ weak gravity, Idefix will be able to land directly on the moon without the assistance of a landing vehicle.
The MMX probe is expected to reach Mars in 2027 after a journey of around a year and enter orbit around the planet. In 2029, the spacecraft is due to release Idefix from a height of about 40 metres above Phobos, allowing it to free-fall to the surface.
Once it has landed, the rover will right itself autonomously before beginning its mission.
Phobos and Deimos are the only moons in the inner solar system apart from Earth’s moon. Both are much smaller than Earth’s moon and are irregularly shaped rather than spherical. Phobos measures just under 27 kilometres at its widest point, while Deimos is around 15 kilometres across.
Temperatures on Phobos range from around minus 170 degrees Celsius to 70 degrees Celsius.
The mission is intended to help scientists determine whether Phobos and Deimos are captured asteroids or were formed from debris thrown into space by a massive impact on Mars.
Source: dpa.com

14,700 children start 1st grade in Estonia
Approximately 160,000 students will attend general education schools this year. Minister of Education and Research Kristina Kallas wished students curiosity and a little rebelliousness in their thinking.
More than 26,000 students will begin vocational education this year. There are more than 47,000 university students this year.
An estimated 45,700 students will attend Tallinn's municipal general education schools in the new academic year. Around 3,600 children will start first grade this year. Exact student numbers will be available by September 10, once schools have entered their data into the Estonian Education Information System (EHIS).
Tallinn has 60 municipal schools and one vocational school.
Fewer than 17,000 children will attend Tallinn's municipal kindergartens in the 2026-2027 academic year. As of September 1, Tallinn has 115 kindergartens, with additional kindergarten groups operating at Tallinn Laagna Kindergarten-Basic School and Tallinn Helen School.
This year, the School Peace title will go to Rapla County for the first time, with Märjamaa Municipality selected as the titleholder. School Peace brings together the communities of six educational institutions in Märjamaa Municipality around the shared goal of keeping schools friendly, safe and caring places.
Minister: A little mischief in thinking
Minister of Education and Research Kristina Kallas said in her message marking the start of the academic year that September 1 is one of the few days of the year when people across almost all of Estonia seem to make a fresh start.
"Some are going to school for the first time, others for the last. Some are standing in front of a classroom as a teacher for the first time. And some parents discover in the very first week that their knowledge of math is not quite as fresh as they thought."
She noted that we live in a time when artificial intelligence can write an essay, solve an equation and provide an answer to almost any question in seconds. This can make it tempting to ask: Why bother learning at all?
"But perhaps the right question is actually the opposite: If answers become cheap, what becomes valuable? Independent thinking. The ability to recognize when a machine is wrong. Creativity. The ability to engage deeply. Understanding other people. And the courage to say: 'I don't know yet, but I want to know.' These things cannot be downloaded with a single click."
Kallas wished students curiosity and a little rebelliousness in their thinking this academic year.
"Don't always settle for the first answer. To teachers, I wish creativity and resilience. Sometimes, after all, the best learning happens precisely when a lesson takes a slightly different direction than planned."
--

Supreme Court lets Trump build White House ballroom as lawsuit continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:58:00 UTC
14:58:00 KST

The Supreme Court, in a split decision Monday, allowed President Donald Trump to continue construction of his controversial White House ballroom as legal challenges to the project play out.
A five-justice majority of the court said the plaintiff challenging the ballroom, the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States, likely lacks legal standing to sue to block the roughly $400 million project.
The majority's unsigned order does not address whether Trump has the legal authority to build the ballroom without approval by Congress, which remains an open question as the Trust's lawsuit continues.
The order said a declaration by a member of the Trust, Alison Hoagland, that having to view the finished ballroom during her periodic visits to the neighborhood would cause her "injuries," was likely insufficient basis for standing.
"Mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury under Article III" of the U.S. Constitution, the order said. "Perhaps nearly any government action or project offends someone's sensibilities."
Chief Justice John Roberts and the court's three liberal members dissented from the order.
"The President ordered the demolition of the East Wing of the White House to make way for a new, privately funded state ballroom in its place," the dissent said. "Construction of the ballroom has proceeded apace for the better part of a year."
"That construction is likely unlawful."
Last week, Roberts issued a temporary stay of a U.S. District Court judge's order, which a federal appeals court affirmed, that had blocked the construction of the ballroom while the National Trust's lawsuit continued.
The chief justice's action gave the full Supreme Court time to consider whether there should be a longer stay as the litigation proceeded.
In his dissent Monday, Roberts wrote that Congress has explicitly barred the construction of any building on federal properties without Congress' "express authority."
"The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds — President's Park — in the District of Columbia," Roberts wrote. "Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling 'express authority' for the Executive's construction of it."
The chief justice also took aim at the majority's finding that Hoagland was unlikely to have legal standing to challenge the ballroom's construction.
"The White House is an iconic American building whose symbolism and history are wrapped up in its architecture," Roberts wrote.
"A historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys," he wrote.
Trump, in a Truth Social post, praised the ruling in his favor.
"We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.," Trump wrote. "When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of."
"The Project, despite the baseless lawsuit brought by the so-called National Trust for Historic Preservation of the United States, which is not in any way affiliated with the United States Government, is under budget and ahead of schedule," Trump said.
Brent Leggs, CEO of the National Trust, in a statement said, "We are deeply disappointed in the Supreme Court's ruling today and respectfully disagree with the majority's opinion on standing. It is noteworthy that the majority did not weigh in on whether the ballroom project was in fact legal.
"We are pleased with [Roberts'] strong dissent, which reiterated what we have maintained from the start of our case — that construction of the White House ballroom is unlawful," Leggs said. "In addition, this is not the final decision on the merits of our case and does not resolve our fundamental argument—that each President is a temporary steward of the People's House and does not have the unilateral authority to demolish and redesign it without the approval of Congress."

In milestone, solar power capacity edges out coal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:51:50 UTC
14:51:50 KST

China's installed photovoltaic power capacity surpassed coal-fired power capacity for the first time, making solar the country's largest power source by installed capacity, the National Energy Administration said on Tuesday.
   
Installed solar power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts at the end of July, edging past coal-fired power capacity of 1.285 billion kilowatts.
"This marks a milestone in China's green and low-carbon energy transition," said Liu Zhiqiang, an expert from the China Electricity Council, adding that the country's new power system, with new energy as the mainstay, is taking shape at an accelerated pace.
By the end of July, solar power accounted for more than 30 percent of China's total installed power generation capacity. 
Measured by newly added capacity, the share rose to more than 40 percent in the first seven months, underscoring the rapid expansion of the sector.
China has built a complete photo voltaic industry chain covering research and development, design and integrated manufacturing. 
Technological advances, including repeated breakthroughs in photovoltaic conversion efficiency, have helped drive continuous upgrades and rapid cost reductions.
China's rapid development of photovoltaic power and other forms of new energy is also making a positive contribution globally.
With the world's largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system, the country supplies more than 80 percent of the photovoltaic modules and 70 percent of the wind power equipment around the world, assisting the green transition in many countries.
In particular, amid uncertainties in global supplies of energy and key raw materials, China's growing new energy capacity helped it meet domestic energy demand while contributing to the stability of global energy markets and supply chains, experts said. (Xinhua)

US teen charged with aiding San Diego mosque shooters share livestream and manifesto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:50:14 UTC
14:50:14 KST

Sarah Santiago, 17, will be charged as an adult, according to a press release issued by prosecutor James O'Neill's office.
A 17-year-old North Carolina girl who recorded a livestream of a shooting that killed three people at a San Diego mosque and then published the attackers’ white-supremacist manifesto has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting, a district attorney said on Monday.
Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O’Neill said at a news conference in Winston-Salem that the girl, identified in court records as Sarah L. Santiago, was arrested last week.
A grand jury indicted her on three counts of murder and one count of conspiracy.
“At this time I can confirm that my client is innocent of all these charges,” Santiago’s attorney, Alan Doorasamy Sr., wrote in an email to the Associated Press news agency.
He said he had not received evidence from law enforcement and did not elaborate on any connection between Santiago and the attackers.
Under North Carolina law, the aiding-and-abetting charges carry the same penalties as if the girl had committed the attack herself, O'Neill said. She is charged as an adult and was being held without bond.
According to the indictment, Santiago agreed prior to the attack that she would record the livestream as the gunmen filmed it, distribute the recording, and release a document written by the attackers. She carried out those tasks, it said.
She's also accused of purchasing a patch bearing a white-supremacist symbol and sending it to one of the gunmen to wear during the attack.
In all, three people watched the initial livestream, O'Neill said. It was not immediately clear if investigators had identified the others, and the indictment did not specify on which platforms the livestream was recorded or shared.
“The individual here, locally, was the person who was recording the livestream," O'Neill said. “She disseminated that information and she published their manifesto.”
Cain Clark, 17, and Caleb Vazquez, 18, stormed the Islamic Centre of San Diego on 18 May before being driven back outside by a security guard who exchanged gunfire with them as he initiated a lockdown, helping to protect 140 children who were just steps away.
The pair killed the guard, Amin Abdullah, and two other men before taking their own lives in a vehicle nearby.
They left behind rambling writings full of vitriol against a wide range of people and cited the shooter who killed 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand in 2019, as one of the models for their violence.
Clark and Vazquez also planned subsequent attacks on two other targets: a Jewish temple and a predominantly Black high school, O'Neill said. He credited the guard and other victims at the mosque with having saved countless lives.
The attackers' writings cited a range of far-right ideological inspirations, including the notion that white people are being replaced by other populations, and detailed their motives and goals.
They included hateful rhetoric toward Jewish people, Muslims and Islam, as well as the LGBTQ+ community, Black people, women, and the political left and right.
They indicated they were trying to accelerate the collapse of society. Vazquez wrote of having “some mental health issues” and being rejected by women.
In a written statement, the Vazquez family said Caleb Vazquez was on the autism spectrum and had grown to resent parts of his identity. The family said they believed that, combined with exposure to hateful rhetoric online, contributed to his radicalisation.

Warriors of Israel rebrands as over 90,000 wounded Israeli veterans need lifelong care, community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:49:05 UTC
14:49:05 KST

After years of war, Israel is facing the largest rehabilitation effort in its history, and Friends of Irgun Nechei Zahal, or Beit Halochem USA, announced on Tuesday that it will be renamed Warriors of Israel after 75 years of experience in providing services for Israel's wounded soldiers.
The organization is the official US branch of Zahal Disabled Veterans Organization (ZVDO), a non-profit organization established after the War of Independence with the goal of rehabilitating and supporting wounded soldiers.
Warriors of Israel stated in a press release that its mission boils down to a promise: "Their sacrifice. Our responsibility, a commitment to stand behind Israel's wounded warriors and their families for every step of the path ahead."
Referring to the organization's choice to change its name, Sam Zussman, Chair of the Board of Warriors of Israel, said, “The name Warriors of Israel reflects the strength and courage of those we stand by. Thousands are beginning a recovery journey that will last a lifetime. Our responsibility is equally enduring: to ensure every wounded warrior can live with dignity, independence, and purpose. That is the promise carried by our new name.”
According to the organization, more than 26,000 soldiers have been wounded since the start of the war on October 7, 2023. ZDVO and Beit Halochem provide rehabilitation and community services to around 80,000 wounded soldiers.
Soldiers who face physical injuries, PTSD, anxiety, depression need support
According to the press release, soldiers have faced "physical injuries, PTSD, anxiety, depression, and other invisible wounds," and the Defense Ministry "estimates that more than 90,000 wounded warriors will require lifelong rehabilitation and support."
Over the past 10 years, over 30,000 American supporters have contributed to Warriors of Israel with resources to meet the quickly growing needs of Israel's wounded soldiers and their families.
Beit Halochem hosts five rehabilitation centers across Israel, where "Wounded warriors regain strength and independence through physical rehabilitation, specialized mental health care, adaptive sports, education and career development, peer connection, and programs that support their spouses and children."
More than rehabilitation: Community
The press release contends that Beit Halochem offers much more than rehabilitation. It offers a community for people wounded in war to progress in life alongside people who share a journey and understand one another's struggles.
"Those beginning rehabilitation today draw strength, guidance, and mentorship from those who have walked the same path for decades," the statement reads.
“Today’s wounded warriors are younger than ever before, and many are living with invisible wounds alongside physical injuries,” said Iris Reff Ronen, CEO of Warriors of Israel. “Their recovery will not be measured in weeks or months, but over a lifetime. We must invest in the opportunities, resources, and community that empower and enable wounded warriors and their families to rebuild their lives and claim the future they have earned.”
Warriors of Israel calls on Americans to take part in helping to ensure that soldiers who have sacrificed a part of themselves in defense of their country have support in rebuilding their lives.
Warriors of Israel is part of a global network of 15 official Friends organizations supporting Israel’s wounded warriors. Learn more: www.warriorsofisrael.org

Jury finds ex-gang leader guilty of murder in Tupac case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:48:44 UTC
14:48:44 KST

An ex-street gang leader accused of orchestrating the drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur three decades ago in Las Vegas was convicted of murder on Monday for his role in a long-unsolved crime that silenced one of rap music's most influential voices.
A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours before finding Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a downtown Las Vegas courtroom. Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13.
Davis told the judge "he plans to appeal this matter." Several people in the gallery wiped away tears and hugged a prosecutor as the court adjourned.
Representatives of the Clark County District Attorney's Office and Davis' lawyer did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
Binu Palal of the Clark County District Attorney's Office told jurors that under the code of respect in street gangs, Davis could not let the beating of his nephew slide.
"So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr. Shakur," Palal said.
Police say they long suspected Davis but did not have enough evidence to charge him until he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir, which, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, make up most of the prosecution’s case.
Davis lawyer calls case fiction not fact
Davis' lawyer Michael Sanft told jurors during his closing argument that his client's story could not be corroborated by evidence and should not be trusted. He also said the case was tainted by police corruption, mismanagement and missing files.
“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact, but the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession," Sanft said, referring to Davis' 2019 memoir "Compton Street Legend."
Over the past two weeks, prosecutors played hours of recordings for jurors in which Davis said he was enraged after Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew.
Davis and three other men, including his nephew, went looking for Shakur and his record executive Marion “Suge” Knight in a white Cadillac on the night of the beating, he told police during an unrelated investigation. Davis said he passed a gun to the backseat, and when they found Knight and Shakur’s car, one of the two men in the back opened fire.
Prosecutors have not named the shooter
Prosecutors have not named the shooter, and the three other men in the car have since died. Under Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder even if he did not pull the trigger.
Davis was a leader of the South Side Compton Crips, a Los Angeles-area street gang that feuded with rival gang Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur and his record label Death Row Records.
Shakur's 1996 killing became a seminal moment in rap history and heightened hip-hop culture's violent image during “gangsta” rap’s heyday, an era defined by feuding between East and West Coast artists.
