What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:27:30 UTC
10:27:30 KST

President Donald Trump on Aug. 28 announced plans to establish a U.S. Space Academy to bolster the country’s workforce and educate “the next generation” of space experts.
The announcement quickly drew comparisons to existing military academies—in a speech at NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, Trump himself likened it to the Army’s United States Military Academy at West Point. But the White House executive order issued in conjunction with the president’s announcement indicates the vision is for a new kind of federal service academy, one led by NASA and designed to train space operators and engineers across the civil, military, and commercial sectors.
“To continue to lead the world in space exploration and technology, while securing and defending our national interests in space, the Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the order states. “It is my administration’s policy to strengthen the nation’s space workforce by expanding opportunities to educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”
The President doesn’t have the authority to create the academy on his own—that would require an act of Congress—but his order establishes a commission to explore questions around the academy’s structure, potential military or civil service requirements, location, funding, and eligibility requirements. The group will be led by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and other commissioners will include leaders from the White House and the Pentagon, including the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Air Force. The commission is meant to issue a report with recommendations by late December.
As those recommendations take shape in the coming weeks and months, experts say they’ll be watching for more detail on the academy’s mission and scope as well as efforts to garner feedback from members of Congress. They’ll also be tracking the U.S. military’s role in the organization and how it might impact the U.S. Air Force Academy, whose 2026 class included 93 Guardians. A Department of the Air Force spokesperson declined to comment for this story. In a statement, USAFA’s Association and Foundation, its alumni organization, said it will “closely monitor developments” and share relevant information with graduates.
Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence, said the concept of a NASA-led “space center of excellence” makes sense given NASA’s deep knowledge and legacy operating in the domain.
“For decades, NASA has been the repository of knowledge when it comes to space operations,” Galbreath said. “It stands to reason that it would be useful to codify that, to create an academy where NASA experts could pass on that knowledge to the next generation.”
While the President’s order doesn’t specify the primary audience for the new academy, Galbreath said there’s an opportunity to reach a wide swath of the space community—from undergraduates to mid-career operators—with programming that ranges from certifications to academic degrees. For the military, the academy could eventually serve as a means for commissioning officers, but Galbreath said that may not be necessary immediately given the Space Force’s small size.
“At some point in the future, it could grow and become a commissioning source, I suppose,” he said. “But we’re still a long way from that.”
Todd Harrison, a space policy expert at the American Enterprise Institute, said that while he agrees there’s a need to expand the space workforce, it’s not clear that a new federally run academy is the right answer. In an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, he cited concerns about operational costs, blurring the line between military and civil space missions, and setting up unnecessary competition with the universities that already exist to train the aerospace workforce.
Harrison suggested that rather than create a separate academy, the administration could start a scholarship program similar to the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps, or ROTC. In this scenario, the government would offer scholarships to students pursuing relevant, space-related degrees in exchange for a period of service in the Space Force, NASA, or another federal agency.
“Instead of competing with our world-class institutions . . . you would let them produce the best and the brightest talent with a commitment to go into the government and work for the government for a period of time,” he said. “Establishing a physical academy is going to take years, whereas if you make it a scholarship program, you could literally start awarding scholarships next school year.”
While a scholarship program is one way to address the government’s workforce pipeline, Galbreath argued there’s also value in creating the consolidated hub of space expertise that would come with the academy model.
“When you have people that are colocated, they’re going to breed new ideas as well,” he said. “If you’re a student and you’re learning about orbital mechanics from a NASA PhD who designed the trajectories for a multi-planetary flyby, you’re getting the best.”
Another key question for the commission is where to locate the academy. Galbreath said it’s worth considering whether the academy should be located in a single campus or dispersed across multiple hubs, adding that cost will be an important factor as the commission considers its footprint.
Harrison cautioned that opening that discussion—which is often loaded with parochial politics—too soon could muddy the process. In fact, some lawmakers have already started to pitch their districts to house the Space Academy, including Rep. Dale Strong, R-Ala., who said on Aug. 31 that Huntsville, Ala., has been floated as a potential location. Although the commission has months to recommend a location, Trump indicated he may select one sooner.
Political headwinds may become a problem for Trump’s Space Academy proposal, especially if Republicans lose their majority in either the House or Senate after midterm elections in November. Harrison said there’s likely not enough time for the commission to complete its work and put the decision to a vote before the end of this legislative session.
But Galbreath noted that creating a new academy could garner bipartisan support, similar to the creation of the Space Force in 2019 during Trump’s first term.
“It’s really going to come down to the cost-benefit—can they make a compelling case that this Space Academy is going to be worth the investment of time and money and personnel,” he said. “If they can, then I think they’ll get bipartisan support. I don’t think this is one of those areas that you can get unilateral support.”
Some Democrats, including Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., have already indicated they’re intrigued by the concept. In an Aug. 28 post on the social media site X, Whitesides said the idea “deserves consideration” but raised concerns about funding and the lack of congressional representation on the commission.
“I am open-minded to hear thoughtful answers to these questions, but I recommend that Congress be engaged quickly and substantively or else this intriguing idea will be stuck on the launch pad,” Whitesides said.

SC: Externment orders cannot be passed routinely, require reasons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:26:51 UTC
10:26:51 KST

SC rules externment orders cannot be routine, quashes Raigarh DM order, says multiple criminal cases alone not grounds for such action.
NEW DELHI: Holding that forcing a person to stay out of a city or district affects freedom guaranteed by the Constitution, SC on Monday ruled that a govt cannot pass an externment order routinely and must pass a reasoned order to justify such harsh measures.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed an externment order passed by Raigarh district magistrate directing a person to remove himself from the district and contiguous districts for one year. The order was passed against him as multiple criminal cases were pending and the district authority apprehended that his presence would create further problems in the area and nearby districts.“An order of externment directly impinges upon valuable fundamental freedoms guaranteed to a citizen and, therefore, cannot be made as a matter of routine. Further, merely because multiple criminal cases have been filed against a person would not, ipso facto, be a ground for ordering externment,” the bench said.Before exercising such power, the DM is required to arrive at a bona fide and informed subjective satisfaction that circumstances warrant such an extreme measure and externment is necessary, it said.
The bench said the authority is not expected to render a judgement as a court of law but the order must nonetheless disclose, at least in broad terms, the reasons for such satisfaction.
“The existence of objective material and a discernible nexus between such material and the conclusion reached are indispensable safeguards against arbitrary exercise of power,” it said.Quashing the order under Chhattisgarh Rajya Suraksha Adhiniyam, SC said the externment order fell short of statutory requirement. “The order does not indicate the material on the basis of which such conclusion was reached. No reasons are forthcoming to demonstrate why the third respondent (Raipur DM) considered the situation grave enough to necessitate the appellant’s externment,” it said.

Then a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home. The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Dawadi, the principal, had little time to act. US Army Secretary Driscoll tenders resignation, source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:25:47 UTC
10:25:47 KST

US Army Secretary Driscoll tenders resignation, source says
WASHINGTON, Aug 31 - U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation to the White House following months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Driscoll, who officials said is close to U.S. Vice President JD Vance, becomes the latest senior official who has either been fired or pushed out in Hegseth's Pentagon. It also comes as the United States is still engaged in a war with Iran, with thousands of U.S. Army soldiers deployed in the Middle East.
It was unclear if the White House had accepted his resignation.
"Driscoll brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth's blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible," the source said, referring to his efforts to modernize the Army.
The Army declined to comment on the news, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
"Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.
The source said that Dave Fitzgerald, the deputy undersecretary of the Army who was focused on innovation within the Army, was also expected to resign. Fitzgerald did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
BREWING FRUSTRATION WITH HEGSETH
Driscoll, who was confirmed for the top Army position in February 2025, pushed the Army to be more nimble in acquiring cheaper weapons and chastised large weapons makers. The Army Secretary is responsible for training and equipping soldiers.
"(The) defense industrial base broadly, and the primes in particular, conned the American people and the Pentagon and the Army," Driscoll said last year in a reference to large defense companies.
One U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that Hegseth saw Driscoll as a threat within the bureaucracy and had long wanted to remove him. But his ties to Vance, the official said, made it tough for Hegseth to do so.
Driscoll gained prominence outside the Pentagon when he was tapped by Trump to take part in talks with Moscow and Kyiv to end the war in Ukraine – a rare diplomatic task for an Army secretary.
In April, Hegseth fired U.S. Army Chief of Staff Randy George, a major staffing change that came as the U.S. military was fighting a major war in the Middle East.
The official said George's firing caught Driscoll off guard and led to increased frustration with Hegseth.
Driscoll told lawmakers in April that after George was fired, his family drove to the former general's house and gave him a hug.
In June, Hegseth also pushed out the head of U.S. Army forces in Europe and he has personally blocked the promotion of senior Army officials.
"Driscoll brought urgency to an institution that cannot afford complacency," Republican Congressman Pat Harrigan said.
"Dan's service to this country is far from over," Harrigan added. REUTERS

Zelensky enacts NSDC decision on regions' preparations for winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:25:00 UTC
10:25:00 KST

Zelensky enacts NSDC decision on regions' preparations for winter
The decision is set out in Decree No. 838/2026, dated August 31 and published on the president's website, according to Ukrinform.
"To enact the decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine dated August 5, 2026, 'On the status of implementation of comprehensive resilience plans for individual regions and approval of the Comprehensive Resilience Plan for the Kyiv territorial community'," the decree states.
Under the decision, the authorities took note of the prime minister's information on the implementation of comprehensive resilience plans by regional state (military) administrations and mayors, including the scope of measures already completed and the realistic prospects for implementing them before the start of the 2026/2027 heating season.
Officials were warned of personal responsibility for failure to implement the comprehensive resilience plans, as well as for delays or improper implementation.
The decision also approved the Comprehensive Resilience Plan for the Kyiv territorial community. In addition, the mayor of Kyiv was reminded of personal responsibility for preparations for and the stable operation of the city's 2026/2027 heating season.
The Cabinet of Ministers, for its part, must immediately update the comprehensive resilience plans, taking into account the realistic prospects for completing the measures envisaged before the start of the 2026/2027 heating season. The government must also, together with the Kyiv City Military Administration and the mayor of Kyiv, continue co-financing the city's Comprehensive Resilience Plan and take measures to ensure the resilience of critical infrastructure operators.
Together with Ukrzaliznytsia, the Cabinet of Ministers must also take measures to restore and replenish rolling stock, including locomotives, damaged or lost as a result of Russian aggression. This includes introducing state aid programs, attracting international funding and simplifying public procurement procedures.
Regional and Kyiv city state (military) administrations, together with businesses regardless of ownership, must conduct command-and-staff exercises within a month to prepare for possible emergencies at heating, electricity, gas and water supply facilities. Before the start of the heating season, they must also increase backup power capacity for essential services, including heating and water supply facilities, by 20% in line with the targets set out in the comprehensive resilience plans.
In addition, local authorities must maintain fuel reserves sufficient for at least two weeks, prepare apartment buildings for autonomous operation and equip them with independent backup power supplies. Heat and electricity companies must protect critical components of their facilities and create reserves of equipment, spare parts and materials for emergency repairs before the start of the 2026/2027 heating season. Regional and Kyiv city military administrations will monitor implementation of these measures.
Control over implementation of the decision has been assigned to National Security and Defense Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.
The decree took effect on the day of its publication.

SC questions CBI, ED's tardiness in Leaps and Bounds probe linked to Abhishek Banerjee, seeks interrogation details by Sept 7.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday lashed out at CBI and ED for getting active in the probe against ‘Leaps and Bounds’ — a company allegedly linked to former West Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee’s nephew and Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee and tainted in the SSC recruitment scam — for getting huge sums from the previous TMC govt, and questioned the state police’s sudden alacrity to probe it for the same illegalities.While seeking custodial interrogation of Sumit Roy, PA to TMC general secretary Abhishek Banerjee, in the illegal sale of govt land as private property, solicitor general Tushar Mehta mentioned Roy’s involvement in the transfer of Rs 30 crore from a party account to Leaps and Bounds.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, “The less said about Leaps and Bounds investigation, the better it is.” It noted Calcutta HC judges’ frustration over the dragging of feet by CBI and ED in investigating the firm.

Roy’s counsel Gopal Sankaranarayanan said he had mistakenly submitted during the last hearing that accused had the right to silence.
He said Roy had answered questions put to him during 11 days of interrogation.Bench asked Bengal police to submit by Sept 7 details of the interrogation relating to financial transactions. It said, “When we see a case like this, the court’s job is to enable a fair investigation.” It said it wanted to examine agencies’ “eagerness” to arrest.

Sony, Warner Music sue Anthropic over songs used in AI training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:21:00 UTC
10:21:00 KST

Sony, Warner Music sue Anthropic over songs used in AI training
- Sony Music and Warner Music have sued Anthropic for using their copyrighted song lyrics and sheet music to train its AI model, Claude, without permission.
- The lawsuit claims Anthropic pirated works from famous artists like The Beatles and Taylor Swift, and that Claude can reproduce these lyrics exactly.
- Sony and Warner seek damages up to US$150,000 (S$191,000) per infringement and want a court order to stop Anthropic from using their works in AI training.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – The music publishing branches of Sony Music and Warner Music have sued Anthropic in California federal court for allegedly misusing their copyrighted song compositions to train its Claude AI models.
Sony and Warner said in the complaint, filed on Aug 28, that Anthropic pirated hundreds of song lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson and hundreds of other artists to train Claude to respond to human prompts.
The lawsuit is the latest in a wave of cases brought against tech companies by copyright owners including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets over the use of their work to train artificial intelligence systems.
Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and earlier in 2026 over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training, in lawsuits that are still ongoing.
Anthropic became the first AI company to settle one of the disputes in 2025, when it paid US$1.5 billion (S$1.91 billion) to resolve a class action from a group of authors.
“Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” Sony and Warner said in their complaint.
“And US$1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering two-trillion-dollar valuation.”
“This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts,” an Anthropic spokesperson said on Aug 31.
The spokesperson also said that the company will defend itself “robustly” and that AI training makes fair use of copyrighted material, citing the judge in the authors’ case against it.
Spokespeople and an attorney for Sony Music and Warner Music did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the case on Aug 31.
The complaint alleges Anthropic illegally obtained the publishers’ lyrics and sheet music through torrent downloads to train Claude, and that Claude can reproduce copyrighted lyrics “verbatim” when prompted.
Sony and Warner also said Anthropic used their lyrics to teach Claude to “generate vast quantities of purportedly ‘new’ AI-generated song lyrics, which compete with Music Publishers’ legitimate copyrighted works as harmful market substitutes”.
The labels are seeking damages of up to US$150,000 for each infringed copyright and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works. REUTERS

African NGOs demand probe into six bodies found in Guinea mass grave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:17:59 UTC
10:17:59 KST

African NGOs demand probe into six bodies found in Guinea mass grave
The bodies were found bound and blindfolded in the Forecariah administrative prefecture on August 24.
A group of 20 African civil society organisations has called for an independent investigation into the discovery of six unidentified bodies in a mass grave in Guinea.
The call on Sunday came after local men gathering firewood stumbled upon the six male bodies in the village of Alassoya in Lower Guinea’s Forecariah administrative prefecture on August 24.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4One ‘party state’: Guinea dissolves main opposition parties
- list 2 of 4‘Before, the land sustained us’: Who benefits from Guinea’s bauxite wealth?
- list 3 of 4Advocacy groups file complaint against Ghana over Trump deportations
- list 4 of 4Photos: Towering landfill collapse kills 30 in Guinea’s capital, Conakry
The bodies were found bound and blindfolded.
Guinea’s Armed Forces have confirmed the discovery.
The NGOs included the Afrikajom Centre and several branches of the Tournons La Page (TLP), an organisation that unites citizens’ movements across a dozen African countries.
They demanded that “all hypotheses be examined as part of an independent, impartial and transparent investigation”. They also called for the investigation to be conducted “with the support of national and international forensic experts in order to formally identify the victims”.
The groups said the discovery of the mass grave comes on top of “at least 35 cases of enforced disappearances documented by TLP-Guinea since September 5, 2021”.
They added that the circumstances in which the bodies were found “raise fears that the victims may have been subjected to extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions”.
Guinea’s Armed Forces have promised an inquiry.
The military said in a statement that the six bodies have been transported to the hospital in Forecariah “to proceed with identification and, if possible, determine the circumstances of their deaths”.
It added that “all measures were being taken to shed light” on the discovery and stated that “investigation results will be made public”.
The discovery comes amid a wide-ranging crackdown on dissent in Guinea following General Mamady Doumbouya’s seizure of power in a coup in 2021.
Since the power grab, several political parties have been suspended and protests suppressed, while numerous opposition and civil society leaders have been arrested, sentenced, or forced into exile.
Civil society groups have also documented cases of opposition activists being abducted or disappearing under the military government.
France has also called on Guinean authorities to conduct a transparent and independent investigation into the mass grave, according to Africanews, a news outlet based in the French city of Lyon.
Africanews said another mass grave was found in the same region of Guinea last year, but investigations have yet to determine the identities of the victims or their causes of death.

Power failures at two Jaipur examination centres disrupted the AIIMS Common Recruitment Examination 2026 a day after a similar glitch hit NEET-PG at the same locations
NEW DELHI: A day after a power failure disrupted NEET-PG 2026 at two examination centres in Jaipur, the AIIMS Common Recruitment Examination (CRE) 2026 was hit by a similar power supply failure at the same centres, forcing AIIMS to cancel the test there and schedule a fresh examination for September 7.Barely 24 hours after the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare constituted a three-member committee to probe the power failure at the Jaipur centre, the same TCS-operated iON Digital Zone in Sitapura witnessed another disruption during the AIIMS CRE. The examination began at 9 am as scheduled but was interrupted by internal power supply issues at centres RJ0101 and RJ0102. AIIMS said the examination was cancelled at the two centres to safeguard the interests of affected candidates and maintain the integrity and fairness of the examination.A total of 2,000 candidates were registered at the two centres. Of these, 1,342 candidates at RJ0101 and 436 at RJ0102 appeared for the examination before the disruption. The affected candidates will now have to take the test afresh on September 7. AIIMS said suitable examination centres in Jaipur are being identified to accommodate them, either together or in smaller groups.
Across the country, 21,098 candidates were registered for the first shift of the CRE on August 31, of whom 16,193 appeared.
The examination was conducted as scheduled at all other centres except the two Jaipur centres.AIIMS has asked TCS to submit a detailed report on Monday's incident. It has also directed the examination service provider to preserve all relevant system logs, CCTV footage and control-room communications to facilitate a comprehensive assessment of the circumstances leading to the disruption.
The CRE is conducted for recruitment to Group B and Group C posts across AIIMS and other Central government and autonomous healthcare institutions. The current examination covers posts including Junior Administrative Assistant, Senior Administrative Assistant, Data Entry Operator, Personal Assistant, Stenographer, Private Secretary, Assistant Security Officer, Receptionist, Junior Medical Records Officer, Junior Warden, Hostel Warden, Telephone Operator and Social Security Officer.The CRE 2026 is being conducted over August 31 and September 1 in three shifts, allowing candidates who have applied for multiple posts to appear for all examinations for which they are eligible. A total of 30,142 candidates have registered for the recruitment examination

US university to pay US$2.1 million settlement over claims it didn’t disclose China ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:14:55 UTC
10:14:55 KST

US university to pay US$2.1 million settlement over claims it didn’t disclose China ties
Justice Department alleged Ohio State failed to reveal employees’ links to China in applications for federal grant funding
A prominent American university has agreed to pay a US$2.1 million settlement to resolve allegations that it failed to disclose employees’ ties to China when applying for federal grant funding, the Department of Justice announced on Monday.
Both Nasa and the NSF required the public university to disclose “foreign government support received by any principal investigator (PI) or co-PI on the grant application”, according to a Department of Justice press release.
The NSF was established by Congress in 1950 and funds scientific research through grants, while Nasa oversees the US space programme, conducting research in areas including aeronautics and space exploration.
The US$2.1 million settlement will specifically resolve allegations that, since 2014, annual faculty activity reports submitted to OSU identified affiliations with Chinese universities and state-run research organisations, but the university did not disclose this information to Nasa or the NSF.
In addition, the university learned in 2019 that a principal investigator on Nasa grants was a participant in the Thousand Talents Programme, which the department said was established by the Chinese government “to recruit individuals with knowledge or access to foreign technology intellectual property”.

Türkiye joins NASA’s Artemis Accords as 71st signatory to peaceful space exploration pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:14:03 UTC
10:14:03 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Türkiye has joined NASA’s Artemis Accords, becoming the 71st country to sign an international framework aimed at promoting peaceful, transparent, and cooperative exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
Turkish Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir signed the accords on behalf of Türkiye during a Monday ceremony at NASA headquarters in Washington, hosted by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
“It is my privilege to welcome the Republic of Türkiye as the 71st signatory of the Artemis Accords,” Isaacman said, according to a NASA statement highlighting Türkiye’s growing role in space exploration.
The accords, established in 2020 by NASA, the US State Department, and seven founding countries, set principles for international cooperation in space, including peaceful exploration, sharing scientific data, providing assistance when needed, and protecting historically significant sites and artifacts.
Türkiye’s signing comes amid growing activity in the country’s space program. In 2024, Alper Gezeravci became Türkiye’s first astronaut, traveling to the International Space Station and doing scientific research with NASA astronauts. Tuva Atasever later flew on Virgin Galactic’s VSS Unity as part of the Virgin Galactic 07 mission.
Türkiye is also preparing to launch its first lunar mission, AYAP-1, joining the small but growing group of countries building and launching their own satellites to the Moon.
The signing precedes the International Astronautical Congress, which Türkiye will host in the city of Antalya in October. The event is expected to bring together dozens of Artemis Accords signatories to discuss the future of peaceful and transparent space exploration.

Air Force Pulls ICBM Testing Device After Finding Likely Carcinogen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
01:11:07 UTC
10:11:07 KST

The Air Force has pulled a piece of testing equipment for its Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles after discovering some appeared to be contaminated with a possible carcinogen.
The order to stop using the AN/PRM-10 test oscillator set came after an Airman discovered polychlorinated biphenyl, or PCB, residue on one of the units during a routine inspection in August, Air Force Global Strike Command said in an Aug. 28 statement.
The Airman, who was at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo., reported the residue and received medical attention for the exposure before returning to duty, according to the statement
The EPA has concluded PCBs are a probable cause of cancer in humans, as well as having negative immune system, reproductive, developmental, and neurological effects. PCBs were regularly used in electrical, heat transfer, and hydraulic equipment for about 50 years due to the compound’s electrical insulating properties, high boiling point, and nonflammibility, until they were banned in 1979 as evidence grew that the compound was toxic to people and the environment.
The AN/PRM-10 test oscillator set is a signal generator used to examine ICBM communications systems, per the Global Strike Command statement. After the Airman reported the issue and tests confirmed the presence of PCBs on that test unit, the 20th Air Force—which oversees ICBM bases—ordered all AN/PRM-10 kits be inspected.
That review of all AN/PRM-10 kits was done within three days, and officials found potential PCB residue on six of eight systems. Samples collected from those systems are now being tested. Officials also ordered safety warnings, precautions, and mandatory personal protective equipment requirements be updated where other legacy test units are still used.
But all AN/PRM-10 systems have been pulled from use in the 20th, and units are transitioning to a modern replacement tester that is free of PCBs, Air Force Global Strike Command said. Leaders are working with the Minuteman III systems program office to dispose of any existing AN/PRM-10 kits and identify any other test equipment pieces that may have PCBs.
The “20th Air Force takes the responsibility to protect our Airmen very seriously,” Commander Maj. Gen. Colin Connor said in a statement. “As our Airmen are our greatest asset, their safety and health are my top priority.”
Concerns about rates of cancer among missileers and other Airmen who work with ICBMs has grown in recent years. In 2023, the Air Force launched a study dubbed the Missile Community Cancer Study to review the possibility of clusters of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma at ICBM bases, as well as other specific cancer concerns raised by the community.
The Torchlight Initiative, an organization made up of current and former ICBM community members and their families that pushes the government to address higher rates of cancer and other illnesses among ICBM airmen, called the swift removal of those units “a great start.” But more work remains to be done, the organization said on social media.
“We need to create a culture where Airmen recognize hazards, speak up, and leaders respond—making the mission safer for those serving today and tomorrow,” Torchlight said in a post on LinkedIn.
Torchlight Initiative public affairs director Erin Dick said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine that while it was encouraging the Airman in this situation knew enough to recognize the potential PCB exposure and say something, it is concerning to think of how many Airmen may have used such contaminated equipment over the decades before PCB hazards were fully known.
Dick said the Air Force should work to determine how widespread potential exposures were, identify and document anyone who may have been exposed, and make sure their health is monitored over the long term, potentially including screenings.
The Air Force said in its release that the Airman in this incident returned to duty “with no adverse effects.” But Dick said it could be too soon to make that conclusion.
“It’s really not possible to say, because of the way these chemicals work, if there will be long-term health effects for this particular Airman,” Dick said. “There is often a very long latency period before illnesses appear. But at least now he’s got [PCB exposure] documented, and that is something we’re trying to encourage all people who are currently serving [and those who previously served] in the community to make sure that their service is documented.”
Retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, a former commander of the 341st Missile Wing at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont., told Air & Space Forces Magazine the recent discovery of PCBs underscores how important it is for the Air Force to remain vigilant against these kind of contaminants.
As part of the Missile Community Cancer Study, the Air Force in 2023 took air and swipe samples from all three of its active ICBM bases: Malmstrom, F.E. Warren, and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. The swipe tests involve gauze wetted with a solution run over surfaces and then analyzed for suspected contaminants. The tests showed a few samples with elevated PCB levels at Minot and Malmstrom, while F.E. Warren had trace amounts not in excess of the EPA’s acceptable limit.
“Typically the command has been actually pretty good, once [PCBs have] been found, about dealing with them,” Reeves, now a senior resident fellow for space studies at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, said. “It’s really old stuff from back when we really weren’t tracking major chemicals and other things that are not good for humans. So now it’s about how well the command can react when things like this are found.”
Reeves said that because ICBMs still use many components from the years before PCBs were banned, the chemicals may still be out there in facilities. It’s crucial for the Air Force to keep looking for PCBs, she said, and the service needs to keep track and follow up with Airmen who may have come down with unusual conditions.
Air Force Global Strike Command also needs to come up with a way to go through its legacy equipment systematically and test them for PCBs, to make sure more potentially harmful gear isn’t out there, she said.
“The bigger context is not, ‘we found an isolated thing’” contaminated with PCBs, Reeves said. “This may be building a bigger picture that we may not yet be fully witting of.”

ZAGREB, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The first-ever World Aquatics Water Polo 4x4 Open Championships began Monday at the Old Town Harbour in Dubrovnik, Croatia.
The seven-day championships feature 17 men's teams and eight women's teams, including two men's teams from Hong Kong, China.
Similar to 3x3 basketball, the 4x4 format reduces the number of players on each side from seven to four and shrinks the playing area from about 25 by 20 meters to 15 by 12 meters, creating a faster-paced version of the sport suited to open-water and urban settings.
Each match is played over a maximum of four sets, with the first team to win three sets taking the match. If the teams are tied 2-2 after four sets, the winner is decided by a penalty shootout.
"WP4 has become World Aquatics' new event to combine sport with tourism, and Dubrovnik is the right place to start," World Aquatics President Husain Al-Musallam said.
World Aquatics hopes the format will lower barriers to participation, attract new audiences and help expand water polo in countries and regions with limited access to standard competition facilities. ■

Feature: O'Sullivan fights to cure "disease" that has plagued his game
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:00:12 CST
10:00:12 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Seven-time snooker world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan says he has a "disease."
It is not a medical diagnosis. It is how he describes a technical problem he has spent nearly four years trying to cure, one he says has robbed him of the power, direction and confidence that once made him the dominant player in world snooker.
"I call it a disease because it feels like the method that I took on has ruined me," the 50-year-old said after reaching the semifinals of the World Snooker Wuhan Open last week. "I've got no cue power, got no sense of direction. I don't know where the balls are going."
His latest withdrawal from the British Open, which begins Monday in Cheltenham, came for medical reasons. But just days earlier in Wuhan, O'Sullivan was still wrestling with the technical problem that has increasingly defined this stage of his career.
Last Thursday, in an all-English quarterfinal against four-time world champion Mark Selby at the Wuhan Open, O'Sullivan fell 2-0 behind before winning three frames in a row. Selby leveled at 3-3, but O'Sullivan finished the match with breaks of 80 and 129 to win 5-3.
Sky Sports called it "his most impressive performance of the season yet." O'Sullivan called it ugly.
"To be honest, I don't really have much hope to regain the kind of level that I was at before," he said at the news conference afterward. "But as it stands, it's pretty ugly out there for me, and maybe ugly for you guys to watch me play."
The next day, the difference between what O'Sullivan saw and what others saw became even more striking.
In the semifinal, he faced China's 24-year-old Chang Bingyu, whom he had coached about a decade ago.
This time, O'Sullivan seemed to lose his connection with the table. Several important shots caught the edge of the pocket and bounced away. At one point, a frustrated O'Sullivan swung his cue through the air, then sat down and shook his head. He eventually lost 6-3.
"Just embarrassing," he told Xinhua. The "disease" in his game, he added, had "come back big time."
According to O'Sullivan, the problem dates back six years. At 44, he could have relied on decades of experience and continued playing largely as he always had. But he didn't. Instead, he decided to learn a technique called "SightRight," a coaching method designed to help players align their eyes correctly with a shot.
"A lot of people kind of thought it was good," O'Sullivan said. "It kind of turned against me after three or four years of doing it. So I'm trying to unlearn that, which is really hard to do."
For most players, experience is supposed to provide something to fall back on when a shot goes wrong. But O'Sullivan said he has lost that safety net.
"As a player, you always have some anchors to hang onto," he said. "I used to have four or five where if one wasn't working, I'd try another one, and then that would just get me going. But at the moment, I just have nothing. I haven't for four years, so it's just been like a nightmare."
O'Sullivan has not won a ranking title since January 2024. His seventh world championship came in 2022. Before Wuhan, he had won only one match at each of the Shanghai Masters and China Open this season. He even described himself as a "very poor snooker player."
Yet there are contradictions in that diagnosis. A player who says he has no sense of direction remains No. 14 in the world, while a player who calls his own technique ugly can still beat some of the biggest names in the sport.
For Wuhan spectator Chen Can, the O'Sullivan he watched was very different from the player O'Sullivan described.
"He beat Carter 5-2, downed Yao Pengcheng 5-1, knocked out Maguire 5-2 and defeated Selby 5-3," Chen said. "I feel he still has it. His attacking game is still smooth, and he can adjust quickly when he is in trouble."
Some British fans commenting online offered a simpler diagnosis, saying O'Sullivan "can't cure it. It's called 'age'."
But O'Sullivan does not buy that explanation. At an age when many players have long since retired, he is still taking his game apart and trying to rebuild it.
"I've been trying to do it for a year. I thought I was there, but I wasn't, and now I'm kind of back to the drawing board," he said.
He has also sought advice from Steve Davis and Stephen Hendry, who told him they continued playing for perhaps a decade after entering similar slumps.
"I give myself 18 months, maybe, to get into the 2028 world championships, to see if I can get somewhere back to how I used to hit the ball," he said. "If I hit the ball half decent, then I can still win tournaments."
An eighth world title in 2028 would give O'Sullivan the outright record for modern-era world championships, moving him beyond Hendry's seven.
"I'll try my hardest," he said. "We'll have to wait and see." ■

Duane “Keffe D” Davis found guilty in Tupac Shakur murder

Duane 'Keffe D' Davis found guilty in Tupac Shakur murder
Duane “Keffe D” Davis was found guilty Monday of orchestrating the 1996 murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur, becoming the first person convicted in the decades-old case. The 63-year-old faces a possible life sentence after a Las Vegas jury deliberated for less than three hours.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
A jury found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur, marking the first conviction in a case that has gripped hip-hop fans for decades.
The 63-year-old Davis was convicted Monday of a single count of murder with a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison. The jury deliberated for less than 3 hours after a weekslong trial in Las Vegas.
After the verdict was read, Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, cried and hugged the prosecutors. Also in the courtroom was Davis’ son, who covered his face with one hand.
Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in closing arguments that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night.
Palal acknowledged that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but argued those differences reflected Davis’ changing motivations and efforts to protect himself. One critical detail, he said, remained consistent: Davis repeatedly placed himself inside a white Cadillac from which the shots were fired.
The panel of 16 jurors, four of whom are alternates, heard testimony from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses over nine days.
“The core facts remain. The material facts remain,” Palal said.
The prosecution said Monday evening that the state would dismiss the gang enhancement part of the charge due to witness logistics.
A decades-old case reaches a verdict
The trial brought to a head a decades-old case that for years has drawn the attention of hip-hop fans and true crime experts alike. Shakur, who was considered one of the most influential rappers of all time, was in Las Vegas on Sept. 7, 1996, and stopped at a red light when a white Cadillac pulled up beside him, and shots were fired. He died six days later from his wounds. Knight was also wounded but survived.
For years, nobody had been charged in the rapper’s death until Davis began making public statements, saying he was in the Cadillac and gave the gun to others in the backseat. Davis described the shooting as an act of retaliation after Knight and Shakur’s entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting.
Read moreTupac's accused murderer out for 'revenge', Las Vegas jury hears
Under Nevada law, someone who helps another person commit murder can be convicted of the crime. Davis is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac. The man who prosecutors say originally gave the gun to Davis is also dead.
Palal told jurors that if they believed Davis' statements, they did not have to be independently corroborated with additional evidence.
Still, he pointed to the rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru, the fight with Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson and testimony that members of Shakur’s circle identified Anderson and Davis as suspects the night of the shooting. Witnesses had testified to the heated gang rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru, which were associated with dueling record companies Bad Boy Records and Death Row Records.
“Who fired is not the question,” Palal said. Prosecutors haven't argued that Davis pulled the trigger, but instead that he was criminally responsible because he provided the gun and ordered the attack.
Palal also argued the shooting was premeditated, pointing to testimony and Davis’ accounts that the group searched for Shakur before spotting him on the road and making a U-turn. “It’s a plan, not an impulse,” Palal said.
Palal held up Davis’ 2019 memoir, “Compton Street Legend,” and played an interview in which Davis encouraged people to buy it to get the “real truth.” Although the book contains a disclaimer saying some facts were changed, Palal argued that names, hotels and other details changed while the central account did not.
Palal also rejected the defense’s contention that Davis fabricated his accounts to make money. “It is an entirely different proposition to be profiting from a murder,” Palal said. “And that is what Mr. Davis is doing.”
Sanft also turned to his client’s memoir during his closing argument. While reading an excerpt, he said the N-word aloud, prompting people watching in an overflow courtroom to recoil and shake their heads.
In multiple interviews, Davis said he handed the gun to the back seat, but in others as well as in his book, Davis wouldn’t say who pulled the trigger.
In a rebuttal argument, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo pointed to a scrapbook Davis kept containing articles about Shakur.
“This guy's scrapbooking his murder, for God's sake,” DiGiacomo told jurors.
Prosecutors and defense clash over Davis’ role
The prosecution's witnesses included a gang expert who described Davis as the shot caller that younger gang members had to obey. Sanft asked jurors if there was any evidence that Davis had ever called the shots before or after the shooting.
During the trial, investigators said a Las Vegas hotel bill was found at Davis’ residence during a police search, but it wasn’t clear when it was dated — or where that evidence is currently located.
The case is nearly 30 years old, which has affected the kind of evidence presented in court. Prosecutors warned jurors that material collected in the ’90s is different from what law enforcement collects today, including hotel surveillance video from the night of the shooting.

Reigning In Big Tech: How California lawmakers plan to regulate AI and social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
00:57:01 UTC
09:57:01 KST

Reining In Big Tech: How California lawmakers plan to regulate AI and social media
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SACRAMENTO — Long the epicenter of the global tech industry, California is taking more action to shield its children, communities and workers from the threats posed by the very industry that’s become central to the state’s identity and enviable economy.
State lawmakers on Monday passed new safeguards around social media, artificial intelligence and data centers at a time when technology has become intertwined with people’s daily lives.
Efforts to rein in the power of Big Tech extend beyond concerns that TikTok, Instagram and other social media platforms are harming young children.
Unions and workers worry that AI will take their jobs, and lawmakers are trying to tackle privacy and safety issues as AI features get added into smart glasses and toys. Californians are concerned that the proliferation of data centers will increase their electricity bills and strain water supplies.
“There’s a heightened level of tech anxiety right now, and that manifests itself from social media to data centers to AI taking jobs,” said Assemblyman Josh Lowenthal (D-Long Beach). “People are coalescing and they’re demanding that policymakers make change.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has previously vetoed some bills aimed at adding restrictions on Silicon Valley businesses, will still have to weigh in on whether to sign the pieces of legislation into law.
The Democratic governor has acknowledged the challenge of adopting regulations that protect the public without going too far and potentially stifling the technology industry’s growth, which brings critical revenue to the state budget.
“I think that’s the constant tension,” Newsom said in an interview earlier this summer. “We’re constantly sort of fighting that balance.”
The governor, who has close relationships in the technology industry from his time in San Francisco, said only a couple of other states have attempted to regulate artificial intelligence like California. The state, he said, leads on regulation of social media.
“We’re not rolling over, certainly,” Newsom said. “We’re leaning forward, and we’re iterating. We will push the boundaries and litigate.”
The looming restrictions on social media follow a landmark Meta Platforms legal settlement aimed at making social media safer for young people. Parents, politicians and child advocacy groups are worried that social media is contributing to depression, anxiety, eating disorders and other issues.
The actions being pushed in the California Legislature are more sweeping than that settlement, however. One of the bills passed by lawmakers on Monday, Assembly Bill 1709, would bar certain online platforms from providing an “addictive feature” to users under 16 years old and add ways to verify users’ ages.
Under the bill, prohibited addictive features include autoplay and feeds that display recommended content.
The addictive nature of autoplay and other features is “harmful, full stop, and that they’re not appropriate for the developing brain,” said Lowenthal, who authored the bill.
Newsom, who chatted with lawmakers at the Capitol on Monday in what will be his last regular legislative session as governor, praised Lowenthal and the bill.
“I’m really proud of the work that we did together on that. My legislator of the year is Josh Lowenthal,” Newsom said. “California will continue to lead in this area as we must continue to lead in this area.”
After watching technology “run free” in California for years, legislators are now seeking to “pump the brakes a little bit,” said Samantha Vigil, a UC Davis researcher who built a registry tracking social media legislation in states across the country.
“They want to reevaluate what is working,” Vigil said. “What is healthy and beneficial, and what is progress just for the sake of having a new iteration of something?”
All 50 states have introduced or passed some type of digital media or technology-related legislation, tackling smartphone use in schools, social media and chatbots, Vigil said.
Other countries have taken more stringent steps to limit social media use among young people. Australia banned social media use for those under 16, but enforcing the law has been challenging because young people have tried to get around the restrictions.
California isn’t trying to ban social media; instead, it’s trying to limit how platforms design their features.
Parents and state attorneys general have not waited for policy makers to act. They have sued Meta, Google and other tech companies over the alleged harms their products have done to young people.
In late August, Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, agreed to pay up to $17 billion and make child-safety changes to resolve a multi-state lawsuit alleging the tech company designed and deployed harmful features while misleading the public about potential harms. Meta and YouTube also lost a social media addiction lawsuit earlier this year in Los Angeles.
Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states
Assembly Bill 1709 goes further. For example, Meta’s settlement gives teens the option to pick a non-algorithmic feed and turn off autoplay but, unlike in the legislation, it’s not mandatory. The bill would also apply to other platforms outside of Meta. Meta declined to comment.
Tech industry and business group opposing the bill say it is too blunt and could cut off access to social media’s benefits, according to the bill’s analysis.
“The durable path is to enforce the targeted laws California already has and to strengthen parental tools rather than an overlapping framework whose scope can be redrawn by regulation,” said Robert Boykin, TechNet’s executive director for California and the Southwest.
California lawmakers passed another Lowenthal bill aimed at holding social media liable for harm caused to children. Under Assembly Bill 2, social media companies could face fines of up to $1 million per child for negligent harm.
California lawmakers this year also attempted to tackle two other perils of the technological world — the rapid development and implementation of artificial intelligence and the proliferation of the massive data centers that are essential to sustaining the AI universe.
National and state union leaders have urged California legislators and Newsom to protect workers from being replaced by AI, saying it posed an existential threat to the foundation of a healthy, productive democracy.
“AI must remain a tool controlled by humans, not the other way around,” said Sen. Jerry McNerney (D-Pleasanton).
The state Legislature on Monday approved McNerney’s Senate Bill 947, which would bar employers from “solely” using automated decision-making systems to discipline or fire employees. If an employer primarily relies upon this system, a human must verify the decision.
Lawmakers also approved Senate Bill 951, introduced by Sen. Eloise Gomez Reyes (D-Colton), which would require employers to provide a 60-day advance notice to workers and local and state governments before AI-related layoffs. Lawmakers also approved Assembly Bill 1609, which requires large private businesses that serve customers to provide access to human customer service representatives and to disclose to use of chatbots.
They passed another bill by Sen. Steve Padilla (D-Chula Vista) that enacts a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of AI-chatbot powered toys over concerns that the technology can harm children.
On Friday, lawmakers agreed on a compromise on proposed legislation to regulate energy use by California’s growing data center industry, measures prompted by community fears about the massive complexes. Lawmakers say the legislation, which passed Monday, would help protect consumers from growing electricity costs driven upward by the sprawling facilities and to track the centers’ immense energy and water consumption.
At a June hearing on Senate Bill 886 to regulate data centers’ energy use, Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo (D-Chatsworth) said it’s just “a handful of companies that are gonna make trillions of dollars” from AI. They should pay for related utility infrastructure upgrades, she added.
“People, I would argue, are not even begging to use AI,” she said. “They’re struggling to figure it out to keep up with the times, but don’t even really want it.”
The California legislature is expected to vote on two of the bills to regulate the controversial industry within the next day.
Whether Newsom will embrace the legislature’s efforts to corral big Tech in California — in part of in whole — remains unclear.
Newsom last year vetoed a similar AI bill from McNerney to ban automated decision-making systems to discipline employees over worries that it could restrict companies’ ability to use customer ratings. That element was dropped in this year’s legislation.
Newsom last year signed Assembly Bill 56 that required social media platforms to display mental health warning labels to users under 18 starting in January 2027. But he also vetoed Senate Bill 771 that aimed to hold social media platforms liable if they amplified content that contributed to hate crimes and other violent acts, saying that the legislation was “premature” and current civil rights laws might be adequate.
Lowenthal said he’s heard from California families who are anxious about social media and seeking “relief” from their concerns about how the platforms are affecting their children.
“This is a kitchen-table topic,” he said. “I’ve yet to find a family with school-age children in the state of California, any corner of the state, that is not going through this right now.”
Times staff writer Taryn Luna contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s approval rating was stuck at the lowest level of his political career amid broad dissatisfaction over the war in Iran and the Republican’s economic stewardship, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded on Aug 31.
Just 33 per cent of Americans approve of the job Trump is doing in the White House – the third straight Reuters/Ipsos poll with that share of respondents giving the President a thumbs up.
Trump’s political brand looks increasingly like a potential weight on his Republican Party, which will be defending slim congressional majorities in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Democrats appear more fired up about the elections, with 46 per cent of self-identified Democrats describing themselves as “very enthusiastic” about voting in November, compared with 31 per cent of Republicans, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, which surveyed 1,167 US adults nationwide.
Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today, 36 per cent of independents in the survey picked Democrats and 22 per cent said Republicans.
Since mid-August, Trump’s popularity has held at a level it only briefly touched early in his first presidency, and well below the 47 per cent share of Americans who approved of his performance early in his current term.
His rating is lower than the low point hit by his predecessor in office, Democrat Joe Biden – 35 per cent in October 2024.
Like Biden, Trump has been dogged by widespread discontent over high levels of inflation.
Petrol prices have surged since Trump ordered the US to start bombing Iran in February, and just 36 per cent of Americans approve of the war, the Reuters/Ipsos poll showed.
The conflict has had long lulls over the period, but in recent days the two sides have traded missile strikes and, since the war’s outset, Iran has largely blocked a major transit point for the global oil trade.
Some 71 per cent of Americans – including four in 10 Republicans – disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living.
For the last month, registered voters in the survey have been saying the Democratic Party has better ideas for the economy than the Republican Party, the first time Democrats have led on the issue in about a decade.

Indonesia, United States Kick Off Annual Multinational Military Exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
00:52:00 UTC
09:52:00 KST

The United States and Indonesia launched annual multilateral military exercises yesterday, which the two sides said aimed to improve interoperability and bolster deterrence in the region.
Super Garuda Shield, which has been held annually since 2007, will take place in various locations including Bandung, Lampung, Kalimantan, and the Indonesian Army’s Baturaja Combat Training Center in South Sumatra before concluding in Jakarta on September 11.
This year’s iteration will involve more than 4,743 personnel from 13 other countries including Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. A further eight nations will join as observers. While the total number of troops is slightly down on last year’s iteration, which featured a record 5,400 participants, it includes more participating nations than ever, with India taking part as an observer for the first time.
Major General Patrick Ellis, the commanding general of the U.S. Army’s 4th Infantry Division, said that the exercise was critical for “building the human architecture that keeps the Indo-Pacific safe.”
“The security landscape of the Indo-Pacific is complex and readiness cannot be surged when a crisis begins,” he said at an opening ceremony at the Indonesian Armed Forces’ School of Command in Bandung. He added, “We are not just meeting for another annual training cycle. We are writing a historic new chapter in our bilateral relationship.”
TNI Commander General Agus Subiyanto, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, said that “the purpose of the exercise is, first, diplomacy, and then cooperation through the exchange of capabilities.”
The Garuda Shield exercise was established between the U.S. and Indonesian militaries in 2007 and forms a primary pillar of the two nations’ defense relationship. “Super” was added to its title in 2022, when the exercise was expanded into a multilateral format.
This year, the exercises “will include a joint staff exercise, cyber exercise, airborne operations, jungle training, and amphibious exercise,” the U.S. Army said in a statement. U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard personnel will also conduct coordinated maritime training serials with the Indonesian Navy in adjacent waters in order “to strengthen joint interoperability at sea.”
Participating forces will also take part in special forces infiltration drills, cyber defense exercises, the firing of Stinger missiles, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations.
The expanded exercise is the first to take place since Indonesia and the U.S. established a new defense cooperation pact in April. The Major Defense Cooperation Partnership (MDCP) will bolster cooperation in Indonesian military modernization and increase training, joint exercises, and professional military education, with the aim of “maintaining peace and stability” in Asia.
Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said at the time that they “have also committed to enhance joint special forces training,” and to expand existing multilateral exercises, including Super Garuda Shield.
The continued expansion of the annual exercise speaks to the continued good health of the U.S.-Indonesia defense partnership, which has remained stable despite the erratic nature of foreign policymaking under the second Trump administration. However, while Indonesia has welcomed closer U.S. security cooperation, it continues to hew to a policy of foreign policy non-alignment, and to maintain a balanced spread of defense engagements – including with key U.S. adversaries.
For example, on the same day that Sjafrie and Hegseth signed the MDCP agreement in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto was being hosted at the Kremlin by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
And last month, Indonesia agreed to boost its military ties with China during a visit to Jakarta by the country’s foreign and defense ministers. The two sides agreed to increase joint exercises and officer exchanges. They also discussed the establishment of a joint munitions factory in Indonesia that would include a possible transfer of technology from China. Also in August, Jakarta courted controversy when an Indonesian frigate conducted a joint navigation exercise with China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy in the waters east of Taiwan – the first time that China had exercised with a foreign military in the area.
Later this year, China and Indonesia are scheduled to hold their Heping Garuda joint military exercises, which took place for the first time in December 2024. These much narrower drills will focus mostly on humanitarian aid and disaster relief operations.

Supreme Court stays FIR against Uttarakhand gym owner ‘Mohd’ Deepak
NEW DELHI: Granting relief to Dehradun-based gym owner ‘Mohd’ Deepak Kumar against whom an FIR was lodged for confronting Bajrang Dal members, Supreme Court on Monday stayed the proceedings against him and sought a response from Uttarakhand govt on quashing of the case.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta also stayed operation of the order passed by Uttarakhand HC that had restrained Deepak from making social media posts about the incident and the case. Appearing for Deepak, senior advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi said his client had protected a Muslim shopkeeper and intervened after Bajrang Dal members objected to the shopkeeper using the word 'Baba' in his shop’s name.
He said Deepak had gone to assist the shopkeeper after the incident and he had himself lodged complaints regarding the incident, but that no action was taken on them and instead an FIR was registered against him.“How can a good samaritan be subjected to this kind of a complaint?” Singhvi asked.The bench, after a brief hearing, agreed to examine the plea and granted interim protection to Deepak. “Issue notice. In the meantime, proceedings from the impugned FIR, effect and operation of the HC order to remain stayed,” court said.The case against Deepak pertains to offences under BNS sections 115(2) (causing hurt), 191(1) (rioting), 351(2) (criminal intimidation), and 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace).

Pentagon secretly hiring military influencers in social media push – WaPo

The Pentagon tightened press access rules last September as part of a broader crackdown on unauthorized disclosures following reports of turmoil inside the department. It has also reportedly considered using lie detector tests to identify officials leaking information.
Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly clashed with mainstream media over reports based on leaked documents and anonymous sources.
Earlier this month, Trump lashed out over reports that the war on Iran had significantly depleted US stocks of critical missiles and air defense interceptors, insisting no shortage existed.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Voorheis Takes Helm of Life Cycle Management Center with $400B Portfolio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
00:49:27 UTC
09:49:27 KST

Lt. Gen. Jason D. Voorheis has taken command of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, a sprawling organization with a $400 billion portfolio, establishing him as one of the service’s top acquisition officials.
Voorheis moves into the job having jumped the rank of major general. As a one star, he was program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, or C3BM, the office overseeing the Air Force’s effort to create a massive “battle network.”
Voorheis assumed command of AFLCMC on Aug. 27 during a ceremony at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, according to a release.
In his new role, Voorheis will also serve as the PAE for combat readiness and integrating PAE for mission systems.
AFLCMC has more than 21,000 employees and manages acquisition, upgrades, and support for aircraft, engines, munitions, electronics, and cyber systems. In other words, it’s the nerve center of keeping the service’s critical hardware running.
“Just about every aircraft, weapon system, uniform, and piece of gear our Airmen take into harm’s way is acquired, fielded, modernized, and sustained by the expertise within AFLCMC. You are the engine of our nation’s defense,” Voorheis told the center’s personnel at the ceremony.
Voorheis takes the post following the retirement of Lt. Gen. Donna D. Shipton, who also previously worked as the Integrating Program Executive Officer for Mission Systems.
Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams took over Voorheis’ previous role as the head of the C3BM office on Aug. 28, according to a separate release. The Air Force established C3BM in 2022, and Maj. Gen. Luke C.G. Cropsey served as its first commander, followed by Vorheis, who took over in February. Cropsey now serves as the military deputy to the Air Force acquisition executive in the Pentagon.
In bidding farewell to the C3BM office, Voorheis said his six months in the job included some of the “most rewarding experiences throughout my career.”
“The mission ahead does not pause,” Voorheis added. “Never stop challenging legacy processes that slow down capability delivery.”
The main goal of the C3BM office is to create a DAF Battle Network, an integrated system of systems that links sensor, effector, and logistics systems. With about 50 programs of record, it is the DAF’s piece of the Pentagon’s massive Combined Joint All Domain Command and Control effort, which seeks to connect any sensor, shooter, and logistics node to a shared network across all of the services.
But the three-star’s experience isn’t limited to the DAF Battle Network; he previously served as the program executive officer for fighters and advanced aircraft, the materiel leader for the F-15 program office, and system program director for the B-21 bomber, according to his official biography.
AFLCMC stood up in 2012 as part of an effort to consolidate and streamline operations within Air Force Materiel Command. It is one of six centers under AFMC, trimmed from a previous dozen centers the service operated, to lower costs, improve readiness, increase aircraft production, and reduce parts shortages, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
The other centers under AFMC are the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center, the Air Force Test Center, the Air Force Installation Management Center, and the Air Force Sustainment Center.

Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drug use.

The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected.
Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting 10th-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.
The former world number three, who had a famously contentious relationship with Kyrgios, said he was surprised the suspension did not come sooner.
"I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it," Tsitsipas said.
"So, what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, 'Here we go'. I kind of expected it, to be honest."
Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022 , when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple of shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a "bully".
Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt "helpless and alone", though added that "none of that excuses what I did".
Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas.
"I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that," he said.
"I'm not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I'll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviours that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.
"So, when I saw it, I was like, 'Well, pretty much expected, to be honest'. I am surprised it came so late, though."

US President Donald Trump has said that Venezuela's oil reserves represented "unbelievable value" that had gone untapped before a new deal between Washington and Caracas.
"It was also a very good deal for Venezuela because you have the most powerful, the richest companies in the world going into Venezuela, where before it was just this unbelievable value that was sitting dormant," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
"But we're going to be taking all of that. We're going to be taking that oil out," he said.
Trump said "all" of the crude would be directed to the US for refineries to process.
"Our refineries are specifically meant for Venezuelan heavy oil. Heavy oil is good thing, not a bad thing," he said.
"It's good for other things. You know that heavy oil is good for asphalt, roadways, all of that," he added.
Trump called the agreement "a deal that nobody's ever heard of, a deal like that. Maybe the greatest deal ever made."
He also hailed the agreement for Americans and said it would have "a tremendous impact" on prices.
"It's going to ultimately, prices are going to come down," he said.
Trump described relations with Caracas as "great" and called the relationship a "team in a sense."
"We're taking out millions and millions of barrels of oil, going to Houston, going to Louisiana, going to lots of different places in the United States and all over the world," he said.
"We're making a fortune, and they're making a fortune," he added.
Venezuela agreement
Trump's remarks followed a transaction on Friday in which Washington secured majority control over 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela.
Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who assumed power in January following a US military operation that captured Nicolas Maduro, confirmed the agreement would remain in effect for 25 years.
Rodriguez said the agreement involved developing 17 strategic fields, with more than $100 billion in expected private investment and more than $209 billion in tax revenue for Venezuela.
The shift toward Venezuelan oil came as the Strait of Hormuz, the world’s most important oil transit point, remained stranded amid the war with Iran that began on Feb. 28 and was said to have reached a stalemate.

Lebanon will not waive right to sue Israel over ‘genocide crimes’: Parliament speaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
00:47:29 UTC
09:47:29 KST

Naim Berjawi, Mohammad Sio
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Lebanon will not give up its right to pursue legal action against Israel over its “genocide crimes” in the country, the nation’s parliament speaker said Monday.
Nabih Berri made the remarks in a speech marking the 48th anniversary of the disappearance of Lebanese Shiite cleric and Amal Movement founder Musa al-Sadr, whose fate remains unknown since he disappeared in Libya in 1978, according to the Lebanese National News Agency.
Lebanon’s Shiite community holds late Libyan President Moammar Gadhafi responsible for the disappearance of al-Sadr along with his two companions, Sheikh Mohammed Yacoub and journalist Abbas Badr al-Din, during a visit to Libya. The former Libyan regime denied the allegation and said the three had left for Italy.
Berri said Lebanon’s confrontation with Israel requires “a unified national approach free of sectarian calculations.”
“What Israel wants is not Hezbollah, its weapons, Amal, or the Shiite community. Lebanon itself, its unity and civil peace, are the target,” he said, warning against allowing the country to be drawn into internal conflicts
“We reject the (June) framework agreement, and we have repeatedly warned against direct negotiations with the Israeli enemy while under fire,” Berri said.
“What have seven rounds of negotiations achieved? The areas under occupation have expanded, destruction has increased, and the number of martyrs has risen,” he added.
Berri also rejected any move to waive Lebanon’s right to prosecute Israel over “genocide crimes.”
His remarks came ahead of an expected eighth round of direct Lebanon-Israel talks in Italy in September. The seventh round ended on Aug. 6 without agreement on expanding areas from which Israeli forces would withdraw.
Lebanon and Israel signed a US-mediated framework agreement on June 26 calling for a phased Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon alongside the deployment of the Lebanese army. Subsequent talks have focused on mechanisms to implement the agreement and complete the withdrawal.
Israel has continued its aggression against Lebanon since March 2, killing more than 4,000 people and wounding over 12,000, while more than 1 million have been displaced, according to Lebanese authorities.
Israel continues to occupy parts of southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the 2023-24 war, while its latest military offensive has expanded its presence deeper inside Lebanese territory.
