New pressure on PM to allow telehealth for voluntary assisted dying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:16 UTC
04:30:16 KST

South Australian government defies Albanese, urges change to voluntary assisted dying telehealth laws
In short:
South Australia's Labor government has openly defied the prime minister's position on telehealth in voluntary assisted dying (VAD), calling for urgent change to a federal law.
It comes weeks after the ALP national conference endorsed a motion committing Labor to removing telehealth restrictions, despite Anthony Albanese's own personal opposition.
The state government has called on the Commonwealth to amend the definition of "suicide" in the criminal code to exclude VAD care.
South Australia has become the first state to formally urge the Commonwealth to change a federal law preventing doctors from using telehealth in voluntary assisted dying (VAD), openly defying the prime minister.
In a letter to federal Attorney-General Michelle Rowland, senior ministers in the Malinauskas government have "implored" the Commonwealth to "take immediate action", arguing the restrictions disadvantage terminally ill people in regional, rural and remote Australia.
"I doubt that I will be the only health minister advocating for this change," SA Health Minister Blair Boyer told ABC News.
The SA ministers' letter said a provision in the Commonwealth criminal code was preventing doctors from using telehealth for VAD and forcing patients to travel long distances to attend appointments, with some dying before being able to access the care.
The intervention puts the SA government at odds with Anthony Albanese, who has expressed personal opposition to changing the law, concerned about the risk of coercion and elder abuse if telehealth replaced compulsory face-to-face consultations.
The letter comes just weeks after the ALP national conference endorsed a motion committing Labor to removing telehealth restrictions, despite Ms Rowland — the highest law officer in Australia — voicing strong concerns on the conference floor.
Penned by Mr Boyer and state Attorney-General Kyam Maher, and co-signed by VAD practitioners, clinicians and advocates, the letter calls for the Commonwealth criminal code to be amended so VAD care is not treated as "suicide" under federal law.
Some states and territories permit limited use of telehealth in VAD, but the federal code overrides those provisions by prohibiting the use of a "carriage service" to counsel or promote suicide.
It means doctors risk $220,000 fines and a criminal record for using phone, email or video to discuss the self-administration of VAD medication.
VAD at a glance
Read more
- Each jurisdiction has its own VAD laws, but all require at least some face-to-face consultations as part of the assessment and approval process.
- There are also safeguards, including restrictions on when doctors can provide information about VAD and making it an offence to induce someone to request or access the care.
- Anthony Albanese has argued safeguards could be weakened if more consultations were conducted via telehealth.
"We suggest a targeted amendment to the definition of 'suicide' under the criminal code such that the definition explicitly excludes conduct authorised under a state or territory VAD law," the letter said.
"We now implore the Federal Government to address this issue and amend the criminal code to better reflect contemporary healthcare practice and to reduce unnecessary disparities between jurisdictions."
The move fits a pattern of the Malinauskas government pursuing its own agenda on contentious national policy debates.
In recent years, South Australia has outlawed political donations, established a royal commission into artificial intelligence and spearheaded the development of a teen social media ban, an initiative followed by the federal government.
Mr Boyer predicted other states would soon join the push to change the criminal code, signalling broader pressure could build.
"This is not an attempt to water down safeguards that were put in place. It is simply an attempt to make good on the commitment that was made," he said.
"This is something that should be available to people regardless of where they live."
The federal government recently blocked debate of a VAD telehealth bill pushed by independent MP Kate Chaney, with Health Minister Mark Butler telling parliament he was "not convinced" telehealth was "well suited to VAD right now".
Doctors divided
Views on telehealth in VAD care are also divided within the medical community.
While the Australian Medical Association (AMA) has backed calls to change the federal law, some doctors remain opposed.
Ballarat geriatrician Mark Yates argued the risks of elder abuse and coercion outweighed the benefits of expanding telehealth access.
Professor Yates said data showed rural, regional and remote Australians were accessing VAD at rates proportional to the population, suggesting there was no widespread access problem, and that individual cases of people missing out highlighted broader failures in regional health services.
"I think [those cases] are an argument for jurisdictions to get their acts together and provide better support and services, whether it's wider-based VAD services or better palliative care,"
Professor Yates said telehealth made it harder to detect coercion or abuse and argued the risk was compounded by the small number of doctors providing VAD.
"When we started the VAD debate, the idea was that it would be your friendly GP who's known you for 30 years who would help you with this. That's clearly not the case. There are one or two practitioners that have [overseen] 300 people with VAD in the short time we've had it.
"To appreciate where coercion or abuse sits without being face-to-face, I think is incredibly difficult. That is where the risk lies."

Iraq sentences militia member for kidnapping American journalist, in rare move against Iran proxies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:08 UTC
04:30:08 KST

Iraq has sentenced a man to fifteen years in prison for kidnapping American journalist Shelly Kittelson in late March, the victim announced on social media on Monday.
Kittelson was kidnapped on March 31, when she was targeted by Iranian-backed militias, and released in early April.
“Iraq's Central Criminal Court has sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim to 15 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Law after convicting him of being one of several armed men who took me hostage in Baghdad on March 31,” read her X/Twitter post.
She added, “I am grateful to the Iraqi judiciary for its attention to my case, as well as to all those who helped get me out alive. And, of course, to those who love Iraq as much as I do and try to build a better future for it. Thank you from the very depths of my being.”
Rudaw media in Iraq added that “an Iraqi court has sentenced a key suspect to 15 years in prison under the country's anti-terrorism law in connection with the abduction of American journalist Shelly Kittleson in Baghdad earlier this year, a case the US linked to the Iran-backed Kata'ib Hezbollah armed group.”
Rare prosecution of Iranian-backed militia member
The development is important because Iraq rarely prosecutes members of the Iranian-backed militias. In the past, members of the militias have sometimes been detained by authorities, but are often released. There is now pressure in Iraq for the government to rein in the militias, after the US encouraged Baghdad to make progress toward disarming the groups.
The militias have been involved in acts of kidnapping and murder for years. In 2020, Dr. Hisham al-Hashimi was assassinated by gunmen outside his home in the Zeyouneh neighborhood of Baghdad. He was a journalist and security expert. Kataib Hezbollah was also behind the kidnapping of Princeton researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in March 2023. She was released in September 2025.
Rudaw noted that “the Central Criminal Court in Baghdad on Sunday sentenced ‘the convict - Amir Rahim Jabbar Lazem - to fifteen years in prison’ pursuant to Iraq's Anti-Terrorism Law ‘for the crime of kidnapping the complainant - Shelly Renee Kittleson of American nationality - on March 31, 2026, in the al-Saadoun area’ in the Iraqi capital, read a copy of the ruling obtained by Rudaw.”
He has already been detained since April for the kidnapping. Other men were involved in the kidnapping. Video at the time showed other individuals. An eyewitness at the scene at the time told Rudaw that "three people surrounded her [Kittleson] and one of them grabbed her from behind."
Kataib Hezbollah suspected to be behind kidnapping
Kataib Hezbollah, which is believed to have been behind the kidnapping, is one of the most powerful of the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. It has been sanctioned by the US as a terrorist organization. It is part of the paramilitary Popular Mobilization Forces.
Its former leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis was killed in a US drone strike in January 2020. He was driving in a vehicle alongside IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, who was the target of the strike and who was also killed. The fact that Muhandis and Soleimani were in the same vehicle illustrates the close ties between the IRGC and Iranian-backed militias.
It does not appear Iraq will hold Kataib Hezbollah responsible for the kidnapping or other crimes. Kataib Hezbollah was also likely behind a drone attack that killed three American service members in Jordan in January 2024. It has also been behind attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Former French PM Balladur dies at 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:25:36 UTC
04:25:36 KST

Former French PM Balladur dies at 97
PARIS, Aug 31 - Edouard Balladur, who was France's prime minister from 1993 to 1995, has died at 97, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on X on Monday.
A leading figure of France's centre-right, Balladur was the architect of a sweeping privatisation drive that saw the sale of some of France's most prominent companies, including banks Société Générale and Paribas — later part of BNP Paribas — as well as broadcaster TF1. He also pushed through a reform of France's politically sensitive pension system in 1993.
"Edouard Balladur is closely associated with fifty years of the history of the Fifth Republic. From his early days working alongside Georges Pompidou to his appointment as Prime Minister, he was a leading figure in our public life," Lecornu said on X.
"Edouard Balladur was a statesman with a reformist spirit and will remain a role model for many men and women in his political family," he added.
A stiff technocrat, Balladur was often portrayed by his critics as aloof and disconnected. Plantu, a press cartoonist, sketched him as an aristocrat wearing a wig and seated in a sedan chair. The satirical weekly Le Canard enchaîné renamed him "His Courteous Smugness".
Balladur served as prime minister under Socialist President Francois Mitterrand. REUTERS

US targets China’s global trade surplus at G20 meeting ahead of Xi-Trump summit

Nayan Sethin Washington
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday targeted China’s global trade surplus, raising concerns over “excessive imbalances,” weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to arrive in Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump.
“We are confronting persistent global imbalances that undermine prosperity,” Bessent said in his opening address at the G20 Finance Ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. The United States holds the G20 presidency in 2026, leading a forum of the world’s major advanced and emerging economies.
Without naming China, Bessent said that the grouping’s finance ministers and central bank governors “have broadly concurred that it is in the interests of both surplus and deficit countries to address excessive imbalances”.
“We have seen how distorted policies that privileged countries’ own exports have harmed many of the economies represented here today,” he said, adding that a “durable global economy cannot rest on beggar-thy-neighbour acts that stifle fair market-based competition.”
Washington has made trade imbalances a key theme of the G20 ministerial – part of decades-long complaints about Beijing’s high trade surpluses – as a surge in Chinese exports of major products such as automobiles, solar panels and batteries has raised concerns in many countries over Beijing’s alleged “overcapacity”.

Poland sees two fires at defense plants in 24 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:00:53 UTC
04:00:53 KST

- Two fires broke out at Polish defense-linked facilities within 24 hours, one destroying a Lublin aviation composites plant and another hitting a drone-component maker in Skarżysko-Kamienna.
- JFG Composites supplies Leonardo's PZL-Świdnik helicopter plant, while WB Electronics produces drone components used by Polish and Ukrainian forces.
A fire destroyed a two-story warehouse building in Lublin, Poland, Sunday afternoon, gutting facilities owned by JFG Composites, a subcontractor to Leonardo’s PZL-Świdnik helicopter plant, according to Polish outlet Defence24.
The fire broke out around 2:00 p.m. local time on Kasprowicza Street and spread through the building’s warehouse and office sections, PAP reported, according to Slawa. The building burned to the ground. Emergency services received the report shortly before 3:00 p.m., and about 60 firefighters responded to the scene. Gray smoke was visible from several kilometers away.
According to the city’s State Fire Service office in Lublin, no injuries were reported, and no residents needed to be evacuated.
JFG Composites specializes in manufacturing composite materials and components for the aviation industry, according to Defence24. The company operates as a subcontractor for Leonardo, the Italian defense conglomerate that owns PZL-Świdnik, a Polish manufacturer of aircraft including the AW149 helicopter.
Polish authorities have not disclosed a cause for the fire or confirmed whether it is being investigated as accidental or deliberate.
The Lublin fire is at least the second incident this week at a European facility tied to defense or aerospace manufacturing. A fire also broke out overnight Sunday at a WB Electronics facility in Skarżysko-Kamienna, Poland, which produces components for drones used by Polish and Ukrainian forces.
That fire started shortly after midnight in the plant’s assembly department, according to Radio Kielce, which cited a spokeswoman for local police. Five fire crews and police responded, the facility was not operating at the time, and no injuries were reported. Police are investigating the possibility of arson after journalist Jakub Wiech reported that surveillance footage showed a masked person entering the site shortly before the blaze began.
Neither Polish fire nor the incident’s proximity to JFG Composites’ aviation supply chain role has been publicly linked by authorities to the WB Electronics fire or to the broader pattern of suspected sabotage incidents The Defence Blog has tracked at European defense manufacturers this year.

What’s next for NASA’s new Roman Space Telescope?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:57:21 UTC
03:57:21 KST

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is already exceeding expectations.
After reaching the launchpad ahead of schedule and on budget, the spy-satellite-sourced, $4-billion project pulled off a flawless launch to space on Sunday morning. At a postlaunch press conference, NASA officials noted that the performance of the rocket that took the telescope to space was so picture-perfect that Roman will likely need fewer trajectory adjustments than planned. That means Roman’s onboard fuel could instead help extend the observatory’s five-year mission to a full decade.
Lofted onboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, Roman was “exactly where it needed to be,” said Denton Gibson, launch director of NASA’s Launch Services Program, at the press event. “That’s a monumental effort because we know the more accurate the launch vehicle is, the more science we can get.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“A launch is such a transition point,” said Julie McEnery, Roman’s senior project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). “It’s a transition because it’s an end point for the engineers, but it’s a starting point for the scientists.”
Roman “will contribute to world-changing science,” said NASA administrator Jared Isaacman. In addition to the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), “Roman will become a household name alongside those great instruments of discovery.”
Separating from its rocket about 30 minutes after launch, Roman successfully deployed its power-providing solar panels and spacecraft-cooling sunshield and will soon unfurl its high-gain antenna for broadband communications with Earth.
In the coming days, the observatory will perform a midcourse correction burn on its approximately three-month voyage to the second sun-Earth Lagrange point, or L2. There, situated 750,000 miles beyond the moon, Roman will begin its science mission to study dark energy, dark matter and exoplanets.
Along the way, the telescope will power up its two core science payloads: a wide-field infrared camera for panoramic views of the cosmos that will be 100 times wider than Hubble’s and an advanced coronagraph for capturing unprecedented images of exoplanets.
Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, summarized the sheer scale of Roman’s expected discoveries at the press conference: “Billions of galaxies will be found, tens of billions of new stars, tens of thousands of new planets, and thousands of supernovae—all wrapped up in one beautiful telescope.”
The observatory should beam back its first images before the winter holidays, said Jackie Townsend, Roman’s project manager at GSFC. And the telescope’s first year of science observations, slated to begin in January 2027, will be action-packed.
One of the mission’s top priorities will be putting the coronagraph through its paces—presumably by taking snapshots of known exoplanetary systems. “Let’s get that technology demonstration nailed so that we can think about what we might want to do next with that instrument,” McEnery said. Observations with Roman’s coronagraph could unveil Jupiter-like planets around nearby stars and will guide the development of NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, which will target smaller, more Earth-like worlds.
Another early focus for the mission will involve using Roman’s wide-field camera to stare at the Milky Way’s star-packed central bulge. Those observations will constitute “a deeper, sharper view of the center of our galaxy” than ever before, McEnery said, and will ultimately deliver most of Roman’s exoplanet discoveries while initially helping mission controllers gauge the telescope’s on-sky performance.
In its first year Roman will also undertake a “pilot survey” of supernovae popping off across the sky and will separately gaze out of the galactic plane to gain a better view of the far-distant cosmos—similar to previous “deep field” images from Hubble, JWST and other telescopes.
“A year from now, we will have found thousands of new exoplanets, [and] we will have used the coronagraph to demonstrate new technologies in space for the first time,” McEnery said. “We will have conducted our pilot survey..., so we will be making new precise measurements of supernovae. Those same observations will allow us to catch the unexpected.... I’m pretty certain we’re going to find something we didn’t expect with that. And I think that that will probably be the most exciting result [of Roman’s first year of science].”
Roman’s most promising aspect, perhaps, is its synergy with Hubble, JWST and other facilities such as the U.S. Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope. Rubin and Euclid are each performing their own panoramic sky surveys, with significant areas of overlap with Roman’s. All three projects will collectively contribute to better measurements of how cosmic structure is changing over time—crucial information for clarifying the nature of dark energy and dark matter in the universe’s evolution.
And although, as a survey-style telescope, Roman boasts a wider, faster view of the sky than either Hubble or JWST, McEnery emphasized that doesn’t make these more focused missions obsolete. “There are things that Hubble [and JWST] can do that aren’t duplicated on any of our other observatories,” she said. “[With Roman] we’re redefining what it means to find a needle in a haystack—and when we find those needles, Hubble and Webb can then follow up, while Roman continues to go off and find new things.”
One of the postlaunch press conference’s most surprising moments came after Isaacman received an unexpected call midway through the briefing from President Donald J. Trump, who praised the mission’s success via speakerphone. It marks a change of heart for the administration, which had repeatedly proposed deep cuts to NASA’s science that included canceling Roman entirely. In the end, the observatory was saved by congressional intervention.
Isaacman shrugged off the shift. “The president of the United States is excited about our next great exploration asset that’s underway. I think that’s a great moment,” he said. “So I’m incredibly grateful for his support.... I do believe we’re entering a new golden age of discovery right now, and I think I’m going to have a lot to thank the president for on that.”

 Isaac ben Solomon Israeli (ca. 855 – 955 CE), not to be confused with Isaac Israeli the Younger (an astronomer of Spain, d. 1322 CE), served as physician to the founder of the Fatimid Dynasty in North Africa and wrote several philosophical and medical treatises in Arabic which were subsequently translated and widely read in Latin and Hebrew. Mortgage rates surge to the highest since June 2025 as new Middle East attacks push oil prices up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:53:36 UTC
03:53:36 KST

A jump in oil prices after renewed hostilities in the Iran war is pushing bond yields higher, and mortgage rates are following suit.
The average rate on the 30-year fixed loan jumped 6 basis points on Monday to 6.87%, according to Mortgage News Daily. That is the highest level since June 2025. It's now up 12 basis points since Thursday and has risen more than 30 basis points in the last two months.
"While rates are technically at their highest level in more than a year, they haven't exactly exploded with surprising, new momentum," said Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "Instead, it's been more of a slow grind fueled by the usual suspects: inflation expectations, elevated bond issuance, and economic resilience. All three of those factors are subject to at least some variability in the future."
The expectation had been for falling rates this year, but the war with Iran and its resulting rise in oil prices upended that. The day before the war started, at the end of February, the rate on the 30-year fixed was 5.99%.
To put that into perspective, for someone buying a $450,000 home, which is right around the national median, putting 20% down on a 30-year fixed mortgage, the monthly principal and interest payment today would be $2,363. That is $207 a month more than it would have been back at the end of February.
And that's just the payment. When rates go up, fewer borrowers can qualify for a mortgage, as it shifts the debt-to-income ratios that lenders rely on for safe lending.
This comes on top of higher home prices, which seem to now be accelerating again in some parts of the country, due to lean supply.
Nationally, prices in June were up 1.5% year over year, up from the 1.2% rise in May, according to the latest S&P Cotality Case-Shiller home price index.
"As financing costs are kept high for prospective buyers, current homeowners remain reluctant to give up the low mortgage rates secured in prior years," said Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices, in a news release.

The NRSC said that private polling in that state shows Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a "dead heat" with Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown in the special election to fill the remainder of the term for the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance.
In May, Gallup said a survey conducted in March found that "seven in 10 Americans oppose constructing data centers for artificial intelligence in their local area, including nearly half, 48%, who are strongly opposed."
On Aug. 28, Wolfe Research issued a report that said, "In nearly every meeting with investors over the past month or so, we've been asked: How is the voter backlash against data centers going to play out?"
"The pace and scale of the backlash is genuinely breathtaking — we've never seen anything like it," the report said. "We've seen 60-point drops in net support for local data center (DC) construction across party lines over the past 12 months."
The upcoming midterm elections will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress. Republicans hold a narrow majority in the House of Representatives, and a 53-47 majority in the Senate.
AI data centers house computing equipment used to train and operate artificial intelligence models developed by companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
The rush to build data centers has sparked a backlash in communities across the U.S., with opponents raising concerns about electricity costs, power demand, water use and other local impacts.
In its Aug. 18 memo, the NRSC warned that "the current perception is negative" among Americans about data centers as it detailed how the issue is affecting the race for the Senate in Ohio.
"Private polling has been consistent: when voters hear Brown's positions and his record, Husted pulls away. That is still the path in this race," the memo said. "The new ingredient (and the new problem) is data centers.
"Ohio is one of the leaders in building these AI factories," the NRSC said. "Brown has made his opposition to them the centerpiece of his campaign against Husted. Brown is using it because it works."
"More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck. If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one."

Ukrainian anti-corruption agencies to check origin of bail money for suspects in several cases

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31

Ukrainian anti-corruption agencies to check origin of bail money for suspects in several cases
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) are to check the legality of funds transferred to the High Anti-Corruption Court as bail for suspects in several criminal proceedings, including Andrii Yermak, former head of the President's Office.
Source: SAPO Head Oleksandr Klymenko in an interview with the Ye pytannia YouTube channel
Details: Asked whether NABU and SAPO will be checking the source of the funds used to pay bail for Yermak, Klymenko said: "That's quite an interesting question. We did have certain suspicions regarding the payment of various bail amounts in our investigations, and we will check this as far as possible. It's more difficult to confirm everything retrospectively than in real time, but in principle, that's the direction we'll be moving in."
He added that there is an established and effective mechanism for checking the origin of funds.
"There is a mechanism. It's quite effective if it operates in accordance with the law and there is no manual interference. Funds are monitored as they are paid into the bank accounts of individuals, sole traders and legal entities. This is done by the bank's financial monitoring department," Klymenko said.
He explained that if the department notices a suspicious transaction, it is obliged to report it to the State Financial Monitoring Service.
Asked again whether such checks will be carried out with respect to the funds used as bail for Yermak, Klymenko said: "Not just in that particular case. There are many proceedings where we are planning to conduct such checks in general."
He added that the anti-corruption authorities often conduct such checks without criminal proceedings being opened.
Quote: "We contact the financial monitoring service without registering criminal proceedings so that they can trace the entire chain of how the funds entered the financial system. If the chain begins, for example, with unexplained people who have no source of income depositing cash into the bank accounts of certain legal entities, and the money is then transferred along the chain and ends up in the account of the High Anti-Corruption Court, this raises suspicions and they have to investigate it."
Details: Asked whether SAPO currently has grounds to suspect that Yermak's bail followed the same pattern as the bail paid for former energy minister Herman Halushchenko, Klymenko said: "I don't want to put forward any theories or versions of events. We need to gather certain factual data and then work with it and draw conclusions."
Background:
- In May, NABU and SAPO served Andrii Yermak with a notice of suspicion in a case concerning the alleged laundering of UAH 460 million (around US$10.5 million) through a high-end construction project outside Kyiv.
- Sources in political and business circles have told Ukrainska Pravda that Yermak's UAH 140 million bail money was raised across virtually the entire government hierarchy: in the President's Office, in parliament – where Servant of the People faction leader Davyd Arakhamiia was one of those involved – and among ministers. Even former Ukraine national football team coach Serhii Rebrov was reportedly forced to contribute UAH 30 million (around US$675,096).
- Former Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko was served with a notice of suspicion in the Midas case in February. He is suspected of large-scale money laundering. The High Anti-Corruption Court initially ordered him to be remanded in custody with the option of posting UAH 150 million (around US$3.3 million) bail. The court later extended Halushchenko's detention but reduced the bail from UAH 200 million to UAH 150 million. The former minister remained in a pre-trial detention centre from February until almost the end of June. At one point, rumours emerged that he might strike a deal with investigators.
- According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources, the authorities subsequently stepped up efforts to find the money needed for Halushchenko's bail. Sources told UP that the problem was not that the money was unavailable in the authorities' numerous back offices, but that the funds had to be legitimate rather than stolen millions.
- At the time, UP sources among influential businesspeople claimed that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had tasked his chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov with finding and legalising the funds. Budanov, in turn, brought in former MP and property developer Maksym Mykytas.
- On 29 June, UAH 150 million was ultimately posted as bail for Herman Halushchenko. The money was provided by little-known companies with little-known owners.
- On 19 August, it became known that NABU and SAPO had managed to document the operation to "rescue" Halushchenko. According to investigators, the collection and legalisation of the funds for Halushchenko's bail were coordinated by Iryna Mudra, who was deputy head of the President's Office at the time.

IRIS² Satellite Communications Project Secures First €1 Billion Contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:43:45 UTC
03:43:45 KST

Luxembourg-based satellite operator SES has signed a deal with the German company OHB worth nearly €1 billion to develop and build satellites for the European IRIS² communications system.
The German manufacturer will produce 18 satellites for medium Earth orbit, according to European Spaceflight.
The launch mass of each satellite will be approximately 2.6 metric tons.
This contract marks the first major order under IRIS² after the program officially entered the implementation phase in early August 2026.
The total cost of the European project, aimed at creating a secure communications infrastructure for the EU, is estimated at €15.6 billion.
SES’s contribution to the deployment will amount to up to €1.3 billion.
The project is being carried out by the SpaceRISE consortium, in which SES is responsible for the medium-earth orbit, Eutelsat is deploying a low-earth orbit constellation of 330 satellites, and Hispasat is building the ground infrastructure.
The launch of the first IRIS² satellites is scheduled for 2029, and initial services are expected to begin in 2030.
IRIS² is a European Union project to create its own multi-tier satellite communications system.
Its goal is to provide the EU with secure, resilient, and independent communications without relying on private or non-European operators.
The system will serve both government and commercial purposes: from defense, governance, and diplomacy to high-speed internet in remote regions of Europe.
IRIS² is seen as Europe’s answer to Starlink. Part of the project’s budget will be covered by the EU, with the remainder coming from private investors.

Germany funds 100 Humvee-sized heavy robots for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:39:19 UTC
03:39:19 KST

- Ukraine's National Guard received the first 10 of 100 Protector heavy ground robots contracted with German government funding.
- The Humvee-sized vehicles are used for frontline logistics and casualty evacuation, with a payload capacity of 1,480 kilograms in this configuration.
Ukraine’s National Guard just started fielding a robot roughly the size of a Humvee, built to haul ammunition into combat zones so soldiers don’t have to.
Four units of Ukraine’s National Guard have received the first batch of Protector ground robotic complexes, part of a 100-unit contract funded by the German government, the National Guard said. Manufacturer Ukrainian Armor confirmed on X that the first 10 vehicles have already been produced and delivered.
This isn’t a small scout drone rolling on toy-sized wheels. The Protector is one of Ukraine’s largest unmanned ground vehicles, built on a diesel off-road chassis and weighing up to 4,000 kilograms (8,818 pounds), roughly in the weight class of a Humvee. It measures more than five meters (16.6 feet) long and stands nearly two meters (6.5 feet) wide, powered by a 190-horsepower engine.
Ukrainian Armor lists the payload capacity for the version supplied to the National Guard at 1,480 kilograms (3,263 pounds), one of the highest figures among current robotic logistics platforms, and higher than the 700-kilogram rating listed for earlier Protector configurations sold through Ukraine’s Brave1 Market platform, where the vehicle has been listed at $90,000. The National Guard version can also tow a trailer weighing up to 4 tonnes (4.4 tons), adding even more cargo capacity per trip. Soldiers from a separate Ukrainian brigade using the Protector have reported hauling nearly a metric ton of supplies in a single run, enough to resupply a frontline unit for roughly a week.
“Our logistics UGV has already proven itself well in military units subordinate to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine,” said Vladyslav Belbas, general director of Ukrainian Armor. “Based on positive feedback from military personnel and understanding the need to protect people at the front, partners have contracted 100 of our complexes for the National Guard of Ukraine. Robotizing logistics allows important tasks to be carried out without unnecessary risk to personnel.”
The Protector’s core job is to keep soldiers away from the most dangerous stretch of road on the battlefield, the final approach into frontline positions. Beyond carrying ammunition, food, fuel and engineering supplies, the vehicle can evacuate wounded soldiers, removing them from combat zones without putting a driver at risk. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the Protector in June 2025, and the vehicle entered serial production within two months. Depending on the configuration ordered, the platform can also carry electronic warfare equipment, a drone launch catapult, or remote weapon modules, including a version fitted with a 12.7mm Browning M2 machine gun known as the Tavria-12.7.
A Protector is already in frontline use with a separate National Guard artillery brigade and is set to be deployed to the Dobropillia sector, according to the National Guard.
“The complex has already proven itself well in our brigade,” said Sgt. Yevhen Kocherhin of that artillery brigade. “I especially want to note the sensitivity and smoothness of control in conditions far from ideal. The power, speed and payload capacity speak for themselves. For our artillery brigade, one of the key tasks is transporting heavy ammunition, and this is exactly where the Protector can significantly reduce risks to personnel.”
The vehicle’s size hasn’t made it invincible. Protector units operated by other Ukrainian formations, including the 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade “Achilles,” have previously survived FPV drone strikes mid-mission and still completed their deliveries, though other units have been damaged beyond recovery by mines while returning from resupply runs.

AI generated
LISBON - One year after an accident that left 16 dead, Portuguese authorities announced on Aug 31 that the emblematic funicular hit by the disaster would be replaced.
Eleven foreigners were among the dead when the cable on the 140-year-old Gloria funicular broke and a carriage hurtled into a building on Sept 3, 2025.
The Gloria and the city’s two other funiculars have been shut down since.
Investigators highlighted a series of failures but said that an underground cable linking the two carriages on the funicular had broken.
The Carris transport company, owned by Lisbon city authorities, said a tender for a new system would be launched in early 2027 aiming to have a new funicular running by 2029.
Carris president Rui Pedro Gaspar Lopo said the line would be new and “not a reconstruction” of the long-time tourism favourite.
“The future lift will be new, but the site will remain historic,” he said.
“Carris must develop a robust and technically advanced solution. We want a modern project, but one that enhances the historic identity” of the old lift, added Goncalo Reis, deputy head of the city council. AFP

What We Know About ‘Dollyfest,’ the Festival Dolly Parton Planned to Host—and That’s Now Being Held in Her Honor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:28:56 UTC
03:28:56 KST

A festival will be held in Dolly Parton’s honor across consecutive weekends in Tennessee and England next year, the late country music legend’s estate announced on Monday.
Dubbed “Dollyfest,” the festival was initially scheduled to take place in Nashville on Parton’s 80th birthday this past January. Parton was set to serve as both the host and a performer at the event, which was also planned to include performances from several other musicians. In a statement on Monday, Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said that the festival was “a dream of Dolly’s.” But as Parton was dealing with health issues in recent months, she “had to take a step back” from the event, Nozell said.
In the wake of her death last week, Parton’s estate revealed in a press release on Monday that the festival will now be held in 2027 to honor her legacy.
“What Dolly started, we will ensure is brought to life,” Nozell said. “A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!).”
Read More: Dolly Parton's Life, in Pictures
The festival will take place in both Nashville and London, and “will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world,” according to the release. Parton’s estate has not yet shared details about the specific dates it will be held or the performers it will feature, but said that more information about the event would be shared at a later date.
“We are not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in the ways they choose,” Nozell said. “However, as far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted. So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.”
“This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan,” Nozell said.
Last week, Parton’s publicist told news outlets that the country music icon had died after a “brief battle with cancer.” Parton had been dealing with health issues over the past year, postponing and later canceling several shows. She revealed in October that she was having “a few treatments here and there” at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, and said in May that her immune and digestive systems “got all out of whack” over the past few years and that her doctors were “working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those.”
Almost immediately after her family announced her death, tributes for Parton began flooding in—from politicians like President Donald Trump to musical artists like Beyoncé.
“You were the barometer. The North Star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself,” Beyoncé said in a statement. “Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one.”
A private funeral service was held for Parton’s immediate family on Friday, The Associated Press reported.
Parton’s great-niece, Lainey Parton, shared a post on Instagram the following day, in which she wrote a touching tribute to Parton and included photos of them together.
“This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words,” Lainey Parton said in the caption. “From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.”
“It still doesn’t feel real that she’s gone. I’m going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there,” she continued. “Thank you to everyone who has reached out, sent messages, flowers to my house, or done any of the little things to show me love. I’ve noticed every single one, and they’ve meant more than you know. I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny.”
There are no public services planned by Parton’s family and estate, but her family encouraged fans to share tributes online and donate to Parton’s Imagination Library, a program she launched in 1995 that mails books to children for free.

Sweden signs contract for four French-built frigates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:24:26 UTC
03:24:26 KST

- Naval Group signed a contract to build four FDI frigates for Sweden's Royal Navy, with first delivery scheduled for 2030.
- The deal follows Sweden's selection of the FDI class less than four months ago and includes technology transfer to Swedish industry.
Naval Group signed a contract in Stockholm on Monday to build four defense and intervention frigates for the Royal Swedish Navy, less than four months after Sweden announced its selection of the French-designed FDI class.
The signing took place in the presence of French President Emmanuel Macron and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. Mikael Granholm, Director-General of the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration, signed on behalf of Sweden, while Pierre Éric Pommellet, Chairman and CEO of Naval Group, signed for the company. The deal followed exclusive negotiations between Naval Group and Sweden’s Ministry of Defence, conducted with support from the French government.
“I am delighted to be in Stockholm today to sign the contract for the delivery of four FDI frigates to Sweden, a major milestone in the cooperation between our two countries,” Pommellet said. “It is an honour to put our expertise at the service of the Swedish Royal Navy’s sovereignty and naval superiority, and I would like to thank the Swedish authorities for their trust. Naval Group is already fully involved and committed to the delivery of this major project.”
The FDI is a French-designed frigate already in service with the French and Hellenic navies, with two units delivered to date. Naval Group said the existing production line will allow it to meet Sweden’s requirement for rapid delivery, with the first Swedish frigate scheduled for 2030.
The frigate carries anti-air capabilities built around the ASTER missile system and is designed to operate in demanding maritime environments, including the High North, the Baltic Sea and the North Atlantic. Naval Group said the ships will support Sweden’s role in NATO and inter-allied naval operations.
Swedish Navy chief Rear Adm. Johan Norlén wrote in an opinion piece published the same day that the purchase reflects a changed mission for Sweden’s fleet since joining NATO. He said the Navy’s task has shifted from defending only Swedish territory to maintaining operational control over the Baltic Sea and its approaches, including protecting shipping bound for Finland and the Baltic states.
“Sweden’s Navy must now ensure that important shipping can reach us and our allies, such as Finland and the Baltic states,” Norlén wrote.
Norlén said the frigates’ size allows them to carry the weapons and sensors required for air defense against threats ranging from drones to ballistic missiles, and to remain on station for extended periods beyond the Baltic Sea. He addressed criticism that Sweden should invest solely in uncrewed systems, citing a recent meeting with his Ukrainian naval counterpart.
“Today Ukraine mainly uses drones because they lack other capabilities,” Norlén wrote. “They have achieved success in preventing Russia from using parts of the Black Sea for its purposes, but have greater difficulty ensuring the protection of their own shipping there.”
Naval Group said it will build a long-term industrial partnership with Swedish companies as part of the deal, including the transfer of know-how and technology to several Swedish partners.

Ex-gang leader found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
Jury finds Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis guilty of orchestrating drive-by shooting, marking first conviction in decades-old case
An ex-street gang leader accused of orchestrating the drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur three decades ago in Las Vegas was convicted of murder on Monday for his role in a long-unsolved crime that silenced one of rap music’s most influential voices.
A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours before finding Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a downtown Las Vegas courtroom. Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13.
Davis told the judge “he plans to appeal this matter”. Several people in the gallery wiped away tears and hugged a prosecutor as the court adjourned.
Binu Palal of the Clark County District Attorney’s Office told jurors that under the code of respect in street gangs, Davis could not let the beating of his nephew slide.
“So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr Shakur,” Palal said.
Police say they long suspected Davis but did not have enough evidence to charge him until he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir, which, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, make up most of the prosecution’s case.

Breaking Down the Savage Season 1 Finale of Furious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:13:40 UTC
03:13:40 KST

Warning: This post contains spoilers for the finale of Furious.
By the end of the eighth and final episode of the first season of Furious, billionaire Jay Easton (Peter McRobbie) is dead, Catherine (Lola Petticrew) is in prison, and Alice (Emmy Rossum) has secured a full-time position working under Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine) in the Bureau's basement-level sex crimes unit. But not all was as simple as it seemed, as creator Elizabeth Meriwether's cat-and-mouse thriller still had a final twist up its sleeve.
Over the course of its first seven episodes, Furious tracked NYPD homicide detective-turned-probationary FBI duty agent Alice's hunt for serial killer Catherine, a sex trafficking survivor targeting wealthy, high-profile men involved in her past abuse. Along the way, we learned Catherine's primary motive was not simply retributive justice, but rather a desire to uncover the truth about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the death of her best friend and first love Isabel (Larissa Campos) at the Easton estate over a decade earlier. With the help of Nora's corrupt boss Ed (Danny McCarthy), Jay covered up Isabel's death to shield his involvement in a prolific child sexual abuse and trafficking ring. Catherine is convinced Jay himself killed Isabel, but due to the severe memory distortion she suffers from as a result of her trauma, she can't fully remember what happened on that fateful night.
After Catherine's fiancé Alden (Steve Way) gave Alice's former partner Danny (Scoot McNairy) a flash drive containing years of incriminating evidence against Jay and his associates, it was revealed there was a folder containing an illicit video of a then-14-year-old Alice being abused by one of the men within Jay's network. Episode 7 then ended with Alice tracking down Catherine and, instead of arresting her, manipulating her into driving out to Jay's Connecticut estate while Alice followed closely behind in order to orchestrate an incident that would allow Alice to search Jay's compound and arrest him without handing over the flash drive.
Who killed Isabel?
Although Episode 7 led us to believe Jay's daughter Emma (Hope Davis) was going to be exposed as the person who had killed Isabel, Furious had a much more tragic reveal on the way. While Emma was anything but innocent considering she spent years procuring underage girls for her father and destroyed evidence of his crimes to protect their family, in the finale, she helped Catherine remember that Catherine herself was the one who ultimately injected Isabel with the drugs that killed her.
On the night Isabel died, both girls had been brought to the Easton house to be abused by Jay and his men. However, Isabel had only recently given birth to her daughter Elena (Chloe Carrillo) and started hemorrhaging and crying out in pain, which led to Jay hitting her. Isabel then asked Catherine to end her life and put her out of her misery, and Catherine complied. In the present timeline, after Catherine finally came to terms with what actually happened, Alice arrests her. While the other cops who had arrived then take over the scene, Alice goes upstairs to find Jay and ends up witnessing him dying of respiratory failure—though we will soon learn that she did more than just witness his demise.
How does the finale end?
Since Emma had destroyed all the evidence at the house and Jay was no longer around to be interrogated, it initially seemed like everyone in Jay's circle was going to get off scot free while only Catherine went to prison, reinforcing the show's overarching message about our flawed justice system. But after weighing the personal cost of exposing her video, Alice decided to hand the flash drive over to Nora so she would at least be able to take Ed down.
While visiting Catherine in prison, Alice learned that Catherine had caught on to the fact that Alice had killed Jay that night by purposefully stepping on his breathing tube to cut off his oxygen supply. Alice also decided to take Nora's advice and watch the video of her abuse in order to face her trauma head on. The finale then ended with Alice using the FBI's search database to look up a list of everyone who had ever downloaded her file, implying Alice may have acquired a taste for the same method of vigilante justice Catherine had been so fond of doling out. And since it was announced on Aug. 27 that Furious has been renewed for a second season, it seems like we're eventually going to get to see Alice attempting to balance her devotion to her role as a FBI agent with her newfound thirst for vengeance against those who wronged her.
We also get a satisfying closing note to Alice and Danny's relationship, as they decompress from the events of the season during a romantic getaway at the beach house he mentioned several episodes back. As to what will happen between them in the future, Rossum tells Entertainment Weekly it's open-ended. "Now all of a sudden, they could be together, but he’s also processing not being really able to hold the totality of who she is and her secrets now that he knows the tape and has seen part of it," she says. "So I think it’s really complicated, and I think getting to watch the human toll on him, the potential partner of somebody that has been a victim of violence and sexual violence is really interesting.”

KYIV - Kyiv on Aug 31 announced a review of security protocols – especially for public transport – after a dramatic surge in Russian drone attacks it says are aimed at “paralysing” the Ukrainian capital.
After intensifying its missile strikes on Kyiv earlier this summer, Russia has also drastically increased its daily drone attacks.

The metro no longer crosses the Dnieper River, which divides the capital in two, causing traffic chaos.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram he had met with local officials on Aug 31 to discuss changes to security protocols, suggesting one metro line remain open despite strikes.
City hall also announced it was preparing changes for schools, including remote learning, as the school year begins in Ukraine on Sept 1.
Kyiv residents took to social media to question whether it was possible to continue living in the capital, especially with children, with some mulling a move to safer areas.
“The enemy is trying to paralyse economic activity in the capital and major cities,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Facebook on Aug 29.
“Prolonged air-raid alerts affect not only people’s safety, but also the operation of businesses, logistics, transportation, schools, kindergartens,” he said.
He called for adapting security rules “with the aim of better protecting people and preserving the ability to live in our cities and communities”.
Some in Kyiv – a city of three million people – consider the security protocols ineffective, with experts suggesting a more flexible approach.
“If, because of a single drone somewhere in the region, everything or almost everything in the entire capital stops for about 40 minutes every hour, we’re not going to last long like this,” Mykhailo Zhernakov, head of a legal think-tank, said on Facebook on Aug 27.
Overnight from Aug 28 to 29, a Russian strike on an ammunition depot killed 38 people in the capital’s suburbs.
Another attack killed a two-year-old girl in a Kyiv park in broad daylight on Aug 29. AFP

beads, crystals, and steel visualize cloud formations within exhibition in china
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:10:47 UTC
03:10:47 KST

Tia-Thuy Nguyen translates cloud formations into installations
Vietnamese artist Tia-Thuy Nguyen presents Fields of Resonance at Almine Rech Shanghai, her first solo exhibition in China. On view from August 28th to October 31st, 2026, the exhibition brings together nearly twenty paintings, sculptures, and installations produced using oil paint, beads, sequins, thread, quartz, crystal, recycled glass, stone, and stainless steel. The exhibition continues Nguyen’s engagement with clouds, a recurring motif in her work since 2018. Initially associated with memories of her father, a pilot who served during the Vietnam War, clouds later became part of the artist’s visual diary as she traveled between Asia and Europe. Their changing forms provide a way to explore memory, emotion, and the movement of energy through the natural world.
 
 Like a sky breeze / 2026 / quartz, crystal, and stone / 19 × 13 × 23 cm | all images ©Tia-Thuy Nguyen
Cloud forms take shape through embroidery, minerals, and steel
In Fields of Resonance, the cloud moves beyond the painted image and becomes a material structure. Nguyen constructs cloud forms through embroidery, assembles them from mineral fragments, weaves them from stainless steel, and extends them into the gallery space. Across these different approaches, durable materials are used to express movement, impermanence, and transformation. At the center of the exhibition, the monumental mixed-media work Fairer than a Fairy, measuring 200 by 300 centimeters, presents a cloudscape built from oil paint, thousands of beads, and sequins. The dense accumulation of small elements gives the painted surface physical volume, positioning the work between painting and sculpture. Nguyen’s background in fashion and engagement with Vietnamese craft traditions inform the use of embroidery as a structural technique. Each bead receives and reflects light differently, causing the surface to shift as the viewer moves around it. Changes in position reveal variations in density, color, shadow, and depth, preventing the image from settling into a fixed appearance. The repetitive process of stitching and assembling also makes time and manual labor part of the work. The resulting surface combines the precision of craft with the fluid visual qualities of an atmospheric landscape.
Oil painting provides another approach to the exhibition’s central motif. In Passionate in Supernatural, Nguyen uses the density and fluidity of oil paint to evoke the atmosphere following a storm. Turquoise, deep violet, orange, and gold overlap across the canvas, suggesting moisture, changing light, and suspended movement. The painting does not reproduce a specific cloud formation. Instead, the shifting relationship between color and pigment expresses the transition between darkness and light, turbulence and calm. Unlike the structured surfaces of the embroidered works, the oil paintings retain the movement of the medium, leaving their forms open and visually unstable. In Another Day of Sun and Like a Sky Breeze, the artist shifts from painted surfaces to compact sculptural compositions made from quartz, crystal, recycled glass, and stone. Their transparency and reflective qualities allow the surrounding light to become part of the works. 
 
 Enduring Vitality / 2026 / stainless steel / 700 x 150 cm
Completed in 2026, Like a Sky Breeze measures 19 by 13 by 23 centimeters. Quartz and crystal fragments gather over a stone base to form an irregular volume resembling a cloud during condensation. White, pale blue, violet, and golden tones appear across the mineral surfaces as light changes. The sculpture combines the physical weight of stone with the visual lightness of crystal. Its angular surfaces suggest both geological permanence and atmospheric change, reconstructing a transient natural form through materials associated with durability and accumulation. Quartz also carries and refracts light through its structure. Instead of applying brightness to the surface, Nguyen allows the material itself to absorb, redirect, and release light. The appearance of the sculpture consequently changes according to its surroundings and the viewer’s position.
The Pause Between Storms introduces Nguyen’s stainless-steel weaving technique. Fine metal strands are bent, joined, and woven into cloud formations that occupy physical space. The material brings an industrial and structurally resistant quality to a process traditionally associated with softer fibers. Through repetitive weaving, the stainless steel is manipulated into forms that appear lightweight and delicate while retaining the material’s structural properties. From a distance, the restrained gray palette and fine lines recall landscape etchings. At closer range, knots, bends, folds, and joints reveal the physical process behind each work. Nguyen leaves the steel in its original metallic state, allowing light to move directly across the surface. Highlights and shadows shift as viewers change position, producing the visual impression of movement within a physically stable structure.
The works bring together a textile-based method of making and an industrial material. Weaving becomes a sculptural process through which strength and delicacy, permanence and impermanence, are held within the same form. Stainless steel takes on a larger spatial role in Enduring Vitality, a seven-meter-long installation in which branching tree forms extend across the gallery floor and walls. Here, steel replaces the drawn line, moving the image from a flat surface into the architecture. The branches twist, overlap, and separate according to the viewer’s position. Their metallic lines operate simultaneously as drawing, structure, and sculpture, while shadows cast across the surrounding surfaces create an additional layer of lines and forms. The tree introduces a grounded counterpart to the exhibition’s cloud motif. Its roots establish a sense of stability, while its branches extend upward through continuous growth. The two motifs are connected through the circulation of natural energy: water rises, condenses, returns to the earth, and supports new life. The cloud disperses and changes, while the tree remains rooted while continuing to develop.
 
Material contrasts connect painting, sculpture, and installation
The materials throughout Fields of Resonance are selected for their physical and visual properties. Oil paint provides fluidity and depth; beads and sequins introduce texture, reflected light, and volume; thread records repetition and manual labor; quartz and crystal refract light through solid matter; recycled glass introduces fragmentation and transformation; and stainless steel provides strength while functioning as fiber, line, and spatial structure. Nguyen retains the distinct qualities of each material instead of disguising them. Steel does not imitate thread, and crystal does not replicate pigment. Their differences become part of the composition. Soft materials accumulate until they acquire weight, while rigid materials are bent and woven into forms that appear delicate.
This movement between materials parallels Nguyen’s practice across painting, fashion, craft, sculpture, and installation. The boundaries between these disciplines remain open: a bead can function as color, light, texture, and volume; a steel strand can operate as line, structure, and image; a canvas can become a relief; and a drawing can expand into architectural space. Across the exhibition, natural motifs are used as structures through which internal and external states intersect. Clouds, trees, light, and mineral formations connect memory with material processes and the viewer’s physical presence. The title Fields of Resonance refers to this exchange. Memories generate images, light activates materials, movement changes perception, and the viewer’s position establishes new relationships between individual works and the gallery. The exhibition develops through recurring contrasts between light and weight, softness and resistance, stillness and movement, permanence and change. These relationships are expressed through painting, stitching, weaving, joining, bending, and assembly.
Across different scales and materials, Nguyen transforms atmospheric and natural forms into physical structures. Clouds become embroidered surfaces, mineral bodies, and woven metal formations, while trees become steel lines extending through space. Light connects these different materials, continually altering their appearance and relationship to the gallery. Fields of Resonance consequently approaches nature as a changing force that moves between memory, matter, light, and the processes of making.

 The Pause Between Storms / 2026 / stainless steel / 60 x 240 cm
 Fairer than a Fairy / 2026 / beadwork and sequins on canvas / 200 × 300 cm
 Another Day of Sun / 2026 / Quartz, cullet and beads / 30 x 30 cm

 artist Tia-Thuy Nguyen (center)

Sweden signs deal for four French FDI frigates
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:09:32 BST
03:09:32 KST

Sweden has signed a contract with France’s Naval Group for four FDI-based air defence frigates, completing a competition that also included British-Swedish and Spanish proposals, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration signed the procurement contract on 31 August during a visit to Stockholm by French President Emmanuel Macron, with the ships to enter Swedish service as the Luleå class.
The first frigate is planned for delivery in 2030, with the remaining three following successively. Sweden had selected Naval Group’s Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention design in May and subsequently entered negotiations with France over the purchase.
The Swedish Government said construction of the vessels and training of Swedish Armed Forces personnel can now begin following signature of the agreement.
Swedish Defence Minister Pål Jonson said: “This is a strategically important investment that strengthens Sweden’s defence capability and security in light of a deteriorated international situation. The four frigates will triple Sweden’s current air defence capability. This is essential to Sweden’s security and NATO’s capability.”
The Luleå-class vessels will be based on Naval Group’s FDI design but configured for Swedish requirements. The Swedish Government has previously confirmed that the ships will incorporate a number of domestically produced systems.
These are expected to include Saab’s RBS 15 anti-ship missile, lightweight torpedo, Giraffe 1X radar and Trackfire remote weapon station, together with 57mm and 40mm naval guns from BAE Systems Bofors.
The ships will also be equipped for area air defence. The Swedish Government said in May that advanced air defence was a central requirement for the programme and that the new frigates would contribute to NATO’s integrated air and missile defence capability.
Naval Group Chairman and Chief Executive Pierre Éric Pommellet said when the design was selected in May: “We are extremely honoured to have been selected by the Swedish Ministry of Defence. We are now eager to engage with the Swedish authorities and partners in the execution of this strategic project.”
He added: “The FDI will provide the Royal Swedish Navy with a latest-generation frigate and extended capabilities in all warfare domains with rapid delivery timeline, to meet the operational needs expressed by the Ministry of Defence.”
Naval Group faced two other proposals during the Swedish evaluation. Babcock, working with Swedish defence company Saab, offered the Arrowhead 120, a smaller derivative of the Arrowhead family that also includes the 140-metre design forming the basis of the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates.
The Arrowhead 120 proposed for Sweden is approximately 124 metres long and displaces around 4,650 tonnes. Babcock’s proposed configuration included the Saab 9LV combat management system, Sea Giraffe 4A fixed-face radar, Sea Giraffe 1X, RBS 15 anti-ship missiles, Saab lightweight torpedoes and Bofors guns.
Babcock and Saab had already been working on the Luleå programme before Sweden moved towards purchasing an existing foreign design. Saab had been contracted by the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration to undertake basic design work, with Babcock providing engineering support including structural design and auxiliary systems.
The third contender was Navantia’s ALFA 4000. The Spanish shipbuilder offered a 120-metre, approximately 4,300-tonne frigate and had proposed delivering the first two vessels in 2030 and the remaining pair in 2031.
Navantia’s proposed Swedish configuration also incorporated Swedish equipment, including the RBS 15, Bofors 57mm and 40mm guns and Saab Trackfire weapon stations. The company proposed air-defence, anti-submarine and surface-warfare capabilities alongside a hangar and flight deck suitable for helicopters.
Swedish officials said during the competition that the three proposals were assessed against time, capability and price. The government had also stipulated that the programme should concentrate on a mature vessel already in production in order to reduce delivery times.
The FDI is already in production for France and Greece. Naval Group pointed to the maturity of the production line and existing deliveries when making its Swedish proposal. The Swedish Government initially authorised negotiations with France in May for four ships expected to be delivered between 2030 and 2034. At the time, it said the procurement was the first stage of the process and that an order could be placed once negotiations were complete.
That process concluded with the contract signed on 31 August between the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration and Naval Group. Sweden and France also signed a separate framework agreement covering defence cooperation during Macron’s visit, including operational matters, defence equipment and industrial development.

Author-psychiatrist Augusto Cury gains ground in Brazil presidential race polls

Author-psychiatrist Augusto Cury gains ground in Brazil presidential race polls
SAO PAULO, Aug 31 - Augusto Cury, a psychiatrist and best-selling author with no previous elected office experience, has emerged as a surprise contender in Brazil's presidential race, unsettling a contest dominated by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Recent television appearances and strong social media reach have lifted Cury's standing in opinion polls ahead of the October vote.
Cury, 67, placed third in first-round voting scenarios released on Monday, garnering 11% (up from 2%) support in a Nexus poll commissioned by lender BTG Pactual and 7.8% (up from 1.6%) in an AtlasIntel/Bloomberg poll.
The results marked a rare shift in a race that has been dominated by the leftist Lula and the right-wing Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Cury's rise could reshape the dynamics of the campaign in the coming weeks, increasing pressure on the frontrunners to respond to a candidate seeking to appeal to voters dissatisfied with years of polarization.
"When a campaign grows like this, the noise comes along with it," Cury said in a social media post on Monday. "Something much bigger is happening at the same time: Millions of Brazilians are discovering that there's life beyond polarization."
Cury, who is running on the ticket of the little-known Avante Party, has sought to position himself as an alternative to the long-standing political polarization between left and right in the country.
Analysts caution, however, that it is too early to conclude whether his gains will prove durable, as the opposition vote remains fragmented.
The Nexus poll showed Lula leading Bolsonaro by 39% to 33% while AtlasIntel put Lula at 43.4% versus 33.7% for Bolsonaro. If no candidate secures more than 50% of valid votes in the first round, the top two candidates advance to a runoff.
"To threaten Bolsonaro, an alternative conservative candidate would need to rise further in polls and reach roughly 15% around mid-September (with Bolsonaro simultaneously falling to about 25%)," political consulting firm Eurasia Group said in a statement.
Cury has avoided identifying with either the political left or right, instead campaigning under the slogan "Centered on what matters."
NATIONAL PROFILE
A physician and prolific author focused on psychology and emotional well-being, Cury has built a national profile over decades through books, lectures and media appearances.
Cury says he has sold 42 million books in more than 70 countries and describes himself as the world's most-read psychiatrist. Reuters could not independently verify the claim.
With 10.7 million Instagram followers, he has a social media audience approaching Flavio Bolsonaro's 11.4 million, though still smaller than Lula's 14.9 million.
Born in Brazil's most-populous state, Sao Paulo, Cury portrays himself as a political outsider bringing management experience to government. In addition to his medical and publishing career, he says he is a rural producer and business manager.
"My mind is capitalist, my heart is social," Cury recently told reporters, as he criticized some of Lula's policies. REUTERS
