Thailand rallies automakers, oil firms to boost biofuel use amid energy security push
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
23:15:26 CST
00:15:26 KST

BANGKOK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Department of Energy Business said on Monday that it has partnered with 13 car brands, five motorcycle makers, and seven fuel retailers to promote wider use of E20 gasoline, as the government seeks to cut reliance on imported crude amid ongoing Middle East tensions.
Thailand currently has sufficient ethanol production capacity to support wider adoption of E20, with more than 4 million cars and about 80 percent of motorcycles already able to run on the fuel blend, which is priced below standard gasoline, the department said in a statement.
However, E20 sales average just 5.88 million liters a day, 18 percent of gasoline demand, held back by consumer uncertainty over vehicle compatibility and misconceptions about engine performance, said Sarawut Kaewtathip, director-general of the department.
Automakers will publish compatible model lists and confirm E20 causes no engine damage, Sarawut said, adding that the agency maintains strict quality oversight from refineries to retail stations, giving consumers assurance on fuel quality.
Supporting domestically produced biofuels benefits consumers through cost savings and bolsters the Southeast Asian nation's agricultural sector by adding value to farm produce and stabilizing crop prices, he told a press conference.
Officials also called on motorists to switch to E20 to help the country navigate the global energy crisis stably and sustainably and urged the public to help spread accurate information about the fuel's benefits. ■

Majority of Americans oppose Trump's new Canada tariffs, renaming Lake Ontario, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:40:49 UTC
19:40:49 KST

Majority of Americans oppose Trump's new Canada tariffs, renaming Lake Ontario, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
WASHINGTON, Sept 1 -
A majority of Americans oppose President Donald Trump's moves last week to raise taxes on imported Canadian goods and his order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The three-day poll, which concluded on Sunday, showed Americans are wary of the feud with Canada — for decades a top U.S. trading partner — which has escalated since trade talks between the two countries collapsed and Trump last week ordered the hike in tariffs on Canadian goods.
Only 20% of poll respondents supported higher tariffs on Canadian goods compared to 57% who opposed them and 21% who couldn't say where they stood. About one in five poll respondents hadn't heard about the development.
U.S. households are already under financial pressure from the surge in gasoline prices since Trump launched a war on Iran in February, and American voters rate the cost of living as the top issue determining how they will vote in November 3 midterm elections. Trump's Republican allies will be defending slim congressional majorities in the elections. Trump's approval rating in recent weeks has been mired at the lowest level of his political career.
The trade conflict took a theatrical turn last week when Trump on Thursday renamed Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes of North America, as "Lake America." Trump's designation applies to U.S. federal usage about the lake, and does not govern what Canada, international bodies or other organizations call the lake. The president has often ribbed Canada, threatening to annex the longtime ally as a 51st U.S. state. He ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the "Gulf of America" at the start of his second term in January 2025.
Just 14% of Americans in the Reuters/Ipsos poll said they supported changing the name of Lake Ontario, which has gone by that name for more than 400 years. Sixty-three percent of poll respondents opposed the name change and the rest were unsure or didn't answer the question.
The poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from 1,023 U.S. adults and had a margin of error of 4 percentage points. REUTERS

Xi noted that high-level political mutual trust and firm mutual support are crucial to ensuring the steady and sustained development of China-Kyrgyzstan relations.
China firmly supports Kyrgyzstan in safeguarding its national sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, as well as pursuing a development path suited to its national conditions, Xi said, adding that China stands ready to work with the Kyrgyz side to continue firmly supporting each other on issues involving each other's core interests.
For his part, Japarov said he was honored to welcome Xi to Kyrgyzstan on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of the country's independence. The visit further demonstrated the profound friendship and high-level political mutual trust between Kyrgyzstan and China, and marked an important milestone in the history of bilateral relations, he said.
Japarov said Kyrgyzstan and China are neighboring countries, and the ancient Silk Road has closely connected the two nations. In recent years, with the rapid development of the Kyrgyzstan-China comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era, bilateral relations have entered a golden period and reached an unprecedented level, he said.
He expressed gratitude to China for its selfless support and assistance at every critical moment in Kyrgyzstan's development, while extending warm congratulations on the 105th anniversary of the founding of the CPC and the launch of the implementation of China's 15th Five-Year Plan.
Japarov also expressed admiration for the remarkable development achievements China has made under the leadership of Xi, and voiced willingness to learn from China's experience in state governance, particularly Xi's commitment to the people, as embodied in his words, "I will fully commit to the people and never fail them."
China has always been a priority in Kyrgyzstan's foreign policy, as well as Kyrgyzstan's closest friend and most reliable partner, Japarov said, noting that Kyrgyzstan firmly adheres to the one-China principle and stands ready to further develop good-neighborly and friendly relations with China on the basis of mutual respect, equality and mutual benefit.
EXPANDING PRACTICAL COOPERATION, DELIVERING TANGIBLE BENEFITS
Xi urged the two countries to deepen practical cooperation, effectively implement the intergovernmental economic and trade cooperation plan, diversify trade products and develop new growth areas such as digital trade and cross-border e-commerce.
Xi also said the two sides should ensure the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, calling it a major transportation artery that carries the development aspirations of the people across the region.
He called for modernizing border ports and deepening "soft connectivity" in institutions, standards and rules, and urged the launch of more landmark projects in renewable energy, resource recycling and other fields, the implementation of cooperation documents on green minerals, and cooperation across the entire industrial chain.
Xi said China and Kyrgyzstan should make joint efforts to successfully build the Belt and Road Joint Laboratory, enhance artificial intelligence cooperation, and leverage scientific and technological innovation to boost the quality and efficiency of bilateral cooperation.
The two sides should further facilitate exchanges and expand cooperation in youth affairs, media, tourism, sports, health care and local affairs, while continuing to strengthen the social and public support for China-Kyrgyzstan friendship, Xi added.
For his part, Japarov said Kyrgyzstan is willing to strengthen cooperation with China in trade and investment, connectivity, technological innovation, energy, mineral resources and the green economy, as well as deepen exchanges in education, health, culture and youth sectors.
Kyrgyzstan is ready to actively advance the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, so as to turn it into a "steel Silk Road" for the new era and a new bond of friendship between the two countries, Japarov said.
JOINING HANDS FOR PEACE AND DEVELOPMENT
China and Kyrgyzstan should expand cooperation in law enforcement and security, work together to combat the "three evil forces" of terrorism, extremism and separatism, drug trafficking and transnational crimes, and jointly maintain regional peace and stability, Xi said.
China supports Kyrgyzstan in playing a greater role in international and regional affairs, Xi said, noting that China is willing to further enhance collaboration with Kyrgyzstan within the framework of the United Nations, jointly implement the four major global initiatives, oppose hegemonism and power politics, adhere to true multilateralism, safeguard international fairness and justice, and promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system.
Noting that China and Kyrgyzstan are both founding members of the SCO, Xi said the two countries should promote the implementation of the outcomes of the Tianjin Summit, facilitate common development in the region, and advance the development of the SCO to a new level.
For his part, Japarov said that the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi help countries work together to address common challenges and build a more just and stable international order.
Kyrgyzstan stands ready to closely coordinate with China on multilateral platforms, including the United Nations, the SCO, the China-Central Asia mechanism and the World AI Cooperation Organization, to jointly safeguard world peace and stability, Japarov said.
Following the talks, the two heads of state signed a joint declaration of the People's Republic of China and the Kyrgyz Republic on the high-quality development of the comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era and a bilateral treaty on permanent good-neighborliness, friendship and cooperation.
The signing of the bilateral treaty on permanent good-neighborliness, friendship and cooperation will provide an important legal foundation for the everlasting friendship and firm mutual support between the two countries, Xi said.
Echoing Xi, Japarov said the signing of the treaty will open up broader prospects for bilateral relations.
They also jointly witnessed the exchange of bilateral cooperation documents in the fields of investment, transportation, customs, and sister-city relations.
During the visit, the two sides also signed over 20 cooperation documents covering science and technology, education, culture, media, and other areas.■

Photo taken on Aug. 31, 2026 shows the scene of the 21st Bled Strategic Forum in Bled, Slovenia. Leaders from Central and Eastern Europe on Monday called for reform and enlargement of the European Union (EU) amid a rapidly changing global order at the Bled Strategic Forum, Slovenia's major foreign policy gathering. (Photo by Zeljko Stevanic/Xinhua)
BLED, Slovenia, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Leaders from Central and Eastern Europe on Monday called for reform and enlargement of the European Union (EU) amid a rapidly changing global order at the Bled Strategic Forum, Slovenia's major foreign policy gathering.
Prime Ministers Janez Jansa of Slovenia, Peter Magyar of Hungary, Andrej Plenkovic of Croatia and Petr Fiala of the Czech Republic said at a joint panel that the EU needs to strengthen its competitiveness and economic development, better manage illegal migration and accelerate the enlargement process.
"If the European Union does not enlarge, someone else will at our expense," Jansa said, without elaborating.
The EU has not admitted a new member since Croatia joined in 2013. Six countries, mainly from the Western Balkans, are currently at various stages of the EU accession process.
Jansa also criticized what he called the EU's "forced green transition," arguing that strict environmental standards had contributed to the relocation of industries from Europe to Southern Asia, hurting the bloc's economy and increasing its dependence on products from other countries.
In contrast, Slovenian President Natasa Pirc Musar said at another panel that the EU and the international community should seek common solutions to climate change, stressing that the issue should not be left to pragmatism alone.
The two-day forum continues Tuesday with discussions on the future of Europe and the era of multi-alignment.
The 21st Bled Strategic Forum is being held under the theme "The Power to Shape the Future." Launched in 2006, the forum is jointly organized by Slovenia's Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs and the Centre for European Perspective.
It has become a major regional platform for dialogue on international and security issues, bringing together political leaders, diplomats, scholars and business representatives to discuss Europe's future amid a changing global order. ■

To nap or not to nap? Science is still waking up to the question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

To nap or not to nap? Science is still waking up to the question
Sleep strategies need to be tailored to individuals, studies suggest
By Sujata Gupta
Social Sciences Writer
In Muslim-majority Oman, most people wake before dawn for morning prayers. People often go back to sleep afterward or take afternoon naps, says sleep medicine researcher Mohammed Al-Abri of Sultan Qaboos University in Muscat, Oman.
Such segmented sleep is not limited to Muslim countries. Teenagers, new parents, perimenopausal and menopausal women and elderly individuals everywhere can struggle to sleep the recommended seven to nine hours in a single block. Early school and work start times leave night owls without adequate sleep. Shift workers juggle daytime demands with nighttime working hours, cramming in sleep when they can. And people living in some of the world’s hottest regions avoid the midday heat with siestas.
Despite how commonplace various kinds of naps are, scientists have largely focused on monophasic, or single, blocks of shut-eye, researchers report in an Aug. 25 review in Brain Medicine. Yet how people sleep matters as much as how much. That means sleep experts need to pay more attention to patterns in which people combine a core nighttime sleep with one or more naps throughout a 24-hour day.
That requires first thinking about naps beyond the binary of something that people either do or don’t do, another team notes in August in Sleep Health. After all, naps vary in duration, timing, frequency and societal significance. And treating all naps as the same, as is common, has led to wildly divergent findings, with some researchers concluding that naps harm health and others finding the opposite.
Lost in the noise is how to advise the fatigued masses. In theory, splitting up sleep could help people clock in enough snooze-time hours, says occupational health worker Line Victoria Moen, who was not involved with either study. But how that sort of strategic, broken sleep impacts long-term health and well-being remains an open question. “The evidence is too fragmented,” says Moen, of the National Institute of Occupational Health in Oslo, Norway.
A history of ‘two sleeps’
Across the ages, sleep has shown surprising variability, records show. One striking example is medieval Europeans’ two-sleep pattern, described in historian A. Roger Ekirch’s 2006 book At Day’s Close: Night in Times Past. People typically went to bed when the sun went down and then woke in the middle of the night to meditate, complete light chores or have sex, suggests Ekirch, of Virginia Tech in Blacksburg. Then they’d fall asleep again until sunrise.
A sleep intermission no longer jibes with a modern world bathed in electric lights and screens that keep people awake until well past sundown. But could such a biphasic sleep pattern be rejiggered to serve modern populations?
As it stands, people across the industrialized world are chronically sleep-deprived. Not sleeping enough has been linked with numerous mental and physical health woes, including struggles with memory and alertness, weakened performance, heart problems and obesity.
Experts generally advise people to practice better sleep hygiene, such as dimming lights and getting off screens several hours before bedtime. Yet such one-size-fits-all advice overlooks modern realities.
Consider those who work outside a 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. day. Shift workers, who comprise roughly a fifth of industrialized countries’ populations, could try to meet their sleep needs with a single daytime block. But being out of sync with the sun means their sleep will probably be lighter, more fragmented and less restorative than had they slept through the night, sleep researchers João Sena Ribeiros, of the Autonomous University of Barcelona in Spain, and Càtia Reis of the University of Lisbon in Portugal, wrote in October 2025 in Sleep Medicine.
Might such individuals be better off sleeping in blocks before and after their shifts? Science provides no clear answers.
No consensus on long naps
Human biology lends some support for a daytime nap.
Two processes govern when and how we sleep. Sleep pressure builds up the longer we stay awake. And circadian rhythms, governed by natural and artificial light, cue the body to release hormones — melatonin in dim light and cortisol upon waking. Roughly after lunch, shorter “ultradian” rhythms, triggered by sleep pressure buildup and changes to body temperature and blood sugar levels, can trigger a crash.
Honoring that malaise with a power nap of less than half an hour has been linked with increased alertness and cognitive performance. But beware. Shorter naps scattered throughout the day seem to harm mental and physical health, researchers reported in June 2021 in Sleep Health.
But what about a two-sleep pattern better suited to the sleep-deprived modern era, in which people go to bed late and wake up early for school and work? Could such individuals benefit from a big block of nighttime sleep coupled with a long afternoon nap? On this point, the science is murky.
Afternoon naps longer than an hour are linked to a higher likelihood of obesity and elevated blood sugar levels, a risk factor for developing type 2 diabetes, Al-Abri and colleagues reported in October 2022 in Frontiers in Psychology. “I usually urge people, if they have a nap, to have it less than half an hour,” Al-Abri says.
But research on an altogether different population — elite soccer players in Australia — suggests that a long afternoon slumber could help counteract sleep deprivation from early morning practices and late evening games. Researchers brought 12 male soccer players into the lab and connected them to electrodes to measure how long it took them to fall asleep and to monitor sleep stages and sleep quality during either one- or two-hour midafternoon naps.
Though well-rested, the athletes conked out in less than 10 minutes, the team reported in September in Clocks & Sleep. Strategically varying nap length could help with different aspects of performance, the team suspects. That’s because nap length altered the athletes’ sleep patterns.
Sleep cycles are roughly 90 minutes long and involve two stages: light REM sleep, often marked by dreaming, and non-REM sleep, which includes deep sleep. Research suggests REM sleep is linked with improved learning and memory, and deep sleep is linked with recovery from exercise. Athletes who napped for one hour spent a larger fraction of time in deep sleep compared with athletes who slept two hours, who had longer REM sleep. That hints at the possibility that shorter naps could facilitate recovery, while longer naps facilitate new skills, the team notes.
That and other research is starting to show that under the right conditions, long naps may be beneficial, says Anastasi Kosmadopoulos, a sleep researcher at CQUniversity Australia in Adelaide. “Sleeping in two blocks versus one is not detrimental to overall daily alertness or waking performance.”
Sleep advice should be personal
Another question is whether findings in elite athletes apply to the rest of us. Moving forward, sleep advice needs to be personalized to the individual, Sena Ribeiros and Reis say.
Such personalization should include a genetic analysis, researchers reported in January 2025 in Obesity. Propensity for napping is highly heritable, the team reported in earlier work. In this study of more than 1,200 Spanish participants, the team quantified a person’s genetic predisposition for napping using more than a million genetic variants. Individuals who went against their genetic predisposition, by napping when they ought not to or vice versa, showed increased risk of obesity, while those who followed their genetic predisposition did not.
In their August review in Sleep Health, members of that same team outlined eight core features of naps that researchers ought to measure. Besides genetic predisposition and nap frequency, duration and timing, researchers should also consider an individual’s motivation for napping, cultural and home environments, seasonality and sleep status.
Experts don’t need to prove that two sleeps are better than one, Sena Ribeiros says. They just need to address how individuals who cannot get their sleep in a single, nighttime block can get as close as possible to meeting their sleep needs. “We should look at [sleep] in a more personalized way instead of … just saying, ‘OK, try to get those seven hours’ to everyone,” he says.

Making a Space for Ethics: Santa Fe College’s Ethics Club
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Ethics, as a field of study, is often overlooked when students consider their career paths. Some incoming students may see it as a subject better left to the philosophers who created and developed it. However, learning the principles of ethics and practicing its discussion doesn’t require one to devote their life to it. As many of us in Santa Fe’s Ethics club, myself included, have discovered, there’s much to gain from simply discussing the works of Aristotle and exploring hypotheticals. It develops a deeper understanding of our actions, our own guiding principles, and what makes us human.
But how did this club come to be? It started with Professor Ron Claypool, Associate Professor of Philosophy, Humanities, and Ethics at Santa Fe College. He encouraged incoming freshmen from his various classes to join and try out for an academic, team-based ethics discussion competition aptly named Ethics Bowl.
As the name suggests, Ethics Bowl is a collaborative competition in which students analyze complex, real-life ethical dilemmas and issues of contemporary concern. Unlike traditional debate, teams are not expected to defend a position at all costs. Instead, they work together to find the most reasonable and well-supported solutions, promoting civil discussion and critical thinking. Teams are scored based on their ability to structure a presentation, analyze the moral dimensions of a case, anticipate counterarguments, and engage in respectful dialogue about their reasoning. This encourages teams to consider the best course of action for a case rather than simply defend a predetermined position. Whether a team reaches a particular conclusion is less important than how thoughtfully and effectively it reasons through the case.
At the first interest meeting, Professor Claypool led a discussion using simple “would you rather” questions based on realistic situations that everyone could relate to. Many students participated in the initial meeting and stayed, intrigued by this different method of thinking they hadn’t previously encountered. Some were drawn by the prospect of competition; others simply by the desire to develop their reasoning and argument-development skills.
Once members decided whether they wanted to commit to competition, we began by learning the rules of the game. We then moved on to the basics of moral frameworks and the tools needed to apply them to structured arguments. This is where many of us developed an appreciation for ethical reasoning.
Although the work was demanding, it significantly strengthened our understanding of ethics and related topics. From then on, leading up to the competition, we met nearly every day of the week to discuss the facts of the cases and refine our presentations. It was a lot of work, but it was through this effort that our knowledge grew rapidly; not only in ethical inquiry, but also in statistics and global affairs that informed our arguments.
When the season concluded, many team members wanted to continue discussing ethical theories and developing their skills in preparation for the following year. Others wanted to focus on recruiting new members to replace those graduating before the next season. Many members found genuine enjoyment in studying and discussing ethical questions; we didn’t want to give that up for a year. As a result, we established a club that would continue what we had built and would allow us to open the conversation to the broader student body.
With that, the Santa Fe Ethics Club was born. We had to decide what direction we wanted to lead the club, since prospective members might have little to no prior exposure to moral philosophy or logical reasoning as a study. We decided to involve Professor Claypool as an informal guide, as none of us were confident enough in the concepts to teach them accurately to others. He would host monthly sessions, focusing on one ethical theory at a time. He was happy to oblige, as the sessions would not only give us a refresher but also gave him an opportunity to identify new potential members.
To fill the remaining meetings and provide variety, we invited guest speakers. One particularly memorable meeting, we brought in a public defender from the city’s courthouse. He took the time to speak about the moral dimensions of the justice system and offered a perspective on how ethical reasoning is applied in the real world. Other meetings involved reviewing the national competition cases posted by APPE, where club members discussed their perspectives and explored how different moral frameworks applied to each scenario. We also organized informal sessions using games and creative hypotheticals to make ethical discussion more engaging and accessible, reaching students who may never have considered moral philosophy as something relevant to themselves.
Many Ethics Bowl members found genuine enjoyment in studying and discussing ethical questions, and it was especially rewarding to create a free and open space that welcomed all perspectives. Hearing new viewpoints allowed us more experienced members to revisit familiar ideas in a new light.
Ultimately, we aim to continue our journey in competition while also making ethical and philosophical inquiry accessible to all students. Almost anyone, at any stage of life, can benefit from discussion and thinking about the world around them more critically. It develops skills that go beyond a college degree, and we hope to continue providing that opportunity.
The post Making a Space for Ethics: Santa Fe College’s Ethics Club first appeared on Blog of the APA.

India rejects ruling on water-sharing treaty with Pakistan by international court
The court says India must uphold the treaty and curb work on a hydroelectric plant in Kashmir pending a neutral expert’s assessment
India in April last year suspended the treaty that ensures water supply to 80 per cent of Pakistani farms, after India identified as Pakistani two of three assailants in an attack that killed 26 people at a tourist destination in Kashmir that month.
Islamabad denied any role in the attack and took legal action after India last year also began work to boost reservoir holding capacity at two hydroelectric projects in the Kashmir region.
This was seen as a first tangible step by India to operate outside agreements covered by the Indus Waters Treaty between the two countries, which both have honoured since 1960 despite three wars and several other conflicts between them.
The Permanent Court of Arbitration said the Indus Water Treaty remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.
“India must observe its obligations under the Treaty, including those relating to the design and operation of its hydroelectric projects on the Western Rivers,” the intergovernmental court said.

mineral stone wall enclosure frames tectoniques’ cultural center in france
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:45:05 UTC
23:45:05 KST

stone enclosure defines the cultural center in Vaison-la-Romaine
Set at the foot of Mont Ventoux in Vaison-la-Romaine, France, the cultural center by Tectoniques is organized within a square mineral enclosure constructed from locally sourced stone. Behind the perimeter, timber volumes, shaded galleries, and a Mediterranean courtyard accommodate a music and dance school, performance hall, and children’s activity center within a compact, climate-responsive composition.
The project occupies former vineyard land that has been converted into a housing estate. Its position within a fragmented peri-urban context, without a direct connection to the public realm, led Tectoniques to develop an inward-looking layout. The spatial organization draws on the cloister and Roman domus, as well as agricultural building types such as the Provençal mas. Set back from the plot boundaries, the building creates a planted forecourt. A strong geometric framework establishes the cultural center as a landmark within the surrounding territory, defining a 55-by-55-meter square enclosed by massive stone walls. The horizontal perimeter creates a clear architectural line against the landscape dominated by Mont Ventoux.
Three volumes rise within the enclosure: two four-sided pyramids and a half-cylinder. Two opposing sides of the quadrilateral are formed by large walls with wide central openings aligned with the entrance, while the other two sides dissolve into regularly spaced columns. The facades of the heated volumes are recessed behind a planted strip and pergola, creating an intermediate layer between the interior spaces and the surrounding residential fabric. Jasmine, clematis, honeysuckle, and lavender populate this shaded landscape, creating a planted filter around the building.
timber volumes organize the center around an open courtyard
Within the stone perimeter, the design team at Tectoniques Architectes divides the plan into three equivalent parts. Two timber-built wings sit on either side of a central void, which forms the internal landscape of the project through an entrance courtyard designed as a Mediterranean garden and a multi-sports pitch.
A peripheral gallery distributes circulation to each wing. Slender galvanized steel columns form the peristyle and contrast with the mass of the stone enclosure. Each wing accommodates a different part of the program, with the children’s activity center and performance hall positioned on one side and the music and dance school on the other.
The three largest rooms occupy distinct architectural volumes. The performance hall is housed beneath the half-cylinder vault, while the two pyramidal volumes bring zenithal light into the dance studios. Instrumental practice rooms feature slightly inclined walls to meet acoustic requirements. Sound-absorbing wall linings and integrated plywood furniture shape the interior environments, while windows at the rear of the rooms extend views and create cross-visibility through the facility.
climbing plants grow beneath the pergola to form a shaded and fragrant intermediate landscape
Passive strategies respond to the Mediterranean climate
Economy of means and hybrid construction inform the project’s environmental approach, which is tailored to the Mediterranean climate. Locally quarried stone from Vers-Pont-du-Gard forms the outer enclosure, providing protection from the mistral while contributing thermal mass. Pergolas and galleries provide solar protection, while the timber structure forms a high-performance thermal envelope.
The through-plan organization supports natural ventilation across the spaces. Timber slatted panels positioned in front of operable windows allow secure night-time ventilation, while a geothermal system is combined with underfloor heating and cooling. Together, the stone enclosure, timber construction, planted courtyards, and passive environmental strategies establish the cultural center as an inward-looking public building adapted to its Mediterranean setting.

Peru seeks to lead UN labour body amid funding shortfall

Peru seeks to lead UN labour body amid funding shortfall
GENEVA, Aug 31 - Peru has entered the race to lead the International Labour Organization, its website showed on Monday, as the body grapples with a financial shortfall that may force it to cut jobs.
• Peru has nominated its former Foreign Affairs Minister Javier Gonzalez-Olaechea to lead the ILO, a letter posted on the ILO website showed.
• Spain has also nominated Labour Minister Yolanda Diaz and they will both run against current head, Togo's Gilbert Houngbo, who is seeking a second term.
• In his mission statement, Gonzalez-Olaechea, who worked at the ILO for two decades, pledged reform and to help protect dignity in the workplace amid major disruptions caused by artificial intelligence and automation.
• Candidates' hearings are planned in November, followed by a secret ballot. The new Director-General's term begins in October 2027.
• The ILO, like the wider UN system, is facing a challenging financial and liquidity situation due to delayed assessed contributions.
• The U.S. has outlined plans to not pay its ILO contributions for the next fiscal year. Long the largest contributor, the U.S. owes 257 million Swiss francs ($315 million) in assessed contributions and arrears as of July.
• The ILO's governing body will discuss possible job cuts in a meeting next month. A draft document showed it proposes to cut up to 120 full-time positions for the 2026-2027 period, or around 7% of the workforce. REUTERS

Sweden inks French war ship order

Macron seals $6 billion French frigate deal in Sweden
- France and Sweden signed a €4.3 billion deal for Sweden to buy four French frigates to strengthen defence amid increasing Russian threats.
- The frigates will have advanced missiles, and Sweden will support France's nuclear deterrence programme to boost European security.
- Both countries aim to build a stronger, more independent European defence industry and explore further military cooperation, including aircraft projects.
AI generated
STOCKHOLM - President Emmanuel Macron on Aug 31 oversaw the signing of a €4.3 billion (S$6.3 billion) deal for Sweden to buy four French frigates as Paris and Stockholm seek to tighten cooperation against a backdrop of growing Russian threats.
Sweden is racing to boost its defences after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, with the Nordic country becoming a NATO member two years later.
Macron and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson oversaw the signing of the contract aboard the French frigate Amiral Ronarc’h, moored in Stockholm.
“We are sealing a major strategic partnership, one that is reciprocal, respectful and ambitious,” Macron said.
“This demonstrates the strength and importance of this European pillar of defence and how Franco-Swedish cooperation is becoming an essential component of it,” the French leader added.
European NATO allies worry about Washington’s wavering commitment to Europe’s defence under US President Donald Trump as Russia’s war against Ukraine grinds into its fifth year.
Macron and Kristersson stressed the need for greater European autonomy in defence.
“Everyone now knows that in Europe we must take greater responsibility for our own security,” Kristersson said.
“The European pillar of NATO is continuing to strengthen.”
The four frigates will be equipped with Aster 30 air-defence interceptor missiles and possibly naval cruise missiles for long-range strikes, Macron said.
‘Avenues for cooperation’
Sweden will help support a Paris-led nuclear deterrence scheme to bolster security on the continent, Macron added.
In March, Macron unveiled a programme under which France, the European Union’s only nuclear-armed country, would use its atomic stockpile to protect allies, including Sweden.
The two countries held their first meeting on nuclear cooperation in Paris in April.
“Work is continuing and intensifying,” the Elysee has said, without providing further details.
Sweden announced in May it would purchase four defence and intervention frigates from French shipbuilder Naval Group, with the first vessel scheduled for delivery in 2030.
France and Sweden, both boasting robust defence industries, expressed a desire to strengthen Europe’s defence industrial base in the face of overwhelming US dominance within NATO.
The goal is to create “a European defence ecosystem that is more resilient over time, more independent, more competitive, and that enables Europe to be fully sovereign,” Macron said.
This could notably involve joint fighter aircraft programmes following the collapse of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) project, the Elysee said on Aug 28.
“There are many possible avenues for cooperation,” the French presidency added, citing France’s aircraft engine manufacturing capabilities as one example.
The frigate deal follows France’s purchase in December of two GlobalEye airborne early warning and control aircraft from Swedish defence giant Saab for more than one billion euros.
French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin and her Swedish counterpart Pal Jonson also signed a framework agreement aimed at strengthening defence cooperation. AFP

Ukrainian Railways received SHATRO COUNTER-MESH electronic warfare systems free of charge.
The systems are designed to protect rolling stock and critical infrastructure facilities from UAVs using mesh networks, Ukrainian company Unwave told Militarnyi.
Ukrainian Railways officially confirmed the system’s high effectiveness in real-world operating conditions.
The first systems were handed over to railway workers for trial operation at the end of June. Enemy UAVs equipped with mesh modems were detected within the systems’ coverage area at distances of 500 to 1,500 meters.
As they entered the system’s operating area, Russian drones changed their flight paths.
The SHATRO COUNTER-MESH suppresses communication links between a UAV’s mesh modem and other network nodes at a range of up to 1,000 meters. This prevents command transmission and disrupts drone coordination.
The Ukrainian electronic warfare system developed by Unwave was the only system capable of jamming a UAV during the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercise in Latvia.

The backlash against screens in schools is escalating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:36:37 UTC
23:36:37 KST

In New York City, teachers have two more weeks to prepare for the start of school—and no access to the educational technology software they typically use to teach. City officials have issued a tech freeze while they deliberate over how artificial intelligence (AI) will be allowed in classrooms, amid public pressure to place a two-year moratorium on the technology.
Across the country, parents, teachers, school districts and state legislatures are currently grappling with similar questions revolving around how much technology should be allowed in the classroom. Just this week, as part of a massive settlement, Meta agreed to institute “school mode” so that kids can’t access Instagram during school hours. Most states now ban student cell phone use in schools, and a broader movement to limit educational screen use is gaining momentum. In March Utah and Alabama became the first states to limit the use of screens in classrooms.
Educational technology companies claim their apps and tools can make learning fun and boost student achievement. Schools also want to prepare students for a future where technology is ubiquitous. But many parents and educators see screens as an expensive distraction providing little additional benefit over analog learning with pencils and paper. And while the financial and educational stakes of these debates are high, the scientific research on the subject is highly nuanced: the effectiveness of these platforms can vary widely, researchers have found. Broadly speaking, digital tools that merely require students to drill new skills don’t promote learning, whereas platforms that are interactive and creatively engaging and provide real-time feedback show benefits.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Tech in schools “is like a lightning rod,” says Christopher Saldaña, a K–12 education policy researcher at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “In some ways, the backlash is a long time coming because we’ve had all these claims about what education technology can do that haven’t always panned out.”
The educational technology (or “ed tech”) industry generated $48 billion in revenue in 2024 and is projected to grow to $90 billion by 2030. The U.S. has some 13,000 public school districts but no central authority that vets marketing claims and provides guidance on which platforms schools should adopt, Saldaña explains.
Individual districts “don’t have the money to be able to vet any of these claims or verify them themselves,” he adds. “They’re often at the mercy of whatever vendors are telling them.”
Data privacy has also emerged as a key concern among grassroots parent groups advocating for screen-free schools. A Utah State Board of Education investigation surveyed educational software with data privacy agreements and found that 61 percent shared student data with third parties and 36 percent shared data with advertisers.
Under Alabama’s new rules, the state’s Department of Education will be required to institute limits on screen time in early childhood education. Utah’s new law bans screens in classrooms for K–3 students, except for computer science lessons and testing. It also bans sending devices home with K–3 students. The Los Angeles Unified School District, the second largest school district in the country, passed a resolution limiting screen use in classrooms in April.
Still, those rules are the exception. Most school districts are forging ahead with technology in classrooms. In a survey of teachers and school leaders conducted this year by the EdWeek Research Center, 74 percent of respondents said that their schools haven’t reduced their investment in education technology as a result of parent pushback and have no plans to do so in the near future. Teachers reported an overall positive effect of educational technology on students’ engagement in learning and mastery of skills but an overall negative effect on their social-emotional skills, overall well-being and behavior in the classroom.
Though digital learning tools are still widely used, bans on noneducational tech in school are now commonplace. At least 39 states and Washington, D.C., have prohibited cell phone use in public schools. Some of these laws only ban devices in class, while others ban them for the entire school day, including lunch and recess. These measures have become increasingly popular among the general public; a Pew survey conducted this spring found that support has risen across all age groups of U.S. adults since 2024.
Research on the impact of these phone bans is mixed. A study of schools that used lockable phone pouches from the company Yondr found that disciplinary incidents rose and student well-being fell in the first year of the phone ban. But in the ensuing years, disciplinary incident rates reduced and student well-being increased. There was no meaningful effect on test scores or attendance throughout the study period, however.
“Bans are just a starting line. They are never a whole comprehensive solution,” says Larz May, founder of #HalftheStory, a digital wellness nonprofit focused on teens. “What we’ve seen on the ground is that alongside phone bans, there are other cuts and issues that are impacting [kids]”—such as funding cuts to art programs and extracurriculars.
Phone ban policies restrict how teens can interact without providing further resources for connection and flourishing, May says. “What we’re hearing is, ‘You’re taking these things away, but what else do you have to offer?’”
Students’ main concerns around technology in schools now revolve around AI, May says. Research conducted by the College Board in 2025 found that high school students are “on the fence” about the risks and benefits of AI in their schooling, even as 84 percent reported using it to help with schoolwork. The study also found that one in five high schools allow generative AI but have no formal policy on what kind of use is acceptable.
The uncertainty is breeding anxiety among students, May reports. “One kid told me ... that he actually videos himself while he’s doing his homework, just in case he gets accused of using AI,” she says. “Kids are going to extreme measures out of fear.”
Meanwhile, ed tech platforms are integrating AI further into their products, says Silvia Noguerón-Liu, a literacy studies researcher at the University of Colorado Boulder. While she stresses that the educational technology platforms used in classrooms are typically well-vetted by districts, the offerings of ed tech companies are expanding and are often marketed as time-saving measures to teachers.
“The last ed tech conference I attended had the big names [in ed tech], and they all had an AI exploration room that felt a little bit dystopian,” Noguerón-Liu says. “Now where this gets very, very problematic is when you rely on it for content,” she says, because charts, information and lesson plans created with AI can often be inaccurate.
And whether technology in a classroom is helping or hurting depends a lot on the teacher, experts say. Educators need training and resources to use technology effectively, and they don’t always get it. “In my mind, teachers’ knowledge and teachers’ actions,” Noguerón-Liu says, “that’s the most impactful component.”

Ukrainian company BlueBird Tech has unveiled a new version of its fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle called the Bebradrone Kit.
This was reported by the press service of BlueBird Tech.
The new system is based on the Bebradrone airframe, proven in real combat conditions.
The key feature of the Bebradrone Kit variant is that customers can choose the configuration of the UAV themselves when placing an order.
Servicemen can select the control and video transmission systems, cameras, flight electronics, navigation equipment, and other specialized modules according to their specific requirements.
The company offers the Bebradrone Kit in four main configurations designed to meet customers’ varying levels of expertise and operational requirements.
The Base version is a basic mechanical airframe designed for self-installation of all equipment.
The ARF configuration comes with the pre-installed motors, while the Pro version is a platform with a fully configured flight controller.
In addition, the developers offer a custom configuration option, with engineers selecting and integrating equipment tailored to a specific mission.
The UAV is designed for units that already have their own communications systems, cameras, or video transmitters and want to integrate them into a ready-to-use airframe.
In its basic configuration, the Bebradrone Kit has a cruising speed of 90 km/h, while its maximum speed reaches 150 km/h.
The platform has an operational range of up to 45 km, with a flight endurance of up to 30 minutes and an operating altitude of 150 to 500 meters. It is launched using a pneumatic catapult and can carry a maximum payload of 7.5 kg.

Indonesia says forest fire hotspots decline, but risks remain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
22:23:48 CST
23:23:48 KST

JAKARTA, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The number of high-confidence forest and land fire hotspots in Indonesia has declined nationwide, but the risk remains as authorities continue intensive firefighting and prevention efforts, particularly in Kalimantan and Sumatra, the Ministry of Forestry said Monday.
Data from the ministry's SiPongi monitoring system showed 946 high-confidence hotspots nationwide as of Sunday night, down 629 from the previous day. West Kalimantan recorded the highest number at 455, followed by Central Kalimantan with 308.
Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said the decline did not mean the fire threat was over.
As of Sunday, authorities had recorded 93 fire incidents across 12 provinces, with fires at 33 locations extinguished and firefighting operations continuing at 60 others.
Joint teams have deployed ground crews, water-bombing helicopters, aerial patrols and weather modification operations, supported by 52 helicopters across Kalimantan and Sumatra.
Antoni warned that peatland fires could continue to smolder even after visible flames disappeared, potentially reigniting without repeated cooling and wetting operations. ■

BANGKOK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's economic growth increased in July on a monthly basis, supported by the global technology and artificial intelligence upswing, easing conflict in the Middle East, and government stimulus measures, the Bank of Thailand said on Monday.
According to the central bank, merchandise exports excluding gold advanced 2.3 percent in July from a month earlier, mainly driven by electronics shipments that also contributed to improved manufacturing production.
However, exports remained heavily reliant on imported inputs, while private investment dipped 0.3 percent month-on-month as machinery and equipment spending cooled after an earlier acceleration, the central bank said in a statement.
Tourism strengthened on higher receipts and a rise in foreign arrivals, especially from long-haul markets, as flight capacity recovered due to easing tensions in the Middle East and seasonal demand during the summer school break, said the central bank's senior director Pranee Sutthasri.
Private consumption rose 1.2 percent compared to the preceding month on stronger spending in services, particularly dining, supported by government measures and domestic tourism during a special long holiday, Pranee told a news conference.
She noted that headline inflation dropped from the prior month as energy costs fell on lower imported oil prices and reduced contributions to the state Oil Fuel Fund, though core inflation edged up slightly owing to cost pass-through in processed food and food ingredients.
Looking ahead, the central bank expects the Thai economy to continue recovering, yet the rebound remains uneven, with key drivers including exports and private investment.
Meanwhile, government measures, reduced inflation, and rising labor income are lifting household consumption as agricultural prices and tourism strengthen, the official added. ■

Swedish firm tests unique unmanned hydrofoil craft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:13:14 UTC
23:13:14 KST

- Aston Harald Composite completed the first test flight of its unmanned GhostFoiler hydrofoil vessel in Stockholm last week.
- The demonstrator, built on hydrofoil technology developed at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, will next join NATO's REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal.
A Swedish composites manufacturer just flew a boat that doesn’t touch the water.
Aston Harald Composite completed the first test flight of an unmanned hydrofoil vessel called GhostFoiler in the waters of Stockholm last week, weaving among ferries and recreational boats in the city’s archipelago. The company said the craft performed well for a first attempt, after resolving grounding and shielding issues that came up during setup.
“The first flight is always special,” the company said. “The test went according to plan, after sorting out the usual grounding and shielding issues, and we were soon flying among ferries and recreational boats in the Stockholm archipelago. It flew well!”
Hydrofoils are not new. Boats mounted on underwater wings have existed for more than a century, using the same lift principle that keeps an airplane in the sky, but applied to water instead of air. What makes GhostFoiler different is that nobody is standing on it. The vessel has to sense the water’s surface, its own height above it, and constantly adjust to stay stable, all without a human balancing on deck the way a foilboard rider would. That’s a substantially harder control problem than keeping a hull floating on the water in the conventional way, and it’s the reason foiling drones have lagged behind ordinary drone boats.
The technology GhostFoiler runs on traces back nearly two decades to a student project at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. In 2008, naval architecture professor Jakob Kuttenkeuler led a group of 15 students in building an early electric hydrofoil board called Evolo, widely credited as one of the first electric hydrofoils ever built and an ancestor of the eFoil boards now sold commercially around the world. Kuttenkeuler has continued that research at KTH’s Maritime Robotics group, developing Evolo into an experimental hydrofoiling testbed for autonomous control systems, sensor fusion and navigation. That academic work was spun out commercially under the name EvoloFoil, which built the hydrofoil rig and flight-control system now flying on GhostFoiler.
Aston Harald Composite, a small Swedish composites manufacturer, built the physical vessel itself. The company designed the hull and manufactured its composite structures, including a carbon-fiber catamaran hull, the lightweight, high-strength material more commonly associated with racing sailboats and aircraft than with typical drone boats. Propulsion comes from two 10-kilowatt electric outrunner motors built by another Swedish company, Zparq AB, which Aston Harald described as extraordinarily quiet, a useful trait for a vessel that may eventually be used for reconnaissance or surveillance work.
The demonstrator is now headed to Portugal, where it will operate under the GhostFoiler name as part of Team Sweden at NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise. REPMUS, short for Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping using Maritime Uncrewed Systems, is an annual NATO exercise where allied nations bring uncrewed underwater, surface and aerial systems to test them together in realistic maritime scenarios, making it one of the main venues where early-stage technology like GhostFoiler gets evaluated alongside systems from established defense contractors.

Hitting a High Point: The Australia-Indonesia 2+2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

Last week, Australia and Indonesia held their tenth 2+2 defense and foreign ministers meeting in Melbourne. The two countries signed the landmark Jakarta Treaty on Common Security in 2024, and although the Indonesian parliament has yet to ratify the treaty, the 2+2 meeting proceeded with the assumption that this is simply the pace of Indonesia’s legislative processes, and that discussions can turn to how best to operationalize their cooperation.
The headline claim is that the relationship between the two countries is now “at a high point.” The Albanese government has made the relationship with Indonesia one of the central pillars of Australia’s foreign policy, understanding how vital friendly, cooperative, relations with its giant near neighbor is to the country’s security. Indonesia, for its part, has recognized it has a capable partner in Canberra that can help advance its own security interests, while maintaining its strategic autonomy.
Although the two countries are seeking to broaden their relationship, at present, defense and security cooperation remain the core elements and these areas were naturally a major focus of the discussions last week.
Given the nature of their geographies, this has developed into a focus on maritime security. At the 2+2 meeting it was announced that Australia will provide aerial drones and training to Indonesia’s Coast Guard. Given that illegal fishing is a central concern throughout Indonesia’s vast waters, and that Chinese often use maritime militia disguised as fishing vessels, greater maritime domain awareness is considered essential for Jakarta.
Alongside this, Australia and Indonesia agreed to increase cooperation on cybercrime, critical infrastructure, and artificial intelligence, building on their existing memorandum of understanding on enhanced cybersecurity and critical technology cooperation. This includes incorporating a defensive cybersecurity component into their bilateral defense exercise, Keris Woomera. Here, cybersecurity is not treated as a separate technical issue, but as a central pillar of military preparedness and national defense.
There is a similar thinking around economic security as inseparable from traditional security. The ministers announced a number of initiatives designed to make their economies more resilient to external shocks and any disruption to supply chains. This included new cooperation to jointly analyze critical supply chain issues and new scholarship courses that will be focused on economic security and resilience – hoping to develop a new cohort of analysts and bureaucrats focused on these issues.
The two countries have already demonstrated how economic interdependence can provide security benefits, with Indonesia working with Australian industry to facilitate a 250,000-tonne agricultural-grade supply of urea due to disruptions from the war in Iran. Alongside this, Australian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) exports to Indonesia have increased threefold over the past year, again in response to supply chain disruptions in the Middle East.
These practical forms of food and energy security are becoming increasingly intertwined with geopolitics. The two countries therefore have an interest in using the resources of one another to address their vulnerabilities. Given both their proximity to each other, and their current distance from global hotspots, there is an opportunity to build resilience together that can withstand any global shocks.
These shocks include the environment. The 2+2 meeting announced the second phase of KINETIK – the Australia-Indonesia Climate and Sustainable Infrastructure Partnership, which will provide US$430 million over ten years to support sustainable infrastructure and climate investment in Indonesia. Its aim is to mobilize public and private capital into clean energy, water, waste management, and sustainable transport, helping Indonesia build climate-resilient infrastructure and accelerate its energy transition. With the hope of the two countries also developing their green technology capabilities.
The 2+2 meeting also demonstrated considered strategic alignment over the regional order – something that hasn’t always been the case. The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to international law, sovereignty and ASEAN centrality, with both expressing concern about rising tensions in the South China Sea and insisting that the Code of Conduct being developed by ASEAN and China must comply with international law.
The significance of the 2+2 is the growing web of cooperation between Canberra and Jakarta. From defense exercises to maritime surveillance to cybersecurity and economic resilience, there has been a noticeable step up in the relationship. This does not amount to a formal alliance, but more a convergence of interests and a recognition that as neighbors there is a natural interconnectedness. The previous distance in outlook and coordination is starting to be overcome.

What Zheng He’s Changing Role Reveals About China’s Maritime Strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

The Ming Dynasty navigator Zheng He is often closely associated with Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road narrative. But the historical figure has been used as a diplomatic tool for decades, long before Xi launched the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
Zheng He entered the diplomatic storytelling of the People’s Republic of China within a decade of its founding. Under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao he became part of a broader historical argument about China’s rise, a role that remained prominent during the first years of Xi’s presidency.
Much attention has been paid to why Beijing revived Zheng He. But few have noticed how mentions of Zheng He changed: Since 2018, China’s top leaders have increasingly moved away from using him to argue that a stronger China would not become a conquering power.
As early as the late Qing period, Chinese nationalists recast Zheng He as evidence that China had once possessed global reach. During the Republican era he entered Chinese history textbooks and became a domestic symbol of national capacity. Around the time of the Bandung Conference, Beijing began recoding him for diplomacy. Zheng He was increasingly presented as a powerful but anti-colonial emissary of Afro-Asian friendship, particularly in China’s relations with newly independent African states.
Under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao, China’s top leaders systematically invoked Zheng He in diplomatic settings to answer a question at the heart of China’s rise: How would a China that was becoming powerful again use its power? In 2003, while explaining China’s “peaceful rise and development” at Harvard University, Wen described Zheng He as a diplomat who had sought friendly relations with other countries across seven voyages, tying this history directly to the Chinese tradition of loving peace.
In 2005, speaking to the Mexican Senate, Hu again used the Silk Road and Zheng He’s voyages as historical evidence of China’s commitment to peaceful development. In Pretoria in 2007, Hu invoked Zheng He before turning to China’s own experience of colonialism to argue that China would not impose its will on Africa.
The logic of Hu’s argument rested on an asymmetry of power. A fleet incapable of conquest proves nothing by refraining from violence. Only if the fleet is understood to possess the capacity to conquer can its peaceful approach serve as evidence of restraint. To Chinese leaders, Zheng He’s story showed how China would exercise superior power without undertaking conquest. Beijing drew on this argument particularly when it sought to reassure foreign audiences about how China would use its growing power, including in its diplomacy with African, Southeast Asian, and Arab states.
This usage persisted for a while after Xi took office. In 2014, Xi placed Zheng He directly within his argument that the Chinese nation carries “no gene for invading others or seeking hegemony.” At the first Belt and Road Forum in 2017, Xi listed Zheng He alongside Zhang Qian, Du Huan, Marco Polo, and Ibn Battuta as friendly envoys along the Silk Road. As the Maritime Silk Road became central to Xi-era diplomacy, Zheng He remained an obvious historical resource.
The later Premier Li Keqiang was especially consistent in bringing up Zheng He during this period. At the 2015 China-ASEAN Leaders’ Meeting and the East Asia Summit, Li invoked the navigator to argue that the South China Sea had been a sea of peace and freedom of navigation for six centuries. Three years later, at the 2018 East Asia Summit, Li was still using Zheng He in much the same way.
After 2018, however, the pattern of top-level use began to change. The decline was most visible in the field of regional maritime order, where references to Zheng He had once figured prominently. At the 2019 East Asia Summit, Li addressed similar regional issues without invoking Zheng He. By the 2023 Belt and Road Forum, even the language of civilizational exchange and connectivity no longer required name-dropping Zheng He.
One contributing factor may have been the 2016 South China Sea arbitration, which made historical arguments about maritime rights more legally awkward. But the timing does not line up perfectly. Two years after the ruling, Li was still making much the same argument. Instead, the break came in 2019, which means the arbitration alone cannot account for it.
China’s maritime strategy and naval capabilities were themselves changing. In 2012, the 18th Party Congress formally called for China to become a “maritime power.” Three years later, the defense white paper China’s Military Strategy directed the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) to move from a posture centered on “offshore waters defense” toward a combination of “offshore waters defense” and “open seas protection.”
At celebrations marking the PLAN’s 70th anniversary in Qingdao in 2019, Xi introduced the idea of a “maritime community with a shared future.” He also stressed that China followed a defensive national defense policy and that the navy would safeguard international sea lanes, shoulder international responsibilities, and provide more public goods for maritime security.
The U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 China Military Power Report describes the PLAN as fielding Asia’s largest force of principal surface combatants, submarines, and amphibious warfare ships. As China built aircraft carriers, sustained far-seas escort missions, established overseas support facilities, and expanded its shipbuilding capacity, Beijing increasingly shifted the basis of its reassurance from historical precedent toward declared policy and contemporary behavior.
The growth of China’s naval capabilities reduced Zheng He’s value as evidence of maritime power. It also changed the analogy itself. In the 2000s, the official narrative constructed by Hu and Wen used Zheng He to show that maritime capability and peaceful intent could coexist. But by the late 2010s, China’s expanding naval power had become an observable reality, increasingly open to judgment through the navy’s actual conduct. The more the Zheng He narrative linked formidable maritime power with voluntary restraint, the more it invited foreign audiences to apply the same standard to China today. The analogy had therefore become more politically demanding.
Zheng He still appears, but mostly in bilateral settings to discuss historical ties with specific countries or communities. In April 2025, Xi’s signed article in the Malaysian press mentioned sites in Malacca associated with Zheng He. On April 21, 2026, during a meeting with Mozambican President Daniel Chapo, Xi noted that Zheng He’s fleet had visited the Mozambican coast more than six centuries earlier. In June of the same year, the Chinese embassy in Tanzania again presented Zheng He’s voyages as a historical symbol of long-standing exchanges between Chinese and Swahili civilizations. Later that month, Jakarta launched a series of cultural exchanges under the banner of “Zheng He’s Voyage: Envoys of Friendship.” In these settings, Zheng He primarily serves as a marker of shared history. In that sense, Beijing is returning Zheng He to the more limited diplomatic role he played in the 1950s and 1960s.
Zheng He’s visibility remains high. Exhibitions in Jakarta and Nairobi marked the 620th anniversary of his voyages; an academy in Angola now bears his name, as do international freight links. But in recent top-level diplomacy, he no longer serves primarily as evidence of China’s national character.
That retreat has also made the difference between Zheng He and another historical icon, Zhang Qian, easier to see. Zhang Qian, the Han Dynasty envoy sent to the Western Regions, has long been regarded as a pioneer of the overland Silk Road. Compared with Zheng He, he represents the active opening of new routes and spaces for exchange. Existing discussions often treat the two as equivalent historical precursors of the Belt and Road. Yet Zhang Qian cannot easily perform Zheng He’s old role of providing reassurance as to China’s peaceful intentions.
The shift has also been uneven across Zheng He’s main diplomatic settings. He appears to have receded more sharply in Africa than in Southeast Asia. In its diplomacy with Africa, Beijing increasingly draws on 20th century anti-colonial solidarity and the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation to narrate historical ties. In Southeast Asia, by contrast, physical sites associated with Zheng He in Malacca, local memories of his voyages, and the Maritime Silk Road continue to sustain a highly localized political afterlife for the navigator.
Another round of China-ASEAN leaders’ meetings and the East Asia Summit will take place this November, while Shenzhen will host the APEC summit in the same month. Whether Zheng He reappears will be worth watching. If Beijing invokes him again, the more revealing question will be what it asks him to prove this time: restraint six centuries ago, or simply a shared local past.

The second system was hit on August 30 near the military airfield in Yeysk, Krasnodar Krai.

The Pantsir-S1 is a Russian short-range self-propelled system designed to protect civilian and military facilities from drones, cruise missiles, and aircraft.
The system is armed with two twin-barrel 2A38M 30 mm automatic cannons and 12 guided surface-to-air missiles. The cannons have an engagement range of up to 4 km, while the missiles can engage targets at ranges of up to 20 km and altitudes of up to 15 km.

Popular sweeteners may leave effects that last for generations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:04:01 UTC
23:04:01 KST

Popular sweeteners may leave effects that last for generations
Popular zero-calorie sweeteners changed the gut and metabolism of mice, with some effects unexpectedly echoing into future generations.
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Two widely used zero-calorie sweeteners, sucralose and stevia, may have effects that linger far longer than the sweet taste itself. In mice, researchers found that both sweeteners altered the gut microbiome, reduced beneficial compounds produced by gut bacteria, and changed the activity of genes involved in metabolism and inflammation. Some of those changes were also detected in later generations that had never consumed the sweeteners themselves.
- Share:
Choosing the diet version of a favorite soda often means consuming non-nutritive sweeteners. These additives provide sweetness without the calories found in sugar. However, some health organizations have begun raising questions about their possible long-term effects, including whether they may disrupt energy metabolism and eventually contribute to a higher risk of diabetes or cardiovascular disease.
New research in mice adds to those concerns. The study suggests that sucralose and stevia, two widely used sweeteners, can alter the gut microbiome and gene activity in ways that may affect metabolic health. Some of these biological changes were also observed in later generations.
"We found it intriguing that despite the growing consumption of these additives, the prevalence of obesity and metabolic disorders such as insulin resistance has not declined," said Dr. Francisca Concha Celume of the Universidad de Chile, lead author of the article in Frontiers in Nutrition. "This does not mean that sweeteners are responsible for these trends, but it raises the question of whether they influence metabolism in ways we do not yet fully understand."
Testing Sucralose and Stevia Across Generations
Researchers began by dividing 47 male and female mice into three groups. One group received plain water, while the other two received water containing either sucralose or stevia. The doses were designed to resemble amounts that a person might reasonably consume as part of a normal diet.
The mice were then bred for two successive generations. Unlike the original animals, both later generations were given only plain water.
"Animal models allow us to control environmental conditions very precisely and to isolate the effect of a specific factor, such as a dietary compound, while also following several generations within a relatively short time," explained Concha.
Tracking Blood Sugar, Gut Bacteria, and Gene Activity
Researchers tested each generation for oral glucose tolerance, a measure used to evaluate how effectively the body handles glucose and identify signs of insulin resistance, which is an important warning sign for diabetes.
They also collected fecal samples to examine changes in the gut microbiome and measure concentrations of short-chain fatty acids. These compounds are produced by gut bacteria and can influence biological processes related to gene regulation. Changes in their levels could therefore point to epigenetic effects that may be transmitted from parents to offspring.
Scientists think sweeteners may alter short-chain fatty acid production by disrupting normal gut microbiome function. Those disruptions could ultimately influence gene expression.
The team also measured the activity of five genes in the liver and intestines. The genes are involved in inflammation, the integrity of the gut barrier, and metabolism. By examining them, researchers hoped to identify possible epigenetic changes connected with gut function, inflammation, and metabolic health that could help explain some of the suspected negative effects of non-nutritive sweeteners.
Sucralose and Stevia Produced Different Effects
The two sweeteners did not affect the mice in exactly the same way, and their effects also shifted between generations.
Among first-generation offspring, signs of impaired glucose tolerance appeared only in males descended from mice that consumed sucralose. By the second generation, researchers found elevated fasting blood sugar in male descendants of the sucralose group and female descendants of the stevia group.
Mice that consumed either sweetener also developed more diverse fecal microbiomes, but they had lower levels of short-chain fatty acids. That pattern suggests their gut bacteria were producing fewer beneficial metabolites. Reduced short-chain fatty acid concentrations were also found in both subsequent generations.
The effects associated with sucralose were stronger and more persistent. Mice exposed to sucralose showed larger changes in the composition of their fecal microbiomes, including greater numbers of potentially pathogenic bacteria and fewer beneficial species.
Sucralose Changes Persisted Longer
Sucralose also appeared to increase the activity of genes linked to inflammation while reducing the activity of genes associated with metabolism. Those effects were still detectable two generations after the original exposure.
Stevia also altered gene expression, but the changes were weaker and did not persist beyond one generation.
"When we compared generations, these effects were generally strongest in the first generation and tended to decrease in the second generation," said Concha. "Overall, the effects linked to sucralose were more consistent and persistent across generations."
"The changes we observed in glucose tolerance and gene expression could be interpreted as early biological signals related to metabolic or inflammatory processes," said Concha. "For example, the animals did not develop diabetes. Instead, what we observed were subtle changes in how the body regulates glucose and in the activity of genes associated with inflammation and metabolic regulation. It is possible that such changes could increase susceptibility to metabolic disturbances under certain conditions, such as a high-fat diet."
What the Mouse Study Does and Does Not Show
The researchers caution that the findings show associations between sweetener exposure and changes in metabolic health, but they do not prove that the sweeteners directly caused all of the observed effects.
The results also come from mice, meaning the biological response to non-nutritive sweeteners may differ in humans.
"The goal of this research is not to create alarm, but to highlight the need for further investigation," said Concha. "It may be reasonable to consider moderation in the consumption of these additives and to continue studying their long-term biological effects."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Francisca Concha Celume, Francisco Pérez-Bravo, Fabien Magne, Ricardo Olivares, Martin Gotteland. Artificial and natural non-nutritive sweeteners drive divergent gut and genetic responses across generations. Frontiers in Nutrition, 2026; 13 DOI: 10.3389/fnut.2026.1694149
