More flooding feared at Grand Canyon after storm leaves 15 missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

More flooding feared at Grand Canyon after storm leaves 15 missing
LOS ANGELES – Storms forecast for Aug 31 could trigger new flash floods in the Grand Canyon, the National Weather Service said, as crews looked for around 15 people missing in a flood that claimed at least one life.
The floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area on Aug 29, forcing dozens of people to evacuate and damaging the sole water pipeline serving the park, one of the most popular national parks in the US.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on the evening of Aug 30 near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River in northern Arizona, the park service said.
The National Weather Service said that rain and thunderstorms are expected again on the afternoon of Aug 31.
“Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas. Raging killer currents will be possible in side canyons and narrow slot canyons. Low-water crossings may be flooded,” it said in a bulletin.
Video footage taken by hikers showed a torrent of muddy water rushing by trails and under footbridges, as well as logs and other debris floating down swollen rivers, accompanied by a rumbling roar.
The park service said it was working with the Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for missing individuals.
As at the morning of Aug 30, 62 people had been evacuated, with others scheduled for later, it said.
It said around 15 people were thought to be missing.
Water pipeline damaged
The flooding damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said, announcing water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires.
The 20km pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park’s website.
The flooding resulted in “significant impacts to infrastructure”, destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said.
Overnight accommodations were closed beginning on Aug 31.
“These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park service said.
The flash flood, which began about 2.30pm on Aug 29, was caused by rain on the Kaibab Plateau, it said.
Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments there have little capacity to absorb rain, the park’s website said, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September.
The Grand Canyon – considered one of the greatest wonders of the natural world – is the result of the Colorado River eating away at layers of red sandstone and other rock for millions of years, leaving a chasm up to 29km wide and more than 1.6km deep.
In 2025, almost five million people visited the site. AFP

Compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du 31 août 2026.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:10:00 CEST
22:10:00 KST

COMMUNICATION
- Rentrée scolaire 2026
MESURES D’ORDRE INDIVIDUEL
Retrouvez le compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du lundi 31 août 2026.
31 août 2026 - Compte-rendu
Compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du 31 août 2026.
COMMUNICATION
RENTRÉE SCOLAIRE 2026
Le ministre de l’éducation nationale a présenté une communication sur la rentrée scolaire 2026.
La rentrée concerne cette année 11,6 millions d'élèves et 1,2 million de personnels de l’éducation nationale, dans plus de 55 000 implantations sur toute la France. Cette rentrée est marquée par l’accélération de la chute démographique, avec 161 000 élèves de moins dans notre système éducatif. Une évolution qui devrait se poursuivre, avec une baisse attendue de 1,7 million d’élèves entre 2025 et 2035. Cette rentrée est caractérisée par l’entrée en vigueur de nouvelles mesures, dédiées à la fois à améliorer la qualité de notre service public et à renforcer la protection des élèves, mais aussi de chantiers de long terme, car ce que la France sera dans vingt ans – ses innovations, sa cohésion, sa capacité à s'adapter – se décide aujourd'hui, dans chaque salle de classe.
En conséquence, quatre priorités guident l'action du ministère pour répondre à ces enjeux :
- Instruire avec une exigence renforcée, pour élever le niveau des élèves et former de futurs citoyens. Les mesures déjà engagées portent leurs fruits : dédoublement des classes en éducation prioritaire, plafonnement à 24 élèves en grande section, évaluations nationales des élèves du CP à la seconde, refonte totale des programmes de la petite section à la troisième avec des objectifs annuels. Pour poursuivre cet élan, l'accent est mis sur deux priorités absolues : la maîtrise du langage d’une part, avec un effort centré sur le vocabulaire (objectif de 2 500 mots acquis en fin de maternelle), sur l’apprentissage par cœur, et sur la lecture et l’écriture ; le raisonnement scientifique et les mathématiques d’autre part, en replaçant les automatismes et la résolution de problèmes au cœur des apprentissages, et avec la création dès cette rentrée de plus de 300 classes à horaires aménagés en mathématiques et sciences. Cette ambition s'étend à tous les établissements, avec une attention particulière portée à la lutte contre la grande difficulté scolaire, notamment au collège, ainsi qu'à la valorisation de l'excellence.
En lien avec la ministre déléguée chargée de l'enseignement et de la formation professionnels et de l’apprentissage, la carte des formations continue d'être adaptée et le dispositif AvenirPro sera déployé dans l'ensemble des lycées professionnels afin d'améliorer l'insertion des futurs diplômés. Le conseil national de la refondation consacré à l'attractivité de cette voie sera lancé en octobre 2026.
Enfin, la réforme du recrutement et de la formation des enseignants, permettant désormais de recruter et former les professeurs dès la licence, s’est traduite par l’amélioration de l’attractivité des concours, avec une hausse de 50 % du nombre d’admis pour 40 % de postes ouverts en plus. Pour mémoire, les lauréats des concours en fin de L3 débutent en ce mois de septembre leur formation rémunérée en master.
- Protéger : la protection des élèves et de l'institution constitue une priorité absolue.
Il s’agit d’abord de protéger les élèves contre les violences sexuelles. Alors que près de 10 % des mineurs seraient victimes de viols ou d’agressions sexuelles, dans plus de 80 % des cas dans le cercle familial, tous les élèves de la grande section à la terminale pourront faire part de leur situation, grâce à un questionnaire adapté à l'âge des enfants distribué dès novembre, avec la possibilité pour chaque élève de solliciter un entretien avec un adulte de confiance s’il le souhaite.
Il s’agit ensuite de protéger les élèves contre la surexposition aux écrans, dont les effets sur l'attention, le sommeil, la santé mentale et les facultés intellectuelles des élèves sont désormais scientifiquement établis. C’est le sens de l'interdiction du téléphone portable au lycée, prévue par la loi promulguée la semaine dernière par le Président de la République. Pour la première fois, les élèves français auront une scolarité complète sans téléphone. Des alternatives sportives, éducatives et culturelles seront proposées pour offrir de nouveaux espaces de sociabilité aux élèves. En outre, 300 emplois d’infirmiers, assistants sociaux et psychologues de l’éducation nationale sont créés en cette rentrée.
Enfin, la protection des personnels est renforcée par un décret permettant de changer d'affectation un élève dont les parents menaceraient gravement un membre du personnel éducatif, tout en garantissant un suivi scolaire renforcé.
- Unir : car l'École est la fabrique de l'unité républicaine et de la citoyenneté. Cela implique de garantir une Ecole inclusive, laïque, luttant contre toutes les formes de discriminations et capable de rassembler autour de valeurs communes.
Depuis 2017, l'École inclusive a été profondément renforcée : 70 % d'AESH supplémentaires ont été recrutés et près de 2 800 ULIS ont été créées dans le premier et le second degré. Aujourd'hui, nos écoles accueillent 200 000 élèves en situation de handicap de plus qu’en 2017. Cette politique d’inclusion se poursuit en renforçant notamment l’attention portée à l’accessibilité, afin de permettre une scolarisation réussie et de faciliter les adaptations pédagogiques.
Dans le cadre d’un travail conjoint avec plusieurs ministères, le plan de formation à la laïcité, le plan de lutte contre le racisme et l'antisémitisme et le plan de lutte contre les haines et les LGBTphobies ont été mis en place.
Enfin, le 11 novembre, journée nationale de la Victoire et de la Paix et d’hommage aux « morts pour la France », sera désormais commémoré dans toutes les écoles élémentaires et établissements scolaires. La cohésion nationale implique en effet de faire mémoire de celles et ceux qui ont risqué leur vie pour défendre les principes de liberté, d’égalité et de fraternité qui nous fondent.
- Prévoir : les changements majeurs qui bouleversent notre société – baisse des naissances, changement climatique, intelligence artificielle – emportent des conséquences profondes sur l’organisation et le fonctionnement de l’Ecole. Le ministère se dote donc d’une capacité à prévoir ces évolutions et à mener les adaptations nécessaires.
La baisse démographique impose de sortir d’une logique strictement annuelle pour renouer avec une politique d’aménagement du territoire par et autour de l’Ecole. L'expérimentation en cours dans 18 départements pilotes permettra de construire, en étroite collaboration avec les élus locaux, une carte de l’offre scolaire pluriannuelle. Afin d’appuyer cette nouvelle méthode qui a vocation à s’appliquer à l’ensemble des départements dès 2027, le ministère procèdera à la création d’une direction de la politique territoriale de l'École et de l'anticipation avant le 1er novembre.
Le changement climatique exige également une réponse concrète et planifiée, en appui aux collectivités territoriales, qui sont propriétaires du bâti scolaire : un plan accéléré d'adaptation sera mis en œuvre pour 2 500 écoles vulnérables identifiées pendant l’été, tandis que le plan de gestion des vagues de chaleur sera renforcé d’ici au printemps prochain. Toutes les épreuves des examens de 2027, à l'exception des quelques épreuves qui durent toute la journée en voie professionnelle, se tiendront uniquement le matin.
Enfin face à l'intelligence artificielle, une approche pragmatique a été adoptée. En lien avec le Premier ministre, un enseignement obligatoire de l'IA en classe de seconde sera mis en place dès 2027, afin que les élèves en gardent l’entière maîtrise. Le programme de cet enseignement et la formation des professeurs seront mis en place cette année.
S’agissant enfin des conditions techniques de la rentrée, le ministère de l’éducation nationale a fait face à une série de cyberattaques pendant l’été qui l’ont conduit à prendre des mesures de protection. A titre de précaution, l’accès aux applications informatiques a ainsi été fermé ou très fortement réduit dans les académies de Toulouse et de Nantes pour les jours à venir. Cette situation, complexe pour les équipes, n’empêche pas l’accueil des élèves dès la rentrée et le début des cours dans des conditions ordinaires.
MESURES D’ORDRE INDIVIDUEL
Le conseil des ministres a adopté les mesures individuelles suivantes :
Sur proposition du Premier ministre :
- M. Vianney BOURQUARD, conseiller référendaire à la Cour des comptes, est nommé conseiller maître à la cour des comptes (1er tour), à compter du 1er septembre 2026 ;
- M. Paul TEBOUL, conseiller référendaire à la Cour des comptes, est nommé conseiller maître à la cour des comptes (2ème tour), à compter du 1er septembre 2026 ;
- M. Pierre ROLLAND, conseiller référendaire à la Cour des comptes, est nommé conseiller maître à la cour des comptes (3ème tour), à compter du 1er septembre 2026 ;
- M. Christian CHAPARD, conseiller référendaire à la Cour des comptes, est nommé conseiller maître à la cour des comptes (4ème intérieur), à compter du 1er septembre 2026.
Sur proposition de la ministre des armées et des anciens combattants :
- M. le contrôleur général des armées Sylvain MATTIUCCI est nommé chef du contrôle général des armées, à compter du 1er septembre 2026 ;
- M. l'ingénieur général de 1ère classe de l’armement, ingénieur du grade transitoire des ingénieurs de l'armement Bruno BELLIER est nommé directeur général de l’Ecole Polytechnique, à compter du 1er septembre 2026 ;
- Il est mis fin aux fonctions de directeur stratégie de défense, prospective et contreprolifération de la direction générale des relations internationales et de la stratégie exercées par M. l’ingénieur général hors classe de l’armement, ingénieur du grade transitoire des ingénieurs de l’armement Bertrand LE MEUR, à compter du 1er septembre 2026.
En outre, ont été adoptées diverses mesures d’ordre individuel concernant des officiers généraux de l’armée de terre et de la direction générale de l’armement.
Sur proposition de la ministre de la transition écologique, de la biodiversité et des négociations internationales sur le climat et la nature :
- M. Alexis VUILLEMIN, ingénieur des ponts, des eaux et des forêts du grade transitoire, est nommé secrétaire général, à compter du 1er septembre 2026.
Sur proposition de la ministre de l'agriculture, de l'agro-alimentaire et de la souveraineté alimentaire :
- Mme Marion ZALAY, ingénieure des ponts, des eaux et des forêts du grade transitoire, est nommée directrice générale de l’Établissement national des produits de l’agriculture et de la mer (FranceAgriMer), à compter du 1er septembre 2026 ;
- Mme Maud FAIPOUX, ingénieure des ponts, des eaux et des forêts du grade transitoire, est nommée directrice générale de l’enseignement et de la recherche.

Spectator calls low stadium flyover a top life moment: "Amazing"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
13:07:55 UTC
22:07:55 KST

Spectator stunned by low flyover at Cape Town rugby stadium: "Probably one of my top-5 moments in my life"
An extremely low flyover above a rugby stadium in South Africa has left many people asking: How low is too low?
Two passenger jets — one following the other — swept just above the packed DHL Stadium in Cape Town on Saturday, coming really close to more than 56,000 people below.
For a spectator who witnessed the passenger jets soaring overhead and captured it on video, it was a moment to remember.
"I didn't feel any danger from my side. I was just like, 'Wow, this is insane,'" said Marcel Opperman.
"It was amazing," he said. "Probably one of my top-five moments in my life."
Preliminary flight data estimates the planes cleared the stadium by only about 50 feet, which airline captain Laura Einsetler said is "really low and really tight for an airliner."
She said the full-size jets are very different from the fighter jets often seen in flyovers.
"It was just too low for this situation with this type of jet at those speeds and angles," Einsetler said.
The spectacle has roots going back more than three decades. Back in 1995, just a year after South Africa's first democratic elections, a South African Airways 747 flew low over a Johannesburg stadium during a Rugby World Cup final, as the country emerged from apartheid.
In a statement, Airlink said the planes in Saturday's flyover were operating safely, telling CBS News: "The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude. ... The South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby."
Airlink said the pilots were senior and experienced, and that they stayed within the altitude and speed limits set by the South African equivalent of the FAA.

US visa delays leave Chinese students stranded with ‘frozen’ plans and ‘constant anxiety’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US visa delays leave Chinese students stranded with ‘frozen’ plans and ‘constant anxiety’
International students are being forced to defer enrolment at US universities as background checks and visa bottlenecks put them in limbo
Under a provision of US immigration law known as “administrative processing” or visa checks, applicants may be asked to submit supplementary documents and undergo additional security reviews before their visas can be approved.
Social media posts and interviews with affected students indicate these extended background checks are sweeping up a wider cross-section of applicants and fields of study.
Ray Zhou, a Beijing resident admitted to a master’s degree programme in computer science, said the prolonged checks – now stretching beyond two months – had forced him to defer his enrolment until next year. Zhou, like the other students interviewed, asked not to give his full Chinese name or university because his visa was still being processed.
“My mindset experienced a drastic shift,” he said. “At first, I felt relief from avoiding an immediate refusal and thought I would simply wait it out. But as the start of the semester got closer, the anxiety became overwhelming.”

Iceland to seek new security partnerships after voters reject EU accession talks
Unknown

Iceland to seek new security partnerships after voters reject EU accession talks
REYKJAVIK, Aug 31 - Iceland needs to find new ways to strengthen its security after voters rejected restarting accession talks with the EU, the country's foreign minister told Reuters on Monday, including by seeking bilateral cooperation and deepening ties with the bloc.
The comments came after Icelanders on Saturday voted to reject a government push to reopen EU membership talks.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly said he wants to acquire neighbouring Greenland and has cast doubt on Washington's commitment to NATO, has sharpened the security debate in Iceland in recent months.
"We didn't vote away the geopolitical situation, it's still there and we will have to find other ways to increase our security," Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir told Reuters in parliament after meeting the foreign affairs committee.
In rejecting EU membership talks voters brushed aside government warnings that EU membership could bolster its security.
"The EU is still a very important partner for Iceland, and we need to strengthen our cooperation further. We will look at bilateral agreements, we already have such agreements with Finland and Norway," she said, also mentioning Japan and Canada as important partners.
Iceland, an Arctic island of 400,000 people, is a NATO member but has no standing army of its own. Its defence is based on a bilateral defence agreement with the United States from 1951 and NATO membership.
In Saturday's referendum, 52.8% of ballots cast were against the government's proposal to hold negotiations with Brussels, 47.2% were in favour, with 82.5% of eligible voters taking part.
Iceland has been part of the European Economic Area since 1994, an agreement with the EU that grants Iceland access to the EU's single market but without being a full member.
"We will have to strengthen cooperation within the EEA. A very positive outcome of the referendum is that all Icelandic parties are now united behind the EEA agreement," she said. REUTERS

How monogamous and polyamorous individuals envision multiple romantic partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
13:00:19 UTC
22:00:19 KST

When people imagine having two long-term romantic partners at the same time, a majority envision two people with similar, well-rounded traits, though monogamous men often show a preference for one partner focused on physical attractiveness and sexual skill. These findings highlight how intended time and emotional investment shape human mating preferences in non-monogamous contexts. The research was published in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships.
Historically, research into human mating preferences has centered on monogamy, an exclusive relationship between two people. In this context, researchers have mapped out how individuals prioritize traits like kindness, intelligence, and physical attractiveness in a single long-term partner. Consensual non-monogamy and concurrent mating structures have been present throughout human history and across various cultures. This historical prevalence led researchers to question whether human mating psychology is adapted to generate distinct preferences when multiple partners are involved.
Ashley J. Coventry, a researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and her colleagues initiated a project to determine whether people prefer the same traits in multiple concurrent partners or if they seek different characteristics in each person. The research team hypothesized that the costs and benefits of certain traits might shift depending on how many partners a person has. For example, a single wealthy partner could theoretically provide enough financial stability for a whole family unit, potentially decreasing a person’s need to seek out high financial prospects in a second partner.
In their first study, the researchers recruited 267 primarily monogamous individuals. Participants completed a budget allocation task, a method where they received a fixed amount of 70 points to spend on specific traits for two hypothetical long-term partners. This forced-choice format creates artificial scarcity among traits like ambition, physical attractiveness, intelligence, and kindness. The researchers then used a statistical technique called cluster analysis to group the hypothetical partners based on how participants distributed their limited points.
The analysis revealed two primary categories of ideal partners, the first of which was labeled “well-rounded” because participants distributed their points evenly across traits. The second category was labeled “good in bed and attractive,” where points were heavily concentrated on physical appearance and sexual skill. Nearly three-quarters of the participants preferred two partners of the same type, but over a quarter of the respondents preferred distinct traits for each partner. In this group, male participants were much more likely than female participants to design at least one partner who prioritized attractiveness and sexual skill.
To confirm these patterns, the researchers conducted a second study with 227 mostly monogamous participants. This study replicated the point-spending methods of the first but added questions about how participants would divide their resources between the two hypothetical partners. Participants rated how they would allocate their financial investment, their daily time, and their emotional closeness across the two relationships.
The second study produced the exact same two partner categories as the first, with most participants again preferring two well-rounded partners. Among those who desired different partner types, men frequently preferred one well-rounded partner and one partner focused on attractiveness and sexual skill. The investment questions revealed that participants who designed two different types of partners planned to divide their resources unequally. These individuals typically intended to invest more time, money, and emotional energy into the well-rounded partner compared to the partner valued primarily for physical and sexual traits.
In a third study, the research team recruited 169 individuals who currently identified as polyamorous. Polyamory is a relationship structure where people can have multiple consensual, romantic partnerships at the same time with the knowledge of everyone involved. The participants completed the same budget allocation and investment tasks as the previous groups. This allowed the researchers to test whether the patterns found in monogamous people applied to those actually practicing non-monogamy.
The cluster analysis for this group yielded slightly different categories. While the well-rounded partner type remained the most common, the second category centered on kindness and sexual skill rather than physical attractiveness. Similar to the previous studies, nearly three-quarters of the polyamorous participants preferred two partners of the same type. Unlike the monogamous groups, polyamorous men and women displayed no statistical divergence in their partner preferences.
Both men and women in the polyamorous group most commonly designed two identical partner types. While participants who designed two different partner types again reported intentions to divide their time unequally, the polyamorous group generally aimed for more equal investment across both partners. The sex-based variations seen in the monogamous sample simply did not appear among the polyamorous respondents.
The researchers note a few limitations to the project. The statistical clusters represent general patterns of point allocation in a specific task rather than rigid, real-world categories of human beings. The reliance on a point-spending system forces participants into trade-offs that might not capture how human attraction naturally unfolds.
The total number of polyamorous participants was lower than initially planned, which can reduce a study’s statistical power to detect minor behavioral patterns. The survey also did not ask polyamorous participants about their specific relationship structures. Some polyamorous individuals practice a hierarchical structure with primary and secondary partners, while others avoid relationship hierarchies entirely. These structural differences likely influence how people imagine investing their time across multiple partners.
The monogamous participants may have inherently imagined a primary and secondary relationship dynamic when asked to envision two partners, prompting them to assign different traits to each. Additionally, the participant pool was limited to individuals living in the United States. Future studies could explore how specific types of consensual non-monogamy alter these preferences in different cultural settings. The authors also suggest exploring these questions with larger groups of non-binary individuals, as they were excluded from the current analysis to maintain sample parity across binary sex categories.
The study, “Preferences and Polyamory: Investigating Ideal Mate Preferences for Concurrent Partners in Monogamous and Polyamorous Individuals,” was authored by Ashley J. Coventry, Benjamin Gelbart, Kathryn V. Walter, Tamsin German, and Daniel Conroy-Beam.

Rolls-Royce completes $1bn US defence investment
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:00:14 BST
22:00:14 KST

Rolls-Royce has completed a decade-long $1 billion investment programme in Indiana, expanding manufacturing, assembly and engine-test facilities supporting US military aircraft including the B-52, C-130J, V-22 and MQ-25A, according to the company.
Rolls-Royce announced completion of the programme on 27 August, describing it as the largest investment the company has made in the United States.
The work has modernised manufacturing facilities across the company’s Indianapolis campus and added full engine-test capability. It also includes new ground-test facilities and an altitude-test facility at West Lafayette. Rolls-Royce said more of its defence products are now built in Indianapolis than at any other company site worldwide.
Adam Riddle, President of Defence and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America, said in the company release: “This billion-dollar investment is about more than buildings and test cells — it is about delivering for the American warfighter, on time and at the standard our customers expect. We made this investment because it was the right thing to do for U.S. national security and for the future of Rolls-Royce.”
The Indianapolis site builds and tests engines for a range of current and future US military aircraft. Rolls-Royce identified future propulsion work for the US Air Force’s B-52 strategic bomber and the US Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne among the programmes supported by the campus.
Current production also supports the V-22 Osprey, Lockheed Martin C-130J and the US Navy’s MQ-25A Stingray uncrewed carrier-based tanker. The investment therefore spans both established fleets and aircraft currently entering or preparing for future service, with the Indiana facilities covering manufacturing as well as assembly and testing.
Rolls-Royce employs approximately 3,500 people in Indianapolis, including a unionised manufacturing workforce, and says its operations support additional employment through suppliers elsewhere in Indiana. Indiana Governor Mike Braun said in the release: “Rolls-Royce has called Indiana home for three decades, and this billion-dollar investment is a vote of confidence in Hoosier workers and our state.”
He added: “Advanced manufacturing like this is exactly what keeps Indiana’s economy strong and growing. We are proud that Indiana is home to Rolls-Royce in the U.S., and we look forward to their continued success for generations to come.”
The company has also invested elsewhere in its American industrial base. According to Rolls-Royce, expenditure over the past decade amounts to more than $1.5 billion across US facilities and almost $2.5 billion in research and development.
The Indianapolis campus is also home to LibertyWorks, Rolls-Royce’s advanced research organisation. Its work includes propulsion technologies and high-temperature materials, supported in part through a $75 million, ten-year research alliance with Purdue University.
US Senator Todd Young said: “This investment is a testament to the hard-working Hoosiers who power this facility. Rolls-Royce understands the importance of producing advanced military technologies here in the United States, and this billion-dollar investment shows that Indiana is leading the way in meeting the needs of our defense industrial base.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index ended above 46,000 points Monday after recovering from heavy early losses, as global markets retreated amid growing expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index (TAIEX) fell more than 800 points in early trading, briefly dropping below 45,000, before recovering most of its losses. It ended down 202.98 points, or 0.44%, at 46,128.47, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Turnover totaled NT$1.2 trillion (US$37.9 billion). The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$150.79 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
For August, the TAIEX gained 3,009.72 points, or 6.98%, recovering from levels around 43,000 points at the beginning of the month.
Among the market’s largest weighted stocks, TSMC fell 0.62% to NT$2,405, closing below its five-day moving average. MediaTek declined 1.51% to NT$3,925, according to Anue.
Foxconn lost 1.19% to NT$250, while ASE fell 5.96% to NT$584. Delta Electronics rose 0.55% to NT$1,840.
Printed circuit board maker Unimicron Technology closed limit-down at NT$999, losing NT$181.9 billion in market capitalization after authorities searched its offices Friday. The company is suspected of labeling China-made PCBs as Taiwan-made products, according to SETN and Liberty Times.
Unimicron is one of the market’s major large-cap electronics companies and ranks 10th by market capitalization. Data released after the market closed showed that foreign institutional investors and investment trusts were net buyers of the stock, purchasing 2,206 lots, or 2.206 million shares, and 42 lots, respectively.
Plastics stocks provided support for the broader market. Nan Ya Plastics and Formosa Chemicals & Fibre both closed limit-up, while Formosa Plastics gained 5.58%.
Stable global oil prices and seasonal restocking ahead of autumn have supported a recovery in prices for petrochemical intermediates and general-purpose resins. The plastics sector rose 8.91%, making it the best-performing sector of the day, according to Sinotrade.
Investors also favored stocks linked to co-packaged optics (CPO). The technology places optical communications components alongside computing chips to improve data transmission, according to StockFeel.
Largan Precision rose 8.28% to a record NT$7,735. Genius Electronic Optical also closed limit-up at NT$1,005, setting a new high.
Gallium arsenide-related stocks recorded gains. Visual Photonics Epitaxy closed limit-up, while LandMark Optoelectronics gained 6.81%. The shift toward Wi-Fi 7 and stronger demand for satellite communications have supported demand across the compound semiconductor supply chain.
Memory stocks serving niche markets were another area of strength. ESMT gained 8.53%, AP Memory rose 3.58%, and Etron Technology advanced 1.72%.
Major global memory manufacturers have shifted production toward HBM and DDR5, tightening supplies of DDR4 and niche memory products. Prices have risen, while stronger restocking demand from the automotive and internet-connected device sectors has provided additional support.
Senior analyst Lee Hsiu-li (李秀利) said trading volume increased in the final session as MSCI index adjustments took effect. The increased activity helped narrow the TAIEX’s losses, according to CTEE.
MSCI reviews its indexes four times a year, adding or removing companies and changing their weightings based on factors such as market value, liquidity, and trading activity. The indexes are used by funds and institutional investors as investment benchmarks, according to Sinotrade.
First Capital Management Chair Huang Yi-ting (黃詣庭) said the TAIEX had faced resistance after testing the 46,500-point level last week, limiting its room for further gains. She suggested that investors focus on individual sectors and stocks in the near term and maintain a relatively high cash position to respond more easily to market volatility and rapid shifts in investor interest between sectors.
This information is not intended as personalized financial advice. Investors are encouraged to conduct their own research and analysis before making investment decisions.

Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:53:45 UTC
21:53:45 KST

Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- Georgia Tech
- Summary:
- A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.
- Share:
Many important choices seem to pit reason against emotion. Popular culture often describes that tension as a contest between two parts of the brain: a newer, more advanced center for rational thought and an ancient "lizard brain" that runs on instinct.
But the evolutionary history of the brain appears to be far more complicated than a simple struggle between old and new.
"There was a theory proposed in the '50s that the brain evolved in layers starting with basic bodily functions, to emotions in the reptilian brain, leading up to sophisticated reasoning in humans," explains Nabil Imam, an assistant professor in the School of Computational Science and Engineering and a faculty member with Georgia Tech's Institute for Neuroscience, Neurotechnology, and Society (INNS). "This is not how an evolutionary biologist would think about the problem."
Research published in Science Advances suggests that brain evolution may be better understood in terms of wiring rather than newer regions being stacked on top of older ones.
By examining the organization of both biological brains and artificial neural networks, Imam and his colleagues found evidence that evolution may involve allocating a limited amount of brain space among competing wiring strategies. Their model describes a computational tug of war between two fundamentally different kinds of neural organization, both of which are established even before birth.
The findings could help explain a long-running puzzle in brain evolution and may also point toward new ways of building AI systems that use less data and energy.
Why the "Lizard Brain" Model Falls Short
Terms such as "logical brain" and "lizard brain" actually refer to groups of brain regions with very different functions. The neocortex, often associated with higher-level thought, forms the outer layer of the brain and is involved in vision, perception, reasoning, and other complex abilities.
The so-called lizard brain is harder to define so neatly.
"The limbic system, sometimes called the 'reptilian brain,' controls emotion broadly speaking -- but it also has other components with distinct functions," explains Imam. The system contains separate regions involved in memory, smell, navigation, and emotional regulation. "Why do people group all these different regions into one big system? There hasn't been a good theory for what is common between these different circuits."
To explore that question, the researchers compared how these brain systems change across species. Rather than looking at individual regions one at a time, they examined how the limbic system and neocortex vary together over evolutionary history.
A clear pattern emerged. When one part of the limbic system was relatively large, the other limbic regions also tended to be larger. At the same time, the neocortex was generally smaller.
That suggests the regions are not evolving independently.
"Rather," says Imam, "it's a coordinated expansion of these regions across species."
The pattern points to the limbic system behaving more like an integrated network than a collection of unrelated structures. Across evolution, its different components appear to expand and contract together.
The next question was what might cause that coordinated shift.
Two Different Ways to Wire a Brain
Imam's explanation centers on the way different brain systems are wired before birth.
Neural circuits in the neocortex are arranged as spatial maps. Brain regions that process nearby parts of the body, such as the thumb and index finger, are also located near one another. Similar spatial organization appears in systems that handle sight and sound.
The limbic system is organized differently. Instead of being laid out spatially, its wiring works more like a bar code, with distributed patterns of activity representing particular smells or complex memories.
The researchers used AI models to test whether these differences arise from built-in architecture or are mainly learned through experience.
When an AI network was created with localized, spatial connections, it was naturally well suited to processing vision, sound, and touch. In contrast, distributed "barcode-style" networks were necessary for strong performance on smell recognition and memory.
An Evolutionary Competition for Brain Space
The researchers then investigated why the relative size of these brain systems changes so consistently among species.
The basic idea is that the brain has limited resources. Space and energy are finite, so natural selection may favor whichever wiring system is most useful for survival in a particular environment.
To test this, the team created a multimodal artificial network in which spatial and distributed systems competed for "real estate."
When the simulated environment rewarded smell, every region within the distributed system expanded while the neocortex became smaller. When vision was favored instead, the pattern reversed.
This trade-off may help explain striking differences between real animals. The nine-banded armadillo, which depends heavily on smell, has a very large limbic system. The squirrel monkey, which relies strongly on vision, has a brain dominated by the neocortex.
Across the 182 species included in the study, the findings suggest that brain evolution is less about adding progressively newer layers of "logic" and more about shifting space between different wiring systems according to what helps an animal survive.
What Brain Evolution Could Teach AI
The same principle may have implications beyond biology.
If engineers can reproduce some of this built-in neural organization in artificial intelligence, they may be able to create systems that learn more like biological brains and require far less training data and energy.
"Today's artificial neural networks are trained by vast amounts [of] data -- it's about nurture," says Imam. "But the brain is not a blank slate that gets trained by experience. It is a mix of nature and nurture, and the nature is that pre-wired architecture."
"We could translate that architecture to AI systems to make it more brain-like, or make it learn or function as efficiently as the brain."
This work was a collaboration with Cornell University and was supported by the National Science Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Georgia Tech. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nabil Imam, Matthew Kielo, Brandon M. Trude, Barbara L. Finlay. Dual computational systems in the development and evolution of mammalian brains. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (17) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aec6112

The dialogue session also forms part of the ministry's ongoing efforts through Clean Brunei to encourage greater participation from all levels of society, particularly youth, in playing an active role in creating a cleaner, more comfortable, and sustainable environment in Brunei. ■

PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:40:35 UTC
21:40:35 KST

PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
Aastha Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 31, 2026, 21:56 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
PM Modi during his visit to meet naval personnel aboard INS Vikrant (left); Rahul Gandhi during 'Chhattron ki Goonj' programme (right)
From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Narendra Modi's carefully curated bandhgalas, from Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and sunglasses to the Thackerays' colour-coded political imagery, what Indian politicians wear has often been more than a question of personal style. Their clothes have helped construct identities, signal ideology, project modernity, invoke tradition and increasingly generate the kind of visual moments that social media loves.So when Rahul Gandhi appeared in a pink shirt and later in a yellow one, the change from his usual white clothing drew attention online. The yellow shirt, along with the line "Smash the patriarchy", became part of the social-media conversation. The interest was less about the shirt itself and more about how unusual it looked compared with his regular public appearance.
But this is not the first time that a politician's attire has made more headlines than their speech. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's clothes have often drawn attention, from his signature jackets and bandhgalas to the regional outfits he wears during visits across the country. Over the years, they have become a familiar part of his public image.
As designer Gaurav Jai Gupta puts it, "Fashion can communicate before a politician has spoken a single word. Clothing conveys identity, ideology, relatability, authority and even regional or cultural affiliation almost instantly." Politics, he adds, is fundamentally about perception, and "an outfit can become the visual shorthand for an entire political moment.
Indira Gandhi, elected as Prime Minister on January 14th, 1977, adresses to the crowd in the Rae Bareli Lok Sabha constituency (Credit: Magnum Photos)
PM Modi: How his wardrobe became part of his public image
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has taken political dressing into the era of personal branding.His wardrobe moves easily between traditional Indian clothing and sharply tailored modern silhouettes. The signature kurta, sleeveless jackets and bandhgalas have become instantly recognisable, while his international appearances often combine Indian craftsmanship with global tailoring.Some of the looks have become headline-makers in their own right.His wardrobe has since offered plenty of other visual moments.A burgundy bandhgala during his first overseas trip as prime minister created a polished diplomatic look. A signature khadi kurta during his Bhutan visit emphasised Indian textiles and craftsmanship. In Nepal, saffron attire paired with a rudraksh mala made a strong cultural and religious statement at Pashupatinath Temple.This habit of dressing for the country he's visiting — or the region of India he's in — is itself a strategy, according to Gupta: "I would definitely consider it a form of fashion diplomacy. Clothing can be a very subtle way of acknowledging the culture of the country you are visiting while siultaneously representing your own identity." Retaining elements of one's own traditional identity alongside that, he says, "reinforces national representation."His recent looks have been more state-centric. From sporting the gamcha look in Bihar, to a turban in Punjab, and even the traditional mund in Kerala, Modi has worn his "vocals for locals" tag.
PM Modi in several traditional attires
Pink, yellow, blue – Rahul's pattern?
For years, Rahul Gandhi's public wardrobe has largely stayed within the safe territory of political dressing — white kurta-pajamas, jackets and understated casual wear. It is a familiar uniform in Indian politics, one that keeps the focus on the politician rather than the clothes.But the pink and yellow shirts were different.Bright, instantly noticeable and far removed from the monochrome political wardrobe, they became an unlikely talking point. Gupta explains why a single garment can take on a life entirely of its own online: "The internet loves symbols that are simple, recognisable and easy to reproduce. A yellow shirt is, in itself, just a yellow shirt. But once social media attaches a narrative to it, the garment can acquire an entirely new meaning." The audience, he says, effectively co-authors the outfit's significance — "memes, edits, captions and commentary can transform an ordinary look into a cultural reference point," helped along by the fact that "colour is highly emotional and visually immediate."
Rahul's shade of politics through the years
He did not wear it just anywhere, either. He wore it to the 'Chhatron ki Goonj' programme, where the audience was predominantly Gen Z. But this is not the first time the Leader of Opposition has made news for his fashion. In 2019, Rahul attended a Kerala college event in a t-shirt and jeans, taking a break from his classic white kurta look, with his "You can call me Rahul" reels still going viral.Likewise, it was not a conincidence that he went with a blue t-shirt, when he held up the red book in his hand and said "Save the Constitution", or a black one to protest outside the Parliament.It's a pattern. Every Rahul Gandhi's politics has reflected in his preference for colours.
The Thackerays: When colour carries politics
If PM Modi's wardrobe demonstrates the power of personal branding, the Thackerays show how colour and clothing can become political shorthand.Bal Thackeray initially adopted the shirt-and-trouser look of the urban office worker, appealing to an aspirational Maharashtra audience. Later, as Hindutva became central to his political positioning, orange became a defining element of his public appearance.Fashion designer Nivedita Saboo, who has dressed several politicians, explains why colour carries this kind of political weight in the first place: "Colour communicates emotion before language does. Saffron can evoke spirituality, sacrifice, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity. White can communicate simplicity, peace, authority or the traditional Gandhian vocabulary. Electric or deep blue has powerful associations with social justice, equality and Ambedkarite politics." But, she cautions, "colour is never universal. Its meaning changes with culture, history, political association, fabric, styling and even the person's body language. That's why political dressing is fascinating: you can say something without saying anything."Uddhav Thackeray developed his own visual identity through simple, brightly coloured sadra-pajamas closely associated with Maharashtrian culture.
Uddhav and Raj Thackeray, whose political styles reflect the Thackeray family's use of colour and cultural imagery
Aaditya Thackeray, meanwhile, represents another generational shift, combining traditional Indian clothing with contemporary fashion.Three generations. Three styles. And three different ways of speaking to their audiences without saying a word.
Mamata, Kejriwal and the politics of looking 'aam'
Then there are politicians whose biggest fashion statement is that they appear to have made very little effort at all.Mamata Banerjee's white cotton saree with a blue border and hawai chappals have become almost inseparable from her political identity. Arvind Kejriwal's muffler achieved a similar status.The appeal is simple: don't look like a politician; look like the people who vote for you. As Gupta puts it, "politics is about recognition and relatability, not necessarily luxury." A consistent, uncomplicated look, he says, "can become incredibly powerful because people can immediately identify it" — Mamata Banerjee's saree and Kejriwal's muffler "function almost like logos," communicating accessibility in a way an expensive designer wardrobe rarely can. "In a country like ours, simplicity is more relatable," he says. "In mass politics, that emotional connection can be far more valuable than sartorial sophistication."The repetition is what makes it powerful. Eventually, the garment becomes a logo.See the white-and-blue saree, think Mamata. See the muffler, think Kejriwal. See the kurta and jacket, think Modi.And now, in the age of viral fashion moments, perhaps even a yellow shirt can enter the political visual dictionary.
Arvind Kejriwal’s signature muffler became a recognisable part of his political image
Vijay: Breaking Tamil Nadu's white-shirt, veshti political dress code
When Vijay took oath as Tamil Nadu chief minister, he broke from the traditional white shirt-and-veshti look, arriving instead in a sharply tailored black suit. He has since made black-and-white suits a regular part of his public image.Addressing the attention around his wardrobe, Vijay said, “Many people have been talking about the new suit that I have been wearing recently. Are we not allowed to wear a coat and suit? Is it meant only for people in positions of authority? There is nothing like that.”Explaining his choice, he added, “I am not wearing many colours. It is just black and white, like all our hearts. The choice of these colours is to show that I will remain transparent and simple in everything, just like black and white.”
Tamil Nadu CM Vijay in his iconic black and white suit
Indira Gandhi: The saree that became a power statement
Long before politicians had to worry about going viral, Indira Gandhi had already mastered the art of having a recognisable political look.Her sarees, from Banarasi silk to handlooms and Tanchois, became an important part of her public image. They projected tradition and authority at the same time, allowing her to appear deeply rooted in Indian culture while commanding political spaces at home and abroad.The saree wasn't simply a sartorial choice. The way she wore it, with the pallu covering her head from the loose end of the saree, made it distinct.
Indira Gandhi in one of her signature sarees during a public event
Gupta points to exactly this kind of repetition as the foundation of a political fashion identity: "Consistency is the key to creating a fashion identity. When a politician repeatedly wears a particular silhouette, colour palette, accessory or garment, it becomes part of their visual vocabulary." Indira Gandhi's sarees, he notes, "became inseparable from her public image," much "like branding in fashion or advertising: repetition creates recognition." Eventually, he says, "you don't need to see the entire person; a particular silhouette, colour combination or accessory can be enough to trigger recognition." But he's careful to add a caveat: "successful political style usually feels authentic rather than overly constructed. The strongest personal brands emerge when the clothes reinforce something the politician already represents."For women in politics especially, clothing has always carried an extra layer of scrutiny. Too traditional, and a leader can be boxed into convention. Too Western, and questions about cultural authenticity can follow.Moreover, most female political leaders of the time or the ones who preceeded her wore sarees the same way.Indira's style largely sidestepped that binary. She made traditional Indian clothing look powerful.
Nehru's jacket, Rajiv's sneakers: Political wardrobe evolves
The political fashion story goes back even further.Jawaharlal Nehru's iconic jacket became so closely associated with him that his name effectively became part of the garment's identity. The jacket was a descendant of the northern Indian achkan, a closed-neck, coat-like garment traditionally associated with Indian nobility. It was largely when the style was marketed to Western audiences that it took the "Nehru" name, after the prime minister popularised it through his public appearances. The minimalist look later found fans beyond politics, including the Beatles and Sammy Davis Jr, who reportedly owned more than 200 Nehru jackets.
Jawaharlal Nehru in his signature Nehru jacket, which later became a global fashion symbol
Khadi and handlooms carried an even bigger political history, associated with nationalism, self-reliance and the freedom movement.Then came Rajiv Gandhi.Dark sunglasses, sneakers, sleeveless fleece jackets and khadi kurta-pajamas gave him a distinctly more contemporary appearance. His wardrobe reflected the image he projected politically — younger, modern and more comfortable with the technological future.
Rajiv Gandhi sporting a pair of sneakers
In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.
Mao & Castro: The outfit of revolutionaries
In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.
Mao Zedong’s uniform-like suit became a visual shorthand for his revolutionary politics
Fidel Castro, meanwhile, swapped the traditional military and political imagery for tracksuits later in life. He was famously photographed wearing a red, white and blue Adidas tracksuit while recovering from surgery in 2006. The look soon became part of his public image, with Castro later wearing sportswear from brands including Fila, Puma and Nike.
Fidel Castro in his guerrilla boots during his early political years (left); Castro in a tracksuit in his later years (right)
What would it take to dress for Gen Z?
If a yellow shirt at a college event can trend for days, the question naturally follows: what does it actually take for a politician's wardrobe to land with a generation raised on Instagram and short-form video?Saboo, who has worked closely with politicians on exactly this brief, is blunt about the trap most of them fall into. "Gen Z has grown up in a visual culture where identity is communicated through what you wear," she says. "But breaking the dress code simply to look young can backfire. Gen Z is extremely good at detecting what feels manufactured. The clothes have to feel like the person, not like a stylist has dressed them to look young." A politician who "wears the traditional kurta beautifully and owns it completely," she argues, can be "far more compelling than somebody wearing sneakers and a T-shirt because someone told them that's what young people like." For her, the real shift isn't from tradition to trend — it's "from dress code to personal code."Asked to imagine one outfit that could say "young India" without a single slogan, she describes something quietly hybrid: a relaxed, engineered jacket in a lightweight Indian textile over a tapered trouser, perhaps a modernised kurta with sharper, almost architectural proportions underneath, finished with one unexpected element — an unusual seam, a technical fabric panel, a monogram, a contemporary sneaker.
The palette, she says, would be "sophisticated rather than loud — ivory, charcoal, deep blue or earthy neutrals with one energetic accent." The test, in her words: "It shouldn't look like 'politician trying to be fake and dress young.' It should look like India's next generation has naturally evolved its own version of Indian clothing."Her advice to politicians boils down to five principles: don't dress younger, dress more authentically; modernise proportions rather than identity; find one recurring signature — a colour, a silhouette, a jacket, a watch — rather than constantly changing the wardrobe; make sure the clothes actually function in a country that "lives fast"; and, above all, stop being afraid of personality. As she puts it, "politics has traditionally rewarded conformity. Gen Z is attracted to people who appear comfortable in their own skin." Fashion, she concludes, "cannot manufacture relatability. It can only amplify it."
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

Feature: Iceland referendum highlights domestic challenges, divided views on EU path
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:22 CST
21:40:22 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhu Haochen, Weng Xinyang and Meng Fanyu
REYKJAVIK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- At a polling station inside the Kringlan branch of Reykjavik City Library on Saturday, voters streamed in and out as Icelanders cast ballots in a nationwide referendum on whether to restart accession talks with the European Union (EU).
For a country of around 400,000 people in the middle of the North Atlantic, the ballot offered only two choices: "Yes" or "No." A "Yes" vote would authorize the government to reopen membership negotiations with the EU.
Yet conversations with voters across the country suggested that the issues behind the referendum were far from a simple binary choice.
A staff member at the Kringlan polling station told Xinhua that public interest in the referendum had been high.
"Iceland has long faced many problems, particularly in the economic and financial fields, and domestic policies alone are not enough to solve them," he said. "Many people hope that moving closer to the EU could offer Iceland another way forward."
At the same polling station, an elderly voter who had just cast his ballot saw things very differently.
He acknowledged that Iceland faced long-standing challenges but insisted they were for Icelanders themselves to address.
"These are Iceland's own affairs. We should handle our own affairs ourselves," he said, arguing that the country should remain independent and avoid outside interference. "Besides, the EU itself is beset by crises."
The contrast was echoed elsewhere in the capital.
At a polling station in Reykjavik City Hall, three students from the University of Iceland said they had all voted "Yes."
One of them, Frodi Gunnlaugsson, said fluctuations in the Icelandic krona and inflation had caused serious difficulties for both the economy and ordinary households. High housing prices, he said, had also left many young people unable to afford a home and settle down.
He also voiced dissatisfaction with what he described as problems concerning government integrity and governance. For him, closer integration with Europe could offer a way to break out of Iceland's current difficulties.
For other Icelanders, however, some issues should not be placed lightly on the negotiating table.
Fisheries, both an economic pillar and an important part of Iceland's national identity, have long stood at the center of the country's debate over EU membership. Official data show that marine products accounted for nearly 40 percent of Iceland's total goods exports in 2025.
Sveinn Margeirsson, a senior executive at major Icelandic seafood company Brim, told Xinhua that Iceland had spent decades building a fisheries system based on expanded jurisdiction over its surrounding waters, science-based quotas and higher value-added production.
If Iceland were to restart accession talks and eventually join the EU, its fisheries could come under the bloc's Common Fisheries Policy, raising questions over how management powers and fishing quotas would be determined and whether Iceland's existing restrictions on foreign ownership could be maintained.
Margeirsson said keeping control of fisheries resources in Icelandic hands was crucial because it affected the entire chain from harvesting and processing to employment and trade, and ultimately whether the value created by the industry would remain in Iceland.
He said he had voted "No."
Foreign policy and geopolitics also weighed on the debate.
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly made remarks about taking control of Greenland, another North Atlantic island. U.S. media have also reported that Billy Long, nominated to serve as U.S. ambassador to Iceland, once joked that Iceland could become the "52nd state" of the United States.
Such remarks, together with doubts over U.S. reliability and concerns about NATO's future, have added to the strategic uncertainty facing Iceland, a NATO member with no standing army.
At the vote-counting center in Reykjavik's Laugardalsholl arena on Saturday night, staff member Bjorn Arnar Karason told Xinhua that he had voted "Yes," partly because of what he saw as a more unsettled international environment and U.S. rhetoric over Greenland.
Joining the EU, he said, might offer Iceland an additional layer of security.
"Greenland is our northern neighbor," Karason said. "The U.S. interest in Greenland makes me feel as if there is always a dark cloud hanging over us."
According to Icelandic public broadcaster RUV, more than 220,000 of the country's roughly 270,000 registered voters cast ballots in the referendum.
Preliminary results showed 52.8 percent voting against restarting EU accession talks and 47.2 percent in favor, securing victory for the "No" side.
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said at a press conference on Sunday that the government respected the result and would not pursue EU accession negotiations during its current term.
The referendum has settled the immediate question of whether Iceland should return to the negotiating table. The deeper issues it exposed, however, remain.
Rejecting renewed talks does not remove the economic and social pressures that helped bring the EU question back into Icelandic politics. At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty continues to complicate the country's security and strategic choices.
For some Icelanders, deeper European integration offers the prospect of greater economic stability and security. For others, preserving national independence and control over fisheries, agriculture and natural resources remains paramount.
The vote may have closed one path for now, but Iceland still faces a broader challenge: how to strengthen its economy and navigate a changing international environment without giving up the degree of autonomy many Icelanders are determined to preserve. ■

Across China: "Sea daughters" fight plastic pollution with love, business model
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:09 CST
21:40:09 KST

Environmental volunteers collect marine plastic waste in Zhoushan City, east China's Zhejiang Province, Feb. 3, 2026. (Xinhua)
HANGZHOU, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- As the sea glimmers under the first dawn light, a cluster of women in red vests spread out along the shoreline of Changtu, a small island in east China, harvesting not shells but plastic bottles, discarded foam, and other debris tide‑washed in overnight.
For years, these once stay‑at‑home wives and mothers, now environmental volunteers, have waged a quiet but persistent campaign against marine plastic pollution, driven by love, faith and a sustainable business model.
"We used to think our duty was just waiting at home while men ventured out to the sea," said Hu Songsu, 66, founder of the "Gold and Silver Island Association of Fishermen's Wives," at the town, known for rich in large yellow croaker and hairtail herring, in Zhejiang Province.
In 2017, Hu, together with a group of like‑minded women, launched the association, initially focusing on fishing safety. "When a wife tells her husband 'come home early and stay safe,' the husband listens," Hu explained.
But over time, Hu noticed a troubling change: the sea was becoming choked with trash. Discarded fishing nets tangled propellers, while used dry-cell batteries were dumped into the sea -- a scene unimaginable back in her childhood.
"The sea feeds our families. We can do more," Hu said.
The association quickly rolled out a "Blue Sea Rescue" project. Starting with 19 boats whose captains were respected village leaders, they persuaded fishermen to bring their waste back ashore.
For those who balked at the extra hassle, their wives appealed to their beliefs: "You pray for safe voyages every year. But prayers alone aren't enough. Bringing back waste is your real merit."
Even more compelling was the practical argument: polluted waters mean fewer fish. "How can fish survive in a polluted sea? Where will our livelihoods go?" Hu said.
To boost incentives, the association set up a transfer station where marine waste is sorted and sold to recycling companies.
Part of the profits goes to impoverished fishing families, while the station's managers -- most of them fishermen's wives -- also receive monthly pay of 1,000 yuan (about 147 U.S. dollars) to 1,500 yuan.
Fishermen can redeem recycling points earned from handed‑in waste for rice, cooking oil and other daily necessities, or purchase new batteries at subsidized prices when they return old ones.
Evolving from gentle persuasion into a well‑run operational model, the association has recovered over 350 tonnes of marine debris, including 75,000 used batteries.
In 2025, the association won the national March 8th Red Banner Collective award, one of the highest honors conferred by the All‑China Women's Federation. Their work also contributed to the Blue Circle project, which claimed the United Nations' Champions of the Earth award.
This year, Hu was named one of the country's top 10 ecological and environmental volunteers by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
What began as a small circle of fishermen's wives has grown into a group with 235 registered volunteers, now widely known as the "East China Sea Daughters."
Researchers and university students visit the island, some shadowing fishermen and their wives at docks, on boats and at the sorting station. "They come to see how ordinary women are changing the ocean," Hu said.
Hu is never alone. Across China, the spirit of these "sea daughters" resonates with volunteer groups operating in vastly different landscapes.
In south China's Shenzhen, "eco‑sentinels" patrol the city's streets and waterways, addressing environmental complaints before they escalate. In northwest China's Qinghai Province, volunteers on horseback travel to summer pastures to collect plastic waste along the shores of Qinghai Lake.
This August marks China's first ecological and environmental volunteer service month. According to the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, 30 provincial‑level regions have rolled out action plans, mobilizing some 38,000 volunteers for more than 650 activities.
For the fishermen's wives in Changtu, August is also the busiest time of year. They repair fishing gear and stock supplies as the peak fishing season is approaching.
Still, Hu never misses her dawn patrol along the shore.
"For us, a healthy ocean is our real wealth," she said. ■

Analysis: Four things we learned in Spain's Matchday 3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:07 CST
21:40:07 KST

MADRID, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The third round of La Liga matches saw Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid turn in impressive displays, while Villarreal is still searching for its first win under new coach Inigo Perez. Here are four things we learned this weekend in Spain.
1. Real Madrid impresses in free-scoring start to season
Real Madrid cruised to a 4-0 win over newly-promoted Malaga at the Santiago Bernabeu on Sunday. Although Malaga was missing key players in defense, that should not take too much away from a confident Madrid display in which Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe stood out.
Both have carried their World Cup form into La Liga and have been vital as Real Madrid has scored eight goals in the first two home matches of the season.
Meanwhile, the confidence Jose Mourinho has instilled in his players also appears to be a major factor in Real Madrid's strong start.
2. Villarreal needs home comforts
Villarreal finished third in La Liga last season, and there are high hopes that dynamic young coach Inigo Perez can maintain that level after the excellent work he did with Rayo Vallecano.
However, after three games this season, Perez is still looking for his first win following a 1-0 defeat away to Alaves. Villarreal had more than 70 percent possession and seven shots on target but lost to one of Alaves' two efforts on target.
Perez has not been helped by his side having to play all three of its opening games away from home because of refurbishment work at the Estadio de la Ceramica. He will hope two consecutive home games can help Villarreal return to winning ways.
3. No Julian, no problem for Atletico Madrid
Julian Alvarez's wish to leave Atletico Madrid and the club's determination not to sell him to Barcelona have dominated the headlines over the past week, especially after he missed training for three days. But whatever the outcome of the summer transfer saga, Atletico's first-half performance in its 3-1 win away to Sevilla showed the club can thrive without him.
Spain international Alex Baena scored twice and Ademola Lookman also found the net as Atletico tore Sevilla apart in the first half. Buoyed by an impressive World Cup, Baena looked back to the form that persuaded Atletico to sign him from Villarreal a year ago.
Atletico will look to sign a replacement forward if Alvarez leaves, but Saturday's performance showed his departure would not necessarily be a disaster.
4. Racing and Elche thrill, but both have defensive concerns
Racing Santander fans celebrated their side's first La Liga win in 14 years with a 3-2 victory over Elche on Friday, but the game also highlighted defensive issues that could cause problems for both teams this season.
Racing found holes throughout Elche's defensive line, which left plenty of space to exploit, and players such as Inigo Vicente, Yassir Zabiri and Andres Marin showed they could pose a threat to many opponents.
However, when Elche got back into the game through a deflected shot in the 78th minute, Racing struggled to maintain its composure at the back.
Two games at El Sardinero have produced nine goals. That promises plenty of entertainment for supporters, although perhaps not much peace of mind. ■

Marine heatwaves leave coral reefs less time to recover: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:06 CST
21:40:06 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The world's coral reefs are losing the time they need to recover between increasingly frequent marine heatwaves and global bleaching events driven by human-induced climate change, a report said on Monday.
The Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025, published by the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN), is the most comprehensive assessment of coral reefs to date, drawing on more than 40 years of global data from 21.1 million observations, 87,299 surveys, representing 36,886 sites across 124 countries, territories and economies, according to a GCRMN statement.
"Climate change is driving more frequent and severe marine heatwaves, but local pressures such as poor water quality, overfishing and coastal development are making reefs even less able to withstand them," said the report's lead author Manuel Gonzalez Rivero from the Australian Institute of Marine Science.
Global hard coral cover declined by about 9.5 percent, from an average of 30.2 percent during 1980-2009 to 27.3 percent in 2020-2024, with climate change-driven heat stress identified as the primary cause.
Four major global bleaching events since 1998 have reduced hard coral cover, with reefs only partially recovering between events.
Major bleaching events previously occurred about once a decade. Since 2010, they have occurred approximately every five to six years. However, many corals need at least five years just to mature and begin reproducing.
"Coral reefs once had decades to recover after major bleaching events. Today, they're lucky to get five or six years," said Gonzalez Rivero.
The report said ambitious reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, combined with effective management of local pressures, offer the strongest pathway to maintain hard coral cover. ■

Feature: Back to school in war zones
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:03 CST
21:40:03 KST

BEIRUT, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- For 21-year-old university student Reine Nasrallah, the start of a new academic year is marked by concerns about how to reach her university and cover the cost of daily transportation, rather than the usual excitement of reuniting with familiar classmates and professors.
After the Israel-Hezbollah war forced her family to flee their home in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh, Nasrallah transferred to the Lebanese University's Hadath campus near Beirut, while she and her mother moved into a rented home in the Chouf District.
"The war turned my life upside down," Nasrallah told Xinhua. "We left our home in a hurry after it was destroyed. We could not even take our clothes or belongings with us."
Life in displacement is difficult. The family now pays about 500 U.S. dollars a month to rent the apartment in Chouf, while Nasrallah spends about 20 dollars a day commuting to and from the university, according to her mother, Rana.
"Some days, we simply can't afford the cost of getting to university," Nasrallah said.
For Nasrallah, an even greater challenge has been keeping up with her studies amid the conflict. She said the disruption has prevented her from meeting academic requirements on schedule. She has also developed vision problems, frequent headaches and dizziness.
"My mother had to sell a piece of her jewelry to cover my medical treatment and some of my education expenses," Nasrallah said.
Nasrallah's experience reflects the hardships faced by many students from war zones in Lebanon, as they prepare to start another academic year amid continued uncertainty.
A nationwide assessment conducted by Lebanon's Ministry of Education and Higher Education in June found that 340 public, private, and technical and vocational schools had been damaged during the war, including 17 that were completely destroyed.
The damage affected several governorates, including Nabatieh and South Lebanon. The UN Children's Fund warned in July that at least 100,000 children could be left without a classroom when the new school year begins unless urgent repairs are carried out before September.
Even for students who are able to return to campus, the challenges of learning do not go away. With Israel still carrying out occasional strikes in southern Lebanon, the sounds of explosions and drones continue to weigh heavily on the students, creating an atmosphere of fear and anxiety that can disrupt learning.
"Studying while hearing the sounds of drones, airstrikes, and artillery shelling, and after losing relatives and loved ones, makes it difficult for students to concentrate," Hassan Jaber, a professor from Lebanese University, told Xinhua.
Such conditions, he added, directly affect academic performance and increase the pressures students face both inside and outside the classroom.
Psychologist Amani Hamdan said the effects could linger long after the conflict ends.
"The living, economic, and security conditions experienced by students have created high levels of anxiety and stress," Hamdan told Xinhua, adding that many have lost the sense of stability needed to concentrate and learn.
Displacement, the loss of homes, financial pressure, and fear of renewed strikes can affect students' mental health, she said.
Hamdan called for psychological support and counseling in schools, as well as academic accommodations for affected students, including greater flexibility in examinations when necessary.
With the new academic year approaching, Rana has once again parted with a pair of earrings she treasured for years to help pay her daughter Nasrallah's tuition. Life goes on, but the end of the war remains a distant prospect.
"I don't know how much longer I can hold on," she murmured. ■
