Families of those missing after Nepal floods struggle to cling to hope as death toll passes 1,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:39:10 UTC
20:39:10 KST

Nepal flood rescue recovery efforts keep hope alive for desperate families as death toll passes 1,000
Kathmandu, Nepal — Five days after a rocky mountainside and the glacier it supported collapsed near Nepal's border with Tibet, unleashing torrents of flash floodwater, mud and debris on the valleys below that swept away everything in their path, rescuers were still searching Monday for reasons to hope.
Over the weekend, a 6-year-old girl was miraculously pulled from the mud-covered rubble, fueling hope that some of the nearly 4,000 people still listed as missing in the wake of the disaster could be found alive.
The death toll in Nepal and China passed 1,000 on Tuesday, authorities said, and the fear is that the toll will spiral as recovery efforts continue along the scars carved into the landscape by the raging floods.
But the danger hasn't passed. The sacred Trishuli River was surging again Monday, this time from heavy monsoon rains that have spurred search and rescue teams to try and move even faster to find anyone still alive in the ruins.
Samarth Srivastav was among the thousands of people desperately hoping a loved one might still emerge from the layers of thick mud and rubble in the Himalayan valleys.
"We're just trying to hope for good news now," Samarth told CBS News from Atlanta.
His father Vivek was on the Nepal-Tibet border when the disaster struck last week.
Samarth said his father joked with him on their last phone call about how steep the river valley walls around him were, saying, "You know, if I fall down there, like, I'll get swept away."
Just hours after the call, a tsunami of glacial ice, water and mud swept away Tibet's immigration checkpoint on the border, and Vivek hasn't been heard from since.
"Initially after hearing about it, you know, it was kind of like, okay, you know, maybe by the end of the day, you know? Might hear something back. And then the next day came and we didn't hear anything all day. And then more and more," he said. "As the number of missing people on record started to increase and, like, the severity of the situation actually started to hit, you know — we're seeing all these videos pop up on social media of people recording the disaster and everything that actually happened — I think that's when we actually started to get worried and realize that something might actually be wrong. This is actually a really bad situation."
Since then, Samarth said it has been nothing but "increasing anxiety" for his family.
"We still have the hope that he's probably okay — he's able to come back, he's probably doing fine out there," he said. "But, it's the fact we don't know anything yet, is just so scary to us."
The torrents of floodwater and everything they picked up and carried with them pushed as far as 150 miles away, into neighboring India.
At Nepal's biggest hospital, in the capital Kathmandu, an outside wall has been all but covered in posters bearing the photos of bodies recovered from the calamity. Another wall, on a smaller street nearby, was starting to fill up Monday.
They are walls of the unknown dead — photos of some of the people still likely listed as missing.
Many of the images are deeply disturbing, but desperate family members have no choice but to step up to pore over the grim images, pleading for any information about missing loved ones.
In Georgia, Samarth said he was trying to keep calm, despite a lack of any information from officials in Nepal, or at home in the U.S.
"Honestly, I haven't really heard as much from the U.S. government," he said. "There's not really much else we can do except just, like, sit and pray."
Other American families with loved ones missing told CBS News over the weekend that they want more help from U.S. authorities, as well as the Chinese and Nepalese governments.
One Virginia family told CBS News on Monday they had experienced a rollercoaster of emotions as conflicting information about survivors comes out, and while some members had lost hope that a husband and wife last thought to have been in Tibet could still be found alive, others were determined to wait for confirmation.
So far, Chinese authorities have not confirmed whether any foreign tourists survived the disaster in Tibet.

Hongkonger jailed 3½ years for molesting girlfriend’s daughter, filming assaults
Defendant, 47, jailed after police found nude photo of 11-year-old girl in his wallet during response to family quarrel
A moving services manager has been sentenced to 3½ years in prison for molesting his girlfriend’s 11-year-old daughter at home and filming and photographing the assaults, with a Hong Kong judge imposing a heavier penalty to reflect the impact on the vulnerable child.
Deputy District Judge Ivy Chui Yee-mei said on Monday that a deterrent sentence was necessary for the 47-year-old defendant, whose offence was “far worse” than most indecent assault cases because he possessed 233 videos and photos taken during the attacks between August 2023 and March 2024.
Citing a psychologist’s report, Chui noted that the defendant was not a paedophile but had shown a sexual interest in his then-girlfriend’s daughter.
The defendant told the psychologist he had been under the influence of alcohol and had mistaken the girl for his girlfriend.
He pleaded guilty to 18 charges: seven counts of indecent assault and 11 counts of possession of child pornography.
He admitted using his phone to take photos and a home security camera to record videos during the assaults. A nude picture of the girl was found in his wallet when he was arrested.
The judge said that as the defendant was seen as a stepfather to the girl, the case involved a serious breach of trust.

Ukrainian drone attacks damaged production infrastructure at the Novoshakhtinsk and Yaroslavl oil refineries, forcing one of the facilities to halt operations.
The Dnipro OSINT community published the satellite imagery.
Analysis of the Novoshakhtinsk refinery shows additional damage to two CDU units, which had also been damaged in previous attacks.
In addition, the imagery shows repair cranes being used for restoration work.
On August 25, 2026, Ukrainian drones attacked the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, after which the facility suspended operations.
The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery’s design capacity is estimated at approximately 7.5 million tonnes of crude oil per year, equivalent to around 112,000–115,000 barrels per day. However, some sources estimate the facility’s capacity at between 5.6 million and 7.5 million tonnes per year, depending on the calculation method used.
The oil refinery was commissioned in 2009. It was one of the first major oil refineries built in Russia after a long period without significant new refinery construction.
Main oil pipelines operated by Transneft, as well as railway lines, connect to the facility. They provide supplies of crude oil and the shipment of finished products. Petroleum products are also transported by water via a terminal on the Don River.
The Yaroslavl oil refinery was also damaged. On August 28, 2026, Ukrainian drones attacked the facility.
According to an analysis of satellite imagery, two strikes hit the area of the process racks.
Meanwhile, the available satellite imagery does not allow for reliable confirmation of reported damage to the AVT-3 crude oil distillation unit. The relevant area is obscured by cloud cover, preventing a detailed assessment of its condition.
Thus, satellite imagery confirms that both refineries sustained damage. However, the extent of the attack’s impact on each processing unit at the Yaroslavl refinery remains unclear.
Slavneft-YANOS is the largest oil refinery in Russia’s Central Federal District. The refinery has the capacity to process up to 15 million tonnes of crude oil per year. It is located more than 700 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
The facility produces a wide range of petroleum products, from automotive gasoline to jet fuel and lubricants.

GiveDirectly’s AI experiment left vulnerable flood victims behind in Nigeria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:17:47 UTC
20:17:47 KST

Share & more
When GiveDirectly launched an AI-powered flood relief programme in 2024 for Ibaji, a key Nigerian farming district, its algorithm was meant to help deliver anticipatory aid to one of the world’s most chronically flood-battered regions. It was meant to be an improvement on aid responses that arrive too late, after homes and fields have been submerged.
After the programme was completed, the New York-based cash aid NGO announced that 4,600 people received anticipatory aid, doubling their incomes, lowering food insecurity by 90%, and leaving 93% feeling more prepared for future floods.
But an investigation by The New Humanitarian – based on interviews with at least 10 flood-affected farmers, mostly in Ibaji’s Unale ward – has revealed gaps in the technology-driven pilot project that prevented some of the area’s neediest people from accessing aid before floods destroyed their farms. Would-be aid recipients said they were excluded for submitting personal data that did not perfectly match government or bank records or because they could not afford the cost of keeping their phones charged to receive verification calls.
Some of these farmers said they took on debt, expecting aid that never came.
Meanwhile, the programme’s verification and targeting systems allowed some aid payments to go to relatively wealthy people and people living outside the programme’s flood-affected target area – sometimes to multiple members of the same family.
This is not the first GiveDirectly programme to encounter pitfalls while experimenting with technological aid solutions. In 2023, the organisation reported that its anticipatory response to Cyclone Freddy in Mozambique ended up targeting villages that were relatively unaffected by floods while bypassing villages that were hit hardest.
GiveDirectly voluntarily reported to The New Humanitarian in 2023 that its own staff in the Democratic Republic of the Congo had defrauded beneficiaries of $1.2 million by stealing their SIM cards and intercepting mobile money transfers. GiveDirectly eventually paid the victims what they had been promised, but six told The New Humanitarian that the payments were not enough to cover debts they or their neighbours defaulted on because of the fraud.
After receiving questions from The New Humanitarian about the Ibaji programme, GiveDirectly updated an article on its website to acknowledge that the programme’s design inherently excluded some of the area’s most vulnerable residents, including people with limited phone access and “poor people who may have moved to higher grounds before the programme began [and] may have incurred flood-related losses but did not benefit”.
Stella Luk, GiveDirectly’s vice president of programmes, told The New Humanitarian that the design involved intentional tradeoffs meant to reach more people more quickly.
“We worked to mitigate the downside of those design choices and study the impact, so we can improve further,” she said. “We think we made the right tradeoffs in our Nigeria pilot and have been incorporating the lessons there into our future work.”
How the system worked
Every year between July and October, catastrophic floods hit the lowlands of Ibaji, displacing tens of thousands of Nigerians from farming villages along the Niger and Benue rivers.
These fertile floodplains are a powerhouse of cassava, maize, yam, and rice production. But the absence of basic infrastructure like paved roads and electricity – as well as a lack of protection from seasonal floods – leaves local Igala-speaking farmers impoverished and unable to harness their full agricultural potential.
In 2024, GiveDirectly and the International Rescue Committee jointly received a $4.6 million Google.org grant to roll out AI-assisted early-warning systems aimed at delivering anticipatory cash to help farmers prepare for floods before they hit. (The IRC implemented its programme in another part of Nigeria.)
Using historical flood data from Google, wealth indicators, and insights from the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA), GiveDirectly narrowed down Ibaji’s 10 wards to the six most at risk of flooding. Within those wards, nearly 39,000 applicants pre-enrolled by submitting personal and bank information via short codes on their mobile phones, which the organisation said saved at least $80,000 in staff costs. Almost half of these applicants were automatically disqualified for self-reporting that they did not live in any of the six eligible wards.
Nearly 1,000 additional applicants failed to pass ID and name verification conducted via Smile ID, a biometric identity verification platform that cross-checks against telecommunications and government databases.
The remaining 18,000 applicants then underwent further verification, which involved calls from a third-party call centre and in-person visits. Over 13,000 people were disqualified because they could not be confirmed as living in an eligible area, including a “small minority” who could not be reached after five outreach attempts, according to GiveDirectly spokesperson Yonah Lieberman.
Cash payments followed a “trigger” based on information from Google’s AI-driven Flood Hub and hydrology analysis by the risk management firm JBA Global Resilience, according to GiveDirectly’s website. If 20% of a given community’s area was forecasted to flood, an automated payout command was issued to verified residents there: $105 up front to help them flee before floods struck, plus $210 later to help them rebuild.
“Satellite/AI flood modelling determined which communities [got paid] and when,” Federico Barreras, GiveDirectly’s senior manager for emergency cash, told The New Humanitarian.
He added that the organisation is now studying the anticipatory action model in Kenya and Mozambique, as well as in Bangladesh, where “we are running a large randomised controlled trial covering over 100,000 families that is planned for the flood season in the Jamuna River Basin”.
Exaggerated impact
GiveDirectly originally claimed on its website that “4,600 households” received cash transfers. But field reporting in Ibaji revealed that in several households, multiple members received separate payouts.
In response to questions about this discrepancy, GiveDirectly retracted the initial claim.
“The honest answer is that we were imprecise with our language: we used ‘household’ and ‘individual’ somewhat interchangeably in our public materials,” Luk said. “That is a mistake that we’ve since corrected. The programme enrolled and verified 4,600 individuals, not households.”
Despite the perception that this might be unfair to other households with only one recipient or those who received nothing, Luk added that GiveDirectly was “comfortable” with multiple people in the same household getting paid separately because more funds “will only help them more”.
Mismatches and disconnections
When The New Humanitarian visited Unale, one of Ibaji’s eligible wards, in June 2026, local farmers waded through thigh-deep road puddles and struggled to push cargo tricycles through the muck.
Some of the area’s 200,000 residents bore painful memories of the 2024 season and GiveDirectly’s digital experiment.
Joshua Ojoyemenenyo, an Unale resident whose fields were wiped out by floods that year, said he had been disqualified because the name he submitted to GiveDirectly did not perfectly match official records.
Friday Fedegwu, a local community leader, said mismatches in names, phone numbers, and bank verification numbers resulted in applicants being “cut out of the process entirely”.
Data mismatches are a well-documented barrier to financial inclusion and are common in communities where relatives register SIM cards on each other’s behalf.
GiveDirectly’s Lieberman said 939 applicants were excluded for failing identity verification via the Smile ID platform.
Another common verification barrier was Ibaji’s lack of electricity and mobile connectivity. To use their phones, many residents rely on solar or generator-powered charging hubs, which come with exorbitant fees.
Applicants who could not afford to charge their phones missed verification calls, and some were disqualified. GiveDirectly said on its website that it was unable to reach 3,000 applicants by phone, adding that the inability to be reached after “five phone calls and two in-person visits” was a common reason for exclusion.
In the update to their website following questions from The New Humanitarian, GiveDirectly explained further that “people weren’t near their phones when we called (having left their phone to charge, for example), and in some poor-signal areas people had to climb trees or get onto rooftops to make a call”.
Luk said human reviews of database anomalies and in-person outreach attempts were meant to resolve these issues.
But for applicants like Ojoyemenenyo, the organisation’s field staff could not reconcile the inconsistencies. He said he was forced to borrow three bags of rice seeds at a 100% interest rate from a local farmer who had received aid from GiveDirectly. To pay it back, he surrendered six bags of rice from his harvest the following year.
“Excluded without an explanation”
The same system that screened out some of Ibaji’s poorest residents benefited those who were relatively well-off.
One Unale household secured four separate payouts and used the funds to build a new building, according to Fedegwu. In another household, two local politicians received separate payouts and – with capital and agricultural training they already had – reaped a bountiful harvest despite the floods.
Unale residents also told The New Humanitarian that people living in cities, outside GiveDirectly’s rural target area, received cash after convincing the call centre that they were flood-affected farmers. One Lagos-based recipient said he was in Idah, the urban cultural capital of the Igala people, when he received the verification call. Familiar with Ibaji, he answered the agent’s questions over the phone, passed the screening, and secured a cash transfer without an in-person visit.
GiveDirectly defended its programme’s methodology, insisting almost every beneficiary had been rightly targeted with aid.
“We believe the overwhelming majority of recipients were living in extreme poverty,” Luk said, citing recipient surveys. She added that GiveDirectly “screened out the overwhelming majority of enrollees who do not actually live in the targeted rural wards, ensuring that only people actually living in the poorest, most flood-prone areas would get cash”.
The New Humanitarian spoke with several farmers within the programme’s coverage area who said they were excluded without explanation.
Samuel Adejoh said he and several family members gave GiveDirectly’s call centre their National Identification Numbers and account numbers but received no payment or any reason for their disqualification.
“They sent all of us a message that we were not qualified – my mum, my wife, my father, all of us,” he said.
Floods destroyed his rice field, and he was forced to leave Unale permanently the following year, migrating hundreds of kilometres to Ogun State in search of a new means of survival.
Aladi Samuel said her family were disqualified for unspecified reasons, leaving them unable to buy a canoe they needed to salvage their produce when floods destroyed their rice field. When a GiveDirectly team visited Unale later to evaluate the aid programme, she told them network failures prevented her from reaching the organisation’s call centre. She said the team gave her a vague promise of a future resolution.
Ladi Ashoba, the headmistress of Unale’s only public primary school, said some disqualified residents took out loans after GiveDirectly evaluators assured them the system would work “next time”. Although GiveDirectly sent out text messages in December 2024 announcing that the aid programme was “closed”, residents said they believed the verbal promise, hoping to pay off their debt with the next year’s payout.
“Being excluded without an explanation costs trust,” GiveDirectly said on its website. Leaving thousands of pre-enrolled people empty-handed without a clear explanation is “an area we’re actively working to do better”, they said.
Luk told The New Humanitarian similar misunderstandings were “also a risk in programmes that use human field infrastructure”. She added that the organisation conducted “re-sensitisation visits ward by ward” to clarify that the aid programme was a one-time event.
On their website, GiveDirectly said their geographic trigger – designed to pay by area rather than individual need – was “a deliberate tradeoff: speed and coverage over precision targeting”.
But the benefits of that tradeoff were inconsistent. While most beneficiaries received payments before the floods hit, nearly a third only received them in late October 2024, after flooding had peaked, because of identity verification issues, according to the website.
Joel, another Unale resident, recalled seeing local widows unable to access emergency funds as their homes collapsed amid rising waters.
“That is our pain,” he said.

AI generated
TEHRAN – The Iranian authorities have seized a bulk carrier after they said it dumped oil and sludge into the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported on Aug 31.
“Following the publication of images of the discharge of oil into the sea... expert and clean-up teams were dispatched to the site and seized the ship causing the pollution,” the deputy head of the Ports and Maritime Department of the southern Hormozgan province, Esmaeil Makizadeh, told the official IRNA news agency.

The United States fiercely opposes any fees in the strait. AFP

Israel signs $3.5 billion air defence deal with Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Israel signs $3.5 billion air defence deal with Greece
JERUSALEM/ATHENS, Aug 31 - Israel and Greece signed a €3 billion ($3.5 billion) defence deal on Monday under which Israel will build a multi-layered air defence system for Greece as Athens pushes ahead with a broader military modernisation programme.
Israel's defence ministry said it was Israel's largest-ever defence export deal with Greece and one of the biggest in the country's history. The agreement confirmed an earlier Reuters report.
Amir Baram, director general of Israel's defence ministry, said the so-called Achilles Shield deal reflected "Israel's technological edge and the proven track record of our defence systems in the field."
Under the deal, Israel will supply Greece with the David's Sling and SPYDER systems produced by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and the BARAK MX system made by Israel Aerospace Industries, as well as MMR multi-mission radars for air surveillance, manufactured by IAI unit ELTA Systems.
David's Sling was used by Israel to intercept Iranian missiles during the war with Iran this year. Greece becomes the second customer for the system after Finland.
Greece spends nearly 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than many NATO allies due to its long-standing dispute with neighbouring Turkey.
Athens plans to spend about €28 billion by 2036 to build the Achilles Shield multi-layer anti-ballistic, anti-aircraft and anti-drone system, and to buy up to 40 F-35 fighter jets from the U.S. and frigates from France and Italy.
Under Monday's deal, Greece will also receive a new national command-and-control system, developed by Rafael, to integrate the country's air-defence capabilities.
A supplementary €26 million agreement will see Israel supply Greece with Rafael's Drone Dome systems to protect strategic sites against drones and reinforce existing defences.
Israel will also expand defence-industrial cooperation with Greece, including transfers of technology and expertise to local industry. REUTERS

Hong Kong government loses appeal over Fanling golf course housing plan
Court of Appeal’s ruling is likely to result in fresh public consultations on developing 9.5 hectares of land at Fanling course
The government’s push to boost short-term public housing supply has suffered a setback after it lost an appeal against a court decision overturning conditional approval for building 12,000 flats on part of Hong Kong’s oldest golf course.
In a judgment delivered on Monday, the Court of Appeal found that the official endorsement of the project’s environmental impact assessment report was marred by an unfair public consultation process, the imposition of improper conditions and a failure to meet wildlife conservation objectives.
The ruling is likely to result in fresh public consultations on developing 9.5 hectares (23.5 acres) of the 32 hectares that the government took back from the 172-hectare golf course in Fanling three years ago. The project was initially slated for completion in 2029.
The government said it would review the judgment to decide whether to appeal further, adding that an announcement would be made “at the appropriate time”.
The Hong Kong Golf Club welcomed the judgment, describing the course as a “precious living heritage” of the city that remained pivotal to the development of the sport.
“The club will continue to communicate with the government, in the hope of preserving the old course and generating the greatest value for Hong Kong by fully utilising all resources and facilities at the club, which is in line with government policies of promoting golf and sports tourism,” a spokesman said.

ChatGPT becomes first AI chatbot to face tougher EU rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:07:00 UTC
20:07:00 KST

ChatGPT becomes first AI chatbot to face tougher EU rules
- ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox are now designated as "very large" platforms by the EU, subjecting them to stricter rules owing to their large user base over 45 million monthly users.
- They must comply within four months with the Digital Services Act, which requires them to assess and reduce risks related to illegal content, user well-being, and public security.
- This marks the first time an AI chatbot like ChatGPT is regulated under these rules, setting a precedent for future AI system oversight in the EU.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – ChatGPT will have to comply with tougher safety rules after the European Union on Aug 31 added it to a list of digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny, a first for an artificial intelligence chatbot.
Brussels also designated Reddit and Roblox as “very large” online platforms, a label that comes with additional obligations and oversight.
“ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the European Union, in line with their large impact on our citizens and society,” EU technology chief Henna Virkkunen said.
The “very large” designation applies to platforms and search engines with more than 45 million monthly active users in the 27-nation grouping, a threshold ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox reported meeting, the European Commission said.
The three now have four months to comply with additional obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA), a content law that is a major weapon in the legal armoury the EU has deployed to rein in Big Tech in recent years.
These include “assessing and mitigating the systemic risks stemming from their service and algorithmic systems related to the dissemination of illegal content, the negative effects on minors, users’ physical and mental well-being, fundamental rights, electoral processes and public security”, Brussels said.
To bring it under the DSA’s regulatory umbrella, the European Commission qualified ChatGPT as a search engine.
The hugely popular artificial intelligence chatbot developed by US company OpenAI reported more than 159 million users in the European Union at the end of March, representing over a third of the bloc’s population.
ChatGPT said it was “preparing to meet the additional compliance requirements” that came with the designation, while Roblox said it was “proud to be the first gaming platform” to gain the “very large” label in the EU.
“Safety is foundational to everything we do and we look forward to continuing our constructive engagement with the European Commission,” said the US-based platform’s general manager for Europe, Joost Hagesteijn.
Hugely popular with children and known for its immersive world of colourful graphics, Roblox says it has 46.6 million active players in the EU, just above the DSA threshold for tougher scrutiny.
The sprawling US discussion platform Reddit says it has more than 57 million users in the bloc.
The designations come as the EU has stepped up regulatory enforcement against the world’s biggest digital platforms, including many American ones, despite strong US pushback and threats of retaliation.
The EU has separately adopted the world’s most far-reaching rules to govern artificial intelligence. Its flagship AI Act entered into force in 2024, with obligations kicking in over several years to curb potentially dangerous uses of the technology.
Lena-Maria Boswald of German technology think-tank Interface said ahead of the announcement that the expected move would set a precedent and “influence the regulatory expectations for every large generative AI system used in the EU”.
“OpenAI already has risk-management obligations under the AI Act, but the DSA could widen the scope,” she said.
Around 30 services have been listed for extra scrutiny under the DSA, most of them owned by major technology companies such as Google, Apple, Microsoft, TikTok, X, Amazon and Shein.
The list also includes several porn sites and the collaborative online encyclopaedia Wikipedia.
Companies found in breach of the law face heavy penalties, including fines of up to 6 per cent of their annual global turnover and, in cases of serious and repeated violations, a possible ban on operating in Europe.
The EU recently told TikTok to change what it deemed its addictive design or face heavy fines.
To date, the bloc has hit three firms with penalties under the law: shopping giants Temu and AliExpress, and Elon Musk’s social media platform X, which was handed a €120 million (S$177 million) fine for transparency and other violations. AFP

Zircon Is Slower Than Russia Claims & Has Smaller Warhead Than Banderol — DIU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:06:58 UTC
20:06:58 KST

Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has released detailed information on Russia’s 3M22 Zircon ballistic missile.
The agency published an interactive 3D model on the War&Sanctions portal, along with details about the missile’s components, manufacturers, their personnel, and the foreign-made equipment used in its production.
The missile was originally developed to strike targets from surface ships and nuclear-powered submarines equipped with 3S-14 (UKSK) launchers. However, due to difficulties in operating the fleet in the Black Sea, Russia adapted it for launch from Bastion-M coastal systems.
The 3M22 missile’s warhead weighs about 120 kg. By comparison, the compact Banderol cruise missile carries a 150-kg warhead.
The missile is launched from a container using a booster that provides the initial altitude and speed. After its separation, the sustainer motor ignites. Both motors use solid propellant. Initial trajectory correction toward the target is carried out by the missile’s altitude control thrusters. These are housed in a protective fairing that is later separated from the missile.
Russia’s claimed speed of Mach 9 does not correspond to the missile’s actual performance in combat. The recorded maximum speed of the 3M22 does not exceed Mach 6.8 and is not maintained throughout the entire flight.
The missile uses a combined guidance system consisting of two main stages. During the cruise phase, it relies on an inertial navigation system, while in the terminal phase, it uses an active radar seeker.
Onboard computation and control are handled by the Baget-83 digital computing system. This module is standard across most Russian ballistic missiles.
The missile’s maneuvering is controlled by electro-hydraulic steering actuators and deployable aerodynamic control surfaces in the tail section. The control surfaces are folded when the missile is in its transport configuration.
The entire tail section of the 3M22 missile is made of titanium to withstand the associated loads. It houses the missile’s flight controls.
In addition to technical specifications, the DIU published data on 70 companies involved in the production of the missile.
The Zircon uses components from the United States, including the TGA2704 amplifier manufactured by TriQuint Semiconductor and the Altera Cyclone II EP2C5T144I8N KBBD9Y2043U field-programmable gate array (FPGA) from Intel.

IISc sets up quantum computing hub under National Quantum Mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:02:11 UTC
20:02:11 KST

The new Section 8 company will serve as the Quantum Computing Thematic Hub at IISc under the Union Govt’s National Quantum Mission
BENGALURU: IISc has set up a not-for-profit company to help build India’s capabilities in quantum computing, a technology expected to play a role in areas ranging from scientific research and industry to computing and communications in the coming years.Called the Foundation for QC Innovation (FQCI), the new Section 8 company will serve as the Quantum Computing Thematic Hub at IISc under the Union Govt’s National Quantum Mission.It’s one of four thematic hubs set up under the mission and will bring together researchers, academic institutions, industry and startups to develop quantum computing technologies in India.Quantum computers use the principles of quantum physics to process certain kinds of information differently from conventional computers. While the technology is still at an early stage, countries and companies around the world are investing heavily in it because of its potential to solve some problems that are difficult for existing computers.At IISc, the new hub will work across several approaches to building quantum computers, including systems based on light particles, superconducting circuits, semiconductor devices, neutral atoms and trapped ions.
It will also work on quantum algorithms.“The National Quantum Mission provides a unique opportunity to build a strong and globally competitive quantum computing ecosystem in India. Our focus is on bringing together India’s research capabilities, advanced infrastructure, industry and entrepreneurial talent to translate cutting-edge research into indigenous quantum computing technologies and applications,” Shankar Kumar Selvaraja, project director, FQCI and professor, Centre for Nano Science and Engineering at IISc, said.
A major part of the initiative will be the creation of shared facilities for making, testing and characterising quantum devices. The aim is to give researchers and companies access to infrastructure that can help move laboratory research towards working technologies.“FQCI will also focus on building the workforce and startup ecosystem required for the sector. Its programmes will support student research and internships, industry-academia collaboration, startup development and knowledge-sharing. The initiative has launched programmes called QC Rise, QC Bridge, QC Leap, QC Accel and QC Quest as part of these efforts,” IISc said.The larger goal, it added, was to reduce dependence on overseas technology by developing quantum computing capabilities within the country.

American nuke sub skips post-shakedown due to availability
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:00:53 BST
20:00:53 KST

The US Navy has declared the Virginia-class attack submarine USS Massachusetts ready for fleet tasking after completing shakedown trials, waiving the boat’s planned post-shakedown availability because of its material condition and combat readiness.
The U.S. Navy announced the decision on 17 August, saying the submarine had completed extensive testing and evaluation following delivery and would move directly into fleet availability rather than entering the maintenance period normally associated with a newly commissioned submarine.
USS Massachusetts, hull number SSN 798, was delivered by Newport News Shipbuilding on 21 November 2025 following sea trials and commissioned in Boston on 28 March 2026.
The Navy said the decision to waive the post-shakedown availability was based on the condition of the submarine during trials and the requirement to make the boat available for operational tasking.
Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle said in the U.S. Navy release: “USS Massachusetts is ready to fight, and that is exactly where we need her, in the hands of our Sailors and available to the Fleet.”
He added: “Waiving this availability reflects the exceptional condition of the ship and our determination to deliver combat-ready capability faster. It also allows our shipbuilding workforce to focus its talent and capacity where we need it most, building the next generation of submarines our nation requires.”
A post-shakedown availability normally follows the initial period of operations for a new warship or submarine, allowing the Navy and shipbuilder to address defects identified during trials, complete outstanding work and incorporate alterations before the vessel enters routine fleet service. In the case of Massachusetts, the Navy said the submarine met and exceeded the construction and safety standards required during its trials and subsequent shakedown period.
Vice Admiral Rob Gaucher, Director of Submarine Programs, said the decision represented a deliberate departure from the normal process. He said: “Waiving a submarine’s post-shakedown availability is an example of driving efficiency, innovation and speed in shipbuilding.”
Gaucher added: “While it is a calculated risk, we do it without ever compromising the safety of our sailors or the quality of our submarines. By getting this boat into the fight we can continue to maintain an absolute advantage in the undersea domain.”
USS Massachusetts is the seventh Block IV Virginia-class submarine. It was constructed under the long-running teaming arrangement between General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding. The Block IV boats incorporate design and maintenance changes intended to reduce major maintenance periods over their service lives and increase the amount of time available for deployments compared with earlier members of the class. Virginia-class submarines are nuclear-powered fast attack boats designed for anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, strike operations, intelligence collection and special operations support.
Vice Admiral Rick Seif, Commander, Submarine Forces, said in the release: “Massachusetts brings unmatched stealth and lethality to the undersea battle force.”He added: “This decision will immediately add combat readiness and capacity to ensure our nation’s ability to dominate and maintain undersea superiority.”
The U.S. Navy’s decision also avoids placing another newly delivered submarine into a shipyard availability at a time when the US submarine industrial base is supporting construction of additional Virginia-class boats alongside Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines and maintenance of the existing fleet.
USS Massachusetts is the fifth US Navy vessel to carry the name and entered service as the latest addition to the Navy’s fast-attack submarine force. With the shakedown period complete and the planned post-shakedown availability waived, the submarine is now available for operational tasking by the fleet.

Researchers discover preventative immune benefits of a little-known psychedelic compound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:00:12 UTC
20:00:12 KST

A small study in mice suggests that administering a psychedelic compound before an immune system challenge can prevent brain inflammation and associated behavioral changes. The findings, published in the journal BMC Neuroscience, hint that these drugs might prime the nervous system to resist future damage.
Neuroinflammation is a biological response where the body’s immune system activates within the brain or spinal cord. While short-term inflammation helps eliminate infections, long-term or excessive immune activity can damage brain tissue. The brain is usually protected from the body’s general immune responses by a specialized cellular boundary. When severe physical stress or infection occurs, signaling molecules can breach this boundary, causing specialized brain cells to initiate a localized immune response.
When the immune system activates, cells release signaling proteins called cytokines. Some cytokines promote inflammation to attack pathogens, while others suppress inflammation to help the body heal. An imbalance leaning toward pro-inflammatory cytokines can disrupt brain circuits and alter an animal’s mood or behavior. This excessive response is a common biological feature in many brain conditions, from Alzheimer’s disease to severe depression.
Psychedelic drugs have gained attention for their ability to treat certain psychiatric conditions, but researchers are also investigating their physical effects on the brain. Many classical psychedelics bind to a specific protein on the surface of brain cells called the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor. Activating this receptor alters perception, but it also appears to influence how immune cells respond to stress. Researchers Michael Fiorillo and Javier González-Maeso of the Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine wanted to see if these immune-altering effects could work preventatively.
The researchers began by mapping how the mouse immune system reacts to a specific chemical trigger. They injected a small group of mice with lipopolysaccharide, a molecule found on the outer shell of bacteria. This molecule reliably provokes a strong immune reaction without causing an actual bacterial infection. Following the injection, the team measured chemical markers in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and emotion.
They found that levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines peaked four hours after the injection. Specifically, the proteins interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha reached their highest concentrations at this time. This four-hour mark became the target window for evaluating the effects of the psychedelic drug.
In a separate test, the team gave healthy mice varying doses of a psychedelic compound known as DOI. This laboratory chemical activates the same serotonin receptors as drugs like LSD and psilocybin. When they measured brain tissue 24 hours later, they found that DOI alone did not change baseline cytokine levels. The drug did not cause an immune reaction on its own.
Next, the researchers designed an experiment to test DOI as a preventative measure. They injected wild-type mice with either a low or high dose of the psychedelic compound. After waiting 24 hours, they administered the bacterial molecule to trigger systemic inflammation. Four hours after that, they measured cytokine levels in the hippocampus.
Mice that received the low dose of DOI before the immune challenge showed lower levels of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha. Their immune response was notably muted compared to mice that did not receive the psychedelic. The higher dose of the drug did not effectively reduce the inflammatory response, a phenomenon that sometimes occurs when cellular receptors become overwhelmed and shut down.
The team then wanted to know if this protective effect relied entirely on the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor. They repeated the prevention experiment using genetically modified mice that were bred without this specific receptor. In these modified animals, the low dose of DOI failed to prevent the spike in interleukin-6. This outcome indicates that the drug requires the 5-HT2A receptor to suppress this specific inflammatory protein.
However, the drug still successfully reduced levels of tumor necrosis factor alpha in the genetically modified mice. This suggests the psychedelic also interacts with other physiological pathways or different serotonin receptors to manage separate parts of the immune response. The researchers also observed that the modified mice experienced a much stronger overall inflammatory response to the bacterial molecule than unmodified mice. Natural serotonin activity at this receptor normally acts as a biological brake to keep the immune system from overreacting.
To see if the chemical changes in the brain translated to physical actions, the team ran a series of behavioral tests. They placed the mice in an open enclosure monitored by infrared beams to measure general movement and exploration. The bacterial molecule normally causes mice to move less, mimicking the physical lethargy people feel when they are sick.
Pretreating the mice with the low dose of DOI prevented this lethargy. The pretreated animals maintained normal movement levels despite the immune challenge. The team also evaluated the mice using a swimming test that measures passive coping, a behavior often compared to human depression. Mice that received the bacterial molecule spent more time floating passively instead of actively swimming.
Animals given the low dose of DOI beforehand remained active and spent less time floating. The researchers also tracked the animals’ body weight over a single week. The immune challenge typically causes severe weight loss, but the psychedelic treatment lessened this physical toll. The pretreated mice recovered their normal weight faster than the untreated control group.
Finally, the researchers looked for links between the chemical markers in the brain and the animals’ physical behavior. They found that higher levels of the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 matched up with increased passive behavior in the swimming test. Conversely, higher levels of two other cytokines associated with cellular healing aligned with more active swimming. This chemical shift points toward a more resilient biological state.
While these results offer a look at how psychedelics might shield the brain, the research relied on a single strong immune trigger. This acute response does not fully capture the persistent, low-grade inflammation seen in human neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases. Additionally, the study evaluated whole sections of the hippocampus rather than looking at individual cell types. It remains unknown exactly which immune or nervous system cells are actually suppressing the inflammation.
The bacterial molecule and the drug were injected into the animals’ bodies rather than directly into the brain. It is possible that the psychedelic suppressed the immune response in the bloodstream first, which then reduced the secondary inflammation in the brain. The genetically modified mice used in the study lacked the serotonin receptor for their entire lives, which might have caused developmental changes that independently altered their baseline immune system.
All the experiments were conducted using male mice. Future research will need to include female animals to determine if these preventative immune effects apply equally across sexes. Scientists also need to test other psychedelic compounds to see if they offer similar protective benefits.
The study, “Pretreatment with the psychedelic DOI mitigates LPS-induced hippocampal inflammation and behavioral impairments in mice,” was authored by Michael Fiorillo and Javier González-Maeso.

Why Food Keeps Making Everybody Sick This Summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

This summer, every meal feels like a risk.
Just as the US is recovering from a major cyclospora outbreak stemming from tainted iceberg lettuce, salmonella has turned up in jalapeños, eggs, and even dog food. The jalapeño-related outbreak is now responsible for at least 431 illnesses and 57 hospitalizations in more than two dozen states. Meanwhile, a dual-pathogen outbreak of E. coli and salmonella linked to alfalfa sprouts has affected 55 people across 15 states.
But is it just your overactive imagination that these outbreaks are worse than normal?
To answer that, WIRED tallied up publicly available numbers from the Food and Drug Administration’s investigations of foodborne illnesses. The agency has identified more than 12,800 illnesses tied to foodborne outbreaks in 2026, already far surpassing the number it has identified in any year since 2020. For comparison, there were 895 cases related to foodborne outbreaks last year.
Experts say the summer of sickness is the result of chronic underfunding in food safety systems, gaps in federal food policy, and recent cuts to the country’s public health infrastructure by President Donald Trump’s administration.
“What is happening this summer just demonstrates to me the vulnerabilities in the system—and what happens when you stress the system,” says Barbara Kowalcyk, director of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition.
To understand how this summer became so swamped with foodborne illnesses, one needs to understand the scale of the cyclospora outbreak, which “was absolutely unprecedented,” says Jennifer McEntire, a food microbiologist and founder of the consulting firm Food Safety Strategy.
The FDA’s numbers, drawn from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s case count, establish this cyclospora outbreak as the largest the agency has investigated in the US since the 1990s. Yet even this figure undercounts how many people actually got sick, according to the CDC’s own calculations.
The FDA’s figures only count illnesses directly linked to a specific outbreak under investigation. So far, about 67 percent of the CDC’s 17,180 laboratory-confirmed cases in the US have been linked to Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce; the rest are linked to other outbreaks or one-off infections, which require a full-blown FDA investigation. On top of that, the CDC is aware of at least 11,844 additional cases that have either not been confirmed by a lab test or require further analysis for other reasons.
Previously, cyclospora infections were rare compared to other common foodborne bugs like salmonella and E. coli. The previously obscure pathogen typically causes a few hundred to a few thousand illnesses a year in the US. Because it is—or at least was—relatively uncommon, cyclospora isn’t included in standard panels that test for several types of gastrointestinal disease. That can mask the true size of an outbreak, on top of the many people who may have gotten diarrhea from the parasite but decided not to go to the doctor.
Cyclospora is also particularly tricky to get rid of, with its tendency to lodge itself into the crevices and folds of leafy greens, herbs, and berries. These foods are typically eaten raw, and food sanitizers aren’t effective at removing the parasite because it forms a tough, protective outer shell.
But the quirks of a parasite cannot fully explain the scale of the outbreak. Last October, WIRED reported that the CDC had reduced its staff through layoffs and buyouts by about 3,000 employees—roughly a quarter of the workforce—since Trump’s second term began. That includes people who worked in a lab that responded to cyclospora outbreaks. According to the team’s former leader, molecular parasitologist Joel Barratt, the lab’s staff was cut from 11 people to just three.
Fewer staff to handle outbreaks is compounded by the nation’s health agencies lacking leadership at the highest levels. The CDC was without a dedicated director for nearly a year, until the Senate voted in early August to confirm Erica Schwartz to the role. The FDA, meanwhile, has not had a permanent commissioner since Marty Makary resigned in May.
In 2025, the Trump administration cut roughly $12 billion in grants for state health departments, which are the first to respond to outbreaks of foodborne illness. In Michigan, the loss of these funds meant 23 fewer infectious disease workers and 123 fewer county health staff, Reuters reported in late July. Health department employees told Reuters they’ve had to pull staff from other areas—and still didn’t have the resources to investigate the thousands of cyclospora cases in the state that’s been at the center of the outbreak.
Putting new food safety policies in place could help prevent large outbreaks, but a traceability rule issued by the FDA in 2022 has yet to be implemented. The rule requires businesses that manufacture, process, pack, or hold leafy greens and other high-risk foods to maintain more detailed recordkeeping. In November, Congress voted to delay implementation of the rule until July 20, 2028. A coalition of food safety and consumer health groups sent a letter to Congress earlier this month urging members to reconsider the delay, saying the rule “would facilitate faster and more effective investigations.”
Even with the new rule, though, outbreaks like the one tied to Taylor Farms lettuce imported from Mexico would be hard to track due to a loophole. De Ann Davis, senior vice president of science at the Western Growers Association, which represents farmers in Arizona, California, Colorado, and New Mexico, says the rule does not apply to importers, brokers, or trading companies that coordinate the movement of food but do not physically possess or handle it.
“In other words, the food can come in without anybody checking that it actually has the necessary traceability information,” she says. “The importer is the one who has to make sure that the food is compliant with those regulations, but they're not subject to the regulations.”
That makes tracing foodborne illness outbreaks tied to foreign products difficult, especially if the original supplier isn’t keeping detailed records. “We are relying on those foreign countries to be informed about the regulations of the US, but they are not subject to the regulations of the US,” Davis says.
There are also lapses in food safety inspections that predate the Trump administration. A January 2025 report from the US Government Accountability Office found that the FDA conducted an average of 917 foreign inspections per year from 2018 to 2023, far fewer than the 8,353 domestic inspections it conducted over the same period. But CBS News reported that inspections have fallen even further since last year’s budget cuts. Taylor Farms’ Mexico facility linked to the cyclospora outbreak has not been inspected since 2019, according to CBS.
In a statement to WIRED, the FDA says that it asked for expanded state and local information sharing, as well as foreign food facility fee collection authority, in its 2027 budget proposal. The agency says that its “robust response” identifying the source of the cyclospora outbreak “demonstrates exactly how the agency's risk-based oversight system is designed to work,” adding that under the Trump administration, the FDA has “increased the number of unannounced foreign inspections and is actively expanding staffing at foreign posts.”
“Suggesting that the FDA's ability to protect the food supply can be measured by a single inspection statistic ignores the agency's comprehensive oversight system,” the statement continues.
Beyond cyclospora, McEntire says the other outbreaks of foodborne illness are still concerning even if they’re smaller in size than the cyclospora crisis. “Multiple visible outbreaks with different organisms associated with very different types of products is kind of unusual, not unprecedented, but certainly unusual,” she says.
Contaminated jalapeños have caused the biggest salmonella outbreak in the US since 2024, when an outbreak of the bacteria in cucumbers caused 551 illnesses that summer. (That’s far below the worst outbreak, though, when an estimated 224,000 people fell ill in 1994 after eating Schwan’s ice cream.)
It’s also rare to find two different disease-causing pathogens in the same product at the same time, which is the case with alfalfa sprouts contaminated with E. coli and salmonella. The outbreak has caused 55 illnesses, with two people getting infected with both pathogens. Everything Sprouts is recalling certain lots of alfalfa sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands at retailers and grocery stores. The sprouts were grown in a hydroponic facility in Minnesota.
Kowalcyk warns that the summer of sickness isn’t over yet, though the calendar is about to turn to fall. Many pathogens thrive in hot, humid environments. Plenty of warm weather is still ahead, and what’s shaping up to be the strongest El Niño on record could jack up temperatures in some locations even further. That means anyone looking for peace of mind at the drive-thru or in the produce aisle after Labor Day may not find it.
“A lot of our foodborne illness cases peak in August, September, even early October,” Kowalcyk says. “So we're just in the beginning.”

Economic Watch: China's August PMI signals improved sentiment, steady new momentum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:50:40 CST
19:50:40 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) edged up in August from a month earlier, signaling improved business sentiment amid policy support and weakening extreme weather effects, while new momentum drivers continued to gain steam, official data showed Monday.
The PMI for China's manufacturing sector stood at 49.8 in August, up 0.6 percentage points from July, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 reflects contraction.
In August, the manufacturing sector's overall business climate saw notable improvement, said Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the National Bureau of Statistics, citing that among the 21 industries surveyed, 16 reported a higher PMI compared with the previous month.
This sector saw expansion in both manufacturing output and market demand in August. The production sub-index and new orders index climbed to 50.4 and 50.6, up 0.5 percentage points and 2.1 percentage points from July.
Driven by the pick-up in both production and orders, enterprises' willingness to purchase strengthened, with the procurement volume index reaching 50.5, up 1.1 percentage points from the previous month, said Huo.
The development momentum of new growth drivers continued to improve in August, she said.
The PMI for the equipment manufacturing industry and the high-tech manufacturing industry stood at 51.4 and 52.9, respectively, both remaining in the expansion zone.
Affected by recent upward movements in crude oil and non-ferrous metal prices, the purchasing price index for major raw materials and the factory price index for manufacturing stood at 56.6 and 50.4, respectively, up 3.4 percentage points and 2.6 percentage points from the previous month.
The PMI for large manufacturing enterprises came in at 50.6, up 1.1 percentage points from the previous month and returning to the expansion zone.
Wen Tao, an analyst at the China Logistics Information Center, attributed the rebound in domestic manufacturing market demand to multiple factors, including diminishing extreme weather conditions compared with July, further implementation of domestic demand policies, such as the "six major infrastructure networks" initiative, and steady summer consumption.
Wen expected the manufacturing sector to stabilize and pick up further in September, with pro-growth policies set to intensify and extreme weather conditions continuing to ease, while certain segments including automobiles, computers, consumer electronics and textiles are poised to enter their traditional peak season.
The PMI for non-manufacturing sector came in at 49 in August, unchanged from the level in July.
He Hui, vice president of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing (CFLP), noted that while the non-manufacturing business activity index remained below 50 percent in August due to seasonal factors such as high temperatures and heavy rainfall, positive structural changes began to emerge.
The driving effect of summer consumption continued to be visible, with business activity indexes for railway transport, air transport, accommodation, scenic spot services, and cultural, sports and entertainment-related industries all staying in expansion territory, said He.
Online shopping-related activities remained vibrant, lifting the business activity index for the postal industry to above 60 percent, a new high for the year, while service consumption potential is expected to continue releasing in the fourth quarter, he said.
Zhang Liqun, a special analyst at the China Logistics Information Center, said the rise in the August PMI indicates that factors supporting economic stabilization have increased, calling for accelerated implementation of existing policies and timely introduction of incremental ones to further strengthen market confidence.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, existing policies will be implemented at a faster pace, incremental policies will be moderately rolled out, and market-driven growth drivers will accelerate their release, creating favorable conditions for China's economy to maintain steady and sound development, said He. ■

China's chemical engineering large language model upgraded with task execution ability
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:50:29 CST
19:50:29 KST

SHENYANG, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The latest version of China's first large language model dedicated to the chemical industry was released on Monday, marking a significant leap from knowledge acquisition to intelligent execution of chemical tasks, and providing new support for managing complex chemical operations, said northeast China's Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics (DICP) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
The Chemical Engineering Large Language Model (ChemELLM) 3.0 Pro was jointly developed by DICP, iFlytek, Alibaba Cloud Computing, and other institutions and enterprises.
The ChemELLM is a key component of the DICP's new system for intelligent chemical research and development, aiming to bridge the gap between laboratory research and industrial production. To date, more than 300 chemical enterprises, universities and research institutes have registered to use the model, with cumulative API calls exceeding 14 million.
The latest version of ChemELLM has evolved from an assistant for knowledge acquisition into an intelligent engineering partner that can collaborate with professionals on complex tasks, offering a new foundation for the smart transformation of chemical research and development, engineering design and production operations.
The chemical industry involves complex materials, large spans in scale, diverse data types and stringent engineering constraints, making it difficult for general-purpose large models to meet professional needs.
The new version breaks away from the conventional application model centered on knowledge Q&A and content generation, establishing a four-tier architecture comprising a large model, intelligent agents, professional skills and tools, and application scenarios.
In this architecture, the large model functions as the cognitive core, responsible for professional knowledge comprehension, multimodal information parsing, solution generation and task planning. Intelligent agents act as the execution entities, handling process decomposition, tool invocation, result verification and dynamic adjustments around task objectives, forming a closed loop that integrates cognition, reasoning, planning, execution and validation.
According to assessments by a chemical-domain evaluation system, the ChemELLM 3.0 Pro achieved text-based Q&A accuracy and multimodal Q&A accuracy of 81.96 percent and 80.75 percent, respectively, with overall scores showing respective improvements of 20.2 percent and 31.4 percent compared with the 3.0 version.
The DICP said it will develop the ChemELLM 4.0 with enhanced reasoning and multi-tool collaborative planning capabilities. By using typical mature chemical processes such as methanol-to-olefins as validation scenarios, the institute will integrate key stages including laboratory research, engineering design and plant operations to create a novel paradigm enabling a seamless "lab-to-plant" transition in a single step. ■

BRUSSELS, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Monday designated ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox as very large online services under the Digital Services Act (DSA), putting the three services under additional regulatory requirements.
The Commission designated ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE), and Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs). The three services reported that they each reach at least 45 million average monthly users in the European Union (EU), meeting the threshold for such designation, according to the Commission.
The three services will have four months, until the end of November, to comply with additional obligations under the DSA, including assessing and mitigating systemic risks related to illegal content, negative effects on minors, users' physical and mental well-being, fundamental rights, electoral processes and public security.
The designations also give the Commission investigative powers to assess the functionalities behind the services and related systems.
The Commission said ChatGPT qualifies as an online search engine because it can respond to users' prompts and queries, including by searching the web. Reddit and Roblox qualify as online platforms because they enable users to disseminate third-party content to the public.
The Commission has now designated a total of 28 very large online platforms and search engines under the DSA. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) has stepped up efforts this year to deepen business cooperation within the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), spokesperson Yang Fan said Monday.
Yang told a regular press conference that the efforts have focused on industrial and supply chain cooperation, business matchmaking and commercial legal services. The CCPIT serves as the lead Chinese organization for the SCO Business Council.
Six SCO member states participated in the fourth China International Supply Chain Expo in Beijing in June. Kazakhstan organized 11 companies to exhibit, while four major Pakistani banks showcased cross-border settlement services. The China-Belarus Industrial Park was cited as a flagship example of industrial-park cooperation. Companies from Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan also exhibited their products alongside firms from northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in the Clean Energy Chain.
The SCO has participated in all four editions of the expo in different forms, with an SCO Business Forum taking place during the third edition.
The CCPIT has also organized Chinese business delegations to SCO member states and dialogue partners, including Belarus and Türkiye. In June, a delegation of 29 Chinese companies attended the SCO Investment Business Forum in Kyrgyzstan, which holds the SCO's 2025-2026 rotating presidency.
It has also hosted several business delegations from SCO countries and organized events such as a high-level meeting between Tajik President Emomali Rahmon and Chinese business leaders, which resulted in strong interest in future cooperation.
In the first seven months, China's national trade promotion system issued 669,500 certificates of origin for exports to SCO member states, up 9.62 percent year on year, and 561 ATA Carnets, international customs documents used for temporary imports and exports, up 45.71 percent.
Yang said the CCPIT would continue to promote closer cooperation among regional business communities and contribute to building a closer SCO community with a shared future.
This year marks the SCO's 25th anniversary. China's trade with other SCO members reached 523.5 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, accounting for 8 percent of China's total foreign trade, according to the Ministry of Commerce. ■

BISHKEK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Peng Liyuan, wife of Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Aigul Japarova, wife of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, visited the National Historical Museum of the Kyrgyz Republic on Monday.
Peng and Japarova watched the welcome performance together before jointly visiting a traditional culture exhibition of Kyrgyzstan.
Peng said the costumes, carpets and other items on show, exquisitely crafted and richly colored, reflect the Kyrgyz people's long-standing handicraft traditions and unique customs.
Both China and Kyrgyzstan attach great importance to preserving and passing on traditional culture, she said, expressing the expectation that the two countries will continue to expand people-to-people and cultural exchanges and further enhance bonds between their peoples.
They also visited an art exhibition on ancient Chinese civilization organized by both sides and watched a Kyrgyz ethnic costume show, where they expressed willingness to promote cultural exchanges and mutual learning between the two countries.
The National Historical Museum of the Kyrgyz Republic is the highest-level national museum in Kyrgyzstan, housing a collection of artifacts that traces the history and development of the Kyrgyz people. ■

Philippines’ Jollibee eyes Hong Kong over US to list international unit
The company is separating its international business, Jollibee Foods Corporation International, ahead of its planned spin-off and listing
Philippine fast food giant Jollibee Foods Corp said on Tuesday it was planning to spin off and list its international operations on the Hong Kong stock exchange, abandoning earlier plans of a US listing.
Jollibee Foods said it was progressing in separating its international business, Jollibee Foods Corporation International, ahead of its planned spin-off and listing.
The fast food restaurant operator now plans for a Hong Kong listing citing its existing presence in the city and brand recognition in Asia.
The Hong Kong listing could give the company a better price discovery as investors are familiar with its regional growth story and potentially better positioned to understand where the value is going to come from, said Dilin Wu, a strategist at Pepperstone.
“HKEX also provides access to a broad base of global and regional investors, making it well suited to support a business with ambitions that extend well beyond Asia, including continued growth in North America,” Jollibee said.

How much should a dinosaur cost?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:52:41 UTC
19:52:41 KST

How much is a Tyrannosaurus rex worth? If you ask the person who bought “Gus,” one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, last month, the answer is $50.1 million.
The price is eye-popping, but it underscores the rising value of dinosaur fossils—and the threat these prices pose to paleontologists.
Fossils didn't always command such steep prices. At least until the late 1990s, dinosaur skeletons didn’t cost more than $1 million, says Kirk Johnson, Sant director of the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. “If you’re a paleontologist or a scientist, $1 million seems like a huge amount of money. So suddenly [$50 million], like, your brain explodes,” Johnson says. Still, it’s the consequence of dinosaur bones being treated—and sold—like fine art.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Gus” is the most expensive dinosaur ever sold, but the previous record holder, “Apex” the Stegosaurus, sold for around $44.6 million in 2024. The first fossil sold at action—and the first to sell for more than $1 million—was “Sue” the T. rex: in 1997 it sold to Chicago’s Field Museum for $8.3 million.
Each fossil is unique, says Craig Kissick, vice president of natural history at Heritage Auctions. Unlike more common collectables, such as coins or baseball cards, “there is not one dinosaur bone that is the same as another,” Kissick says. “Any collectible category that is not graded and commoditized is going to have its own unique set of rules.”
As a result, fossils are appraised based on what auctioneers know—the completeness of a fossil and the price that the last one sold for.
“If you talk to the auction houses and say, ‘What do you think this is worth?’ they’ll say, ‘I don’t know what it’s worth, but I can tell you how much it’s sold for,’” Johnson says. “When Apex the Stegosaurus sold for $44 million, Stegosauruses [became] worth $44 million.”
Who exactly buys these fossils is sometimes a mystery. Hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin bought Apex and then loaned the dinosaur to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City. Another sold-at-auction specimen, the $32-million “Stan” the T. rex, disappeared from public view for years before reappearing at a natural history museum in Abu Dhabi.
“The people buying the expensive dinosaurs are not necessarily hardcore natural history collectors or museums. They’re hedge fund managers. They’re celebrities,” Kissick says. “If you’ve already got five homes and 10 cars, what’s next? Well, maybe a dinosaur.”
Like fine art, some economists believe fossils are more than unique collectibles and status symbols—they can be alternative investments. The benefit is that “their value may be less prone to volatility” compared to stocks, says Simon Condliffe, an economist at West Chester University. That said, they don’t appreciate the same way shares do. Comparing the prices of the most recently sold T. rexes to returns on the S&P 500 for the same period, “the S&P 500 wins comfortably,” Condliffe says.
Increasingly high fossil prices are a problem for paleontology, says Kristina Curry Rogers, a vertebrate paleontologist at Macalester College, because they “encourage the perception that dinosaur fossils are investment assets rather than irreplaceable pieces of our collective natural heritage.”
They also encourage fossil hunters—commercial paleontologists and hobbyists looking to turn a profit on dinosaur bones—no matter the cost to science.
Booming Commercial Paleontology
Fossil hunters aren’t a new phenomenon, Johnson says, and many work with museums, academics and collectors to find dinosaur bones ethically and legally. Cary Woodruff, curator of vertebrate paleontology at Frost Science in Miami, says he has a “wonderful relationship” with Jason Cooper, the paleontologist who found Apex, for example. Sue the T. rex was found during a commercial excavation trip, too.
“There have been so many amazing fossils that, frankly, just would not have been found” without commercial fossil hunters, Woodruff says. But the work isn’t charity. “A lot of them are very nice people, but in that simple respect of what they’re doing—digging to sell—they are not benefiting the scientific discipline,” Woodruff says.
Increasing payouts for fossils present an ethical problem, researchers say. They could incentivize poaching, illegally excavating fossils from federal land or fabricating information about a fossil to buyers.
“If you’re a land manager, you’re like, ‘I'm going to be watching for illegal digs now because there’s a $50-million dinosaur out there for somebody,’” Johnson says.
“As [we see] these higher and higher dollar values, we’re seeing more crimes,” says Woodruff, citing lawsuits and even the brandishing of weapons at dig sites. Rogers says she’s personally witnessed fossil poaching from active excavation sites—and later seen those fossils up for auction.
“I really think that, in a very short period of time, we will see someone killed in the United States over a dinosaur,” Woodruff says.
Are Private Fossils Lost to Science?
Some of the most expensive fossils are also some of the most complete ever found: Gus, Stan and Apex are among them, and access to them would help researchers understand of how their species looked, moved and evolved. Other dinosaurs are extremely rare finds, such as Archaeopteryx, of which just 14 fossils have ever been unearthed. Each specimen changes our knowledge of the animal, but at least one was hidden away for years before it could be studied.
In theory, scientific research can be done on privately owned fossils. But whether that research is worthwhile depends on who owns them and how they’re stored. The issue, Rogers says, “isn’t whether fossils are discovered. It’s whether, after discovery, their scientific value can be preserved for future generations.”
“When done right, amateur and commercial paleontologists add a great deal to the lexicon of our knowledge of the science,” Kissick says. “When we auction something, I don’t think it’s lost to science. I think it’s brought in front of the whole world.”
Certainly, many museums, such as the American Museum of Natural History, have accepted dinosaurs on loan from private collections. It makes the specimen available to the public, Johnson says, but this also amounts to a public institution storing an individual’s asset for them. “It’s certainly not unethical or illegal,” he says. “I just don’t think it’s very prudent.” And museums can bid for fossils at auction just like any other buyer, says Johnson—so long as it is within their budget, of course.
Auctions and acquisitions aren’t the only way these institutions obtain fossils: Museums have the legal right to excavate fossils on federal land, whereas commercial paleontologists don’t, for example.
But if a rare fossil that is important to science is being sold on the art market for an exorbitant price, the reality is simple: “Museums are not trying to buy these dinosaurs at this price rate,” Johnson says. “They can’t afford it.”

The brain, solved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:52:17 UTC
19:52:17 KST

It took years, an international consortium and a small army of volunteer proofreaders. That effort led to the first full map of every neuron and synapse in an animal brain—139,000 neurons, 50 million connections, none of them left unaccounted for. The animal brain being mapped? A fruit fly’s. In comparison, the human brain has upward of 86 billion neurons, connected by some 100 trillion synapses. It is easily one of the most complex objects we know—including the universe itself. In this special edition, Scientific American surveys that complexity—the everyday mechanics of a working brain, what keeps it healthy or lets it fail, and the odder mysteries scientists have yet to solve.
The brain, it turns out, is less a fixed organ than a system in constant negotiation with the rest of the body and the world around it. Sleep, for instance, isn’t downtime but active maintenance, when the brain flushes out cellular waste in ways that may help stave off dementia. That body-mind entanglement means that physical exercise may slow cognitive aging in the long run; synchronized movements such as dancing forge surprisingly deep connections between people. And new weight-loss drugs are exposing the neural circuitry behind hunger, pleasure and satiety and, in the process, complicating what we thought about food addiction.
But even a well-tended brain can falter, and nowhere is that more apparent than in people with Alzheimer’s. A more nuanced picture of the disease is now yielding a wider range of treatment strategies, including those that involve insulin and immune-modulating drugs. Some hope lies in prevention, as evidence suggests diet, exercise and social engagement may lower one’s risk. Meanwhile new blood-based biomarkers are offering better detection.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If illness shows how memory can be lost, a parallel line of discovery is illuminating how it is built in the first place. The machinery switches on earlier than long assumed, as brain scans of infants reveal. Decades of work have now identified specific molecules that lock memories into place, with the search for others underway. And it turns out the act of forgetting may be less a flaw than a feature: everyday memory lapses are increasingly understood to be part of how learning happens.
Minds can be found everywhere in nature, often in places we’d never think to look for them—even without a brain to house them, clusters of cells no bigger than a speck can learn, remember and make surprisingly complex decisions. Consciousness itself can hide in unexpected places, too, with some patients in comas who seem entirely unresponsive revealing signs of a mind at work.
The search for awareness is now centered on machines, with the debate over artificial-intelligence sentience forcing scientists to take a hard look at what cognition and consciousness actually mean. The discourse is reshaping how we see other species as well. Growing evidence of even insects’ cognitive sophistication raises real ethical questions about how we should treat them.
The complexity of the mind guarantees that generations of scientists to come will be well occupied trying to understand it. But the tactics to help yours thrive are refreshingly unmysterious: whole foods, sleep, movement, friends. You don’t need to solve the brain to take good care of it.
